text:
Title
Engineering enhancer bias to reset autophagy from cytoprotective to lysosomal cell death in advanced cancers

Central hypothesis-question
Can locus-specific epigenetic editing that lowers the activation threshold of lysosomal cell-death modules and raises that of cytoprotective autophagy modules reprogram the stress-gated TFEB/TFE3–FOXO–p53 network so that therapy stress triggers lethal, not adaptive, autophagy in advanced tumors? This targets the stage-dependent duality of autophagy (tumor-suppressive early; tumor-promoting in progression) by encoding a chromatin “bias” rather than inhibiting autophagy globally. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/mog2.70064?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Install an enhancer-level barrier asymmetry: use CRISPR–dCas9 epigenome editors to decrease the energetic/epigenetic threshold for activating lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP)-linked, p53/DRAM1- and cathepsin-centered death modules while simultaneously increasing the threshold for activating MiT/TFE- and FOXO-driven cytoprotective autophagy/antioxidant modules. The same endogenous stress gating by mTORC1/AMPK then preferentially engages lethal autophagy outputs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6826502/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale
- Autophagy’s valence depends on transcription factor availability and chromatin accessibility: TFEB/TFE3 drive the CLEAR lysosome–autophagy program; FOXO induces multiple ATG and stress-resistance genes; p53 can route stress responses toward autophagy and/or cell death depending on target selection and localization. Their activity is tuned by mTORC1 (retains TFEB/TFE3 in the cytosol) and AMPK (favors catabolism). Enhancer accessibility constrains which targets are selectable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6826502/?utm_source=openai))
- LMP converts autophagy from a buffering process into a death-executing route via cathepsin release and p53-regulated DRAM1, providing a mechanistic pivot for “lethal autophagy.” ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30125440/?utm_source=openai))
- CRISPR–dCas9-KRAB can durably repress distal enhancers, while dCas9–p300 can selectively activate genes from enhancers; both operate in vivo via AAV or related delivery systems, enabling programmable enhancer bias. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26501517/?utm_source=openai))
- Tumors frequently depend on lineage- or state-specific super-enhancers; restricting edits to tumor-enriched regulatory elements yields a therapeutic window. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrc.2016.62?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define the enhancer grammar of cytoprotective versus lethal autophagy under stress in advanced cancer models.
- Models: two autophagy-dependent solid tumor systems (e.g., TNBC and PDAC) and matched normal organoids.
- Perturbation to reveal valence: graded nutrient limitation and transient mTORC1 downshift/AMPK upshift to mimic tumor stress; do not block flux so that the endogenous gate remains intact.
- Phenotyping:
  - Autophagy flux: tandem mRFP–GFP–LC3 reporter.
  - LMP: galectin-3 puncta assay and cytosolic cathepsin B/L translocation. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/15548627.2015.1063871?utm_source=openai))
  - Cell fate: caspase activation, clonogenic survival.
- Multi-omics under each phenotype:
  - ATAC-seq and H3K27ac ChIP–seq to map accessible/active enhancers.
  - ChIP–seq for TFEB/TFE3, FOXO3, and p53 to assign factor occupancy.
  - Infer co-regulated modules that associate with “survival-autophagy” (CLEAR+antioxidant/repair) vs “lethal-autophagy” (LMP/cathepsin, DRAM1, pro-apoptotic p53 targets). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6826502/?utm_source=openai))
- Output: a prioritized set of tumor-enriched enhancers predictive of autophagy valence.

Go/no-go: If no enhancer sets correlate with valence, the central premise fails; pivot to non-epigenetic control is indicated (ideation stop).

Aim 2. Install enhancer bias with CRISPR epigenome editors and test conversion of autophagy from cytoprotective to lethal.
- Tooling:
  - dSaCas9–KRAB for compact AAV delivery to repress survival enhancers (e.g., top CLEAR/FOXO antioxidant enhancers identified in Aim 1).
  - dCas9–p300 for activation of lethal enhancers (e.g., DRAM1, LMP-sensitizing loci, and pro-death p53 enhancer clusters). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349887/?utm_source=openai))
- Editing strategy:
  - Multiplex gRNAs per enhancer (tiling) to ensure robust epigenetic remodeling; validate with ChIP–qPCR for H3K27ac gain (activation) or H3K9me3/HDAC recruitment (repression).
  - Confirm TF re-routing: measure TFEB/TFE3, FOXO3, and p53 occupancy shifts by ChIP–seq after editing.
- Functional tests under standardized stress:
  - Autophagy flux vs LMP and death readouts; quantify bias index = LMPhigh/FLUXhigh cell fraction.
  - Mechanism controls: rescue LMP-mediated death with cathepsin inhibitors; DRAM1 loss-of-function to test p53/DRAM1 dependency. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30125440/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criterion: edited cells display a ≥3-fold increase in LMP-coupled death at matched stress relative to controls without compromising basal viability at rest.

Aim 3. Establish tumor selectivity and translational feasibility in vivo.
- Tumor-enriched targeting: intersect Aim-1 enhancers with tumor vs normal H3K27ac/ATAC differences to build a “precision gRNA set” per tumor type; exclude elements active in matched normal tissues. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrc.2016.62?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery: AAV8/9 or dual-vector AAV for dSaCas9–KRAB and sgRNAs; LNP-mRNA for dCas9–p300 with sgRNA AAV, tested in orthotopic xenografts and PDX. Track on-target epigenetic remodeling in situ. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349887/?utm_source=openai))
- Efficacy and safety endpoints:
  - Tumor growth delay, apoptosis, and LMP biomarkers (galectin-3 puncta immunostaining; cytosolic cathepsin profiles).
  - Off-tumor toxicity: histopathology and serum chemistries; transcriptional off-targets by CUT&RUN for KRAB/p300 footprints. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/15548627.2015.1063871?utm_source=openai))
- Biology stratification: compare p53WT versus p53def tumors to quantify the p53/DRAM1 contribution and the p53-independent LMP route. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11071813/?utm_source=openai))

Key predictions and falsification
- Prediction: Enhancer biasing will not alter autophagy initiation per se but will switch outcome from stress buffering to LMP-coupled cell death upon native mTORC1 downshift/AMPK upshift; death will be abrogated by cathepsin inhibition or DRAM1 loss (in p53WT). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6826502/?utm_source=openai))
- Falsification: If enhancer edits do not change TF occupancy or histone marks, or if LMP/death does not increase under matched stress, the model is refuted. If equal toxicity occurs in normal organoids despite tumor-enriched targeting, the therapeutic window assumption is false.

Milestones
- Months 0–6: Define valence enhancers and build gRNA libraries (Aims 1–2).
- Months 6–12: Demonstrate enhancer biasing and lethal-autophagy conversion in vitro; mechanism controls (Aim 2).
- Months 12–24: In vivo delivery, efficacy, and selectivity across p53 states; finalize translational gRNA sets (Aim 3).

Innovation and feasibility
This proposal treats “autophagy memory” as an enhancer-programmable attractor state, not a static pathway node. It leverages established but underexploited capabilities—enhancer-targeted dCas9–KRAB/p300 and tumor super-enhancer dependency—to reset autophagy’s valence under native mTORC1/AMPK gating, aiming for lethal, lysosome-centered cell death specifically in advanced cancers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25849900/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Resonance-breathing–driven CSF–autonomic entrainment as an awake surrogate for sleep’s restorative dynamics under time-restricted sleep

Background and Rationale
- Sleep expands interstitial space by ~60% and accelerates convective CSF–interstitial exchange, facilitating metabolite clearance; this effect is strongly modulated by noradrenergic tone. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24136970/?dopt=AbstractPlus&utm_source=openai))
- Human sleep features coupled low-frequency neural, hemodynamic, and CSF oscillations; these macroscopic rhythms coordinate clearance and autonomic downshift. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))
- In awake humans, respiration is a dominant driver of CSF flow; slow/deep breathing and paced-breathing paradigms augment CSF pulsatility measured by real-time MRI. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Breathing at the individual cardiorespiratory resonance frequency (~0.1 Hz) maximizes baroreflex gain, HRV, and vagal afferent signaling—the same axis sleep leverages to impose parasympathetic predominance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4179748/?utm_source=openai))
- Vagal efferent activity mediates the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex; augmenting vagal tone acutely restrains pro-inflammatory cytokine production. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17273548/?utm_source=openai))
- Lateral decubitus positioning enhances glymphatic transport relative to supine/prone in rodents, suggesting posture can modulate human perivascular patency. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26245965/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic Strategy
Exploit 0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory resonance breathing—augmented by lateral decubitus micro-bouts—to mechanotransduce sleep-like CSF and venous pulsations and to impose a synchronized parasympathetic state during wakefulness, thereby partially substituting for sleep’s clearance and homeostatic control across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes. The causal kernel is mechanical and timing-based: entrain low-frequency pressure oscillations that drive CSF movement while simultaneously maximizing baroreflex-mediated vagal output.

Hypothesis (also the research question)
Can brief, scheduled bouts of resonance-frequency breathing during wakefulness, optionally performed in lateral decubitus, induce a multiaxial recovery state—indexed by enhanced CSF pulsatility, improved autonomic balance, dampened inflammatory signaling, and stabilized cognition/metabolism—that approximates the restorative effects seen after sufficient sleep? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims
- Aim 1 (Mechanistic): Quantify the effect of resonance breathing on CSF flow dynamics and autonomic tone during wakefulness.
- Aim 2 (Efficacy under sleep restriction): Test whether scheduled resonance-breathing micro-bouts improve neurocognitive performance, metabolic control, and inflammatory markers after acute sleep restriction.
- Aim 3 (Optimization): Determine whether lateral decubitus positioning during resonance breathing enhances mechanistic and clinical effects.

Design and Methods
- Population: Healthy adults (ages 18–40) with normal sleep; within-subject, randomized, counterbalanced crossover.
- Sleep manipulation: Two conditions separated by ≥7 days: (a) normal sleep (≥7 h, night −1), (b) restricted sleep (4 h, night −1).
- Interventions (day 0, 09:00–17:00):
  - Resonance breathing (RB): 12-minute guided breathing at individual resonance frequency (4.5–6.5 breaths/min) with HRV biofeedback to sustain high-amplitude LF oscillations; four sessions spaced every 2 hours. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2020.570400/full?utm_source=openai))
  - Control breathing (CB): Iso-attention audio guidance at 0.25 Hz or spontaneous breathing without HRV feedback (matched duration; counterbalanced).
  - Posture sub-condition (optimization): In 50% of RB sessions, subjects lie lateral decubitus with 10° head elevation; remaining RB sessions are seated. Posture order randomized. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26245965/?utm_source=openai))

Primary Endpoints
- CSF/vascular mechanics (Aim 1):
  - Real-time phase-contrast MRI in aqueduct and foramen magnum (visit-level lab substudy, n=24): mean and peak CSF velocity, stroke volume, and respiratory vs cardiac spectral contributions during RB vs CB. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
  - Resting-state fMRI (global BOLD power in 0.01–0.1 Hz band) during RB vs CB; coherence with respiratory belt signal. ([alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/alz.079182?utm_source=openai))
  - Autonomic: HRV (RMSSD, HF power, LF power, LF/HF), baroreflex sensitivity (sequence/transfer-function methods) during sessions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10412682/?utm_source=openai))
- Multiaxial recovery (Aim 2):
  - Neurocognitive: Psychomotor vigilance task lapses and median RT; 2-back accuracy; task-switch cost; subjective sleepiness (KSS).
  - Metabolic: Oral glucose tolerance test AUC (08:30 baseline, 14:30 repeat); resting energy expenditure via indirect calorimetry pre/post day; capillary lactate every 2 hours.
  - Immune: Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, CRP at 08:00, 13:00, 17:00. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17273548/?utm_source=openai))
  - Autonomic carryover: Post-intervention HRV and baroreflex sensitivity (17:00 seated rest).
- Optimization (Aim 3):
  - Compare RB-lateral vs RB-seated for MRI CSF metrics (lab substudy) and PVT performance.

Key Procedures
- Resonance frequency determination: Standardized stepped-breathing protocol with HRV biofeedback to identify the rate yielding maximal LF power and baroreflex gain. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2020.570400/full?utm_source=openai))
- MRI protocol: 3T scanner; PC-MRI velocity encoding aligned to respiratory belt; pseudorandomized RB/CB blocks; head immobilization; lateral decubitus feasibility assessed in subset with appropriate coils. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: Continuous SpO2 and end-tidal CO2 during breathing tasks; abort criteria for dizziness or hypocapnia.

Predicted Outcomes
- Aim 1: RB will increase respiratory-band CSF pulsatility and stroke volume versus CB and augment HRV and baroreflex indices; magnitude of CSF change will correlate with HRV amplitude across individuals. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Under sleep restriction, RB days will show fewer PVT lapses, improved working memory, reduced IL-6/TNF-α, more favorable OGTT AUC, and higher post-day HRV compared with CB.
- Aim 3: Lateral decubitus during RB will further increase CSF pulsatility and modestly enhance cognitive outcomes relative to seated RB. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26245965/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic Interpretation
- If RB increases CSF respiratory pulsatility and improves multiaxial endpoints under sleep restriction, this supports the claim that low-frequency cardiorespiratory entrainment can substitute key sleep-linked clearance and autonomic functions during wake, via a single mechanotransductive and reflexive pathway rather than stimulant masking. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))

Statistical Plan
- Mixed-effects models with fixed factors Condition (Sleep: normal vs restricted), Breathing (RB vs CB), and Posture (lateral vs seated in RB), random intercepts for subjects.
- Primary mechanistic effect: RB>CB on CSF stroke volume and HRV (α=0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
- Power: n=40 main cohort detects d=0.45 on PVT lapses (within-subject) at 0.8 power; n=24 MRI substudy detects d=0.65 on CSF stroke volume.

Novelty and Feasibility
- Novelty: Directly tests whether a single, scalable, wake-time, timing/mechanical intervention can induce sleep-like CSF–autonomic dynamics and cross-axis recovery. Prior work has not linked resonance breathing to glymphatic-relevant CSF mechanics and multiaxial outcomes under sleep restriction in humans. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility: RB and HRV biofeedback are safe and field-deployable; MRI protocols for respiratory-modulated CSF flow are established.

Go/No-Go Criteria
- Go if RB significantly increases respiratory-band CSF stroke volume and HRV versus CB and improves at least two domains (neurocognitive performance and one of metabolic/immune/autonomic) under sleep restriction.
- No-Go if mechanistic effects on CSF pulsatility are absent or if multiaxial outcomes do not trend in the predicted direction despite confirmed autonomic resonance.

Potential Extensions
- Closed-loop RB using real-time HRV and respiratory–BOLD coupling to phase-lock low-frequency neural–vascular oscillations.
- Application in operational settings requiring sustained performance with constrained sleep; integration with lateral micro-rest postures. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Ultradian Nutrient-State Oscillation as a Wakeful Sleep-Mimetic: A randomized crossover study to induce cellular maintenance and multidomain recovery during sleep restriction

Background and rationale
- During consolidated NREM sleep, noradrenergic tone falls and parasympathetic influence rises; fasting physiology predominates, suppressing mTORC1 and engaging AMPK/SIRT1-dependent programs that support autophagy and mitochondrial quality control. Glymphatic clearance in rodents scales with low norepinephrine and vascular/CSF dynamics in NREM, implicating state-dependent fluid mechanics and cellular maintenance in sleep’s restorative effects. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41325105/?utm_source=openai))
- Feeding time strongly entrains peripheral clocks independent of the SCN, and metabolic-sensing nodes (AMPK, SIRT1, mTORC1) interface bidirectionally with clock machinery. Thus, nonphotic, nutrient-linked zeitgebers can phase specific cellular programs during wake. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7182033/?utm_source=openai))
- Starvation or amino-acid restriction acutely suppresses mTORC1 via Ragulator/GATOR pathways, derepresses ULK1, and initiates autophagy; theoretical and experimental work shows AMPK–mTORC1–ULK1 can generate oscillatory autophagy under sustained deprivation, suggesting trainable maintenance pulses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8536509/?utm_source=openai))
- Ketone bodies are not only fuels; β‑hydroxybutyrate (BHB) modulates signaling (HCAR2/GPR109A, class I HDAC inhibition) and redox. Nutritional ketosis increases the brain NAD+/NADH ratio in humans, a milieu associated with SIRT1 activity and proteostatic programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640868/?utm_source=openai))
- Gaps: human interventions typically use daily-scale fasting or time-restricted eating; early TRF alters clock and autophagy markers, and 6‑month intermittent programs can increase PBMC autophagic flux, but no trial has tested short ultradian nutrient-state oscillations to entrain wakeful “maintenance phases” during sleep restriction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31151228/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question
Can repeated ultradian nutrient-state oscillations during enforced wakefulness—alternating brief “scarcity” windows that suppress insulin/mTORC1 and activate AMPK/SIRT1 with short, non‑insulinogenic ketone support—entrain a wakeful cellular maintenance phase that restores neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic homeostasis to levels approximating adequate sleep?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the intrinsic oscillatory dynamics of the AMPK–mTORC1–ULK1 axis by imposing 90‑minute nutrient-state cycles: 70 minutes of low‑insulin/low–essential‑amino acid scarcity to de-repress ULK1 and initiate autophagy, followed by 20 minutes of ketone-supported, non‑glycemic fueling to sustain cognition without reactivating mTORC1; repeat to establish anticipatory maintenance pulses during wake. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8536509/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish on-target cellular effects during wakefulness under sleep restriction:
- Primary: increase in autophagic flux in PBMCs during ultradian cycles versus isocaloric control feeding. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40345145/?utm_source=openai))
- Secondary: reduced mTORC1 activity (pS6K1↓; ULK1 Ser757 phosphorylation↓), increased markers of mitophagy/proteostasis, and increased brain NAD+/NADH in a subsample assessed by 31P‑MRS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5869864/?utm_source=openai))

2) Demonstrate multidomain recovery despite restricted sleep:
- Neurocognitive: sustained executive function/working memory under partial sleep deprivation. 
- Autonomic: higher HRV (RMSSD/HF power), improved baroreflex sensitivity during cycles and next day. 
- Immune: lower IL‑6/TNF‑α/CRP deltas across the intervention day vs control. 
- Metabolic: improved insulin sensitivity (OGTT-derived Matsuda index) and higher fat oxidation (RER). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40252198/?utm_source=openai))

3) Test entrainment:
- Show phase‑locked peaks in autophagy/clock outputs during cycles (PBMC clock gene expression, autophagy gene transcripts; BOHB and NAD metabolite rhythms) and partial maintenance of these peaks after protocol learning. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7182033/?utm_source=openai))

Study design
- Population: healthy adults 18–40 y, BMI 20–28, regular sleepers; exclude diabetes, GI malabsorption, ketogenic intolerance, major psychiatric illness.
- Design: randomized, controlled, two‑period crossover; each period is 3 days in-lab, separated by ≥2 weeks. Nights 1–2: 4 h time‑in‑bed (02:00–06:00) to induce partial sleep loss; intervention delivered during wake day 2.
- Arms:
  a) Ultradian Oscillation (UO): five 90‑min cycles (total 7.5 h). Each cycle: 70‑min scarcity (water/electrolytes only; no carbohydrate; ≤1 g protein; ≤30 kcal permitted from non-insulinogenic fat if needed) followed by 20‑min ketone support (either 10 g caprylic MCT or ketone ester dose titrated to BOHB 0.5–1.0 mM). Aim: suppress insulin and amino acid signaling (mTORC1↓), activate AMPK/SIRT1→ULK1, provide BHB fuel/signaling without reversing catabolic signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8536509/?utm_source=openai))
  b) Isocaloric Control Feeding (ICF): five matched 90‑min blocks with isocaloric mixed snacks (30–40% carbohydrate, 15–20% protein, remainder fat) to maintain euglycemia/insulin pulses and minimize ketosis.
- Standardization: identical caffeine-free beverages; light exposure and posture controlled; activity restricted to light ambulation; macronutrient intake matched at day level across arms; water/electrolytes ad libitum.

Outcomes and assessments
- Cellular/autophagic:
  - PBMC autophagic flux: ex vivo bafilomycin A1–augmented LC3‑II accumulation and p62 turnover from serial draws at baseline and mid‑cycle peaks; immunoblot/flow. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40345145/?utm_source=openai))
  - mTORC1/ULK1: pS6K1 (Thr389), 4E‑BP1 phosphorylation; ULK1 Ser757 and Ser317; TFEB nuclear localization (subset). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5869864/?utm_source=openai))
  - Redox/ketones: plasma BOHB/AcAc; subset 31P‑MRS brain NAD+/NADH pre‑ and post‑day. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6052097/?utm_source=openai))
- Circadian/entrainment:
  - PBMC clock gene panel (BMAL1, PER2, REV‑ERBα) and autophagy transcripts (MAP1LC3B, ATG5) every 90 min across the day to assess phase‑locking vs control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7182033/?utm_source=openai))
- Neurocognitive:
  - Psychomotor vigilance (PVT), N‑back, task switching, and Stroop at baseline and after cycles; subjective sleepiness (KSS) as manipulation check.
- Autonomic:
  - HRV (5‑min seated and 20‑min quiet rest, RMSSD/HF power), baroreflex sensitivity; salivary cortisol diurnal profile. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40252198/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune/metabolic:
  - IL‑6, TNF‑α, hs‑CRP; OGTT with insulin/glucose for Matsuda index the following morning; indirect calorimetry (RER) during cycles. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22292421/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted signatures of success
- Within‑day: versus ICF, UO yields higher PBMC autophagic flux and lower pS6K1/ULK1‑S757 during scarcity windows; BOHB rises without insulin spikes; HRV increases or is preserved despite sleep loss; inflammatory cytokine excursions are blunted. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5869864/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross‑domain recovery: better or preserved PVT lapses and executive function; improved next‑morning OGTT insulin sensitivity; higher RMSSD and lower waking cortisol AUC. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167876026001200?utm_source=openai))
- Entrainment: emergence of 90‑min phase‑locked peaks in autophagy/clock readouts during UO, absent in ICF. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7182033/?utm_source=openai))

Sample size and analysis
- Effect sizes for HRV/cortisol and autophagic flux from prior SB/HRV‑B and iTRE/flux literature suggest n=28 completers to detect within‑subject differences of d≈0.5 with 80% power (two‑tailed α=0.05). Mixed‑effects models with subject as random factor; period and sequence tested for carryover; Holm correction for secondary endpoints.

Feasibility and safety
- Ketone dosing anchored to human data showing nutritional ketosis can raise brain NAD+/NADH and support cognition; dose ceiling set to minimize GI intolerance. Continuous glucose monitoring and adverse‑event tracking; exclusion of hypoglycemia‑prone participants. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6052097/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Moves beyond day‑scale fasting/TRF toward a wake-executable, ultradian “maintenance oscillator” that leverages known AMPK–mTORC1–ULK1 dynamics and ketone signaling to concentrate cellular repair programs into scheduled wake windows—under explicit sleep restriction. To our knowledge, no controlled human study has tested 60–120‑minute nutrient-state oscillations to entrain autophagy/repair during enforced wakefulness and measure multidomain recovery. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10143760/?utm_source=openai))

Risks to inference and contingency tests
- If autophagic flux increases but neurocognitive or autonomic outcomes do not improve, extend cycle count or adjust scarcity amplitude (greater amino‑acid restriction) to deepen mTORC1 suppression while titrating ketone support to sustain cognition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8536509/?utm_source=openai))
- If ketone support reactivates mTORC1 (unexpected), switch to lower‑calorie BHB dosing or pure caprylic MCT to limit insulinogenic byproducts; verify with pS6K1 monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6640868/?utm_source=openai))
- If entrainment signatures are absent, increase schedule regularity across two consecutive days to strengthen food-entrainable clocks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7182033/?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes and impact
Positive results would establish a physiologically grounded, wake‑deployable method to induce sleep‑like cellular maintenance across neurocognitive, immune, metabolic, and autonomic axes without extending total sleep time, enabling countermeasures for operational settings where time in bed is limited.

Title
Transition-mimetic 0.1 Hz respiratory–vasomotor entrainment to induce a wakeful multi-axis “recovery” state after sleep restriction

Hypothesis–Question
Can actively entraining 0.05–0.1 Hz cardio-respiratory–vasomotor oscillations and respiration-driven CSF/venous coupling during wakefulness, immediately after acute sleep restriction, approximate the systemic recovery normally observed after catch-up sleep across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the state-transition signature itself: reproduce the slow, high-amplitude oscillatory pattern that couples cortical slow activity, vasomotion, baroreflex resonance, and CSF/venous flow (present at NREM transitions) using 0.1 Hz nasal diaphragmatic breathing with mild inspiratory loading in a lateral posture, thereby broadcasting a repair/clearance “go” signal without extending sleep. This is a single control-layer intervention; no stimulants or sedation.

Rationale
- Sleep promotes metabolite clearance via coordinated neurovascular dynamics and glymphatic exchange; loss of sleep impairs this clearance and perturbs cognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic homeostasis. Recreating key oscillatory features during wake may reinstate the clearance-permission state. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24136970/?dopt=AbstractPlus&utm_source=openai))
- Slow (~0.05–0.1 Hz) vasomotion and noradrenergic dynamics during natural sleep couple with CSF oscillations and appear to drive brain-wide solute transport; these transitions, rather than tonic variables alone, are prime candidates for the endogenous “recovery signal.” ([websites.ucy.ac.cy](https://websites.ucy.ac.cy/neurology/documents/brain_oscillations_and_sleep_Fultz_et_al_2019.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Respiration is a dominant driver of CSF flow and venous outflow in awake humans; deep inspirations amplify CSF mobility. This provides a direct, voluntary handle on the fluid-information pathway during wakefulness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6605608/?utm_source=openai))
- Breathing at baroreflex resonance (~0.1 Hz) increases vagal modulation, HRV, and baroreflex sensitivity and strengthens connectivity in the central autonomic network—an autonomic backdrop consistent with a low-sympathetic, repair-permissive state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Lateral body posture improves glymphatic transport in rodents and may favor cerebral venous drainage in humans; combining posture with resonance breathing should maximize CSF–venous coupling during the intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4524974/?utm_source=openai))

Study design
- Design: Randomized, within-subject, counterbalanced crossover after acute sleep restriction.
- Participants: 48 healthy adults, 18–40, habitual 7–9 h sleepers, no sleep, cardiovascular, or respiratory disorders.
- Sleep manipulation: Each arm begins with one night of restricted time-in-bed (04:00–08:00, 4 h). Washout ≥7 days between arms.
- Arms:
  1) Transition-mimetic entrainment (TME): 0.1 Hz nasal diaphragmatic breathing with mild inspiratory threshold load (5–10 cmH2O) in right-lateral decubitus, eyes dimmed, isocapnic guidance. Three 20-min blocks separated by 10-min quiet wake over 90 min beginning 90 min after wake time. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31361032/?utm_source=openai))
  2) Control: Quiet wake, semi-recumbent supine posture, spontaneous breathing paced to non-resonant 0.25 Hz via metronome, matched eyes-open luminance; same schedule.
- Blinding: Outcome assessors and data analysts blinded. Participants informed of two breathing conditions without emphasis on “active” vs “control.”

Mechanistic verification (subset, n=18)
- MRI session during first 20-min block:
  - Simultaneous ultrafast BOLD to quantify low-frequency CBV oscillations and fourth-ventricle/aqueduct CSF inflow signals; coherence with respiratory belt and end-tidal CO2. Primary mechanistic endpoint: enhancement of 0.05–0.1 Hz CSF–BOLD coupling during TME vs control. ([websites.ucy.ac.cy](https://websites.ucy.ac.cy/neurology/documents/brain_oscillations_and_sleep_Fultz_et_al_2019.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Primary outcomes (multi-axis, acquired across 6 h post-intervention)
- Neurocognitive:
  - Psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) lapses and median RT.
  - Working memory (N-back 2/3), sustained attention (CPT).
  - EEG during resting wake: delta/theta power and aperiodic 1/f slope as noise proxy.
- Metabolic:
  - Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) variability; standardized mixed-meal test AUC glucose/insulin; HOMA-IR.
- Immune:
  - Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, IL-10; leukocyte NF-κB target gene expression (qPCR panel).
- Autonomic:
  - Beat-to-beat BP and ECG for spontaneous baroreflex sensitivity, HF-HRV; ambulatory BP “daytime dipping” over the subsequent afternoon/evening.

Secondary outcomes and proxies of clearance
- Internal jugular venous Doppler (flow pulsatility, collapsibility index) and optic-nerve sheath diameter variability during TME vs control blocks.
- Salivary/serum lactate and adenosine kinetics across the session (exploratory).
- Subjective sleepiness (KSS) for context only; not a success criterion.

Intervention details
- Breathing: 6 cycles/min, I:E 1:1. Titrated to maintain end-tidal CO2 within ±2 mmHg of baseline using visual feedback to avoid hypocapnia confounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Inspiratory threshold load: 5–10 cmH2O via threshold trainer; chosen to amplify intrathoracic pressure swings and cardiac–baroreflex resonance without straining. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31361032/?utm_source=openai))
- Posture: Right-lateral decubitus with neutral neck; pillow support to avoid jugular compression. Periodic brief left-lateral switches allowed for comfort. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4524974/?utm_source=openai))
- Vigilance control: Low-arousal auditory oddball and eye-tracking to ensure wakefulness.

Analysis plan
- Primary composite “Recovery Index” (RI): z-scored average of four domain anchors—PVT lapses (neurocognitive), MM AUC glucose (metabolic), IL-6 (immune), HF-HRV (autonomic). Pre-registered.
- Hypothesis test: TME > control in RI (paired t-test or linear mixed model with session order, sex as covariates). Family-wise error controlled for domain-specific secondary endpoints.
- Mechanistic mediation: Within MRI subset, test whether 0.05–0.1 Hz CSF–BOLD coupling gain during TME predicts RI improvement (path analysis).
- Power: For medium within-subject effect (d=0.5), n=48 gives >0.9 power at α=0.05 (two-tailed).

Success criteria
- Statistical: RI improvement with TME vs control and ≥3 of 4 axes individually significant or showing consistent directional benefit.
- Biological: Demonstrable enhancement of 0.05–0.1 Hz CSF–BOLD coupling and jugular flow indices during TME; correlation with outcome gains. ([websites.ucy.ac.cy](https://websites.ucy.ac.cy/neurology/documents/brain_oscillations_and_sleep_Fultz_et_al_2019.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Safety and feasibility
- Exclusions: Cardiopulmonary disease, OSA, orthostatic intolerance, migraine with aura, intracranial pathology.
- Adverse event monitoring: Hypocapnia symptoms, dizziness, paresthesia; protocol pauses and CO2 re-equilibration as needed.

Contingencies and falsification
- If MRI and hemodynamic data show no augmentation of 0.05–0.1 Hz CSF–vascular coupling under TME, the mechanistic premise is falsified.
- If coupling is enhanced without multi-axis recovery, the oscillatory signature is insufficient as a recovery signal; future work should add state-transition ingredients (e.g., sensory gating or light manipulation) without adding sleep time.

Innovation and impact
- Recasts recovery as an engineered state-transition broadcast rather than molecule-by-molecule replacement, using a single, physiologically grounded actuator that is operable during wake. It leverages known sleep-linked glymphatic/vasomotor physics, respiration-driven CSF flow, and baroreflex resonance but, to our knowledge, has not been tested as a wakeful, cross-system recovery induction after sleep restriction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24136970/?dopt=AbstractPlus&utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic anchors (select)
- Sleep–glymphatic clearance coupling. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24136970/?dopt=AbstractPlus&utm_source=openai))
- Slow vasomotion/NE dynamics and CSF oscillations in sleep. ([websites.ucy.ac.cy](https://websites.ucy.ac.cy/neurology/documents/brain_oscillations_and_sleep_Fultz_et_al_2019.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Respiration as a dominant CSF driver in awake humans. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6605608/?utm_source=openai))
- Resonance breathing enhances vagal/central autonomic network function. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Lateral posture facilitates glymphatic transport/venous drainage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4524974/?utm_source=openai))

Optional exploratory extension
- Closed-loop entrainment: adapt breathing phase and depth in real time to maximize 0.1 Hz coherence among respiratory belt, finger PPG-derived Mayer waves, and HF-HRV, using a simple on-device biofeedback algorithm; evaluate whether stronger coherence yields steeper RI gains. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8090775/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Coincidence‑gated fever‑range hyperthermia to induce waking multisystem recovery after sleep restriction

Question–Hypothesis
Can brief, fever‑range whole‑body hyperthermia (WBH) pulses delivered during wakefulness, timed by autonomic and metabolic sensors, engage endogenous coincidence detectors (HSF1–chaperone titration and post‑heat parasympathetic rebound) to selectively activate proteostatic, metabolic, immune‑resolution, and autonomic recalibration programs and produce a composite recovery state that approximates sufficient sleep after time‑restricted sleep? The prediction is that sensor‑timed WBH pulses will yield superior neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic recovery versus sham thermoneutral control at equal wake time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794010/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit intrinsic coincidence gating: (i) HSF1 activation is restrained by Hsp70/Hsp90 and is released when misfolded proteins titrate these chaperones; tissues with higher proteostatic strain cross the activation threshold first, enabling selective HSP induction under a global temperature trigger. (ii) WBH elicits a biphasic autonomic response with a cooling‑phase parasympathetic rebound that engages the cholinergic anti‑inflammatory reflex. Space submaximal WBH pulses at the timescale of HSP persistence to prolong the restorative window without large peaks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794010/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Test whether sensor‑timed, submaximal WBH pulses acutely improve composite recovery (neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, autonomic) after sleep restriction versus sham.
- Aim 2: Determine whether WBH‑induced HSP72 upregulation and reduced JNK/IKK signaling mediate metabolic and proteostatic recovery in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and skeletal muscle microdialysate.
- Aim 3: Quantify whether the magnitude and duration of the parasympathetic rebound (HRV indices) mediate reductions in circulating inflammatory markers (IL‑6, TNF) after WBH.

Design
- Participants: Healthy adults (18–40) undergo two counterbalanced in‑lab conditions: (a) restricted sleep (4 h time‑in‑bed) + WBH pulses; (b) restricted sleep + thermoneutral sham. One‑week washout.
- Intervention: Two WBH “micro‑sessions” per experimental day using a controlled sauna or liquid‑conditioned suit to target 38.5–39.0°C core for 15–20 min, followed by standardized passive cooling to thermoneutral. Morning pulse delivered when RMSSD (5‑min) is below individualized baseline (autonomic stress), afternoon pulse delivered when postprandial CGM slope indicates impaired glucose disposal. Sham reproduces time/ritual without elevating core temperature. ([discoveryjournals.org](https://www.discoveryjournals.org/medicalscience/current_issue/v29/n161/e114ms3604.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Rationale for dose/time: HSP70/90 induction occurs within hours and persists up to days; spacing pulses by ~6–8 h leverages persistence while minimizing cumulative heat load. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4088327/?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes
- Primary composite recovery index (CRI): z‑scored mean of four domains measured 2–6 h after each pulse and end‑of‑day:
  - Neurocognitive: PVT lapses, N‑back accuracy; EEG theta power drift during a sustained‑attention task (optional).
  - Metabolic: CGM‑derived 2‑h postprandial glucose AUC; Matsuda index from a standardized mixed meal test.
  - Immune: plasma IL‑6, TNF, hsCRP; lipid‑mediator panel (resolution markers) exploratory.
  - Autonomic: HRV (RMSSD, HF power), baroreflex sensitivity (sequence method).
- Mechanistic biomarkers: PBMC HSP72 protein, HSF1 DNA‑binding (ChIP‑qPCR at HSEs), JNK and IKKβ phosphorylation; serum eHSP70; salivary cortisol (context control). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1097276516001362?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic justifications
- Proteostasis and neurocognition: WBH activates HSF1 and induces HSP70/HSP90, enhancing refolding, proteasome/autophagy flux, and synaptic proteostasis; HSP induction in neural tissue is a conserved neuroprotective program. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11113869/?utm_source=openai))
- Metabolic signaling: HSP72 upregulation improves insulin signaling in preclinical and human models via antagonism of stress kinases (JNK/IKK) and improved mitochondrial function; acute OGTT effects may be limited, supporting repeated submaximal dosing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2234214/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune modulation: The cooling‑phase parasympathetic rebound increases vagal output, engaging the α7nAChR‑mediated cholinergic anti‑inflammatory pathway that suppresses proinflammatory cytokines; HRV‑inflammation inverse associations support this mediator model. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31331560/?utm_source=openai))
- Autonomic recalibration: Sauna/WBH shows acute HRV increases during recovery/cooling, consistent with durable parasympathetic dominance post‑stress. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31331560/?utm_source=openai))
- Coincidence gating: The chaperone‑titration model ensures stronger HSF1 activation where misfolded‑protein burden is highest, providing local selectivity to a global trigger. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794010/?utm_source=openai))
- Persistence tuning: HSP70 persists for tens of hours post‑induction, allowing small, well‑timed pulses to extend the restorative window without high peak stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4088327/?utm_source=openai))

Procedures
- Sleep restriction verification by actigraphy and PSG subset.
- WBH delivery: servo‑controlled heating with real‑time ingestible telemetry pill for core temperature; terminate at 39.0°C or earlier if safety criteria triggered.
- Cooling: standardized passive cooling to 36.8–37.2°C; hydration and electrolyte matching across arms.
- Sensing and timing: wearable HRV (5‑min windows) to trigger morning pulse when RMSSD <20th percentile of personal baseline; CGM slope (>1 mg/dL/min for ≥10 min in 60‑min postprandial window) triggers afternoon pulse. Pre‑registered algorithms and locked thresholds.

Analysis
- Primary: CRI difference WBH vs sham by linear mixed models with subject random intercepts; familywise error control across domains by Holm method.
- Mediation: test whether ΔHSP72 and ΔRMSSD mediate CRI improvements via path models.
- Dose–response: relate core‑temp AUC and recovery HRV AUC to biomarker changes.

Power
- n=40 crossover provides ≥80% power (α=0.05) to detect a 0.35 SD CRI difference (within‑subject correlation 0.5).

Safety/monitoring
- Exclusions: cardiovascular disease, autonomic neuropathy, dermatologic heat intolerance.
- Adverse‑event stopping rules: core >39.2°C, symptomatic hypotension, or arrhythmia.

Falsification criteria
- Null finding if WBH fails to increase PBMC HSP72 vs sham or fails to increase recovery‑phase RMSSD, and CRI shows ≤0.15 SD improvement; indicates inadequate engagement of the coincidence gates. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31331560/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty
- Prior work shows WBH induces HSPs, improves insulin signaling with repeated exposure, and yields a recovery‑phase parasympathetic rebound, but it has not been tested as a sensor‑timed, coincidence‑gated intervention to approximate sleep‑derived multisystem recovery during wakefulness. This study operationalizes that architecture in humans. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3670665/?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If acute metabolic effects are modest, increase pulse frequency (three shorter bouts) within safety limits to exploit HSP persistence.
- If autonomic rebound is blunted, extend cooling duration or schedule the second pulse later in the circadian day to enhance vagal dominance, then retest mediation.

Deliverables
- A validated, wake‑compatible WBH protocol and sensor rules that reproducibly induce a multi‑axis recovery state after sleep restriction, with mechanistic evidence for HSF1–HSP and vagal‑mediated pathways. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794010/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Resonant Convection Microbursts (RCM) to approximate sleep-dependent recovery during wakefulness under time-restricted sleep

Rationale
- During non-REM sleep, reduced locus coeruleus noradrenergic tone expands interstitial space volume and enhances CSF–ISF exchange, accelerating metabolite clearance; pharmacologic adrenergic blockade in awake rodents partially restores this clearance toward sleep levels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3880190/?utm_source=openai))
- In awake humans, respiration is a dominant, modifiable driver of CSF movement; 0.1 Hz hemodynamic oscillations (Mayer/vasomotor waves) couple to cerebrovascular tone. Slow breathing at ~6 breaths/min increases baroreflex sensitivity and vagal modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Carotid baroreflex activation reduces sympathetic outflow, augments parasympathetic tone, and can lower inflammatory cytokines in patients with cardiovascular disease; neck-chamber suction provides a noninvasive, brief, controllable baroreflex stimulus. ([acc.org](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/articles/2022/12/02/13/14/barostim-baroflex-activation-therapy?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–question
Can ultra-brief, wakeful “resonant convection microbursts” that synchronize 0.1 Hz respiration with transient carotid baroreflex activation safely increase CSF–ISF convection and rebalance autonomic/immune/metabolic tone enough to preserve neurocognitive performance under 4–5 h/night sleep schedules?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the physiological resonance between respiratory pumping of CSF and baroreflex/vasomotor 0.1 Hz oscillations to create minute-scale “convection bursts” during wakefulness, increasing brain solute clearance and shifting autonomic/immune set points toward a sleep-like recovery state—without inducing unconsciousness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Demonstrate that RCM acutely increases CSF flow and perivascular transport markers during wakefulness compared to sham. Primary mechanism readouts: phase-contrast MRI of aqueductal and cervical CSF flow; CSF-signal low-frequency power in resting-state MRI; jugular/vertebral venous outflow distribution by ultrasound. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jmri.20427?utm_source=openai))
2) Test whether daily RCM during a 5-day, 4 h/night sleep restriction preserves the four axes versus sham:
   - Neurocognitive: psychomotor vigilance (PVT-lapse rate), N-back accuracy.
   - Autonomic: baroreflex sensitivity (sequence/transfer), HRV (HF power, LF/HF).
   - Immune: plasma TNF-α, IL‑6, IL‑1β, IL‑10, CRP.
   - Metabolic: continuous glucose metrics (MAGE, mean nocturnal glucose), indirect calorimetry RQ, fasting HOMA-IR.
3) Identify mediators linking autonomic resonance to clearance and inflammation: relate RCM-induced changes in baroreflex sensitivity and 0.1 Hz hemodynamics to MRI CSF-flow metrics and cytokine suppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))

Study design
- Population: Healthy adults, 18–45 y, habitual 7–9 h sleepers, randomized, crossover (RCM vs sham), 3-week washout. Exclusions: cardiopulmonary disease, arrhythmia, hypertension, OSA risk, pregnancy, MRI contraindications.
- Sleep restriction: 4.5 h time-in-bed/night for 5 consecutive nights per period.
- Intervention (RCM):
  - Paced breathing at 6 breaths/min (1:1 I:E) for 60 s every 10 min during wake periods (total ~36 min/6 h work block). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
  - Synchronous neck-chamber baroreflex pulses: −15 mmHg suction in 5-s ramps, 5-s hold, 5-s release, repeated 4–6 times within each 60-s breathing window; duty cycle targeted to 0.1 Hz coupling. Safety capped at −30 mmHg, with automated abort on MAP drop >15 mmHg or presyncope. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7854574/?utm_source=openai))
  - Posture/airway standardization to optimize cranial venous return without jugular compression: head elevated ~20°, neutral neck, avoid tight collars; coaching to minimize Valsalva. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jmri.20427?utm_source=openai))
- Sham: breathing at 12 breaths/min with desynchronized metronome; neck chamber sealed at 0 mmHg with identical sounds/tactile cues; identical posture guidance.
- Safety monitoring: beat-to-beat BP, SpO2, capnography (EtCO2), ECG; adverse-event stopping rules.

Measurements and endpoints
- Primary mechanistic endpoint (Aim 1): Change from baseline in aqueductal CSF stroke volume and cervical CSF flow during 5-min RCM vs sham, assessed by phase-contrast MRI; secondary: resting-state MRI CSF-signal 0.1 Hz power and coupling to peripheral photoplethysmography. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jmri.20427?utm_source=openai))
- Primary efficacy composite (Aim 2): Preservation index combining z-scored PVT lapses (inverted), BRS gain, HF-HRV, and inverse log(IL‑6) over days 3–5.
- Secondary endpoints:
  - Neurocognitive: N-back d′, subjective sleepiness (KSS).
  - Immune: TNF‑α, IL‑1β, IL‑6, IL‑10, CRP trajectories. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42024569/?utm_source=openai))
  - Autonomic: baroreflex sequence method, transfer-function BRS at 0.1 Hz, LF/HF ratio; muscle sympathetic nerve activity (subset).
  - Metabolic: CGM time-in-range (70–140 mg/dL), fasting HOMA‑IR; exploratory OGTT on day 6.
- Mediation analysis (Aim 3): Structural equation modeling to test whether increases in BRS and 0.1 Hz cerebrovascular oscillations mediate CSF-flow and cytokine changes.

Feasibility and mechanistic anchors
- Sleep-state clearance primitives can be partially reinstated during wake by lowering NE tone and engaging vasomotion; respiration in awake humans is a strong CSF driver. RCM leverages these without sedation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3880190/?utm_source=openai))
- Slow breathing reliably increases baroreflex sensitivity at ~0.1 Hz; brief baroreflex activation via neck suction is established and noninvasive. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11790690/?utm_source=openai))
- Autonomic down-bias is linked to anti-inflammatory effects in humans receiving baroreflex activation therapy; cytokine suppression with vagal neuromodulation provides convergent biological plausibility that RCM will shift immune tone. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42024569/?utm_source=openai))

Statistical plan
- Power: N=36 completes (within-subject crossover) gives >80% power (α=0.05) to detect a 0.3–0.4 SD difference in the composite primary endpoint and a ≥10% change in CSF stroke volume during RCM vs sham.
- Analyses: Linear mixed-effects models with condition, day, and their interaction; mediation with bootstrapped indirect effects; multiplicity control via Holm-Bonferroni across secondary endpoints.

Success criteria
- Mechanistic: RCM increases aqueductal/cervical CSF flow and CSF 0.1 Hz power vs sham during wake. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jmri.20427?utm_source=openai))
- Systems-level: Under sleep restriction, RCM preserves the composite primary endpoint vs sham, with significant improvements in BRS/HRV and reductions in IL‑6 or TNF‑α. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))

Risk management
- Hemodynamic safety via automated thresholds; exclude high-risk cardiopulmonary conditions.
- MRI markers prioritized are non-contrast; no intrathecal agents.
- Interim safety review after first 10 participants.

Exploratory extension (optional second period)
- Add an auricular tVNS arm applied only during RCM windows to test whether augmenting the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex further reduces cytokines without impairing performance. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrd1797?utm_source=openai))

Impact
If RCM reproducibly augments wakeful CSF–ISF convection and rebalances autonomic/immune tone, it establishes a deployable, physiologically grounded method to interleave sleep’s restorative primitives into waking hours, addressing neurocognitive, autonomic, immune, and metabolic stressors under restricted sleep—without extending sleep time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3880190/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Inducing a wakeful recovery microstate with resonance nasal breathing: a minimal-signature, threshold-crossing test under partial sleep restriction

Rationale
- Sleep’s restorative phenotype co-expresses: cortical slow-wave/spindle synchrony, autonomic parasympathetic dominance with strong baroreflex, and large-amplitude low-frequency hemo-CSF oscillations; these processes are coupled in humans during NREM sleep. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))
- Nasal respiration entrains human limbic-cortical activity and modulates cognition; bypassing the nose reduces this entrainment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Respiratory mechanics are a dominant driver of CSF motion in humans, measurable with real-time/ultrafast MRI. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Slow-paced breathing near 0.1 Hz (≈6 breaths/min) maximizes vagally mediated HRV and baroreflex sensitivity via cardiovascular resonance, with clinical effects on inflammatory tone in RCTs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Sleep–wake transitions are regulated by mutually inhibitory “flip‑flop” circuitry exhibiting threshold/bifurcation dynamics; brief, well-timed inputs may tip the system between operating regimes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22811426/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis/Goal (undistinguished)
A brief bout of nasal, resonance-paced breathing at 0.1 Hz with prolonged exhalation will push the coupled autonomic–neurovascular–cortical network across a control threshold into a transient “recovery microstate,” characterized by: increased HF-HRV and baroreflex gain; strengthened respiration‑locked limbic–cortical synchrony; amplified low-frequency CSF oscillations; and reduced pro‑inflammatory signaling—sufficient to partially normalize neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic markers after partial sleep restriction, without sleep. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/J.NEUBIOREV.2022.104576?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit nasal 0.1 Hz breathing as a single actuator that simultaneously entrains neural timing and drives intracranial fluid dynamics while shifting autonomic set‑points; deliver it in short, phase-precise bouts to cross a state threshold rather than provide continuous stimulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define and validate a minimal “recovery signature” S during wakefulness
- Components: HF‑HRV and baroreflex sensitivity (autonomic); respiration–EEG phase‑locking in limbic–frontotemporal leads (neurocognitive); ultrafast MRI (MREG or rt‑PCMRI) indices of respiration‑coupled CSF oscillation amplitude (metabolic); plasma IL‑6 as a rapid immune proxy; pupil oscillations at breathing frequency as a noninvasive proxy for LC‑NA coupling. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/J.NEUBIOREV.2022.104576?utm_source=openai))

2) Test efficacy under partial sleep restriction
- Question: Do brief, scheduled “recovery bouts” (3–5 min each hour) maintain or restore S and performance over a 10‑hour wakeful day after a 4‑hour time‑in‑bed night relative to control breathing? Outcomes: working memory (OSPAN), psychomotor vigilance, and fatigue; secondary: mood/stress. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40392328/?utm_source=openai))

3) Map threshold behavior
- Determine whether S exhibits nonlinear (bifurcation-like) transitions as a function of bout duration/intensity and exhale:inhale ratio, predicting sharp state changes near critical parameter values. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-025-02091-1?utm_source=openai))

Design and methods
- Participants: Healthy adults, within-subject randomized crossover across two laboratory days separated by ≥7 days. Each day follows one night of partial sleep restriction (4 h time in bed).
- Conditions:
  a) Active: nasal breathing at 0.1 Hz (paced by visual/auditory cue), 2:1 exhale:inhale, light recumbent or seated posture; 5-min bouts delivered hourly (total 8–10 bouts).
  b) Control: quiet rest with mouth breathing at spontaneous rate, matched for guidance/attention.
- Safety/monitoring: End‑tidal CO2 to avoid hypocapnia; SpO2; dyspnea ratings.
- Measurements:
  - Autonomic: ECG for HRV (HF power, RMSSD), sequence/spectral baroreflex sensitivity using finger arterial pressure.
  - Neurocognitive/EEG: 32‑channel EEG; compute respiration–EEG phase‑amplitude coupling and coherence in theta–delta bands over limbic–frontotemporal leads; working memory (OSPAN), PVT.
  - Pupil/LC proxy: infrared pupillometry; quantify breathing‑frequency pupil oscillations and mean diameter.
  - Metabolic/CSF: Subsample (n≈20) undergoes MREG or rt‑PCMRI during a breathing bout to quantify respiration‑locked CSF velocity/volume changes.
  - Immune: plasma IL‑6, TNF‑α at baseline, mid‑day, and day‑end.
- Primary endpoint: ΔS (z‑scored composite) during and after each bout, and area‑under‑curve across day.
- Secondary endpoints: Cognitive performance change and biomarker deltas relative to baseline and control.
- Analysis: Mixed models with condition×time; nonlinear regression to test for threshold (piecewise) vs linear dose–response; mediation analysis of S on cognition.

Operational details for S
- S integrates standardized metrics: HF‑HRV, BRS, respiration–EEG coupling strength, CSF oscillation amplitude (subsample), inverse IL‑6, and inverse mean pupil diameter with positive weight on breathing‑frequency pupil oscillations. We define S* as the 75th percentile of each participant’s baseline‑night (well‑rested) quiet‑wake distribution; bouts are considered successful when S≥S* during the final 60 s and for 3 min post‑bout. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/J.NEUBIOREV.2022.104576?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes
- Active bouts acutely increase HF‑HRV/BRS and respiration‑EEG coupling; amplify respiration‑locked CSF oscillations; reduce IL‑6; entrain pupil oscillations at 0.1 Hz without sustained dilation—yielding higher S versus control. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/J.NEUBIOREV.2022.104576?utm_source=openai))
- Across the day, periodic bouts maintain working memory and vigilance relative to control despite sleep restriction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40392328/?utm_source=openai))
- ΔS versus bout parameters exhibits a steep, threshold‑like transition consistent with bifurcation dynamics. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-025-02091-1?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and impact
- Repurposes nasal 0.1 Hz breathing as a unifying actuator to approximate sleep’s coupled recovery signature during wake, directly testing CSF–neural–autonomic coordination rather than isolated endpoints; prior work has not evaluated this as a sleep‑surrogate, multi‑axis recovery induction in a controlled, sleep‑restricted model. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))

Key risks and mitigations
- Risk: Hypocapnia blunting autonomic effects. Mitigation: CO2 monitoring, titrate to comfortable tidal volume.
- Risk: Mouth leaks reducing olfactory entrainment. Mitigation: nasal‑patency screening; instruction; optional external nasal dilator.
- Risk: MRI subset feasibility. Mitigation: prioritize rt‑PCMRI single‑slice aqueduct/cistern measures during one bout. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28152239/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- Primary: S exceeds S* during ≥70% of active bouts and remains elevated ≥3 min post‑bout; composite cognitive performance non‑inferior to well‑rested baseline or superior to control day under restriction.
- Mechanistic: Demonstration that breathing‑locked neural entrainment and CSF oscillation amplification co‑occur with autonomic/immune shifts during wake. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and deliverables
- Phase 1 (months 0–6): Optimize pacing protocol; validate S components in rested wake.
- Phase 2 (months 7–18): Crossover trial under partial sleep restriction with MRI subset; preregistered analyses.
- Phase 3 (months 19–24): Dose/threshold mapping; open dataset of multimodal signals and S computation code.

References (selected)
- Coupling of slow waves, hemodynamics, and CSF in human sleep. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))
- Nasal respiration entrains human limbic oscillations and cognition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Respiration as a dominant driver of CSF motion in humans. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6705733/?utm_source=openai))
- Resonance breathing maximizes HRV/baroreflex and reduces IL‑6 in RCTs. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/J.NEUBIOREV.2022.104576?utm_source=openai))
- Sleep–wake flip‑flop and bifurcation dynamics. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22811426/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Quota-triggered replication of sleep architecture under time-restricted sleep: a closed-loop trial to restore neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic homeostasis without extending total sleep time

Premise and rationale
- In humans, non-REM slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.75–4.5 Hz) indexes homeostatic sleep pressure (Process S) and dissipates during sleep; REM is governed by a separate ultradian homeostatic process (“REM pressure”) that builds between REM bouts and partially discharges during REM, shaping REM timing and density. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/074873099129000894?utm_source=openai))
- SWS is mechanistically tied to glymphatic/CSF hydrodynamics and solute clearance; neural slow waves drive hemo‑CSF oscillations in humans, and sleep increases interstitial space and β‑amyloid clearance in rodents. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))
- Selective SWS suppression (without reducing total sleep time) impairs morning glucose tolerance, linking SWS quantity/quality to metabolic control. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602132/?utm_source=openai))
- Sleep loss elevates systemic inflammatory markers (e.g., IL‑6, CRP); a daytime nap after sleep loss can normalize cortisol/IL‑6 profiles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12856123/?utm_source=openai))
- Closed‑loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) can enhance slow oscillations and spindle coupling without lengthening total sleep time, though memory benefits are mixed—supporting physiological feasibility but motivating outcome tests beyond memory. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23583623/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use individualized, deficit-triggered “quotas” for slow-wave energy (SWE) and REM propensity as control targets. During a restricted sleep opportunity, deliver phase-locked CLAS only until the individual’s SWE target is met; the next day, schedule a short nap at a circadian phase of high REM propensity and terminate the nap when a REM-density target is achieved. By meeting state-specific quotas rather than extending time, the protocol aims to reconstitute the endogenous sequence of restoration and normalize four-axis homeostasis.

Hypothesis (inseparable from the goal)
If individualized deficits in NREM slow-wave energy and REM propensity are corrected to prespecified quotas via closed-loop, state-timed nudges within a fixed, short total sleep allotment, then markers of neurocognitive performance, insulin sensitivity, inflammatory tone, and autonomic flexibility will be statistically non-inferior to a normal-sleep baseline.

Study design
- Population: Healthy adults (n=48), 21–40 years, regular sleepers, no sleep/medical disorders.
- Design: Randomized, within-subject, three-condition crossover with ≥10-day washouts.
  1) Restricted-sleep + closed-loop quota protocol (RS+CLQ)
  2) Restricted-sleep + sham (RS+Sham)
  3) Normal-sleep baseline (NS)
- Restriction schedule: 3 consecutive nights at 4.5 h time-in-bed (TIB 01:30–06:00) in RS arms; 3 nights at habitual TIB in NS.

Closed-loop quota protocol (RS+CLQ)
- Night module (architecture: NREM/SWE)
  - Wearable frontopolar EEG + EOG. Real-time sleep staging and slow-wave detection onboard smartphone. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.10111?utm_source=openai))
  - Target definition: For each participant, compute baseline-night cumulative SWE (0.5–1.5 Hz) per unit NREM from NS. Set per-night SWE quota in RS to the model-predicted Process S dissipation needed to offset prior wake, capped at 75th percentile of individual baseline NREM SWE to avoid over-stimulation. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/074873099129000894?utm_source=openai))
  - Intervention: Deliver 40–60 dB pink-noise clicks time‑locked to up-states of detected slow oscillations during N2/N3. Suspend stimulation in micro-arousals and REM. Controller stops stimulation once cumulative SWE matches the nightly quota. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23583623/?utm_source=openai))
- Day module (architecture: REM/propensity)
  - Timing: Single 60‑min nap scheduled at the participant’s individualized early‑afternoon circadian phase with historically higher REM propensity (inferred from prior nights’ sleep history and a validated REM timing model). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7385183/?utm_source=openai))
  - Target definition: REM quota set to the participant’s baseline first‑cycle REM density (rapid eye movement counts per minute) or an equivalent propensity threshold from the ultradian REM model; nap ends when REM density target is reached or at 60 min, whichever comes first. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7385183/?utm_source=openai))
  - No stimulation during naps; eyes-closed quiet if REM fails to emerge.

Sham (RS+Sham)
- Identical instrumentation. Night: non-contingent, very low‑volume tones delivered in N2/N3 without phase-locking; no quota logic. Day: fixed 60‑min quiet rest at same clock time, no EEG‑guided termination.

Outcomes and endpoints
- Primary non-inferiority composite (day 4, morning):
  - Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Test lapses; 2‑back d′; paired-associates recall.
  - Metabolic: 2‑h OGTT Matsuda Index (or standardized mixed‑meal with CGM-derived insulin sensitivity proxy). Link to SWS function via prior SWS suppression findings. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602132/?utm_source=openai))
  - Immune: Plasma IL‑6 and hs‑CRP; expectation of RS elevations and nap‑related normalization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12856123/?utm_source=openai))
  - Autonomic: Morning HRV (RMSSD) during 10‑min supine rest.
- Secondary/Mechanistic:
  - Night module efficacy: ΔSWE vs target; spindle–SO coupling.
  - Day module efficacy: REM latency, REM density, and achievement of REM quota.
  - Exploratory hydrodynamics: morning fMRI in a subset to quantify low‑frequency CSF inflow coupling to slow waves (feasibility permitting). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31672896/?utm_source=openai))

Controller specification
- SWE controller: Cumulative integral of band‑limited power within phase‑detected slow oscillations drives a PI controller that schedules CLAS pulses until quota achieved; safety timeouts prevent continuous stimulation and avoid sleep fragmentation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23583623/?utm_source=openai))
- REM quota estimator: Hidden‑state ultradian model updated online with sleep history to predict REM propensity; termination when EOG-based saccade rate × REM duration exceeds the individualized density threshold. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pcbi.1009316&utm_source=openai))

Procedures
- Run-in (NS): Two nights of habitual sleep to estimate baseline SWE/REM metrics and train individual Process S/REM models. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/074873099129000894?utm_source=openai))
- RS arms: Nights 1–3 with or without CLQ; nap module on days 2–4.
- Blood draws: pre- and post‑intervention mornings (days 1 and 4).
- Cognitive/metabolic tests: standardized morning schedule; OGTT on day 4.

Analysis
- Mixed-effects non-inferiority models compare RS+CLQ vs NS and RS+Sham on the composite endpoint; margin pre-specified as 20% of baseline SD per domain.
- Mediation: test whether quota attainment (ΔSWE, REM density) mediates changes in metabolic and inflammatory outcomes.

Power
- With n=48, α=0.05, intraclass correlation 0.4, the trial has >80% power to detect non-inferiority on the composite assuming standardized differences ≤0.3.

Innovation and compatibility with biology
- Targets are endogenous state variables (Process S via SWE; ultradian REM pressure via density/propensity), not proxies like “time asleep,” respecting known sleep control architectures. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/074873099129000894?utm_source=openai))
- CLAS augments slow waves without lengthening sleep; the nap leverages natural circadian/ultradian REM dynamics; no direct manipulation of heart rate or stress responses. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23583623/?utm_source=openai))
- Multi-axis restoration is biologically motivated: SWS links to glymphatic and insulin sensitivity; naps after loss affect IL‑6/cortisol. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24136970/?dopt=AbstractPlus&utm_source=openai))

Risks and mitigations
- Mixed memory outcomes with CLAS: the aim is multi-axis homeostasis; stimulation parameters individualized and suspended on arousals to limit fragmentation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6831893/?utm_source=openai))
- REM emergence in short naps is variable: use individualized REM‑propensity timing and density‑based termination to maximize efficacy within 60 minutes. ([journals.plos.org](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pcbi.1009316&utm_source=openai))

Decision criteria for success
- RS+CLQ non-inferior to NS and superior to RS+Sham on the composite endpoint.
- Quota attainment explains a significant share of variance in each axis (predefined mediation thresholds).

Potential outcomes and implications
- Success would show that correcting state-specific homeostatic deficits—rather than extending total sleep—can approximate the recovery state, providing a principled path to “copy the pattern, not the duration.” If partially successful (e.g., neurocognitive/metabolic restored but immune not), results will specify which quotas or timing require refinement or whether additional state‑specific quotas are necessary. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/074873099129000894?utm_source=openai))
