Title
Tomography-native predictive validation for in situ cryo-ET with acquisition-split cross-validation and optional DNA-origami lattice calibration

Hypothesis/research goal
A validation framework that evaluates a model’s ability to predict held-out raw tilt observations—augmented by direction-aware acquisition splits and, where feasible, periodic DNA-origami lattice calibration—will yield reproducible, anisotropy-aware confidence estimates that enable democratized, reliable in situ structure determination by cryo-ET. This reframes “resolution” as predictive generalization under real microscope physics rather than agreement between correlated tomograms. The question and goal are identical: Can we make in situ cryo-ET trustworthy by demanding that reconstructions predict raw data they did not use, with direction- and location-specific uncertainty?

Atomic strategy
Shift the locus of truth from reconstructed volumes to raw projections: hold out selected tilts or sub-apertures, fit on the remainder, and score predictive likelihood/residuals on the held-out data with a physically correct forward model. Optionally anchor directional calibration using known Fourier peaks from a co-imaged DNA-origami lattice. This single change converts missing data into a falsifiable constraint, isolates correlations that plague tomogram-level splits, and yields spatially adaptive confidence without assuming uniform imaging. Prior art establishes leave-one-out, projection-vs-reprojection tests in ET; we generalize and standardize them for in situ use and pair them with anisotropy calibration. ([immunology.ox.ac.uk](https://www.immunology.ox.ac.uk/publications/104039?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Define and validate a predictive, tomography-native metric on raw tilts.
  - Develop a per-tilt forward model that accounts for per-tilt CTF, dose-weighted noise, defocus gradients, and 3D-CTF/missing-wedge geometry. Compute predictive log-likelihood and calibrated residual maps on held-out tilts (noise-compensated leave-one-out extended from prior ET work). Report per-voxel confidence by aggregating residuals in spatial blocks to respect local correlations. Benchmark against even/odd-tilt FSC(e/o) and conventional STA FSC to show improved calibration under anisotropic sampling. ([immunology.ox.ac.uk](https://www.immunology.ox.ac.uk/publications/104039?utm_source=openai))

- Aim 2. Enforce independence and expose anisotropy with acquisition-split cross-validation.
  - Partition the tilt series into angular sub-apertures (e.g., interleaved sectors) to create disjoint training/validation sets with complementary angular coverage. Reconstruct each sub-aperture independently under identical priors and require cross-prediction: each sub-aperture reconstruction must predict raw images from the complementary sub-aperture. Differences between sub-aperture reconstructions provide an empirical, direction-resolved point-spread characterization that directly reflects the missing wedge and lamella thickness. This replaces global thresholds with direction-aware uncertainty reporting. ([immunology.ox.ac.uk](https://www.immunology.ox.ac.uk/publications/104039?utm_source=openai))

- Aim 3. Optional DNA-origami lattice module for directional calibration and targeting.
  - When compatible with the specimen, co-image a thin 2D or low-order 3D DNA-origami lattice in montage tomograms adjacent to the cellular region. Use the lattice’s known reciprocal-space peaks to measure angle-dependent attenuation and phase distortions along the same optical path, providing a local anisotropic transfer estimate that informs per-direction regularization and confidence scaling. The same structures have been imaged by cryo-ET and used as cryo-ET-compatible signposts, supporting feasibility; however, their use as periodic, in-tomogram calibration for anisotropy and independence-preserving unit-cell splits has not been standardized. ([ebi.ac.uk](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-49289?utm_source=openai))

- Aim 4. Package a low-resource, standardized pipeline for broad adoption.
  - Implement streaming predictive scoring that operates per tilt on a single workstation GPU, with optional CPU fallback. Provide containerized integration points for IMOD, emClarity, Dynamo/EMAN2, and RELION subtomogram modules. Release reference datasets, SOPs, and pass/fail acceptance criteria to enable inter-lab reproducibility.

Experimental plan
- Datasets
  - In situ lamellae from adherent cells prepared by dose-symmetric schemes; include regions with recurring endogenous complexes (e.g., ribosomes, clathrin). Acquire montage cryo-ET to capture both cellular and optional lattice regions within one acquisition when feasible.
- Baselines and controls
  - Compute even/odd-tilt FSC(e/o) and conventional STA FSC where applicable; use published reviews and workflows to ensure standard baselines and to highlight limitations under anisotropic sampling and tomogram-level correlations. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34003255/?utm_source=openai))
- Predictive scoring protocol
  - Split tilts into K folds (K≈5) by interleaving angles to avoid dose/defocus drift confounds. For each fold: reconstruct from K−1 folds; compute per-tilt predictive likelihood/residuals for the held-out fold; aggregate to per-voxel confidence via spatial block pooling that respects the local missing-wedge footprint.
  - Report direction-aware confidence by binning residuals over Fourier cones aligned to the tilt axis; visualize as per-voxel confidence and per-direction PSF maps.
- Sub-aperture cross-prediction
  - Form two disjoint angular sectors (e.g., low-tilt vs high-tilt interleaved). Reconstruct each sector; forward-project each reconstruction into the other sector’s angles; score predictive residuals and quantify anisotropic blur. Use these measurements to set direction-specific regularization weights in iterative reconstruction.
- DNA-origami lattice calibration (optional)
  - Design a sparse 2D lattice (d≈15–30 nm) deposited on grid regions adjacent to cells prior to vitrification; acquire montage tomograms so that the lattice and cell share defocus gradient and lamella thickness. Fit per-angle attenuation/phase of lattice harmonics to estimate a local, direction-resolved transfer function; use it to scale predictive residuals and to set unit-cell-based independence splits if the lattice spans the FOV. Feasibility is supported by cryo-ET imaging of origami lattices and by origami “signposts” compatible with cellular cryo-ET. ([ebi.ac.uk](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-49289?utm_source=openai))

Analysis and success criteria
- Calibration quality
  - Predictive likelihood must improve monotonically with added tilts from complementary directions; failure to improve indicates overfitting or alignment/CTF errors.
  - Direction-aware PSF estimates must reproduce known anisotropy from the missing wedge and thickness, evidenced by poorer prediction in poorly sampled directions. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2011/sm/c0sm00441c?utm_source=openai))
- Biological validity
  - Regions containing known complexes should show higher predictive confidence and better cross-prediction than surrounding background. Confidence should track with subtomogram averages’ resolvability but need not match SPA-style FSC thresholds.
- Reproducibility and accessibility
  - Across ≥3 labs and ≥2 microscope platforms, the predictive score distributions and pass/fail thresholds should agree within predefined tolerances when using the same acquisition scheme and reconstruction settings, on a single-GPU workstation.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: Held-out tilts at extreme angles have systematically worse SNR; mitigation: noise-compensated weighting and angle-balanced folds to avoid inflating residuals due to dose/thickness, following prior NLOO principles. ([immunology.ox.ac.uk](https://www.immunology.ox.ac.uk/publications/104039?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Optional DNA-origami module may not be co-localizable with every biological target; mitigation: treat it as an external calibration that sets instrument/geometry priors when montage co-imaging is feasible; otherwise rely solely on acquisition-split predictive validation.

Deliverables
- A vetted, tomography-native predictive validation metric and software with streaming per-tilt scoring and direction-aware confidence maps.
- Reference datasets and SOPs for acquisition-split CV and, when applicable, origami-lattice calibration.
- Benchmark report showing improved falsification power versus FSC(e/o)/STA FSC under anisotropic sampling and low SNR, and guidance for dose- and angle-aware stopping rules.

Significance
By requiring models to predict raw tilts they did not use—and by exposing directionality explicitly—this framework aligns validation with cryo-ET physics, mitigates tomogram-level correlation artifacts, and yields spatially adaptive confidence that respects the missing wedge. Optional DNA-origami lattices offer a principled, periodic calibration for anisotropy when feasible. The result is a reproducible, resource-efficient path to trustworthy in situ structure determination. ([immunology.ox.ac.uk](https://www.immunology.ox.ac.uk/publications/104039?utm_source=openai))

Title
Rotation-invariant information tensors for tomography-native validation and democratized in situ structure determination

Background and significance
- In cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), incomplete angular sampling (the missing wedge) yields anisotropic resolution and elongation along the beam, which confounds biological heterogeneity with acquisition artifacts. Dual-axis tilting reduces but does not eliminate these effects, and throughput remains a bottleneck. Directional and conical FSC variants quantify anisotropy but rely on data splits and do not resolve in situ artifact-versus-biology at the tomogram level. Existing wedge-aware approaches (e.g., wedge-masked differences, inpainting, deconvolution) treat the wedge as a deficit rather than a measurable signal tied to acquisition geometry. These gaps impede robust validation and limit adoption in smaller labs. ([rupress.org](https://rupress.org/jcb/article/202/3/407/54592/Cryo-electron-tomography-The-challenge-of-doing?utm_source=openai))

Central question-hypothesis
- Can we convert the acquisition-locked anisotropy induced by the missing wedge into a quantitative, rotation-invariant “information tensor” that distinguishes true in situ variability from direction-dependent imaging artifacts without half-set splitting or heavy compute?

Atomic strategy
- Treat the local directional power on the unit sphere as a measurable field and fit a symmetric 3×3 tensor per patch that summarizes anisotropic information transfer; then test whether this tensor rotates with the acquisition frame while the biological structure stays fixed in the specimen frame.

Specific aims
1) Define and estimate a tomography-native local information tensor.
- For each tomogram patch, compute directional energy E(n) by integrating Fourier amplitude over narrow cones on the sphere, with per-tilt CTF/dose weighting. Fit a second-order spherical model E(n) ≈ n^T T n to obtain tensor T, its eigenvectors, and a fractional anisotropy (FA_info) score. This generalizes directional/local anisotropy mapping to a compact tensor that is amenable to rotation tests and does not require split maps. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940361/?utm_source=openai))

2) Use controlled reorientation to test invariance and separate artifact from biology in situ.
- Acquire minimal redundancy via either (a) sequential short tilt subsets before/after a 90° grid in-plane rotation (dual-axis hardware or manual stage rotation) or (b) lamellae prepared with distinct in-plane orientations of the same cellular region. Invariance test: if T’s principal axes rotate with the acquisition geometry while biological frames (e.g., membrane normals, filament tangents) remain fixed in the cell, the anisotropy is wedge/CTF-driven; if T aligns with biological axes across rotations, it reflects true heterogeneity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2776717/?utm_source=openai))

3) Create tomography-native validation via sector-partitioned semblance and reprojection residuals.
- Reconstruct sub-volumes from complementary angular sectors (e.g., ±60° vs orthogonal sectors) and compute multi-sector coherence (semblance) and view-dependent reprojection residuals. Features with high cross-sector coherence and low residuals are specimen-locked; features whose appearance flips across sectors are acquisition-locked artifacts. Report voxelwise coherence maps alongside FA_info as routine QC. ([repository.gatech.edu](https://repository.gatech.edu/entities/publication/df7d7f60-db8c-49b8-b72c-b6ee552e7e63?utm_source=openai))

Methods
- Data acquisition: Cryo-FIB lamellae from cultured cells; for each ROI, collect a single standard tilt series (±60–70°) plus one complementary short series after a 90° in-plane rotation where feasible; otherwise, collect on adjacent lamellae cut at rotated in-plane orientations. Record per-tilt defocus and dose for dose-weighted, CTF-corrected reconstructions. Use any standard alignment/reconstruction toolchain; our method is reconstruction-agnostic. ([pure.mpg.de](https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3265230_1/component/file_3266643/content?utm_source=openai))
- Tensor estimation: For each 32–64 voxel patch, compute a local 3D FFT, tabulate cone-averaged power vs direction, correct first-order CTF/dose, and fit T by least squares on S2. Output FA_info and eigenvectors; store as low-bit maps to minimize storage.
- Rotation-invariance test: Register rotated acquisitions in the specimen frame using fiducials or common landmarks, then compare T fields after rotating into a shared coordinate system. Quantify alignment via principal-angle error between eigenframes; report per-patch p-values by bootstrap over directions.
- Semblance/residual validation: Build sector-partitioned reconstructions by angular masking in weighted backprojection or SIRT; compute normalized cross-correlation across sectors per voxel or along detected membranes/filaments; forward-project each sector volume to original tilts and measure view-stratified residuals.
- Compatibility with existing anisotropy metrics: Compare FA_info to conical/directional FSC maps to ensure consistency and to calibrate thresholds for actionable QC. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847715000726?utm_source=openai))

Test systems and analyses
- Filament-rich cytoskeleton and ER/mitochondrial membranes where biological frames are well-defined. Expectation: missing-wedge anisotropy eigenvectors rotate with acquisition; biological axes (filament tangents, membrane normals) do not.
- Benchmarks: Public tomograms and in-house datasets with both single- and dual-axis acquisitions to probe dynamic range of anisotropy and verify reduction to a missing pyramid. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847715000726?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes and endpoints
- Deliverables: (i) Open-source CPU-only code producing FA_info/eigenvector fields and coherence maps; (ii) a rotation-invariance validation protocol requiring at most one additional short tilt subset or a second lamella; (iii) reporting standards to accompany in situ subtomogram averaging and model building.
- Primary endpoints: (a) reduction in false-positive features flagged by low coherence/high FA_info; (b) improved STA alignment stability when down-weighting orientations with low E(n); (c) agreement with cFSC/directional FSC while avoiding half-set dependence. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847715000726?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and novelty relative to prior art
- Prior work quantifies anisotropy using directional/conical FSC or local-directional resolution (MonoDir/MonoRes) and mitigates wedge effects via classification or deconvolution. Our contribution is to (i) recast anisotropy as a local tensor field explicitly designed for rotation-invariance testing across minimal reorientations, and (ii) introduce tomography-native coherence/residual validation that does not rely on independent half-sets. This complements, rather than competes with, cFSC/3DFSC and wedge-aware classification. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940361/?utm_source=openai))

Risk mitigation
- Limited ability to rotate: fall back to adjacent rotated lamellae or to sector-based semblance alone; document reduced confidence. ([pure.mpg.de](https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3265230_1/component/file_3266643/content?utm_source=openai))
- Patch size trade-offs: adapt cone width and patch size to SNR; aggregate tensors on biophysical manifolds (along membranes/filaments) to stabilize estimates.
- Confounding from alignment/CTF errors: use per-tilt CTF/dose modeling and include controls where conical FSC predicts near-isotropy to verify specificity. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847715000726?utm_source=openai))

Validation plan
- Simulations: generate ground-truth cellular phantoms with controlled anisotropy and known biological frames; simulate single- vs dual-axis acquisition to test tensor recovery and rotation behavior. Compare to cFSC and MonoDir maps. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940361/?utm_source=openai))
- Experimental: apply to microtubule bundles and ER sheets; show that FA_info eigenvectors track wedge rotation, while filament/membrane axes remain specimen-locked; demonstrate that down-weighting low-E(n) directions improves STA class convergence.

Milestones and metrics
- Month 3: Prototype tensor estimator, release CLI; reproduce known anisotropy on public tomograms. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847715000726?utm_source=openai))
- Month 6: Rotation-invariance experiments on 10 ROIs across 3 lamella orientations; threshold FA_info for QC; integrate semblance/residual module.
- Month 9: STA integration with orientation down-weighting; report gains in alignment stability and reduced artifact rates.
- Month 12: Community release with documentation and example datasets; propose reporting guidelines pairing FA_info/coherence maps with reconstructions.

Impact
- Provides a low-compute, acquisition-aware validation framework that uses the wedge as a measurable, rotating signal. It replaces half-set assumptions with rotation-invariance tests, aligns with existing anisotropy metrics, and lowers the barrier for small labs to perform reliable in situ structure determination. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847715000726?utm_source=openai))

Title
Imaging-center deployment of in situ DNA-origami rulers with provenance-rich tomography to standardize and validate cryo-ET structure determination

Hypothesis-question
Can programmable DNA-origami “rulers” colocated with native cellular structures provide a ground-truth geometric reference that (i) yields a tomography-native, wedge-aware local information metric and (ii) becomes portable across imaging centers through provenance-complete data standards, thereby enabling reproducible in situ structure determination at scale? The practical test is whether ruler-derived quality layers and metadata allow independent labs to predictably recover equivalent structures from different sites for the same biological target despite missing-wedge and low-SNR constraints. ([rupress.org](https://rupress.org/jcb/article/202/3/407/54592/Cryo-electron-tomography-The-challenge-of-doing?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Introduce rigid, asymmetric DNA-origami rulers into the same microenvironments as the macromolecular targets to instantiate a local geometric truth and absolute orientation frame. Use deviations of recovered inter-feature distances/angles from design to estimate a local, wedge-aware transfer function and an information-density field; embed these fields, together with full acquisition/reconstruction provenance, in a standardized, provenance-rich container so that multi-center datasets are directly comparable and queryable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7956247/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and validate cryo-ET ruler constructs and targeting modes
- Ruler design: 30–80 nm 3D DNA-origami bodies with (a) three non-collinear, high-contrast landmarks (dense DNA bundles ± small AuNPs), (b) asymmetric spacing to remove orientation degeneracy, and (c) an internal calibration ladder (e.g., two fixed inter-landmark distances 20 and 40 nm). Designs leverage demonstrated origami rigidity/orientation control in cryo-EM and facile geometric addressability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7956247/?utm_source=openai))
- Targeting to cellular locales: start on the extracellular side (SPOT-like tags binding GFP fusions on membranes/viruses/vesicles) where in situ cryo-ET labeling is already feasible; then extend to intracellular delivery using nanobody/aptamer handles and permeabilization/electroporation or microinjection in adherent cells on EM grids. This staged path acknowledges that intracellular origami labeling remains an open challenge and treats it as an experimental variable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7895908/?utm_source=openai))
- Physical/chemical stability: assess folding integrity in cryo buffers and on-grid adsorption; verify by SPA 2D class averages and low-dose cryo-ET of purified rulers to obtain a “reference tomogram” of the construct as manufactured. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7956247/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: quantify recovery of known distances/angles across tilt and depth in ice; measure orientation error distributions relative to the tilt axis.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Extracellular ruler localization with ≥80% detectability and ≤5° median orientation error relative to design in tomograms. 
- M2: Demonstrated intracellular delivery with ≥40% detectability in lamellae without aggregation artifacts.

Aim 2. Derive tomography-native, wedge-aware quality metrics from the rulers
- Local anisotropic transfer characterization: for each ruler instance, fit the reconstructed landmark coordinates to design using a wedge-constrained error model; infer local elongation tensors and direction-dependent attenuation attributable to the missing wedge and dose history. Compile these into a voxel-level WEDGE_MASK and LOCAL_INFO_DENSITY (LID) field that explicitly encodes where resolvable information survives. This avoids direct import of SPA gold-standard assumptions that do not hold for a unique tomogram. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847705001085?utm_source=openai))
- Half-set partitioning without tomogram-level leakage: use the per-ruler absolute orientation frame to stratify subtomograms by angle relative to the tilt axis before splitting, minimizing interhalf correlations introduced by shared tilt-series features. Evaluate resolution/overfitting by wedge-aware FSC variants that restrict shells to supported Fourier sectors and weight by local SSNR inferred from the rulers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8133831/?utm_source=openai))
- Validation tasks: 
  - Predictive test: use the LID and WEDGE_MASK fields to predict where specific macromolecular features (e.g., membrane curvature, filament periodicities) should be recoverable; score agreement between predictions and observed recoverability across independent datasets.
  - Reference consistency: for purified rulers, compute FSC against the known 3D model filtered by the measured wedge support as a calibration of absolute performance. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1047847705001085?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- M3: A reproducible pipeline that outputs WEDGE_MASK and LID fields whose values predict local feature recoverability with ROC AUC ≥0.85 across test tomograms.
- M4: Demonstration that wedge-aware, ruler-referenced FSC yields tighter confidence intervals than conventional FSC in STA of a test complex imaged in situ.

Aim 3. Build a provenance-rich, federation-ready tomography container and archive workflow for imaging centers
- Data model: adopt FITS-like container semantics with explicit headers for tilt geometry, lamella normal, CTF model, per-tilt dose, alignment model, and full processing HISTORY; include WCS matrices to map voxel indices to specimen space and wedge support. Store auxiliary planes (WEDGE_MASK, LID, VARIANCE, QUALITY flags) as image extensions. Provenance follows the IVOA Provenance Data Model to make acquisition-to-reconstruction chains auditable and comparable across centers. ([archive.stsci.edu](https://archive.stsci.edu/fits/fits_standard/node40.html?utm_source=openai))
- Services: publish center outputs to a catalog that supports query-by-quality (e.g., LID thresholds, wedge half-angle, lamella thickness bands) and subsetting/streaming of only required planes for downstream analysis to reduce compute/storage load for small labs.
- Correlation control: assign a CORRSET identifier based on deterministic hashes of acquisition and reconstruction parameters; downstream STA software can track and limit per-CORRSET particle contributions per half to reduce hidden correlations.

Milestones and success criteria
- M5: Reference implementation and validator that round-trips a tomogram with all header keywords and planes; public example datasets and schema.
- M6: Query service enabling cross-center selection by LID and wedge geometry; successful reproduction of a published in situ average at an external site using only the standardized container and metadata.

Aim 4. Multi-center ring trial with traceable physical references
- Protocol: participating imaging centers bracket biological sessions with a short run on a traceable physical reference (e.g., NIST RM 8012/8013 AuNPs for size/contrast and magnification bias checks) collected under the same optics/dose conditions as the biological tilt series. Use ruler-only grids as an additional cross-check of reconstruction bias. ([tsapps.nist.gov](https://tsapps.nist.gov/srmext/certificates/8012.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Analysis: compute per-center bias/variance in magnification anisotropy, wedge-induced elongation, and LID scaling; include these as priors/corrections in downstream STA. Publicly report uncertainty budgets per center/session.

Milestones and success criteria
- M7: Inter-site variability in predicted LID reduced by ≥30% after applying center-specific corrections derived from SRM and ruler measurements.
- M8: Cross-site reproducibility: independent centers obtain subtomogram averages of the same cellular target that agree within 10% in reported resolution and show indistinguishable angular anisotropy profiles after correction.

Methods overview
- Sample prep: adherent mammalian cells on EM grids; extracellular SPOT-like ruler application for Aim 1 baseline; intracellular delivery by electroporation or microinjection for advanced studies; plunge freezing; cryo-FIB lamella fabrication.
- Data acquisition: standardized tilt schemes; per-tilt dose tracking; energy-filtered TEM where available.
- Reconstruction and analysis: fiducial or patch-tracking alignment; CTF estimation per tilt and Z; ruler landmark detection and geometric fitting; computation of WEDGE_MASK and LID; STA with wedge-aware half-sets and FSC; containerization and archive deposition.

Evaluation plan
- Technical validation: show that ruler-derived elongation tensors match analytical predictions of wedge geometry and measured tilt coverage; demonstrate that LID correlates with local STA classifiability and alignment precision.
- Biological validation: choose a membrane-associated complex with known quasi-periodicity; test whether LID predicts recoverable periodicities across orientations and depths within the same lamella.

Risks and mitigations
- Intracellular ruler delivery efficiency may be low: begin with extracellular targets and lamella-adjacent cytosol regions; evaluate delivery aids (nanobody fusions, electroporation) in parallel; continue to treat intracellular targeting as an engineering variable, not a dependency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7895908/?utm_source=openai))
- Ruler interference with local ultrastructure: restrict occupancy and binding valency; monitor for clustering artifacts and exclude affected regions using QUALITY flags.

Expected outcomes
- A deployable, tomography-native quality framework—WEDGE_MASK and LID—from in situ rulers that replaces SPA-derived assumptions and quantifies the local impact of missing wedge and dose.
- A provenance-complete, queryable container and archive workflow that makes multi-center benchmarking and data reuse practical for small labs.
- Evidence that ring-trial calibration with traceable references plus on-specimen rulers leads to reproducible, center-agnostic in situ structure determination.

Impact
By turning a local, programmable geometric truth into a measurable transfer function and embedding it in a provenance-rich, federated data product, imaging centers can deliver cryo-ET datasets whose quality is explicit, comparable, and predictive of downstream success. This addresses the core limitations—missing-wedge anisotropy, low SNR, and validation without independence—without claiming to break physics, and provides the operational standardization required to democratize reliable in situ structure determination. ([rupress.org](https://rupress.org/jcb/article/202/3/407/54592/Cryo-electron-tomography-The-challenge-of-doing?utm_source=openai))

Title
Tomography-native self-validation and refinement by missing-wedge autofocus: a reference-free quality metric and correction loop for in situ cryo-ET

Integrated hypothesis–question
If the missing wedge is treated as a deterministic constraint rather than a loss, then the only reconstructions consistent with the data and biology are those that (i) minimize energy mapped into geometrically forbidden Fourier sectors and (ii) maximize cross-ray consistency across tilts. Can a wedge-informed autofocus objective—optimized directly on the acquired tilt series—yield a tomogram-native validation metric and simultaneously refine per-tilt phase/geometry to improve in situ structure determination without half-set splitting? Prior work offers wedge-aware classification (WMD), anisotropy-aware STA validation, and powerful CTF/geometry refinement, but no map-level QC that penalizes forbidden-sector energy or uses it to drive per-tilt correction. We ask whether such a metric can be made robust, biologically compatible, and computationally accessible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2556382/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit SAR-style autofocus self-consistency to refine per-tilt phase and geometry by minimizing a wedge-leakage objective: reduce energy reconstructed in known-forbidden k-space while enforcing projection–reprojection agreement. Use empty ice as an internal baseline to calibrate the leakage penalty so that optimization is driven by physically interpretable error, not over-regularization. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/21/7/2370?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define a wedge-informed, reference-free QC metric.
- Ghost Index (GI): ratio of Fourier energy inside the geometrically forbidden wedge to that predicted from ice-only noise propagated through the same reconstruction operator, computed locally and globally. Lower GI indicates fewer algorithmic ghosts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3834153/?utm_source=openai))
2) Build a missing-wedge autofocus (MW-AF) refinement loop.
- Jointly refine per-tilt defocus offsets, low-order aberrations, and small pose parameters by minimizing a compound objective that trades off cross-ray data fidelity and GI. Seed from standard pipelines; no half-sets or external references required. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42185541/?utm_source=openai))
3) Establish tomography-native validation for in situ structure determination.
- Show that MW-AF reduces anisotropy and overfitting in subtomogram averages (3D-FSC cones) and improves classification stability relative to WMD-only workflows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6281437/?utm_source=openai))

Methods

A. Forward model and masks
- Construct a 3D sampling mask S(k) from actual tilt angles, dose weights, and per-tilt CTFs; its complement W(k)=1−S(k) is the forbidden region (the missing wedge). Use the same reconstruction operator as the pipeline under test (WBP/SIRT/TV-regularized). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3991334/?utm_source=openai))
- Segment ice volumes to estimate the tilt-wise noise power spectrum; propagate through the operator to obtain the expected forbidden-sector baseline Eice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3834153/?utm_source=openai))

B. Metrics
- Ghost Index GI(Ω)= Eforb(Ω)/Eice(Ω), where Eforb(Ω)=∑k∈W |F{R(y;θ)}(k)|² within region Ω (global or patch), R is the reconstruction from tilt images y under parameters θ. GI≈1 implies noise-consistent leakage; GI≫1 flags algorithmic ghosts.
- Cross-ray inconsistency C: average squared residual between measured tilts and reprojected synthetic projections from R(y;θ), computed patchwise to respect spatial nonstationarity.

C. MW-AF objective and optimization
- Minimize J(θ)=α·C(θ)+β·GI(θ) over per-tilt parameters θ={Δdefocus, coma/astigmatism terms, in-plane shift/rotation, small tilt corrections}. Initialize θ from AreTomo/emClarity; optimize per-patch with stochastic gradient and multi-scale windows. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42185541/?utm_source=openai))
- SAR autofocus analogy: GI acts like a sharpness/entropy surrogate but anchored to geometry (forbidden-sector energy), while C enforces projection fidelity—together replacing heuristic image-entropy objectives common in SAR with a physics-constrained target. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/21/7/2370?utm_source=openai))

D. Implementation and accessibility
- Patchwise, GPU-light: compute GI and C on 64–128³ subvolumes with mixed precision; accumulate gradients across patches to update global per-tilt parameters.
- Drop-in refinement stage callable from standard stacks (SerialEM → AreTomo/IMOD/WBP/SIRT → MW-AF → downstream denoising/STA). Open-source CLI with optional CUDA; CPU fallback for small labs.

Validation plan

1) Simulations with ground truth
- Generate dose-symmetric tilt series with controlled phase and pose perturbations; reconstruct with WBP/SIRT; quantify recovery of injected errors by MW-AF. Endpoints: error reduction vs. magnitude of initial perturbation; GI reduction; prevention of overfitting (no GI increase when true parameters are correct).

2) Public biological datasets
- EMPIAR ribosome-in-cell and membrane-rich datasets; run baseline (AreTomo/emClarity) vs. +MW-AF. Endpoints:
  - Global/local GI reduction without loss of visible features in allowed band.
  - Subtomogram averages: improved directional 3D-FSC and reduced anisotropy cones; improved classification stability relative to WMD-based pipelines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6281437/?utm_source=openai))

3) Comparative ablations
- Replace GI with image-entropy sharpness; test whether wedge-anchored penalty outperforms generic autofocus criteria and avoids hallucinating detail. ([rfessentials.com](https://rfessentials.com/resources/rf-glossary/autofocus-sar/?utm_source=openai))
- Swap reconstruction operators (WBP vs. SIRT vs. TV) to test metric/operator dependence.

Quantitative success criteria
- ≥30% median reduction in GI across cellular regions; no increase in Eforb within ice (specificity).
- ≥0.02 improvement in 3D-FSC directional average at 1/20–1/10 Å⁻¹ for key complexes; narrower anisotropy cones.
- ≥10% improvement in STA classification consistency (cluster assignment stability across bootstraps) vs. wedge-masked-difference baselines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2556382/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is biologically and methodologically sound
- The specimen is static across tilts; disagreements are due to imaging physics, sampling, or alignment—precisely what MW-AF optimizes. Forbidden k-space contains no measurable specimen information by construction; structured energy there is algorithmic leakage, which GI quantifies and suppresses. The ice region provides an internal, contemporaneous noise baseline, analogous to solvent practices in SPA but adapted to tomograms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3991334/?utm_source=openai))

Positioning vs. prior art
- Wedge-masked differences are used for STA classification, not map-level QC or per-tilt refinement. 3D-FSC anisotropy quantifies averages, not raw tomograms, and requires half-sets. CTF/geometry refinement exists but is not driven by a wedge-informed penalty. MW-AF integrates these gaps into a single, geometry-anchored objective. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2556382/?utm_source=openai))

Potential risks and mitigations
- Risk: Window leakage or mask misestimation can inflate GI. Mitigation: apply spectral tapers; learn per-dataset tapers from ice power spectra; validate against simulated phantoms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7642792/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Over-penalizing high-frequency content near wedge boundaries. Mitigation: normalize GI by the predicted resolution kernel (convolution of S(k) with CTF/dose), ensuring penalties scale with local identifiability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8279804/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Compute cost. Mitigation: patchwise evaluation with mixed precision; cache FFT plans; early stopping when GI plateaus.

Milestones
- M1 (3 months): Build GI and C metrics; release test dataset and CLI; demonstrate GI specificity on ice vs. cell volumes.
- M2 (6 months): Implement MW-AF; show error-recovery on simulations; ablation vs. entropy autofocus.
- M3 (9 months): Benchmark on EMPIAR sets; report 3D-FSC anisotropy and STA classification stability improvements; preprint and open-source release.
- M4 (12 months): Community plugin integration (AreTomo/IMOD hooks); reproducibility protocol and QC dashboards.

Deliverables
- Open-source MW-AF toolkit (Python/CUDA) with CPU mode.
- Public benchmark datasets, scripts, and QC dashboards.
- Protocol describing GI computation, thresholds for gatekeeping tomograms, and integration points with current pipelines.

Anticipated impact
- Provides a tomography-native, reference-free validation metric and a refinement routine that convert the missing wedge from a liability into a self-check and correction signal, reducing overfitting and improving reproducibility of in situ reconstructions without requiring independent half-sets or large compute budgets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2556382/?utm_source=openai))

Title: Design-for-identifiability planning and validation for in situ cryo‑ET via Fisher‑information mapping and tomographic resolution kernels

Premise and need
- In situ cryo‑ET suffers from the missing wedge, dose-limited per‑image SNR, and anisotropic sampling; current acquisition choices (tilt scheme, dose schedule, lamella orientation/thickness) are often made heuristically, leading to irrecoverable information loss and irreproducible outcomes. These limits and their dose dependence are well documented, but are not yet translated into a principled pre‑acquisition design tool or a tomography‑native, anisotropy‑aware validation framework. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
- Optimize cryo‑ET experiments by maximizing biologically weighted, spatially and direction‑resolved Fisher information under fixed dose/time, and by predicting the resulting local, orientation‑dependent resolution kernels before data collection. Then validate only where independent information exists, using noise‑decorrelated agreement between interleaved tilt partitions. This replaces global, isotropic assumptions (e.g., SPA-style FSC) with tomography‑native, local identifiability and independence tests. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3379812/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis-as-question
- If we allocate tilts, per‑tilt dose, and lamella orientation to maximize a specimen‑specific, biologically weighted Fisher‑information functional and to minimize anisotropy of the predicted model‑resolution kernels, will targeted cellular features (defined by their orientation and length scales) become reliably resolvable and reproducible at the same total dose and throughput? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build a fast, specimen‑aware Fisher‑information simulator for cryo‑ET.
- Forward model: linearized image formation per tilt with CTF, dose‑dependent envelope, thickness‑dependent noise (Poisson + additive readout), and lamella tilt/thickness geometry; produce I(x, û, k) and its orientation‑marginals I(x, û) over the region of interest (ROI). The Fisher framework is standard for microscope parameter estimation but has not been operationalized as spatial, direction‑resolved “maps” for cryo‑ET planning. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3379812/?utm_source=openai))
- Biological weighting: encode expected feature orientations/scales (e.g., membrane normals, filament tangents) as wfeature(û, k) from prior biology or low‑mag scouting; compute Jinfo = ∫ROI∫ wfeature·I d û d x to score a candidate plan. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))
- Outputs: voxel‑wise directional ceilings, predicted SNR gain per orientation, and sensitivity to wedge orientation at fixed dose/tilt count; report whether planned data can, in principle, resolve the targeted features. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Predict tomographic model‑resolution kernels and posterior uncertainty for candidate plans.
- Compute the local point‑spread/averaging kernels R(x → x′) and approximate posterior covariance Σ using the chosen reconstruction operator (e.g., WBP/SIRT/NovaCTF‑corrected LS), quantifying spatial/axis‑specific resolving power and voxel‑to‑voxel coupling that arise from the missing wedge and anisotropic coverage. Use efficient approximations from geophysical tomography (e.g., Gaussian target‑kernel fits, randomized trace methods) to keep computation tractable. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/138/1/36/640459?utm_source=openai))
- Planning metric: penalize kernel elongation aligned with feature orientations. Optimize angles, starting tilt, and per‑tilt dose to jointly maximize J = Jinfo − λ·Janiso, where Janiso summarizes kernel anisotropy along biology‑relevant axes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Tomography‑native, independence‑aware validation after acquisition.
- Noise‑decorrelated cross‑validation: split tilts into interleaved partitions; reconstruct two volumes; estimate structured‑artifact covariance (missing‑wedge harmonics, lamella‑thickness gradients, alignment warps) from empty‑ice regions and alignment residuals; apply a whitening/projection operator W to both partitions; measure agreement only in orientation–frequency bands that (i) are predicted informative by Aim 1 and (ii) remain independent across partitions by Σ from Aim 2. This prevents shared artifacts from inflating agreement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3150390/?utm_source=openai))
- Reportables: orientation‑resolved agreement maps, local uncertainty from Σ, and repeated‑motif reproducibility across tomograms as an external test. Avoid isotropic, SPA‑style FSC assumptions known to break under anisotropic sampling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8411978/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan and milestones

M1. Ground‑truthable phantoms and cellular testbeds
- Phantoms: membranes + filaments with controlled orientation distributions; synthetic tilt series with realistic CTF/dose/thickness.
- Biological targets: ER sheets with bound ribosomes; microtubules + MIPs in cell lamellae; dual‑axis and dose‑symmetric baselines for comparison. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

M2. Planning optimization under realistic constraints
- Decision variables: tilt list (bounds ±60–70°), order, start angle, per‑tilt dose schedule, lamella pre‑tilt/orientation; constraints: total dose, time, stage slew overheads, lamella thickness distribution from cryo‑FIB. Optimize J via gradient‑free search with analytic Fisher gradients where available. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

M3. Acquisition and validation
- Collect data under baseline (dose‑symmetric) and Fisher‑optimized plans on identical samples/lamellae. Apply NovaCTF or equivalent for 3D‑CTF correction, then run interleaved‑tilt reconstructions, W‑decorrelation, and orientation‑resolved agreement. Evaluate subtomogram averaging with wedge‑aware scoring as secondary readout. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28743638/?utm_source=openai))

M4. Metrics of success
- Pre‑registered endpoints by feature type:
  - Membranes: improvement in resolvable membrane normal frequency band and reduced kernel elongation along beam axis at fixed dose/time.
  - Filaments: increased angular power in tangential directions and higher correct‑detection rate in template matching at equal FPR.
  - Repeated motifs: higher cross‑tomogram reproducibility after W‑decorrelation without FSC inflation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3150390/?utm_source=openai))
- Throughput/access: wall‑clock planning ≤ minutes on a single GPU/CPU; standardized “planning report” artifact to store with datasets.

Methods highlights (implementation)
- Fisher maps: closed‑form per‑tilt Fisher blocks with CTF/dose weighting; voxel‑wise aggregation across tilts to yield I(x, û, k) and its marginals.
- Resolution kernels: target‑kernel Backus–Gilbert fits and local Gaussianization for R; diagonals/off‑diagonals of Σ via Hutchinson trace/probing.
- Decorrelation operator W: estimate structured noise covariance from empty‑ice/feature‑free ROIs and alignment residual fields; compute whitening/projection; combine with local noise power normalization before agreement scoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3150390/?utm_source=openai))

Risk, falsification, and contingency
- Risk: prior on feature orientations is wrong. Falsify by comparing predicted informative directions with measured orientation‑resolved agreement; if mismatched, re‑optimize plan or revert to unbiased angular schedules. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Fisher/noise models are misspecified. Falsify using tilt‑pair precision and residual statistics; expand noise model if residuals remain structured. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4136738/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: computational burden. Mitigate with multi‑resolution grids and precomputed per‑tilt operators; adopt geophysical approximations for R, Σ. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/226/3/2158/6247624?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and impact
- A principled simulator that predicts, before acquisition, whether planned settings can resolve biology‑relevant orientations at the allowed dose; and a validation protocol that credits only genuinely independent, informative content rather than shared artifacts. This addresses known limits from missing wedge/dose and avoids isotropic SPA metrics unsuited to tomography. By standardizing planning/QA outputs and relying on linear‑operator computations, the approach lowers resource barriers and improves reproducibility across labs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6103461/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- Open‑source planning/validation software with:
  - Fisher‑information and predicted‑resolution maps exportable to standard viewers.
  - Optimization of tilt list, dose schedule, and lamella orientation under user constraints.
  - Tomography‑native, orientation‑resolved validation from interleaved tilts with W‑decorrelation.
- Benchmark datasets and registered protocols comparing baseline versus Fisher‑optimized acquisitions on shared cellular targets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7018747/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Answer-Key Cells: Reversible in situ occlusion to benchmark cryo-ET state discriminability under real acquisition and analysis limits

Hypothesis–Question
Can in situ cryo-ET be made reproducibly testable and democratized by reframing validation from absolute resolution estimation to binary state discriminability, using engineered cells that reversibly occlude or expose a chosen macromolecular target just before vitrification?

Atomic strategy
Embed a reversible, light-tunable condensate “barrier” that transiently assembles around a tagged endogenous target to sterically occlude its interaction surfaces (barrier-on) and then fully dissolves to expose them (barrier-off). Use the barrier state as the intrinsic answer key for tomography-native, wedge-aware discriminability metrics acquired under unchanged cellular, preparation, and imaging conditions. This leverages established, reversible optogenetic clustering/condensate systems (e.g., LARIAT, optoDroplets/Corelets) but repurposes them as a physical visibility switch for tomographic validation rather than for functional perturbation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.2940?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims and work plan

Aim 1. Engineer a reversible “occlusion cloak” around an endogenous target
- Design: Build a two-module system in a human cell line with an endogenously GFP-tagged target (CRISPR knock-in where available). Module A: CRY2–VHH(GFP) to bind the target via a high-affinity GFP nanobody. Module B: a multivalent scaffold that nucleates a low-permeability condensate upon blue light, e.g., CIB1 fused to a multimeric core (ferritin or designed multimer) and an IDR (FUSN/HNRNPA1-IDR) to form an occluding shell. In blue light (barrier-on), CRY2–CIB1 heterodimerization and multivalency drive local clustering/LLPS around the target; in the dark (barrier-off), clusters dissolve. Toggle kinetics and penetrance are tunable by light dose and expression, and fully reversible on minute timescales. As a lower-phototoxicity option, test a red-light variant (R-LARIAT). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.2940?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: (i) VHH(GFP) alone; (ii) CRY2–VHH(GFP) with scaffold lacking IDR (tests steric occlusion vs mere clustering); (iii) cytosolic Corelet/optoDroplet without VHH to quantify nonspecific backgrounds. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28041848/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts before vitrification: live-cell fluorescence to confirm local condensate assembly/dissolution at the chosen locus; time-course quantification of assembly half-times and recovery to ensure practical toggling within vitrification windows. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28041848/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Vitrify matched “on/off” states and acquire state-labeled cryo-ET datasets
- Protocol: Plate replicate grids; set barrier-on with a brief light pulse; set barrier-off on paired grids kept in dark. Freeze within 1–5 minutes to minimize state drift. Use cryo-FM to verify presence/absence of the fluorescent condensate per cell/ROI and to log ground-truth state for downstream correlation. Modern cryo-fluorescence platforms and several fluorescent proteins, including Dronpa and EGFP variants, have been imaged at cryogenic temperatures, although photoswitching is reduced; here fluorescence is used only for localization, not post-freeze switching. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8877847/?utm_source=openai))
- Acquisition: Prepare multiple lamellae per condition with randomized grid positions to break tomogram-level correlations. Record identical tilt-series parameters across states to keep the missing wedge, dose, and SNR matched. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8877847/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Define tomography-native, wedge-aware validation metrics based on state discriminability
- Primary metric: State Discrimination Index (SDI) = AUC for classifying local neighborhoods around the tagged target as barrier-on versus barrier-off using wedge-aware features (e.g., template-free local density descriptors, anisotropy-corrected steerable filters, or shallow CNNs trained with wedge simulation). Compute SDI per lamella with held-out lamellae to avoid half-set leakage.
- Secondary metrics: (i) Orientation Sensitivity Curve: SDI as a function of target orientation relative to the missing wedge; (ii) Dose Robustness Curve: SDI versus accumulated dose; (iii) Cross-site Reproducibility: SDI across microscopes and labs using the same cell line and protocol. These directly test analysis pipelines under physical information ceilings without invoking SPA-style FSC assumptions.

Aim 4. Demonstrate generality across targets and alternative occlusion chemistries
- Orthogonal “rigid shell” variant: Express a bacterial encapsulin nanocompartment targeted adjacent to the protein of interest to create a rigid, high-contrast occlusion volume near the site; use pore engineering to tune permeability. This provides a mesoscale occluder with distinct density for segmentation stress-testing; although assembly is not rapidly reversible, it offers a fixed “hard-negative” benchmark complementary to the reversible condensate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5959871/?utm_source=openai))
- Alternative reversible sequestration: Evaluate RELISR-like dark-assembled/light-dissolved systems or small-molecule–releasable condensates to show that SDI-based benchmarking is actuation-agnostic and robust to different biophysical occluders. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12234719/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory module (optional). Programmable quaternary-geometry switch using pdDronpa
- Rationale: Provide a second, orthogonal binary change—monomeric versus defined oligomeric geometry—without changing the core fold. Fuse a photodissociable Dronpa dimer to selected termini to cage/uncage a designed dimerization geometry before freezing; use cryo-FM for localization only. This tests subtomogram classification on a known geometric rearrangement under identical acquisition. Switching is set pre-freeze (cyan to dissociate, violet to associate) and is well established in cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5589340/?utm_source=openai))

Analysis plan
- Predefine regions of interest by cryo-FM; extract local subvolumes around targets; blind the analysis team to state labels; run multiple standard pipelines (reconstruction, denoising, segmentation, particle picking, subtomogram averaging/classification); compute SDI and secondary curves per pipeline and per site. Release a small, standardized benchmark dataset and containerized evaluation scripts to minimize compute barriers for smaller labs.

Milestones and deliverables
- Month 0–6: Build and validate occlusion cloak constructs; characterize reversible assembly/dissolution kinetics; select 1–2 targets with robust condensate formation.
- Month 6–12: Produce barrier-on/off lamellae; acquire matched cryo-ET datasets; implement SDI and orientation-sensitivity analyses; publish v1 benchmark set and code.
- Month 12–18: Cross-lab reproducibility study; add encapsulin “hard-negative” and pdDronpa “geometry-switch” variants; release expanded benchmarks and SOPs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5959871/?utm_source=openai))

Why this fulfills the goal under stated constraints
- It respects the information ceiling from the missing wedge and dose: the metric is discriminability between two known in situ states, not absolute resolution. It avoids half-set leakage by using lamella-level holds and randomized state assignment. It supplies a tomography-native validation framework grounded in realistic anisotropy and SNR. It reduces adoption barriers by providing turnkey cell lines, light-pulse protocols, compact labeled datasets, and containerized metrics—so small labs can benchmark pipelines without large storage/GPU budgets. And it is built on reversible, biologically proven modules for in-cell sequestration/condensation and for programmable oligomerization, repurposed as an answer key for cryo-ET rather than as conventional actuators. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.2940?utm_source=openai))

Risk–mitigation
- If LLPS occlusion is too permeable or morphologically heterogeneous for a given locus, increase scaffold valency or switch to Corelet-like ferritin cores to amplify local client concentration; if phototoxicity or off-target clustering is problematic, use red-light LARIAT or chemically switchable condensates. If reversible actuation is undesirable for a specific benchmark, deploy encapsulin-based rigid occluders as fixed-state controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12254321/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- A blinded pipeline achieves SDI ≥0.85 on held-out lamellae for barrier-on/off discrimination, with orientation-sensitivity curves that reveal predictable performance degradation along the missing-wedge axis and reproducible values across independent labs and microscopes. All plasmids and cell lines are deposited for community use; datasets and SDI code are released under permissive licenses.

Title
Wedge-aware reference atlas with physics-calibrated validation for democratized in situ cryo-ET

Rationale
Limited tilt range and low-dose imaging impose a hard information ceiling in cryo-ET, producing a missing wedge and anisotropic transfer that bias detection and reconstruction. Existing template-matching workflows already model wedge and CTF effects during scoring, but lack a standardized, dataset-specific calibration and a tomography-native validation metric usable across laboratories with modest compute. An external frequency ruler with discrete, strong Fourier peaks and an endogenous periodic standard with conserved layer lines can together define and verify the per-dataset imaging operator, enabling a recoverability-adjusted identification of cellular structures with pre-degraded templates from a shared atlas. STOPGAP and related packages demonstrate feasibility of forward models for template matching; we operationalize this as a calibrated, standardized library and metric to lower barriers and raise reproducibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8133831/?utm_source=openai))

Question-as-Hypothesis
Can co-vitrified bacteriorhodopsin (bR) 2D crystals and endogenous F-actin filaments together define a per-tilt, per-dataset imaging operator that, when used to forward-degrade a shared template atlas and to validate only the features predicted to survive, yields reproducible, low-compute, in situ structure identification across labs and microscopes?

Atomic strategy
Constrain inference to what physics says is visible. Estimate the dataset-specific imaging operator from an external crystalline calibrant (bR) and verify/adjust it locally using actin layer-line amplitudes; then match only the forward-degraded features predicted to survive, and validate matches with a recoverability-adjusted score.

Specific aims
1) Build an external, per-dataset calibrant using bR 2D crystals.
2) Construct a wedge-aware reference atlas with forward-degraded templates and a recoverability-adjusted validation metric.
3) Implement endogenous, local verification and correction using F‑actin layer lines.

Aim 1. External calibration with bacteriorhodopsin 2D crystals
- Protocol
  - Prepare purple membrane fragments (standard protocols) and spike into fiducial gold solution used for tilt-series; seed sparsely so bR patches lie on the same grid squares as cells but outside cellular regions of interest. Acquire tilt-series encompassing at least one bR patch per lamella or per grid square. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2020.547818/full?utm_source=openai))
- Operator estimation
  - From the bR patch subtomogram, fit lattice parameters and extract lattice-rod amplitudes across tilts. Use their attenuation versus tilt/defocus/thickness to jointly fit the 3D-CTF, dose filter, and anisotropic envelope, and to refine tilt-axis/eucentricity. bR crystals provide discrete, high-SNR peaks suitable for robust fitting. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3172228/?utm_source=openai))
- Deliverable
  - A calibrated per-tilt imaging operator (Ôdataset) with confidence intervals, exportable as JSON.

Aim 2. Wedge-aware atlas and recoverability-adjusted validation
- Reference atlas
  - Curate volumetric templates of common cellular assemblies (e.g., ribosomes, proteasomes, microtubule segments) from public models/maps. For each dataset, forward-degrade each template by applying Ôdataset: per-tilt CTF, dose-weighting, inelastic attenuation, lamella-thickness envelope, and the measured wedge; store degraded volumes and their predicted invariant manifolds (e.g., layer lines, lattice rods, symmetry-constrained harmonics).
  - Precompute across a discretized grid of typical operators to enable reuse and reduce on-the-fly GPU time in small labs. Existing TM frameworks (e.g., STOPGAP) already incorporate wedge+3D‑CTF in scoring; here we shift the burden to a standardized, sharable bank of degraded templates and define explicit predicted-visible feature sets for validation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10769363/?utm_source=openai))
- Matching and validation
  - Perform GPU-accelerated template matching with the forward-degraded templates; compute a Recoverability-Adjusted Template Agreement (RATA) score defined as the ratio of observed-to-predicted energy within the template’s invariant manifolds that remain after degradation, penalized for energy in forbidden regions (e.g., in the gap of the wedge or outside expected Bessel orders).
  - Report matches only if RATA exceeds a per-dataset threshold learned on the bR patch (where ground-truth visible peaks are known).
  - Implement a low-memory mode using FFT tiling and precomputed filters. Recent GPU TM demonstrations show feasibility and speed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11088655/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Endogenous, local verification with F-actin
- Detection and measurement
  - Detect actin segments via coarse helical filters; compute layer-line profiles and quantify amplitudes at conserved orders (e.g., 1/5.9–6.1 nm and neighbors), which are measurable in tomograms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7480112/?utm_source=openai))
- Local operator correction
  - Compare observed layer-line amplitudes against those predicted by Ôdataset for the measured local orientation; adjust local anisotropy terms to produce Ôlocal where deviations are systematic (e.g., due to thickness gradients).
  - Use actin polarity pipelines to further check internal consistency and reject regions with implausible filament geometry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8111420/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-validation
  - Require that high-confidence template matches in nearby volumes co-occur with actin-derived Ôlocal consistent with Ôdataset; flag discrepancies for operator re-estimation or data rejection.

Milestones and methods
- M1. bR-on-grid feasibility and operator fit (Months 0–6)
  - Benchmark on empty-grid and cell-on-grid datasets; show that bR-based operator explains anisotropic attenuation and improves tilt-axis refinement, quantified by sharper bR peaks after reconstruction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3172228/?utm_source=openai))
- M2. Atlas and RATA metric (Months 4–12)
  - Release initial atlas and degraded banks for common tilt schemes/defocus ranges. Validate that RATA correlates with true-positive rate in simulated and experimental ribosome/microtubule TM, and reduces false positives relative to correlation-only thresholds, controlling for wedge bias. Existing reviews document that wedge bias affects cross-correlation; RATA addresses this by restricting to physics-predicted visible features. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8133831/?utm_source=openai))
- M3. Endogenous verification (Months 8–16)
  - Demonstrate that actin-based local corrections increase RATA and detection precision in cytoplasm-rich regions and maintain correct filament layer-line spacings, matching prior in situ measurements. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7480112/?utm_source=openai))
- M4. Multi-site reproducibility and low-compute deployment (Months 12–24)
  - Containerize pipeline; run on mid-range GPUs; show cross-lab reproducibility of RATA thresholds and match lists on shared datasets.

Data, metrics, and success criteria
- Operator fidelity: variance explained in bR lattice-rod amplitudes across tilts; target >80% variance explained.
- Detection performance: at fixed 1% FDR (estimated by spatial bootstrapping and negative controls), RATA-based TM achieves ≥25% higher precision than wedge/CTF-only correlation. STOPGAP-compatible scoring will be run as baseline. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10769363/?utm_source=openai))
- Local consistency: actin-derived Ôlocal improves RATA for nearby targets by ≥10% without inflating FDR; actin layer-line spacings remain within expected bounds seen in tomograms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7480112/?utm_source=openai))
- Accessibility: end-to-end on a 24 GB GPU with ≤16 GB RAM; processing time per tomogram ≤2 hours with pre-degraded banks; atlas and code openly released.

Risk mitigation
- bR interference with cellular imaging: seed bR at low density and outside cellular ROIs; restrict to calibration FOVs; if absent in a lamella, borrow Ôdataset from a same-grid calibration area and verify with actin Ôlocal.
- Actin-poor samples: fall back to other endogenous periodic polymers (e.g., microtubules) in future extensions; initial release focuses on actin-rich cells.
- Overfitting to references: require independent biological plausibility checks (stoichiometry, compartment localization) and penalize energy in forbidden Fourier regions in RATA.

Expected impact
- Physics-calibrated, wedge-aware atlas and a recoverability-adjusted validation metric that align inference with the information ceiling, reduce compute via pre-degraded templates, and standardize reporting across labs. By pairing an external crystalline calibrant (bR) with an endogenous periodic standard (actin), the approach converts wedge-limited tomograms into testable predictions of what should be visible and certifies detections against those predictions. This satisfies the need for a tomography-native validation framework and lowers entry barriers for reliable in situ structure determination. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8133831/?utm_source=openai))

Resources to leverage and related work (for context)
- Wedge/CTF-aware template matching and 3D‑CTF correction exist in open-source tools (STOPGAP, novaCTF), supporting feasibility of forward modeling and GPU acceleration that our atlas will standardize and simplify for small labs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10769363/?utm_source=openai))
- bR 2D crystals provide strong, discrete Fourier peaks long used as imaging standards, here repurposed as a tomographic calibrant. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3172228/?utm_source=openai))
- Actin layer lines are measurable in cryo-ET and can serve as endogenous checks on local operator validity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7480112/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- Open protocols for co-vitrifying bR calibrants with cells.
- Open-source code for operator estimation, forward degradation, TM with RATA, and actin-based local verification; containerized distribution.
- A public wedge-aware reference atlas and degraded-template banks for common acquisition regimes.
- Benchmark datasets and multi-site reproducibility report.
