text:
Title
Catalytically clamping the implant–brain redox state in the first 72 hours using a covalently anchored organoselenium (GPx‑mimetic) polymer brush

Background and gap
- Intracortical implants trigger an immediate oxidative burst (superoxide, H2O2, lipid hydroperoxides) from microglia/macrophages with complement activation and BBB leakage. This acute chemistry seeds glial scarring over days to weeks and degrades electrode materials, elevating impedance and reducing signal quality. Quieting this chemistry in the early hours–days improves chronic outcomes. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fbioe.2018.00009/full?utm_source=openai))
- Conducting polymer coatings (e.g., PEDOT variants) improve initial electrochemistry but suffer oxidative/overoxidative degradation and delamination in vivo, linking interfacial ROS to long‑term loss of function. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1369702121004533?utm_source=openai))
- Antioxidant electrode coatings that mimic SOD or use Mn porphyrins reduce oxidative stress and improve histology/recordings, but they convert superoxide into H2O2; without efficient local peroxide and lipid hydroperoxide removal, peroxidative signaling persists. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6851492/?utm_source=openai))
- Immobilized organoselenium catalysts (GPx‑like) on medical polymers catalytically convert endogenous substrates at interfaces (classically RSNO→NO on blood‑contacting devices), demonstrating long‑term catalytic surface chemistry. However, peroxide‑reducing, organoselenium GPx‑mimetic polymer brushes have not been reported for neural electrodes to target the acute implantation window. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2824255/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question
If a thin, covalently anchored organoselenium polymer brush located at the electrode–tissue boundary catalytically reduces H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides during the first 72 hours post‑implantation—sustained by prepositioned thiol cofactors—will this “redox clamp” durably prevent the pro‑inflammatory program that degrades neural signal quality over months?

Atomic strategy
Create a regenerative, GPx‑mimetic catalytic layer directly at the interface to intercept peroxides and lipid hydroperoxides faster than they can oxidize adsorbed proteins/ECM, thereby aborting NF‑κB/inflammasome priming and stabilizing the interface. The layer’s catalytic cycle is maintained by embedded, immobile thiol/reductant motifs that re‑reduce oxidized selenium intermediates under transiently low extracellular GSH.

Specific aims
1) Synthesize and anchor a GPx‑mimetic organoselenium polymer brush on neural electrode materials with built‑in redox cofactor motifs.
2) Quantify interfacial peroxide/lipid hydroperoxide kinetics and electro‑optical compatibility under injury‑mimetic conditions.
3) Test whether acute redox clamping rescues chronic electrophysiology and reduces gliosis in vivo, including under optogenetic illumination.

Aim 1: Materials design and surface engineering
- Substrate: Pt/Ir, Au, or PEDOT‑modified microelectrodes on Si/SiC or parylene. Grow a 10–50 nm brush by SI‑RDRP (e.g., RAFT/ATRP) from robust primers (avoid siloxane linkers; use diazonium/carbon, Ti–O–P, or Au–S anchoring as appropriate). Crosslink the brush in situ for long‑term stability and minimal swelling. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2022/tb/d1tb02605d?utm_source=openai))
- Catalytic motif: Copolymerize side chains bearing selenide/selenoester groups (GPx‑mimetic) at defined densities. Introduce pendant disulfide/thiol co‑monomers (immobile reductants) at low fraction to re‑reduce selenenic/seleninic intermediates and maintain turnover with micromolar extracellular thiols. GPx‑mimetic organoselenium catalysis and thiol‑driven cycles are established in solution and in immobilized systems. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2015/ob/c5ob01665g?utm_source=openai))
- Anti‑leaching verification: ICP‑MS for selenium in soak solutions; accelerated aging in oxygenated PBS at 37–60°C; adhesion by scratch/tape testing and nanoindentation. Ensure electrical access via nanopatterned windows if needed.

Aim 2: Interfacial catalysis and device compatibility
- Chemical performance:
  - Interfacial H2O2 clearance: amperometric H2O2 microelectrodes scanned within 5–50 μm of the coated surface in a flow cell delivering injury‑mimetic boluses (50–500 μM H2O2; 4‑HNE/lipid hydroperoxides); EPR/spin trapping for lipid radical suppression.
  - Turnover and durability: quantify apparent kcat, KM at physiologic pH/ionic strength and after 10^7 catalytic cycles; verify activity in thiol‑depleted media to demonstrate efficacy of embedded reductants.
- Electro‑optical performance:
  - EIS and CV to confirm minimal added series resistance and preserved charge storage/injection; accelerated electrochemical stress to probe overoxidation susceptibility relative to unmodified PEDOT/metal. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1369702121004533?utm_source=openai))
  - Optogenetic safety: in brain‑mimetic media, measure light‑induced H2O2 formation during blue‑light pulse trains and test whether the brush suppresses this increase without photothermal rise; establish that optical transmission at visible wavelengths is unchanged. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19275-x?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmarks to advance: ≥10× faster interfacial H2O2 clearance than bare/PEDOT controls; no detectable Se leaching; <10% impedance change at 1 kHz; unchanged optical output.

Aim 3: In vivo efficacy in cortex (rodent), acute‑to‑chronic bridge
- Acute redox readouts (6 h, 24 h, 72 h): dihydroethidium oxidation, 4‑HNE adducts, protein carbonyls, and complement C3 deposition within 0–100 μm of shank tracks; BBB integrity markers. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fbioe.2018.00009/full?utm_source=openai))
- Chronic tissue and recording (2, 8, 16 weeks): microglia/astrocyte density and process coverage, neuronal soma density vs. distance, and collagenous matrix markers; longitudinal impedance and unit yield/SNR on awake recordings. Compare to SOD‑mimetic coated and uncoated controls to test whether removing peroxides/lipid peroxides adds benefit beyond superoxide dismutation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6851492/?utm_source=openai))
- Optogenetic challenge (if optical sites present): blue‑light pulse trains within published safety envelopes; quantify lesion size and oxidative markers post‑stimulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4813666/?utm_source=openai))

Key design justifications and feasibility
- Biology‑first target: Peroxide and lipid hydroperoxide removal interrupts the feed‑forward peroxidation that primes NF‑κB/inflammasome and glial scarring. Prior SOD‑mimetic coatings improved outcomes but leave H2O2 to secondary pathways; a GPx‑mimetic brush directly addresses this gap. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6851492/?utm_source=openai))
- Surface‑tethered catalysis precedent: Organoselenium catalysts covalently immobilized on polymers sustain interfacial catalysis for months in blood‑contacting devices (NO generation from RSNOs), supporting the engineering plausibility of a durable catalytic selenium surface on implants. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2824255/?utm_source=openai))
- Stability under physiological stress: Crosslinked brushes with robust anchors resist hydrolysis/delamination long‑term; thin (10–50 nm) layers minimally perturb electrochemistry. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2022/tb/d1tb02605d?utm_source=openai))

Risk and mitigation
- Risk: Insufficient extracellular thiol to sustain Se catalysis in the first 24–48 h. Mitigation: embed a low fraction of immobile thiols/disulfides within the brush to locally recycle oxidized Se; confirm by activity retention in thiol‑depleted media. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2015/ob/c5ob01665g?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Unintended RSNO→NO catalysis alters local NO signaling. Mitigation: directly measure NO flux in brain tissue simulants; modulate Se microenvironment (pKa/electrophilicity) to bias peroxide reduction over RSNO catalysis; compare to established NO‑generating Se coatings as bounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4955746/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Added layer alters stimulation safety. Mitigation: characterize charge injection capacity and reversible potential limits; ensure no increase in overoxidation versus controls. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1369702121004533?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- Year 1: Synthesize brush, verify covalent anchoring, leach‑free selenium, and catalytic activity (kcat, KM) with embedded thiols; EIS within 10% of baseline.
- Year 2: Demonstrate ≥10× faster H2O2/lipid‑OOH clearance at the interface and suppression of light‑generated H2O2 in vitro; 8‑week soak/electrochemical stress without delamination.
- Year 3: In vivo, achieve ≥30% higher neuronal unit yield and ≥20% lower impedance vs. controls at 8–16 weeks, with reduced oxidative and glial markers in the peri‑implant zone; under matched optogenetic protocols, reduce phototoxic lesioning by ≥30% at threshold doses. ([advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/adhm.202503893?utm_source=openai))

Translatability and manufacturing
- Processes (SI‑RDRP, crosslinking) are wafer‑compatible and applicable to metals, oxides, and conductive polymers; organoselenium content is covalently bound and below systemic exposure thresholds (confirmed by leach testing). Ethylene oxide sterilization is compatible with polymer‑coated neural arrays. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41682391/?utm_source=openai))

Comparators and controls
- Uncoated, PEDOT‑only, and SOD‑mimetic (e.g., iSODm or MnTBAP) coatings provide direct tests of the peroxide‑focused mechanism’s added value. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6851492/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcome
A redox‑clamped interface that prevents the injury‑chemistry “teaching signal,” yielding multi‑month stability of impedance and unit yield, and expanded safety margins for optical stimulation by suppressing light‑amplified peroxides—all via a thin, non‑swelling, covalently anchored catalytic layer compatible with existing electrode materials. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391891/?utm_source=openai))

Optional extension (contingency if catalytic turnover is insufficient)
Integrate a 50–200 nm, covalently crosslinked PPS underlayer beneath the Se brush as a stoichiometric ROS sink and cofactor reservoir to front‑load hours‑to‑days scavenging without particulate shedding; PPS anchoring to noble/oxide surfaces is established, and PPS microspheres have validated ROS‑sponge efficacy in injury models. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nmat851?utm_source=openai))

label: debate_bypass
text:
Title
Activity-gated sol–gel microreactors that convert local glucose to L-lactate at the implant–tissue interface to stabilize neurometabolism and blunt the foreign body response

Unsplit hypothesis–question
Can a monolithic, non-swelling silica sol–gel microreactor, patterned on neural implants and tuned to convert a fraction of interstitial glucose to L-lactate in proportion to local activity, maintain peri-implant energy sufficiency and thereby reduce glial encapsulation and preserve recording/optical performance over months? The premise is that neurons can readily use extracellular lactate and that glial inflammatory programs are modulated by lactate signaling; chronic implants fail in part via ischemia/BBB disruption, microglial/astrocytic activation, and vascular injury. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrn.2018.19?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Turn the implant from a passive foreign body into a demand-coupled metabolic neighbor: a thin, covalently anchored silica sol–gel layer that encloses an immobilized, NAD(H)-balanced glucose→lactate enzymatic cascade and K+-responsive pore gates. Net effect: glucose in, lactate out, with internal redox cycling and protein-impermeant pores. When extracellular K+ rises during local activity, pore gating modestly increases flux to match demand. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6190511/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Engineer and validate a silica sol–gel enzyme microreactor (SG-EMR) that is protein-excluding, metabolite-permeable, and redox self-contained.
  - Rationale: Silica sol–gel films can stably entrap dehydrogenases/cofactors; mesopores ~2–5 nm pass small solutes (glucose, lactate) but exclude serum proteins (e.g., BSA, IgG). Durable cofactor anchoring avoids leaching. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0956566301002871?utm_source=openai))
  - Build: Pattern a 5–20 μm-thick silica sol–gel ring around each recording/stimulation site (leaving electrode face and optical window bare). Entrap a minimized glucose→pyruvate→lactate cascade (cell-free enzymatic set per prior work) plus LDH for NAD(H) recycling; tether a small NAD+/NADH pool to the matrix. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6190511/?utm_source=openai))
  - Gate: Functionalize pore mouths with 18‑crown‑6 motifs to yield K+-responsive transport; target a 1.5–3× flux increase from 3 to 10–12 mM [K+]o. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6368432/?utm_source=openai))
  - Metrics: (i) IgG/BSA rejection with fluorescent tracers; (ii) steady-state lactate flux at 1–2 mM glucose; (iii) redox mass balance (no net NAD(H) leak) under continuous flow; (iv) K+-dependent flux modulation.

- Aim 2. Test whether peri-implant lactate support reduces glial activation and preserves unit yield in vivo.
  - Model: Mouse motor cortex, 16‑site shanks with three arms: SG-EMR (active), inert silica sol–gel (no enzymes), and uncoated control.
  - Readouts (1–24 weeks): local extracellular glucose/lactate with enzyme microbiosensors; two-photon/confocal immunohistology (Iba1, GFAP, CSPGs, vascular markers); capillary patency; single‑unit yield, impedance. Expect reduced microglia/astrocyte encapsulation and higher chronic unit yield when lactate support is present. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165027005002931?utm_source=openai))
  - Mechanistic markers: HCAR1 pathway engagement (receptor localization; downstream cAMP/PI3K readouts) and microglial phagocytic tone. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23696276/?utm_source=openai))

- Aim 3. Evaluate optogenetic safety margins with and without SG-EMR.
  - Setup: Red-shifted opsin mice (e.g., ChrimsonR). Deliver defined fiber powers; map temperature rise (MR thermometry/thermocouples) and behavioral/physiologic thresholds.
  - Expectation: Equal optical protocols yield lower photothermal/phototoxic impact metrics with SG-EMR due to better-supported metabolism; quantify safe irradiance/time windows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5129112/?utm_source=openai))

Design and methods
- SG-EMR fabrication
  - Substrate silanization; TMOS/TEOS sol–gel with enzyme-friendly chemistries; co-entrap LDH plus a minimal glucose→lactate route (per cell‑free biosystem literature) achieving net glucose→2 lactate with internal NAD(H) cycling. NAD+ covalently linked via glycidoxypropylsilane; verify retained turnover after 10^8 substrate turnovers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6190511/?utm_source=openai))
  - Pore control: Surfactant-templated mesopores; target 2–5 nm; verify size cutoff by dye/protein panels (glucose/lactate diffuse; BSA/IgG blocked). ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsami.6b06765?utm_source=openai))
  - K+-gating: Immobilize amino‑benzo‑18‑crown‑6 near pore mouths; calibrate ionic transport versus [K+]o; ensure Na+ has minimal effect. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6368432/?utm_source=openai))
  - Fouling resistance: Hydrophilic silica plus thin zwitterionic brush overcoat except at pores to minimize protein adsorption without blocking metabolite flux. Benchmark against known hydrogel coatings that risk swelling/delamination. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038%2Fs43246-024-00541-0?utm_source=openai))

- Bench characterization
  - Continuous-flow microfluidics simulating interstitial conditions (37°C; glucose 1–2 mM; lactate baseline ~1 mM; [K+]o 3–12 mM steps). Quantify fluxes and redox mass balance; accelerated aging (80°C Arrhenius) for lifetime prediction.
  - Mechanical/thermal stability: Nanoindentation of silica layer; cyclic temperature exposure to optogenetic loads; impedance mapping of exposed electrodes (no shunting).

- In vivo studies (rodent)
  - Surgery and grouping as in Aim 2; weekly recordings up to 24 weeks; vascular imaging to assess microhemorrhage correlation with signal degradation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8975777/?utm_source=openai))
  - Microdialysis or enzyme-based biosensors to map peri-implant metabolites; immunohistology at endpoints.

- Scaling and translatability
  - Large-animal pilot (swine cortex) with cm‑scale arrays; evaluate mass-transport modeling and manufacturability (wafer‑level sol–gel; batch reproducibility). Reference prior use of silica coatings on neural microelectrodes to support compatibility. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165027009001071?utm_source=openai))

Key controls and failure modes
- Controls: Inert silica; enzyme-inactivated silica; SG-EMR without K+-gating; hydrogel-coated electrodes (benchmark swelling/delamination risks). ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038%2Fs43246-024-00541-0?utm_source=openai))
- Risks/mitigations
  - Enzyme decay: Use sol–gel stabilization protocols; refresh via patterned re‑deposition ex vivo between implantations in long-term studies. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0956566301002871?utm_source=openai))
  - Cofactor loss: Covalent/tethered NAD(H); monitor leachate; redesign linker density if needed. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0956566311007871?utm_source=openai))
  - Excess lactate/pH shifts: Tune enzyme loading and pore density; K+-gating to limit flux at rest; monitor pH, MCT expression, and HCAR1 engagement. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrn.2018.19?utm_source=openai))
  - Unintended ROS: Avoid oxidase chemistries; use dehydrogenase cascades; verify no H2O2 accumulation.

Outcomes and quantitative success criteria
- Materials performance: ≥90% BSA/IgG rejection with ≥70% glucose/lactate permeability relative to bare controls; stable NAD(H) pool with <5% loss over 30 days of continuous perfusion. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsami.6b06765?utm_source=openai))
- Activity coupling: ≥2× increase in lactate flux when [K+]o rises from 3→10 mM without Na+-driven changes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6368432/?utm_source=openai))
- Biology: At 12 and 24 weeks, SG-EMR arms show (i) ≥30% higher single‑unit yield, (ii) ≥25% lower Iba1+/GFAP+ sheath thickness, and (iii) preserved microvasculature versus controls. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165027005002931?utm_source=openai))
- Optogenetics: For equivalent fiber powers, ≥0.5–1.0°C lower peak ΔT or extended safe illumination duration before exceeding heating thresholds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5129112/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is plausibly novel and impactful
- Enzyme‑entrapped sol–gel layers are common in biosensing, including brain analyte electrodes, but not as chronic, demand‑coupled metabolic support at neural implants; prior neural coatings focus on hydrogels, drugs, or antifouling, which face swelling/delamination risks. K+-responsive crown‑ether gating adds passive, physiology‑linked control absent from existing neuroimplant coatings. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165027009001071?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables and timeline (24–30 months)
- Months 0–9: SG-EMR materials stack validated; pore cutoffs and K+-gating calibrated; redox balance confirmed.
- Months 6–18: Rodent implants; monthly electrophysiology and metabolite mapping.
- Months 18–24: Optogenetic safety window mapping; endpoint histology.
- Months 24–30: Large‑animal feasibility and manufacturing reproducibility.

Translational considerations
- Materials are inorganic, non-swelling, MRI‑compatible; wafer‑scale processes exist. Document chronic safety via absence of protein/fragment release and by histopathology. Position for integration with existing silicon/polyimide probes and optical ferrules. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165027009001071?utm_source=openai))

Title
Threshold-activated, autocatalytic DNA strand-displacement therapeutics for glioblastoma: converting GBM-specific RNA codes into amplified, localized myeloid reprogramming and tumoricidal effects

Central hypothesis and integrated research question
A minimal, composite RNA signature that is consistently enriched in glioblastoma (GBM) cells and tumor-associated myeloid cells—but rare in healthy brain—can be used as the only trigger for an autocatalytic DNA strand-displacement (TMSD) circuit that remains inert elsewhere. Once triggered, the circuit amplifies and releases dual oligonucleotide therapeutics that (i) reprogram immunosuppressive myeloid cells and (ii) disable GBM survival/state-maintenance hubs, thereby overcoming heterogeneity, plasticity, and immune evasion while minimizing neurotoxicity. Is such a thresholded, AND-gated, positive-feedback molecular therapy sufficient to control infiltrative GBM in vivo when delivered systemically with BBB-penetrant carriers and validated for brain selectivity? This leverages GBM’s conserved neuron–glioma activity coupling, myeloid-dominant TME, and BBB/BTB heterogeneity not as obstacles but as contextual filters for localized activation and retention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838971/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Translate GBM-intrinsic RNA context into therapy: use an autocatalytic TMSD circuit to implement AND/threshold logic on two to three GBM/TAM RNA cues; above-threshold binding initiates a self-amplifying hairpin cascade that unmasks and releases dual nucleic-acid effectors in situ. The positive feedback provides steep, local activation without global exposure, addressing microscopic invasion and BTB patchiness. Enzyme-free TMSD circuits have operated in living cells and in mice for nucleic-acid sensing; we will adapt them from diagnostics to therapy with strict anti-leak designs and reversible “antidote” shutdown. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35076991/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define a compact composite RNA trigger set and activation thresholds for GBM/TAM selectivity.
- Rationale: GBM growth depends on neuron–glioma synapses and hyperexcitability; the TME is myeloid-dominant with scarce functional T cells; BBB/BTB is heterogeneous. A trigger restricted to GBM cells and TAMs maximizes selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838971/?utm_source=openai))
- Approach:
  - Integrate single-cell GBM and peri-tumoral cortex datasets to nominate 6–8 candidate RNAs (e.g., miR-21, miR-10b, TK1 mRNA, STAT3 mRNA in TAMs, and low miR-128) and downselect to a 2–3 marker signature with highest tumor/brain contrast and cross-model stability; fit distributions to set circuit thresholds with <1% predicted activation in normal neurons/astrocytes/microglia.
  - Validate in human GBM organoids co-cultured with primary microglia; quantify trigger distributions and leakage risk at single-cell resolution.

Aim 2. Engineer a leakage-resistant autocatalytic TMSD therapeutic circuit implementing AND/threshold logic and dual outputs.
- Rationale: Autocatalytic CHA/HCR-like hairpin cascades and TMSD gates provide enzyme-free exponential amplification and logic in living systems; in vivo TMSD circuits have imaged miRNAs and assembled functional siRNAs. Therapeutic deployment in GBM remains unexplored, representing actionable novelty. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35076991/?utm_source=openai))
- Circuit design:
  - Inputs: two or three RNA triggers (Aim 1). Implement co-localized AND via split-input hairpins and threshold gates that sequester inputs until concentrations exceed preset values. Tune toehold/spacer lengths to set rate constants across four orders of magnitude. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8942360/?utm_source=openai))
  - Positive feedback: autocatalytic hairpins H1/H2 that generate Output A and Output B strands upon activation; include “double-negative” design where an endogenous brain-abundant RNA competitively inhibits activation in healthy cells.
  - Outputs:
    - Output A: antisense/siRNA against STAT3 to reprogram TAMs and reduce immunosuppressive signaling. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/13/17/4255?utm_source=openai))
    - Output B: antisense/siRNA against SOX2/OLIG2 network components to blunt GBM stem-like maintenance and plasticity.
  - Safety: 3′-end phosphorothioate/2′-O-methyl stabilization; multi-layer anti-leak (short toeholds, clamped hairpins, quenched endosomal escape domains released only by circuit activation); exogenous “antidote” strands to terminate amplification on demand.
- Packaging and delivery:
  - Formulate in receptor-mediated BBB carriers (e.g., TfR- or LRP1-targeted lipopolyplexes) sized 60–120 nm; characterize brain uptake and perivascular dispersion. BTB heterogeneity provides increased local exposure in tumor core, while the circuit enforces cellular specificity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34253912/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate efficacy, selectivity, and quality-of-life compatibility in orthotopic GBM models.
- Models: patient-derived GBM xenografts and syngeneic immune-competent glioma; include resection-cavity recurrence and diffusely infiltrative setups.
- Endpoints:
  - Molecular: on-target mRNA knockdown (STAT3, SOX2/OLIG2), TAM polarization shift, neuron–glioma synapse density reduction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838971/?utm_source=openai))
  - Spatial selectivity: activation maps via fluorescent reporter gates; off-target activation in cortex/hippocampus <1%.
  - Systems outcomes: tumor burden (MRI/bioluminescence), seizure frequency, survival, and neurobehavioral scores.
- Optional enhancement (exploratory): single-session, low-intensity, implanted or transcranial focused ultrasound to transiently augment BTB only at tumor regions to improve carrier penetration; clinical feasibility in GBM has been shown with implantable ultrasound devices. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38396134/?utm_source=openai))

Study design and methods

Trigger discovery and thresholding (Aim 1)
- Mine single-cell RNA/miRNA atlases for GBM versus normal brain to derive candidate triggers and decoy inhibitors; fit Gaussian mixture models to set AND thresholds that maximize Youden’s J while constraining false-positive rates in neurons/astrocytes/microglia.
- Validate RNA abundance and covariance in patient-derived GBM organoids with embedded human microglia; perform smFISH and qPCR to parameterize circuit inputs.

Circuit construction and in vitro characterization (Aim 2)
- Build hairpin libraries implementing AND logic with threshold gates; tune toehold lengths and mismatches to set kinetics; quantify leakage and amplification factors in cell-free conditions resembling cytosolic ionic strength.
- Test in GBM cell lines and primary neurons/astrocytes/microglia; measure activation only when composite triggers are delivered; verify antidote strand shutdown kinetics.
- Package circuits in TfR-targeted carriers; assess uptake, endosomal escape, cytosolic availability, and stability in human CSF and mouse serum.

In vivo delivery and efficacy (Aim 3)
- Dose-finding in orthotopic models for brain exposure and safety; whole-brain activation mapping using a reporter circuit variant.
- Therapeutic studies with dual-output circuits; measure TAM reprogramming (decreased ARG1/IL-10, increased phagocytic markers), GBM stemness reduction, synaptic input attenuation, seizure mitigation, tumor control, and survival.
- Neurotoxicity monitoring: EEG, motor/cognitive assays, histopathology for neuronal injury and gliosis.

Innovation
- First therapeutic application of a thresholded, autocatalytic TMSD circuit in GBM to convert endogenous RNA context into amplified, dual-pathway attack on both tumor cells and the dominant myeloid compartment. Prior in vivo uses of TMSD have focused on sensing and imaging rather than GBM therapy. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35076991/?utm_source=openai))
- The circuit’s amplification solves microfocus dosing and BTB patchiness without global BBB disruption; the AND/threshold and double-negative logic address heterogeneity and protect normal brain. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34253912/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and quantitative success criteria
- Leakage: <0.5% activation in healthy brain cell types at 10× therapeutic exposure (in vitro); <1% voxels active outside tumor on in vivo maps.
- Amplification: >50-fold signal gain from trigger to output per cell; >70% knockdown of STAT3 and SOX2/OLIG2 in target compartments.
- TME shift: ≥2× increase in phagocytic/myeloid activation markers; reduction in immunosuppressive cytokines.
- Efficacy: ≥50% median survival extension in orthotopic xenografts; seizure burden reduction ≥40% in models with network hyperexcitability.
- Safety: no significant deficits on rotarod/novel-object tasks; no EEG deterioration outside tumor regions.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Risk: RNA signature instability across patients. Mitigation: maintain modular gates; swap trigger strands per patient transcriptome; retain core AND architecture.
- Risk: circuit leakage. Mitigation: multi-layer threshold/decoy design; antidote strands for shutdown; restrict endosomal escape to activated state.
- Risk: delivery shortfalls. Mitigation: optimize TfR/LRP1 ligand density and size; exploratory localized ultrasound to enhance BTB where needed. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38396134/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline (36 months)
- Months 0–9: Trigger selection, circuit library construction, leakage minimization; in vitro validation.
- Months 10–18: Carrier optimization; brain delivery pharmacokinetics; in vivo activation mapping.
- Months 19–30: Therapeutic efficacy in xenografts and syngeneic models; dose and schedule optimization.
- Months 31–36: Safety profiling, neurobehavioral assessments; manufacturability and IND-enabling plans.

Ethical and safety considerations
- Nucleic-acid therapeutics with reversible “antidote” strands enable rapid cessation. EEG and behavior are continuously monitored to detect off-target neurophysiology changes. Humane endpoints are predefined.

Impact
A single, endogenous-code–driven therapeutic layer that self-amplifies only inside GBM/TAM contexts can overcome intratumoral heterogeneity, plasticity, immune evasion, and BTB patchiness without systemic toxicity. If validated, this would establish a new therapeutic modality for brain tumors based on programmable, threshold-activated molecular computation rather than receptor occupancy or cell therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838971/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Edge Rewriting: A peritumoral heparan-sulfate–mimetic “field shaper” that traps motogenic ligands and tethers BMP cues to enforce astrocytic fencing and GBM cell differentiation

Central hypothesis-as-question
Can we convert the GBM invasive rim from a motility- and stemness-permissive niche into a containment and maturation niche by rewriting the local heparan sulfate (HS) code—sequestering heparin/HS-binding motogens while stably presenting BMP cues—so that astrocytes build a STAT3-dependent border and GBM cells adopt non-migratory differentiated states? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773542/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Engineer a soft, surgically placed, sulfated HS-mimetic polymer ring that lines the resection cavity. Its charge pattern and binding sites are tuned to: (i) high-affinity capture of heparin/HS-binding motogens and chemokines (e.g., FGF2, HB‑EGF, HGF/SF, CXCL12) to collapse haptotactic and chemotactic cues that drive GBM edge migration; and (ii) stable tethering/presentation of BMP2/4 or BMP-mimetic peptides to bias GBM stem-like cells toward quiescence/differentiation and to reinforce astrocyte border formation via STAT3-coupled reactive astrogliosis. As gradients extinguish and matrix remodeling proceeds, inputs that activate invasion fall, passively winding down output—a built-in termination. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5111123/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define HS-mimetic sulfation patterns that optimally sequester GBM motogens and present BMP cues.
- Rationale: HSPG sulfation (N-, 2‑O-, 6‑O-) governs binding of FGF2, HGF, HB‑EGF, and CXCL12; BMP2/4 contain heparin/HS-binding sites enabling immobilized presentation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2021.778752/full?utm_source=openai))
- Approach: Synthesize a panel of HS-mimetic copolymers varying N-/O‑sulfation and aromatic sulfonate density. Quantify binding constants (SPR/ITC) for FGF2, HGF, HB‑EGF, CXCL12 and BMP4/BMP2 or BMP-mimetic peptides; assess ternary complexing with receptors on GBM cells. Select formulations that maximize motogen sequestration while enabling BMP presentation and SMAD1/5 activation in GBM stem-like cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5111123/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test whether polymer-mediated edge rewriting induces an astrocytic fence and GBM differentiation in ex vivo brain models.
- Rationale: Reactive astrocytes form STAT3-dependent border structures that corral inflammatory/fibrotic cells; HS/FGF/heparin signals and HS sulfation patterns modulate astrocyte boundary formation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23904622/?utm_source=openai))
- Approach: In organotypic murine and human cortical slices bearing GBM spheroids, place polymer strips at the tumor–parenchyma interface. Readouts: (i) astrocyte border density/orientation (GFAP/vimentin, STAT3 phosphorylation, CSPG/tenascin deposition); (ii) ligand field mapping (FGF2, CXCL12, HGF) by proximity ligation/immuno-FRET; (iii) GBM invasion metrics and single-cell state shifts (proliferation, motility, stemness markers; SMAD target induction). Compare BMP-tethered versus inert polymers and unsulfated controls. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32848612/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Evaluate safety, efficacy, and self-limiting dynamics of the polymer ring in resection-cavity GBM models.
- Rationale: Intracavitary implants bypass the BBB and can be applied at surgery; efficacy requires limiting edema and neurotoxicity while reducing edge recurrence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11964529/?utm_source=openai))
- Approach: In orthotopic GBM with subtotal resection, line the cavity with compliant HS-mimetic gel rings (storage modulus ~0.2–1 kPa). Endpoints: survival; MRI invasion halo; peritumoral motogen levels; astrocyte border integrity; neurobehavior. Track polymer degradation and ligand occupancy to verify negative feedback (reduced protease/motogen flux correlates with decreased bound cargo and signaling). Compare to empty gel and heparin-only controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8658694/?utm_source=openai))

Design and feasibility
- Material architecture: Soft hydrogel or elastomeric strip with spatially graded sulfation (tumor-facing side enriched for BMP tethering motifs; brain-facing side optimized for motogen capture). BMP is delivered as an immobilized BMP2/4 or as BMP-mimetic peptides with heparin-binding tags to enhance local presentation and receptor engagement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6139562/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic levers exploited:
  1) HS interactome control: Competitive sequestration of FGF2, HB‑EGF, HGF/SF, and CXCL12 blunts FGFR/ErbB/MET/CXCR4 signaling, collapsing invasion-driving gradients. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5111123/?utm_source=openai))
  2) Differentiation cue display: Immobilized BMP engagement drives GBM stem-like cells toward quiescence/differentiation, reducing motility and proliferation and improving therapy sensitivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7072475/?utm_source=openai))
  3) Astrocytic border induction: Local HS signaling biases astrocytes toward boundary-forming phenotypes via STAT3, thickening the physical/biochemical fence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2583788/?utm_source=openai))
- Self-limiting behavior: As invasion and protease-driven remodeling abate, free motogen supply drops; polymer-bound ligand occupancy declines; astrocyte-deposited ECM further dampens diffusion—together reducing active signaling without external shutdown.

Key experiments and metrics
- Binding and presentation
  - Quantify KD and off-rates for target ligands across sulfation patterns; verify BMP receptor activation with SMAD reporter cells on polymers; test ternary FGF2–FGFR–HS inhibition. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2021.778752/full?utm_source=openai))
- Edge control in tissue
  - Time-lapse invasion assays in brain slices ± polymer ring; measure displacement along white-matter–like tracts and perivascular regions. Map ligand gradients with fluorescently labeled or antibody-detected ligands. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8773542/?utm_source=openai))
- Cell-state outcomes
  - scRNA-seq of GBM at the rim for stemness (SOX2/OLIG axis), cell cycle, migration modules, and BMP target programs (ID1/SMAD). Validate with immunostaining and functional assays (temozolomide sensitivity after exposure). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8080762/?utm_source=openai))
- Astrocyte responses
  - Quantify STAT3 activation, border orientation metrics, and CSPG/tenascin deposition; perturb with STAT3 inhibitors to establish necessity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23904622/?utm_source=openai))
- In vivo efficacy and safety
  - Survival, MRI-defined edge recurrence, neurobehavior; cytokine/edema profiling; histology for neurotoxicity. Compare to Gliadel-like intracavitary delivery benchmarks to contextualize translational feasibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11964529/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and decision criteria
- Success criteria: ≥50% reduction in invasion distances, stable astrocytic border formation, durable induction of BMP/SMAD transcriptional programs at the rim, and improved survival without neurological deficits versus controls.
- No-go signals: diffuse off-target gliosis beyond 2–3 mm from rim, seizure propensity, persistent edema, or lack of motogen gradient suppression.

Innovation and distinctness
- Modality shift: A charge-coded, ligand-field therapy that reprograms the peritumoral niche, rather than a cytotoxic, antibody, or standard cell therapy. It exploits GBM’s reliance on HS-bound motogens and the brain’s innate astrocytic fencing to contain and mature tumor cells. Prior GBM work with HS mimetics has shown invasion reduction in vitro, but not a peritumoral, gradient-rewriting implant designed to synchronize astrocyte borders with differentiation cues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6059807/?utm_source=openai))

Risk mitigation and alternatives
- Excess inhibition of neural plasticity by CSPG-like environments: tune sulfation density and mechanical compliance; confine polymer coverage to the immediate rim; incorporate degradable linkers for timed reversal.
- Variable BMP responsiveness across GBM: select BMP2/4 mimetics and dosing informed by ex vivo sensitivity; pair with local low-dose temozolomide if differentiation increases chemosensitivity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-020-0479-9?utm_source=openai))
- If astrocytic fencing is insufficient: add a minimal density of Slit2- or semaphorin-mimetic adhesion–repulsion peptides on the tumor-facing surface in later iterations, without altering the core HS-driven mechanism.

Translational path
- Manufacturability: GMP-synthesis of sulfated polymers and BMP-mimetic peptides is established; ring geometry compatible with neurosurgical placement similar to existing wafers. ([dailymed.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=38962a55-a514-4c48-bea5-f99a8da4beec&utm_source=openai))
- Regulatory starting point: Local implant with non-systemic exposure; staged IDE submission after GLP neurotoxicity and large-animal resection-cavity studies.

In sum, edge rewriting with an HS-mimetic peritumoral ring is a single-lever intervention that collapses invasion-permissive gradients, presents differentiation cues, and recruits astrocytic border formation, turning GBM’s own edge biology into a containment and maturation therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5111123/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Capturing and reprogramming infiltrative GBM via geometry-gated YAP/TAZ suppression and local RNA–resource sequestration

Central hypothesis–question
Can a resection-cavity implant that (i) mechanically traps migrating GBM cells and enforces low-spread, high-curvature morphology to keep YAP/TAZ cytoplasmic and (ii) locally expresses RNA decoys that sequester oncogenic RNA-binding proteins (HuR/IGF2BP3) divert scarce transcriptional/translation resources away from growth programs and bias tumor cells into stable, non-proliferative, astrocyte-like states that support neural function? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12098759/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit GBM’s dependence on mechanotransduction and RBP-mediated mRNA control by converting post-resection space into a “mechano-resource basin”: geometry drives YAP/TAZ-off to reduce proliferative competence, while RBP-decoy RNAs locally siphon HuR/IGF2BP3 from oncogenic transcripts, shifting the limited cofactor and translation economy toward differentiation and homeostatic secretomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10296830/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and evidence
- GBM progression integrates mechanical cues via integrins/FAK→RhoA and YAP/TAZ; small adhesive areas and compliant, high-curvature contexts retain YAP/TAZ in the cytoplasm, reducing growth/invasion. Brain tissue is soft (sub‑kPa to low‑kPa) and anisotropic, shaping glioma migration along tracts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10296830/?utm_source=openai))
- Trapping residual GBM cells in resection cavities with hydrogels is feasible; CXCL12/SDF‑1α traps and macroporous scaffolds concentrate migrators near the cavity for local intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12098759/?utm_source=openai))
- HuR (ELAVL1) and IGF2BP3 stabilize or modulate oncogenic transcripts and translation; GBM depends on these RBPs. Engineered RNA decoys can titrate RBPs in vivo and redirect post‑transcriptional control. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/mcr/article/9/5/648/90812/The-RNA-Binding-Protein-HuR-Promotes-Glioma-Growth?utm_source=openai))
- Forced activation of astrocytic programs (NFIA/NFIB/SOX9/STAT3 axis) suppresses GBM proliferation and links to mature astrocyte markers, indicating a reachable non‑malignant attractor once proliferative pressure is relieved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9890139/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build a one‑way “glioma capture niche” that enforces YAP/TAZ‑off states.
- Design: Implant an anisotropic, ultra-soft hyaluronan–laminin hydrogel into the resection cavity with microchannels (7–10 μm width; high curvature; 100–300 μm2 adhesive islands) aligned to local white‑matter tracts to convert infiltration into guided ingress and residency. Geometry limits cell spread and mitotic rounding, biasing cytoplasmic YAP/TAZ. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10296830/?utm_source=openai))
- Add-on (optional, already validated by others): low‑dose CXCL12 gradients to accelerate capture; no cytotoxins. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12098759/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: nuclear/cytoplasmic YAP/TAZ ratio; pFAK/RhoA activity; traction forces; migration speed/directionality in ex vivo slices; single‑cell RNA‑seq for YAP/TAZ target repression. Benchmarks: ≥50% reduction in nuclear YAP/TAZ and ≥40% drop in invasion metrics vs flat controls.

Aim 2. Reallocate post-transcriptional resources using local RBP-decoy RNAs.
- Construct: AAV or hydrogel‑embedded vector expressing noncoding decoys bearing multimerized AU‑rich and IGF2BP‑binding motifs to titrate HuR and IGF2BP3, respectively, under a promoter active in captured GBM cells. Decoys remain confined by the implant, minimizing off‑target exposure. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/mcr/article/9/5/648/90812/The-RNA-Binding-Protein-HuR-Promotes-Glioma-Growth?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism tests: RBP–RNA CLIP to confirm decoy occupancy; polysome profiling and ribosome‑footprinting to show reduced translation of cell‑cycle/PI3K–MAPK effectors; mRNA half‑life assays for canonical HuR/IGF2BP3 targets; proteomics for oncogenic network attenuation. Success criteria: ≥30% reduction in HuR/IGF2BP3 target stabilization/translation; concurrent upregulation of astrocyte differentiation and homeostatic genes (e.g., ALDH1L1, GLT‑1/EAAT2, AQP4). ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/mcr/article/9/5/648/90812/The-RNA-Binding-Protein-HuR-Promotes-Glioma-Growth?utm_source=openai))
- Functional reprogramming: Assess glutamate uptake, potassium buffering, and trophic factor balance in captured cells; reduced secretion of pro‑invasive cytokines. Threshold: ≥2× increase in EAAT2 function with unchanged viability.

Aim 3. Test efficacy, stability, and safety in orthotopic resection models.
- Model: Patient‑derived GBM xenografts with subtotal resection followed by implant placement. Arms: scaffold only; scaffold+decoy; empty cavity control.
- Endpoints: time to radiographic recurrence; spatial pattern of relapse (distance from cavity edge); survival; seizure burden; neurobehavioral scores; neuropathology for neurotoxicity. Expectation: scaffold+decoy shifts recurrence pattern toward cavity confinement, prolongs survival, and preserves function vs controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12098759/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic durability: Challenge captured cells with growth factors and mechanical stiffening ex vivo; test whether YAP/TAZ remains cytoplasmic and HuR/IGF2BP3 targets remain suppressed.

Design principles and parameters
- Geometry as checkpoint: prioritize microcurvature and minimal adhesive area over bulk softness to avoid contexts where extreme softness can paradoxically enhance invasion in 3D; tune E ~0.5–2 kPa to match parenchyma while letting curvature do most of the YAP/TAZ suppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7984937/?utm_source=openai))
- Anisotropy: orient channels with tractography to turn white‑matter–guided migration into inward capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11803519/?utm_source=openai))
- Local-only gene control: restrict decoy expression to the implant domain via spatial delivery; decoy stoichiometry targets RBP occupancy without global RBP knockdown, minimizing systemic effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7237136/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no‑go
- M1 (in vitro/ex vivo): Achieve target YAP/TAZ cytoplasmic retention and reduced invasion; demonstrate RBP decoy engagement and translational reweighting toward differentiation.
- M2 (short‑term in vivo, 4–6 weeks): Show ≥30% delay in recurrence and capture‑biased relapse pattern without neurologic deficits.
- M3 (long‑term in vivo): Demonstrate survival benefit with preserved behavior; captured cells display stable astrocyte‑like transcriptomes and functions.

Risk management
- If softness increases invasion in certain lines, increase curvature and reduce adhesive area; incorporate graded stiffness only within channels to maintain low spread areas while preventing “free‑swim” zones. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7984937/?utm_source=openai))
- If HuR or IGF2BP3 redundancy blunts effect, multiplex decoys or prioritize the dominant RBP per tumor transcriptome before implantation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6997557/?utm_source=openai))
- If immune response to implant emerges, adjust matrix chemistry (HA/laminin vs collagen) and porosity; existing GBM traps report low inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12098759/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcome and impact
A local, non-cytotoxic, “one‑way niche” that captures migratory GBM cells and deprives oncogenic networks of mechanotransductive and post‑transcriptional resources, enabling a stable, space‑filling astrocyte‑like state with improved quality of life and minimal systemic exposure. This leverages brain‑specific mechanics and tumor reliance on RBPs as therapeutic control points, distinct from cytotoxic drugs or systemic immunotherapies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10296830/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Contact-and-activity-gated conversion of neuron-integrated glioblastoma into permanently hyperpolarized, non-dividing cells

Integrated hypothesis-question
Can we repurpose the very neuron→glioma synaptic activity that accelerates GBM growth to irreversibly switch only synaptically connected tumor cells into a stably hyperpolarized, post‑mitotic, neuron‑like state, thereby collapsing the malignant circuit while sparing normal brain function? This tests whether pathologic depolarization/Ca2+ influx at bona fide neuron–glioma synapses can be converted from a growth driver into a durable anti‑proliferative instruction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use synapse‑proximal calcium activity as the address and trigger for a one‑time genetic state transition in connected GBM cells. The transition locks in a hyperpolarized membrane potential and cell‑cycle exit, converting excitatory drive into its own brake and eliminating the need for global neuronal silencing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and novelty check
- Mechanism: GBM cells form AMPAR‑dependent, Ca2+‑permeable synapses with excitatory neurons; neuronal activity and secreted activity‑regulated factors (for example, NLGN3) promote glioma proliferation and invasion. GBM cells also interconnect via Cx43‑rich networks that propagate depolarization and support resistance. These are stable findings across models and patient samples. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))
- Leverage point: Sustained depolarization favors proliferation; sustained hyperpolarization biases toward growth arrest/differentiation across diverse cell types, motivating a “bioelectric-to-epigenetic” latch as an upstream control of plasticity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2862582/?utm_source=openai))
- Tool precedent: Activity‑gated gene switches (Cal‑Light/FLARE/FLiCRE) and emerging Ca2+‑gated bioluminescent activators (BLADe) demonstrate that intracellular Ca2+ transients can be integrated to drive stable gene expression without external light, supporting feasibility of an activity‑to‑permanent‑program converter in living brain tissue. To our knowledge, this has not been applied to selectively reprogram GBM cells at neuron–glioma synapses. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.3902?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Map and quantify the synaptically connected GBM subpopulation as the dominant growth driver in vivo.
- Approach: In orthotopic patient‑derived GBM xenografts (PDX), combine neuronal stimulation with activity‑integrating reporters to label glioma cells experiencing AMPAR‑dependent EPSCs; validate by patch‑clamp, Ca2+ imaging, and pharmacology. Endpoints: fraction labeled, proliferation indices, invasion metrics versus unlabeled tumor cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer and validate a contact-and-activity-gated flip to a hyperpolarized, post‑mitotic program in glioma cells.
- Sensor: A synapse‑proximal Ca2+ integrator that requires local high‑Ca2+ transients to arm a recombinase; use a Ca2+‑dependent luciferase to generate on‑site light that gates the integrator (no external illumination), ensuring coincidence detection of synaptic Ca2+ and proximity. Readout: permanent recombinase flip. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.3902?utm_source=openai))
- Effector (constitutive post‑flip): (i) a minimal hyperpolarization set (e.g., KCNQ/Kir conductance plus KCC2 to reset ECl−) and (ii) a cell‑cycle exit set (p21/p27). Benchmarks: sustained Vm shift to more negative values, reduced Ca2+ microdomain amplitudes, durable G0 arrest, neuron‑like passive membrane properties. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2862582/?utm_source=openai))
- Selectivity guard: Synapse‑anchored localization of the sensor using AMPAR/PSD‑scaffolding motifs to restrict flipping to neuron‑connected tumor membranes; confirm absence of flipping in non‑connected tumor regions and non‑tumor cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838971/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test in vivo efficacy and network‑level impact while preserving circuit function.
- Approach: Deliver the cassette to orthotopic GBM via CNS‑tropic vectors; trigger only through endogenous neuronal activity. Outcomes: tumor volume, proliferation and invasion, single‑cell Vm distributions, and functional connectivity of the GBM network (calcium imaging/electrophysiology). Measure cortical physiology and behavior to verify preserved host circuits. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16071?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic secondary readouts: decrease in neuron→glioma EPSCs, reduced activity‑dependent GBM subpopulation size, and attenuation of activity‑regulated trophic pathways (e.g., NLGN3). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28959975/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Resistance and heterogeneity stress‑test.
- Approach: Track clonal dynamics by single‑cell transcriptomics and membrane‑potential reporters pre/post‑flip. Test whether residual GBM cells reestablish synaptic integration or are electrically shunted by hyperpolarized neighbors. Explore whether adding a Cx43‑CT decoy post‑flip further dampens network support without broad toxicity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16071?utm_source=openai))

Key design constraints and solutions
- Intratumoral heterogeneity/plasticity: The trigger is a functional phenotype (synaptic Ca2+ microdomains), not a static marker, ensuring that the most aggressive, circuit‑integrated clones self‑identify and self‑convert. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))
- Infiltration and margin control: Synapse‑proximal gating restricts action to tumor–neuron interfaces at invasive edges where BBB/BTB are heterogeneous and where growth is neuron‑driven. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12838971/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune‑suppressive TME: Strategy is cell‑autonomous and electrical; it does not require robust lymphocyte infiltration. Any secondary relief of immunosuppression from network collapse is an exploratory endpoint. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/31/14/2864/763489/Innovative-Therapeutic-Strategies-Targeting-the?utm_source=openai))
- Normal tissue toxicity and QoL: No global silencing or systemic ion‑channel drugs; conversion occurs only in cells receiving pathological synaptic input, preserving upstream neuronal function. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))

Model systems and endpoints
- Systems: Human GBM PDX and patient‑derived organoids co‑cultured with human neurons; adult murine orthotopic models with intact circuits. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary endpoints: durable loss of proliferation in flipped cells, whole‑tumor growth delay/survival benefit, maintenance of normal behavioral performance. Secondary: Vm set‑point shift magnitude, EPSC suppression at neuron–glioma synapses, network fragmentation metrics. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16071?utm_source=openai))

Go/no‑go criteria and failure modes
- Go: ≥70% of synaptically connected GBM cells flip and maintain hyperpolarization and G0 for ≥4–6 weeks in vivo with preserved host behavior. No‑go: widespread off‑target flipping or reversion to division despite hyperpolarization. Contingency: tune Ca2+ integration threshold or add a synapse‑anchoring constraint to improve specificity; if needed, add a modest Cx43 decoy to prevent electrical back‑propagation from unconverted neighbors. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16071?utm_source=openai))

Impact
If successful, this establishes a circuit‑aware, self‑limiting therapy: the very signal that fuels GBM growth (synaptic Ca2+ influx/depolarization) becomes the address and the mechanism for permanent, localized tumor disarmament—conceptually distinct from receptor blockade, cytotoxic drugs, or systemic neuromodulation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31534222/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Turning white matter into a selective conduit: PRG4-grafted, magnetothermally gated OPC couriers for precision treatment of infiltrative glioblastoma

Central question (inseparable from hypothesis)
If we convert oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) into low-friction couriers by grafting a boundary‑lubricant (PRG4/lubricin) onto their membranes and arm them with protease-activatable, magnetothermally gated payloads, can we outpace and intercept glioblastoma (GBM) cells along white‑matter and perivascular routes where the blood–brain barrier (BBB) remains largely intact, thereby reducing recurrence-driving infiltrative disease with minimal off‑target toxicity? GBM preferentially invades along white matter tracts and perivascular spaces; these invasive margins are often non‑enhancing on MRI and shielded by an intact BBB, limiting systemic drugs. MMP-2/9 and ECM lecticans (e.g., tenascin‑C, brevican) are enriched at these margins and perivascular niches. OPCs are motile residents that migrate along axonal tracts and can be SPION‑labeled without losing functionality, while SPION magnetothermal therapy is clinically feasible. These facts motivate an approach that leverages, rather than fights, brain‑specific structure and GBM biochemistry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6254577/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Change the tribology of the courier cell—not the road or the tumor—so OPCs travel farther and faster along myelinated highways with fewer off‑track arrests, then require local GBM protease activity to unlock payload release, with an external alternating magnetic field (AMF) as a second spatial key for repeatable, confined dosing. PRG4’s anti‑adhesive, TLR2/4‑antagonist “molecular brush” properties enable friction reduction and immune quieting; MMP‑cleavable linkers implement biochemical AND logic; SPIONs provide remote steering and heat‑triggered depot emptying under fields already used in GBM thermotherapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4707532/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Cell tribology as a therapeutic lever: PRG4 membrane brushes on living OPCs to bias motion persistence along aligned, myelinated tracts—distinct from chemotaxis‑only designs. PRG4 coatings are strongly anti‑adhesive/anti‑inflammatory on biointerfaces; their use to tune glial motility in CNS tracts is unexplored. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35019542/?utm_source=openai))
- Invasion‑microenvironment logic: Protease‑cleavable linkers keyed to MMP‑2/9 activity at GBM margins restrict activation to where infiltrative cells reside. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/14/2/443?utm_source=openai))
- Noninvasive spatiotemporal control: SPION‑based steering and magnetothermal pulses confine release in space/time and are translatable given ongoing/precedent GBM hyperthermia trials. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6341053/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build PRG4 “molecular brush” OPC couriers and quantify tract‑selective motility and immune quieting.
- Engineering: Insert PRG4 onto human OPC membranes via DSPE‑PEG‑PRG4 amphiphiles and/or enzyme‑tagged anchors; titrate brush density.
- Readouts of motility: 3D aligned‑fiber scaffolds and organotypic brain slices to measure run length, speed, directional persistence along myelinated bundles versus gray‑matter ECM. Endpoints: ≥2× increase in persistence length and ≥50% reduction in off‑tract arrests versus unmodified OPCs.
- Myeloid evasion and tissue compatibility: Microglia co‑culture phagocytosis index, NF‑κB reporter suppression in TLR2/4 agonist challenge, and cytokine panel. Hypothesis: PRG4 brush reduces opsonization and TLR2/4 signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4672561/?utm_source=openai))
- Docking selectivity: Introduce MMP‑2/9‑cleavable spacers within PRG4 tethers so partial shedding in protease‑rich zones increases local adhesion for payload handoff while maintaining lubrication elsewhere. Validation: rMMP‑2/9 cleavage kinetics; adhesion switch on tenascin‑C/brevican ECM under MMP exposure. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470001/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Implement AND‑gated payload release keyed to GBM proteases plus magnetothermal cues.
- Surface‑tethered prodrug vesicles: Load cytotoxic/myeloid‑reprogramming cargo in liposomes tethered to OPC surface with MMP‑2/9‑cleavable peptides (e.g., PLGLAG variants). Only upon cleavage are vesicles freed to bind ECM and fuse with nearby GBM cells. Endpoints: ≥10× higher release in GBM‑conditioned media versus healthy‑brain media; minimal leakage in protease‑inhibited controls. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/febs.15227?utm_source=openai))
- Magnetothermal key: Co‑load OPCs with optimized SPIONs; AMF pulses (clinically used frequency/amplitude) raise local temperature by 3–5°C to trigger liposomal phase transition for secondary AND gating. Calibrate to avoid bulk tissue heating. Endpoints: on‑demand bursts with ≤5% off‑target release outside AMF focus; viability ≥85% after loading and pulsing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3097345/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate tract‑constrained delivery to invasive margins and survival benefit in orthotopic GBM.
- Models and navigation: IDH‑wildtype GBM orthotopic xenografts with DTI tractography to pre‑plan steering along corpus callosum/perivascular routes. Many invasive regions are behind an intact BBB; assess non‑enhancing margins. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11016125/?utm_source=openai))
- Guidance and dosing: External gradient magnets for biasing distribution; serial AMF sessions for repeatable bursts (clinically precedent schedules) while monitoring edema risks. Endpoints: increased payload at tenascin‑C/brevican‑positive invasive fronts; reduced tumor cell density on T2/FLAIR‑correlated regions; extended survival with preserved neurobehavior. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6341053/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: Neuropathology for axon integrity; neurobehavioral battery; off‑target injury mapping. Built‑in OPC safety switch (e.g., HSV‑TK/ganciclovir) if long‑term engraftment occurs.

Research plan and methods
1) OPC source and characterization
- Human iPSC‑derived and primary human OPCs; verify markers (PDGFRα, NG2). Baseline motility assays in aligned microchannels and mouse organotypic slices.

2) PRG4 brush fabrication and validation
- Recombinant human PRG4 with N‑terminal tags; DSPE‑PEG‑maleimide conjugation; density control by feed ratio; stability on membranes.
- Surface characterization: immunostaining, FRAP to assess lateral mobility; single‑cell force spectroscopy to measure adhesion/friction on myelinated substrates.

3) Immune‑interaction assays
- Co‑culture with human microglia; phagocytosis and cytokines ± LPS/HA fragments; TLR2/4 reporter cells to quantify PRG4 antagonism and CD44‑dependence using blocking antibodies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4707532/?utm_source=openai))

4) Protease‑AND gate chemistry
- Synthesize MMP‑2/9‑cleavable linkers (GPLGIAGQ/PLGLAG) between OPC‑bound anchors and cargo vesicles; cleavage kinetics with rMMP‑2/9; stability in CSF simulant; leakage tests.
- ECM targeting on freed vesicles: moderate‑affinity binders for tenascin‑C/brevican to bias deposition where these ECM proteins are enriched at invasion fronts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10046791/?utm_source=openai))

5) SPION loading and magnetothermal calibration
- High‑SAR, biocompatible SPIONs; intracellular distribution; preservation of OPC migration and differentiation potential. AMF parameters modeled on GBM hyperthermia experience to limit edema. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3097345/?utm_source=openai))

6) In vivo efficacy and distribution
- Stereotactic OPC delivery into ipsilateral white matter near tumor; external magnets to bias motion along corpus callosum; serial MRI to track SPION‑OPCs and map to DTI tracts; ex vivo histology for payload deposition versus GBM cell density.
- Outcomes: invasive margin cell‑kill, delay of non‑enhancing FLAIR progression; survival; neurotoxicity.

Therapeutic payload options (modular)
- Low‑dose genotoxic or mitotic agents tuned for slow‑cycling cells in invasive margins.
- Small‑molecule radiosensitizers or DNA‑repair inhibitors for adjuvant synergy.
- Local myeloid reprogrammers (e.g., STING agonist) in sub‑ablative doses to counter myeloid‑dominant immunosuppression without systemic exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9244707/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision gates
- Go/no‑go 1: PRG4 brush confers ≥2× tract persistence without elevating microglial activation.
- Go/no‑go 2: AND‑gated release shows ≥10× protease selectivity and ≤5% basal leakage in brain‑mimetic media.
- Go/no‑go 3: In vivo, tract‑biased OPC distribution and ≥3× higher payload deposition at ECM‑positive invasive fronts versus gray matter; survival advantage with preserved motor/cognitive scores.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Off‑target heating/edema: adopt clinical AMF bounds and interleave short pulses; include real‑time MR‑thermometry where feasible. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35158809/?utm_source=openai))
- OPC differentiation or tumor‑support risk: incorporate suicide switch; cap in vivo persistence; verify no pro‑tumor paracrine effects in controls.
- Protease heterogeneity: k‑of‑n logic by combining MMP‑2/9 linkers with magnetothermal key; optional hypoxia/NF‑κB‑responsive transcriptional gate if needed.

Why this should work system‑wide
- It exploits the same anisotropic conduits GBM uses, but with faster, friction‑reduced couriers that require GBM‑specific proteolysis plus an external trigger to act—converting dispersion routes into treatment lanes where systemic drugs cannot reach due to intact BBB at margins. The biochemistry (MMP‑rich, TNC/Brevican‑positive ECM, myeloid‑dominated TME) and physics (tract anisotropy, SPION AMF actuation) are all real, observed features in GBM and CNS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11016125/?utm_source=openai))

Expected impact
- A tract‑first, activation‑last platform that is orthogonal to conventional small molecules, antibodies, standard CAR‑T, and checkpoint inhibitors. It addresses heterogeneity through repeatable, spatially precise dosing and minimizes toxicity by biochemical and physical coincidence gating.

Key prior‑art anchors supporting feasibility
- GBM invades along white matter/perivascular routes; margins are often behind intact BBB. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6254577/?utm_source=openai))
- ECM at invasive fronts is enriched in tenascin‑C and brevican; MMP‑2/9 are active drivers and markers of invasion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10046791/?utm_source=openai))
- OPCs migrate along axonal tracts and can be SPION‑labeled/tracked without losing function. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11113994/?utm_source=openai))
- PRG4 coatings are anti‑adhesive and antagonize TLR2/4 via CD44/TLR interactions, enabling a low‑friction, low‑inflammation interface. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4672561/?utm_source=openai))
- SPION magnetothermal therapy for GBM is clinically practiced, enabling translatable AMF parameters. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3097345/?utm_source=openai))
