Title
Self-referenced breath-phase tactile micro-violations to recalibrate surprise–affect coupling for everyday emotion regulation

Background and rationale
- Predictive coding accounts of emotion propose that anxiety and depression reflect overly precise priors linking bodily change and unexpected events to threat; the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) signals unsigned prediction error (“surprise”) and modulates learning, while limbic regions like the amygdala bias vigilance and valence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10690029/?utm_source=openai))
- Nasal respiration entrains human limbic oscillations and modulates amygdala-linked cognition, providing a continuously generated, precisely phased internal timing signal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Tactile oddball and omission paradigms elicit hierarchical mismatch responses ascending from somatosensory cortex to insula and mid/dorsal cingulate, offering a low-valence channel to deliver controlled prediction errors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758822/?utm_source=openai))
- Near-threshold vibrotactile stimulation with added noise leverages stochastic resonance to titrate sensory precision and detection probability without high arousal. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2005.01533.x?utm_source=openai))
- Self-generated actions produce efference-copy–based predictions; slight deviations in the expected sensory consequence are encoded as self-attributed prediction errors, typically with reduced defensive responses relative to exogenous surprises. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1334241/?utm_source=openai))

Integrated hypothesis-question
Can repeated, low-arousal tactile prediction errors, time-locked to a person’s own respiratory phase and kept near perceptual threshold via stochastic resonance, reduce the learned coupling between “unexpected” and negative affect by recalibrating ACC-centered surprise signaling and its downstream influence on the amygdala?

Atomic strategy
Exploit respiration as a self-generated temporal prior and deliver subthreshold tactile “micro-violations” (small phase jitter or occasional omissions) at predicted breath phases, so the ACC repeatedly registers surprise in a safe, low-valence context, driving precision reweighting that uncouples unexpectedness from threat.

Specific aims
1) Establish that breath-phase–locked tactile micro-violations increase unsigned prediction-error markers in ACC/insula while minimizing amygdala arousal.
2) Test whether 4–6 weeks of daily training reduces everyday anxiety and negative affect reactivity to surprise.
3) Quantify whether changes are mediated by reduced precision of threat-biased priors (behavioral modeling) and altered ACC–limbic responses to unexpected events.

Intervention
- Hardware: A wrist or forearm wearable with (a) PPG/accelerometer airflow proxy to estimate respiratory phase, (b) a 6–12‑site vibrotactile array operating near individual detection threshold, and (c) a noise injector to implement stochastic resonance (SR).
- Control signal: Online breath-phase tracking; pulses nominally occur at user-specific predicted exhalation peak (or chosen phase) with closed-loop phase locking.
- Micro-violations: On 15–25% of predicted-pulse opportunities, introduce ±20–120 ms phase jitter, spatial relocation to an adjacent tactor, or omissions; hazard rate adapted to keep detection probability ≈0.3–0.5.
- SR tuning: Inject band-limited tactile noise to keep the underlying pulse near threshold and maintain low arousal while preserving detectability variance required for learning. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2005.01533.x?utm_source=openai))
- Self-referencing: Users are prompted to breathe naturally; because the timing prior is self-generated, deviations are labeled as self-referential mismatches rather than exogenous threats. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1334241/?utm_source=openai))

Design
Phase 1 (mechanism, N=72, lab-based, pre-registered)
- Randomized within-subjects, three conditions during fMRI/EEG:
  A) Breath-locked mismatch (phase-locked pulses with micro-violations)
  B) Breath-locked regular (phase-locked pulses, no violations)
  C) Random-timed pulses (yoked count, no breath locking)
- Primary neural outcomes: ACC/insula unsigned PE (BOLD/EEG) > B; amygdala BOLD and SCR minimal vs. C. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758822/?utm_source=openai))
- Behavioral/physiology: Startle and oddball tasks to assess surprise–valence coupling; skin conductance to unexpected neutral sounds/touches; HRV changes during blocks.

Phase 2 (home trial, N=240, everyday efficacy, 6 weeks)
- Parallel-arm RCT:
  1) Active: breath-locked micro-violation + SR
  2) Breath-locked regular (no violations; matched tactile dose)
  3) Random-timed micro-violations (no breath locking)
- Use case: 20 minutes/day during routine sedentary activity.
- Primary outcomes: Weekly EMA of state anxiety/negative affect; STAI‑S, PANAS; reactivity to daily unexpected minor events (EMA probes).
- Secondary outcomes: Lab subset pre/post fMRI/EEG markers (ACC/insula PE; amygdala response to unexpected neutral events), and computational indices of prior precision from probabilistic learning tasks.

Analysis plan
- Mechanistic contrasts (Phase 1): A>B for ACC/insula unsigned PE; A≈B<C for amygdala/SCR. Mediation: ACC PE change mediates startle/affect reactivity change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10690029/?utm_source=openai))
- Efficacy (Phase 2): Linear mixed models on EMA anxiety reactivity slopes; between-arm differences in pre/post computational estimates of precision weighting; correction for multiplicity.
- Generalization: Post-training, surprise tasks in a different modality (auditory oddball) to test cross-modal decoupling of unexpectedness and negative affect. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35017672/?utm_source=openai))

Safety and tolerability
- Arousal safeguards: Adaptive ceilings on violation magnitude/hazard to avoid startle; real-time SCR monitoring to keep within low-arousal bounds; omission events favored over intensity spikes. Startle physiology benchmarks and guidelines inform limits. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-8986.2005.00271.x?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1: Accurate breath-phase locking (<40 ms median error) and stable near-threshold calibration over a week.
- M2: ACC/insula unsigned PE increase without amygdala/SCR elevation in ≥70% participants (Phase 1).
- M3: ≥0.3 SD reduction in EMA anxiety reactivity vs. control arms at 6 weeks; durability at 4 weeks post.

Mechanistic justifications mapped to biology
- Respiration provides a limbic-entrained temporal scaffold; locking neutral tactile events to this scaffold and occasionally violating it elicits hierarchical mismatch responses (S1/S2→insula→ACC) that label “unexpected” without threat. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Stochastic resonance maintains subthreshold, low-valence touch while ensuring intermittent detectability that sustains learning signals. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2005.01533.x?utm_source=openai))
- Repeated self-referenced surprise updates priors via ACC-coded unsigned prediction error, reducing the learned association between surprise and negative affect. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10690029/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and differentiation
- Unlike existing vibrotactile devices geared to soothe or entrain relaxation, this protocol targets prediction-error recalibration using breath-phase timing and controlled micro-violations, a mechanism not used in current anxiety wearables or open-label affective touch devices. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022395625005552?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- If the active arm shows reduced affective reactivity to surprise and stronger ACC unsigned PE with stable or reduced amygdala/SCR, this supports the claim that safe, self-referenced prediction errors can retrain emotional habits for everyday regulation.
- Null findings with elevated amygdala/SCR would suggest that violations were not sufficiently low-valence or that breath-phase scaffolding is insufficient; adjustments would include lower hazard, increased omissions, or alternative phases.

Title
Closed‑loop, cardiac‑locked olfactory micro‑pulses to recalibrate threat‑biased interoceptive priors for everyday emotion regulation

Background and Rationale
- Predictive coding accounts of interoception posit that anxiety involves overweighted precision on interoceptive prediction errors relative to exteroceptive cues; shifting precision allocation can change appraisal of ambiguous bodily signals. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763417303573?utm_source=openai))
- Cardiac cycle timing gates affective perception: stimuli presented at systole (baroreceptor firing) amplify fear/threat processing and alter somatosensory thresholds, identifying millisecond windows where interoceptive signals are most behaviorally potent. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))
- Olfaction provides a rapid route to amygdala and valence encoding, enabling fast, low-load safety tagging without high cognitive demand. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7076187/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety signals can suppress conditioned fear and reduce anxiety responses when paired consistently with potential threat contexts, suggesting a route to reshape priors without explicit exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6981293/?utm_source=openai))
- Wearable olfactory displays and micro‑diffusers now permit brief, directed, low‑intensity odor pulses with sub‑second control, and human olfaction resolves temporal odor structure within a single sniff—supporting precise time‑locking to internal events. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8919918/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic Strategy
Pair brief, near‑threshold, pleasant olfactory micro‑pulses to cardiac systole during everyday activities so that ambiguous interoceptive transients repeatedly co‑occur with a benign, exteroceptive cue. Over time, this shifts precision toward external context during interoceptive ambiguity and re‑maps bodily “blips” to safety.

Hypothesis/Research Question
If near‑threshold, cardiac‑locked olfactory micro‑pulses are delivered at systole during daily life, then:
- threat‑biased appraisal of bodily fluctuations will decrease, and
- interoceptive precision weighting (relative to exteroceptive signals) will down‑shift during ambiguity,
resulting in lower momentary anxiety and improved emotion regulation. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763417303573?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims
1) Establish that cardiac‑locked olfactory pulses reduce fear‑biased perception at systole (laboratory test).
2) Demonstrate short‑term down‑weighting of interoceptive error signals during ambiguity (neurobehavioral markers).
3) Test real‑world efficacy for everyday emotion regulation with a wearable in a 4‑week field trial.

Methods

Device and Control
- Wearable unit: wrist PPG for R‑peak prediction and latency compensation; IMU for movement context; micro‑diffuser (e.g., SAW or micro‑pump) directing faint odor toward nares via a short, unobtrusive nozzle; smartphone controller. Delivery latency <150 ms from detected R‑peak with calibrated advance to hit systole. Odorants are neutral‑to‑pleasant, minimal trigeminal activation, food‑grade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8919918/?utm_source=openai))
- Control modes: (a) true cardiac‑locked (CL); (b) randomly timed micro‑pulses (RT, same dose); (c) no‑odor airflow sham (SH).

Participants
- N=120 healthy adults with elevated trait anxiety but not under treatment; balanced by sex. Power targets d=0.35 within‑subject contrasts across conditions.

Laboratory Phase (Aims 1–2)
- Design: within‑subject, counterbalanced CL vs RT vs SH across three sessions.
- Tasks and measures:
  - Cardiac‑phase fear bias: fear/neutral face identification and intensity ratings with stimuli probed at systole vs diastole; primary outcome is reduction of systolic fear advantage under CL. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))
  - Somatosensory/pain threshold modulation by cardiac phase to check baroreceptor gating sensitivity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23669535/?utm_source=openai))
  - Interoceptive–exteroceptive attention task with heartbeat‑evoked potentials (HEP) and performance indices; prediction: under CL, exteroceptive accuracy and reduced HEP amplitude during ambiguity indicate down‑weighted interoceptive precision. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8153056/?utm_source=openai))
  - Safety‑signal transfer: olfactory cue presented during mild interoceptive perturbations (e.g., brief stair stepping); later test whether the same cue reduces startle/aversive ratings in matched contexts without pulses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6981293/?utm_source=openai))
- Physiological: HRV, skin conductance, respiration; EEG for HEP modulation.

Field Phase (Aim 3)
- 4‑week randomized cross‑over (2 weeks CL, 2 weeks RT/SH). Micro‑pulses delivered only during locomotion and low‑demand tasks detected by IMU to avoid intrusiveness.
- Outcomes:
  - Ecological momentary assessments (EMA): state anxiety, perceived bodily threat, affective valence, 5–6 prompts/day.
  - Passive markers: phone typing error variability and step‑time variability as stress correlates; wearable HRV during daily episodes.
  - Weekly lab check‑ins: interoceptive accuracy/awareness tasks, fear‑bias probe, HEP.
- Primary endpoint: reduction in EMA state anxiety and perceived bodily threat during CL vs control; secondary: durable reduction in systolic fear bias and HEP modulation after 4 weeks. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))

Signal Timing and Dosing
- Pulse onset targeted to 200–300 ms post‑R to coincide with peak baroreceptor influence; individualized by brief calibration using pain/looming probes to map systolic windows. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23669535/?utm_source=openai))
- Odor pulse widths 100–300 ms with PWM intensity control near individual detection threshold to avoid habituation and overt awareness. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26710120/?utm_source=openai))
- Sniff synchronization: optional lockout during forceful inspiration to minimize plume spread and reduce adaptation. ([cir.nii.ac.jp](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1360590043961229824?utm_source=openai))

Analysis
- Aim 1: mixed models with factors condition (CL/RT/SH) × cardiac phase (systole/diastole) on fear bias indices.
- Aim 2: HEP amplitude and decoding of attentional state; mediation by HEP between condition and behavioral fear bias. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11645458/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: hierarchical models on EMA outcomes; durability assessed in final lab probes; exploratory moderation by baseline interoceptive accuracy.

Innovation/Novelty
- First test, to our knowledge, of cardiac‑locked, near‑threshold olfactory micro‑pulses as precision‑reallocation and safety‑tagging for interoceptive ambiguity; prior cardiac‑locked multisensory work used visual/full‑body illusions, not olfaction or wearables for affect regulation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-27698-2?utm_source=openai))
- Leverages amygdala‑proximal olfactory pathways for rapid, low‑cognitive‑load safety tagging during windows of peak interoceptive salience. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12319816/?utm_source=openai))
- Technically enabled by modern wearable olfactory displays and sub‑second pulse control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8919918/?utm_source=openai))

Expected Outcomes and Interpretation
- CL reduces systolic fear‑bias and HEP amplitude during ambiguity vs RT/SH, indicating down‑weighted interoceptive precision when a stable, benign exteroceptive cue co‑occurs with interoceptive transients. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))
- In the field, CL lowers momentary anxiety and perceived bodily threat during daily fluctuations without requiring explicit exposure.
- A safety‑signal association to the olfactory cue emerges, generalizing to matched contexts and supporting real‑world emotion regulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6981293/?utm_source=openai))

Risks and Mitigations
- Habituation or plume persistence: use brief pulses, PWM control, and airflow management to minimize residual odor. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26710120/?utm_source=openai))
- Trigeminal irritation/allergy: pre‑screen odorants; use low‑trigeminal, food‑grade compounds and adverse‑event monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7076187/?utm_source=openai))
- Timing errors: individualized latency calibration and continuous PPG quality checks; fall back to RT if signal quality degrades.

Success Criteria
- Lab: significant condition×phase interaction reducing systolic fear‑bias under CL; concurrent HEP reduction during ambiguity.
- Field: ≥20% reduction in EMA state anxiety and perceived bodily threat during CL relative to control weeks; maintenance of effect in final lab probe.

Timeline and Milestones
- Months 0–6: device engineering, latency calibration, odorant safety validation.
- Months 7–14: laboratory study (Aims 1–2).
- Months 15–24: field trial (Aim 3), analysis, dissemination.

Broader Impact
A low‑burden, non‑invasive wearable that gently re‑tunes precision allocation at natural interoceptive “hot moments” could scale as an everyday aid for anxiety and mood vulnerability, complementing existing behavioral strategies without requiring explicit exposure or high user effort. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763417303573?utm_source=openai))

Title
Limbic Dawn: Pre-awakening olfactory micro‑pulses as a noninvasive zeitgeber to sharpen morning endocrine dynamics and improve next‑day mood in the general population

Premise and rationale
- The olfactory bulb projects to primary olfactory cortex and amygdalar subregions, which interface with hypothalamic autonomic–neuroendocrine control; this provides a direct route for odor signals to bias arousal/regulatory circuits. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK11071/?utm_source=openai))
- Pure olfactory stimulation can be processed during sleep with minimal awakenings, in contrast to trigeminal chemosensory stimulation; odor cueing during sleep reliably modulates brain activity and behavior without overt arousal. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15164891/?utm_source=openai))
- The early‑morning period is a sensitive transition: artificial dawn exposures alter skin temperature, reduce sleep inertia, and modify the cortisol awakening response (CAR), a distinct morning surge with functional significance for day readiness. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20408928/?utm_source=openai))
- CAR–mood associations exist but are heterogeneous; nevertheless, CAR amplitude/timing is a validated, objective readout of morning endocrine dynamics responsive to environmental cues. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/edrv/article/46/1/43/7739741?utm_source=openai))
- To our knowledge, pre‑awakening, low‑dose, pure‑olfactory micro‑pulses timed to the dawn window have not been systematically tested for effects on CAR, sleep inertia, and next‑day mood. (Inference based on literature above.)

Atomic strategy
Use very brief, low‑concentration, pure olfactory “dawn micro‑pulses” in the 45 minutes before habitual wake to act as a limbic access cue that sharpens the morning endocrine/arousal transition (indexed by CAR and sleep inertia), thereby improving next‑day affect—without waking the sleeper or requiring any conscious regulation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15164891/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–question
Do pre‑awakening, pure‑olfactory micro‑pulses delivered at fixed times in the 45 minutes before habitual wake (vs. odorless carrier) sharpen the cortisol awakening response and reduce sleep inertia, leading to measurable improvement in next‑day mood in free‑living adults?

Study design
- Population: Healthy adults 18–65, general population, typical sleep duration 6.5–9 h; exclude current major respiratory illness, anosmia/hyposmia, and fragrance/odorant allergy.
- Design: Randomized, double‑blind, within‑subject crossover; two 14‑day conditions in counterbalanced order with a 7‑day washout:
  - Dawn‑odor condition: 1‑second odor pulses at T−40, T−25, T−10 minutes relative to predicted wake time.
  - Control condition: identical carrier air pulses (no odor).
- Optional mechanistic sub‑study (n=40 subset): third arm with pulses at T+30, T+45, T+60 minutes after wake to test time‑specificity independent of pleasant odor effects.

Intervention engineering
- Odorants: Phenethyl alcohol and vanillin (rotated across days to limit adaptation), selected for predominantly olfactory (non‑trigeminal) profiles to minimize arousal; concentrations titrated to remain below typical wake thresholds during sleep. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306452211000327?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery: Bedside, closed‑loop micro‑olfactometer with validated flow and on‑device timestamping; wake prediction via prior 7‑day actigraphy and adaptive schedule; no light, audio, or haptic co‑stimulation in the primary trial to keep the mechanism atomic.
- Compliance and masking: Identical hardware in both arms; micro‑pulses are inaudible and near‑odorless upon full wake.

Outcomes and measurements
- Primary physiological outcome: CAR area‑under‑the‑curve increase (AUCi) and slope across saliva samples at wake, +30, +45 minutes on days 7 and 14 of each arm, collected per Psychoneuroendocrinology 2022 guidelines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12819873/?utm_source=openai))
- Secondary outcomes:
  - Sleep inertia: 3‑minute psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale within 10 minutes of wake; subset comparison to recent sleep‑inertia odor data. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/49/Supplement_1/A80/8674233?utm_source=openai))
  - Next‑day affect: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) 4 times/day using validated positive/negative affect items.
  - Sleep and light covariates: Wrist actigraphy with light sensor; nightly sleep diaries; optional home EEG subset for stage timing.
  - Autonomic tone: Morning 5‑minute seated HRV (RMSSD).
- Covariate controls: Time‑stamped medication/caffeine/alcohol, menstrual phase where relevant, prior‑day stressor checklist; ambient morning light exposure binned by melanopic lux. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2717723/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted effect pattern
- If the limbic dawn cue is effective: steeper CAR slope/AUCi and reduced sleep inertia vs. control; EMA shows improved average valence next day; effects persist or strengthen by day 14 (entrainment/anticipation). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20408928/?utm_source=openai))
- Time‑specificity: No comparable CAR or inertia benefits when pulses occur post‑awakening (sub‑study).

Statistical analysis
- Mixed‑effects models with participant random intercepts/slopes; condition (odor vs. control) as fixed effect; adjust for within‑day sampling time deviations.
- Primary endpoint: ΔCAR AUCi (odor − control), two‑sided α=0.05.
- Mediation: Test whether CAR change mediates next‑day affect change via multilevel mediation.
- Sensitivity: Exclude days with >5‑minute deviation in first saliva sample timing; re‑analyze with light exposure strata.

Powering
- Assuming a small‑to‑moderate standardized effect on CAR AUCi (d=0.30) and within‑subject correlation 0.5, N=120 yields >80% power for the primary endpoint with two 14‑day periods and two CAR assessment days per period.

Risk management and safety
- Screen for odor sensitivities; start at low concentrations and auto‑abort pulse if device detects movement consistent with arousal.
- Use pure olfactory stimuli to avoid trigeminal co‑activation, which increases arousal risk. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306452211000327?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and feasibility
- Prior work shows: (a) olfactory inputs access amygdala–hypothalamic circuits; (b) pure olfactory stimuli influence brain activity during sleep without awakening; (c) pre‑awakening sensory changes (artificial dawn) shift CAR/inertia. However, pre‑awakening, pure‑olfactory micro‑pulses as a stand‑alone zeitgeber for morning endocrine dynamics and next‑day affect have not been tested. This project isolates that mechanism with objective endocrine, autonomic, and behavioral readouts. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK11071/?utm_source=openai))

Falsification and alternative interpretations
- If CAR and inertia do not change but mood improves, effects may be mediated by non‑HPA arousal pathways; follow‑up will add pupillometry/EEG markers upon awakening.
- If pulses occasionally wake participants, effect estimates will be biased; per‑protocol and intent‑to‑treat analyses will be reported, with arousal‑flag sensitivity checks. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15164891/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extensions (separate future trials)
- Multi‑site population synchronization of dawn pulses to test social zeitgeber augmentation without user effort. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4919368/?utm_source=openai))
- Orthogonal comparison to artificial dawn light to test additivity vs. redundancy of olfactory and photic cues. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306453003001604?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and deliverables
- Months 0–3: Device validation (flow, concentration, timestamp fidelity); preregistration.
- Months 4–12: Recruitment and data collection.
- Months 13–15: Analysis; release anonymized dataset and analysis code; preprint and journal submission.

Impact
A scalable, noninvasive environmental micro‑intervention—pre‑awakening pure‑olfactory pulses—could reduce population‑level morning inertia and improve next‑day affect without training or personalization. The work establishes whether limbic‑access chemosensory cues can function as practical zeitgebers for everyday emotion regulation. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK11071/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Adaptive Social Bandwidth Control for Everyday Emotion Regulation: A privacy-preserving, context-aware JIT intervention grounded in resilient social timing

Rationale
- Social buffering attenuates HPA-axis and sympathetic responses, but effects depend on timing, relationship quality, and context; oxytocin is implicated yet inconsistent in humans. These properties suggest that when and how social input arrives matters for stress regulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3844011/?utm_source=openai))
- Executive control supports top‑down regulation of limbic responses; when working memory is taxed, reappraisal efficacy drops. Therefore, reducing high‑entropy social input during low-capacity windows should preserve appraisal precision. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9081270/?utm_source=openai))
- Batching notifications reduces stress and improves well‑being, but fixed schedules ignore individual state and context. JITAI literature shows promise but highlights weak triggering logic and heterogeneous effects, motivating state‑dependent delivery. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563219302596?utm_source=openai))
- Passive, on‑device extraction of non‑linguistic acoustic features (prosody, turn‑taking) is feasible without retaining audio content, enabling privacy‑preserving estimation of social context and arousal. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17061?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat everyday social input as a controllable throughput variable; when inferred executive capacity is low or arousal high, gate and compress incoming social information until capacity rebounds. This preserves representational precision for appraisals, averts unnecessary limbic escalation, and thereby reduces anxiety/depressive affect.

Hypothesis
A smartphone-based, privacy-preserving Social Bandwidth Controller (SBC) that contextually gates and sequences social input using on‑device acoustic and activity markers will reduce same‑day anxiety and negative affect versus non‑adaptive batching or business‑as‑usual. Effects are mediated by preserved executive control during vulnerable intervals and enhanced recovery following stressors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9081270/?utm_source=openai))

Study overview
- Population: General adult smartphone users (non‑patients), diverse occupations; n≈600 across phases.
- Non-invasive sensors: Phone OS notifications/API logs, lock/unlock/app switches, on‑device acoustic features (no content), optional smartwatch HR/HRV.
- Primary outcomes: Momentary anxiety/negative affect (EMA), daily state anxiety; secondary: HRV indices, voice‑derived arousal indices, sleep regularity, PHQ‑8/GAD‑7 at baseline/week 4/8. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41669161/?utm_source=openai))

Phase 0: Discovery of resilient timing signatures
- Recruit a resilient cohort (top decile on stress recovery indices over 4 weeks). Learn signatures linking social interaction timing/topology and acoustic context to same‑day/laged mood stability (e.g., optimal windows after conversational offsets, low arousal prosody periods). These serve as priors for personalization in later phases. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7453326/?utm_source=openai))

Intervention platform (SBC)
- State estimation (on device):
  - Acoustic scene: speech presence, overlap, turn‑taking tempo, energy/pitch variability as arousal proxies; ambient class (quiet/crowd/vehicle). Raw audio discarded; features computed locally (e.g., openSMILE‑class toolchain). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17061?utm_source=openai))
  - Cognitive load/interruptibility proxies: notification rate, app switching entropy, recent interaction density, time‑of‑day chronotype priors.
- Control policy:
  - During low-capacity/high‑arousal windows, hold non‑priority notifications; release in brief, predictable micro‑batches containing low‑entropy summaries and safety‑relevant items; defer high‑entropy threads until recovery windows inferred from priors and recent acoustic calm. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563219302596?utm_source=openai))
  - During high-capacity windows, permit richer social inflow and promote structured replies.
- Privacy: All feature extraction and gating decisions occur on-device; only de‑identified logits for analytics leave device. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17061?utm_source=openai))

Phase 1: Micro‑randomized trial (MRT) to test proximal effects
- N≈200 for 4 weeks; 4–6 random decision points/day when notifications arrive or conversational offsets are detected.
- Randomized treatment options at each decision:
  1) Adaptive gating (SBC policy).
  2) Fixed‑time batching (3x/day).
  3) Business‑as‑usual (immediate delivery).
- Proximal outcomes within 90 min: EMA stress/anxiety; HRV 10‑min window if available; voice arousal index from brief prompted vowel task (optional). Weighted and centered least squares (WCLS) estimates marginal causal effects and context moderation. Success criterion: mean proximal anxiety reduction ≥0.10 SD vs BAU, ≥0.07 SD vs fixed batching. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03544?utm_source=openai))

Phase 2: 8‑week parallel‑arm RCT for cumulative effects
- Arms: (A) Adaptive SBC; (B) Fixed batching; (C) BAU. N≈300.
- Primary endpoint: Change in daily state anxiety slope and mean negative affect; Secondary: PHQ‑8/GAD‑7 change, HRV RMSSD change, notification burden, engagement.
- Mechanism tests: Weekly 2‑min mobile n‑back/updating probe to index executive capacity; mediation tested via within‑person paths from gating→reduced interruption load→preserved capacity→lower affect. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25947896/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory sub‑study (optional add‑on)
- Safety‑cue micro‑affiliation: In identified recovery windows, prompt 10–20‑second low‑effort affiliative signals (acknowledgment/thanks/emoji) to peers with auto‑reciprocation nudges; test whether repeated pairings function as conditioned safety (CS– or CI) and further shorten recovery tails. Outcomes: time‑to‑baseline after self‑reported stressor; neural plausibility anchored in vmPFC/striatal circuitry for safety learning. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35577553/?utm_source=openai))

Analytic plan
- MRT: WCLS for proximal effects, context moderation by acoustic arousal, prior sleep, time of day. Sensitivity analyses excluding work‑critical alerts.
- RCT: Mixed models for repeated measures; mediation via time‑varying capacity indices; heterogeneity by baseline social load.
- Power: Simulations using prior batching effect sizes (≈0.2–0.3 SD) suggest ≥80% power for hypothesized contrasts at proposed N. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563219302596?utm_source=openai))

Risk management and ethics
- Respect critical communications: Always‑allow lists; emergency bypass.
- Burden: EMA ≤3/day; optional HRV and vowel tasks; immediate opt‑out.
- Privacy: No raw audio stored or transmitted; acoustic features only; transparent on‑device processing. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17061?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and contribution
- Advances beyond fixed batching and generic JITAIs by controlling social information flow based on real‑time, content‑free acoustic/context estimates and resilient timing priors, explicitly targeting the executive‑capacity bottleneck that undermines top‑down regulation. This is distinct from therapy content or generic digital CBT. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563219302596?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and deliverables
- Year 1: Platform build; Phase 0 discovery dataset and priors.
- Year 2: Phase 1 MRT results, open‑sourced anonymized feature schema.
- Year 3: Phase 2 RCT outcomes; policy artifacts for OS‑level notification APIs; preregistered datasets.

Go/no‑go criteria
- Proceed to RCT if MRT shows proximal anxiety reduction ≥0.10 SD vs BAU and no increase in missed critical communications. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03544?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Phase-aligned, latency-staggered multisensory micro-interventions for everyday emotion regulation

Hypothesis–question
Does timing brief multisensory safety cues to (a) endogenous respiratory/cardiac phases that favor parasympathetic dominance and (b) sub-second multisensory temporal binding windows reduce autonomic arousal in everyday contexts more than simultaneous or off-phase delivery, and do personalized timing policies learned from biosignals generalize across contexts? The atomic strategy is to use time (phase and intermodal latency) as the primary control variable to minimize interoceptive–exteroceptive mismatch and permit vagal rebound. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale (mechanistic checks)
- Slow paced breathing near 0.1 Hz maximally engages baroreflex resonance, increasing HRV and vagal indices; heart rate rises during inhalation and falls during exhalation (RSA). Exhalation and diastolic/cardiac-cycle timing modulate interoceptive processing, including heartbeat-evoked potentials. Aligning external cues to these phases should amplify parasympathetic shifts with minimal energy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9088144/?utm_source=openai))
- Nasal respiration phase entrains human limbic oscillations (olfactory cortex, amygdala, hippocampus), and olfactory access is locked to the sniff cycle, supporting phase-precise odor micro-pulses at inhalation onset. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Multisensory inputs integrate within limited temporal binding windows (tens to hundreds of milliseconds). Auditory and tactile channels are processed faster than vision; olfaction is constrained by sniff-timed access with decisions unfolding within a single sniff. Staggering modalities inside the binding window can shape a coherent “single event” safety signal while avoiding additive alerts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3711231/?utm_source=openai))
- Speech acoustics covary with arousal and autonomic markers; while inter-speaker variability is substantial, features such as F0 and rate provide an ecologically available adjunct to HRV/EDA for personalization in the wild. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12289014/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Demonstrate that phase-locked, latency-staggered multisensory micro-interventions acutely increase vagal indices (RMSSD/HF-HRV) and reduce sympathetic indices (EDA) more than simultaneous or off-phase controls in healthy adults. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))
2) Identify subject-specific timing policies that maximize autonomic calming across contexts using online reinforcement learning with HRV/EDA and speech features as reward signals. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/26/5/1584?utm_source=openai))
3) Test generalization to daily life: do personalized timing policies reduce momentary stress and maintain effect without habituation over four weeks?

Design overview
- Population: 150 adults (18–65), no psychiatric diagnoses, screened for scent sensitivities.
- Device: a neck/upper‑sternum wearable delivering low-amplitude vibrotactile cues; ear-level warm auditory tones via open earbuds; collar-mounted micro‑diffused odor pulses; optional ambient light dimming via smart bulb. Sensors: wrist PPG for HRV; microphone for speech features (opt-in); accelerometer; optional finger EDA. All interventions are non-invasive and suitable for everyday use.
- Study phases:
  1) Lab calibration (single session): determine individual resonance breathing frequency; map respiratory and cardiac phase; measure TBW for audio–tactile–visual via simultaneity judgments; calibrate olfactory percept thresholds.
  2) Crossover efficacy (2 weeks, home + brief daily probes): randomized blocks comparing four conditions: A) phase-aligned, latency-staggered cascade; B) simultaneous multisensory off-phase; C) single-modality paced-breathing audio at 0.1 Hz (active control); D) minimal-sham. Each block contains multiple 2–3 min micro-sessions per day during self-reported stress windows.
  3) Personalization/generalization (2 additional weeks): RL policy optimizes the timing parameters of condition A only; evaluate ecological outcomes.

Intervention timing (condition A)
- Respiratory/cardiac phase:
  - Deliver a low-frequency vibrotactile down-ramp during late exhalation to coincide with peak cardiovagal influence; avoid strong cues during early inhalation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))
  - Gate a brief odor micro‑pulse to inhalation onset to exploit sniff-locked olfactory access to limbic circuits; limit concentration to just‑detectable or sub‑threshold familiarity cues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Intermodal staggering inside the temporal binding window:
  - Initiate a soft auditory tone, then vibrotactile cue 40–80 ms later, visual dimming after an additional 80–120 ms; keep total offset within 200 ms so the packet is bound as one event rather than multiple alerts. This sequence leverages faster auditory/tactile latencies relative to vision to preframe the subsequent cues as “benign.” ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20436185/?utm_source=openai))
- Anti-habituation:
  - Apply low-amplitude temporal jitter (±30 ms) to offsets and rotate between 2–3 safe odor notes to preserve novelty without breaking phase alignment. (Inference from binding-window tolerance.) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3711231/?utm_source=openai))

Controls
- B) Simultaneous, off-phase: identical modalities delivered concurrently, triggered randomly with respect to exhale/inhale and cardiac cycle.
- C) Paced breathing only at 0.1 Hz via audio guide.
- D) Minimal-sham: inaudible audio carrier; imperceptible vibration; no odor.

Outcomes and measures
- Primary acute endpoint: within-subject change in RMSSD and HF-HRV (0.15–0.40 Hz) during and 2 min post-micro-session vs 2 min pre, aggregated per condition. Resonance-breathing literature supports HRV/baroreflex sensitivity as responsive autonomic markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))
- Secondary acute endpoints: tonic and phasic EDA; self-reported state stress (single-item EMA); speech-derived arousal index (composite of F0, spectral tilt, speech rate, and pause structure) when speaking occurs, cautiously interpreted due to inter-speaker variability. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/26/5/1584?utm_source=openai))
- Exploratory: phase-specific effects (exhalation vs inhalation) on heartbeat-evoked potentials (subset with EEG headband) and detection of tactile probes time-locked to respiratory/cardiac phase. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11016802/?utm_source=openai))
- Longitudinal outcomes: daily stress EMA, sleep quality single-item, and HRV baseline drift over weeks.

Personalization (aim 2)
- Policy space: timing parameters only (no intensity escalation). The RL agent adapts three knobs: respiratory phase angle of onset, intermodal offsets, and odor-release alignment to the detected sniff onset. Reward is a short-horizon composite: ΔRMSSD (z-scored per subject), EDA reduction, and, when available, a decrease in speech-derived arousal index. This prioritizes a single global control variable—time—without adding modalities. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/26/5/1584?utm_source=openai))
- Safety constraints: maximum odor pulses/hour; minimum inter-session intervals; avoidance of cues during driving (phone motion proxy).

Analytic plan
- Efficacy (aim 1): within-subject linear mixed models comparing condition A vs B/C/D on primary and secondary endpoints; order and time-of-day as covariates.
- Mechanism checks: interaction of respiratory/cardiac phase with autonomic outcomes; mediation by exhalation alignment predicted to explain a significant proportion of A’s effect. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11016802/?utm_source=openai))
- Generalization (aim 3): compare pre- vs post-personalization week in free-living EMA stress and baseline HRV; evaluate whether learned phase/offset parameters converge toward subject-specific optima stable across contexts.

Power
- Detecting a small-to-moderate within-subject RMSSD effect (Cohen’s dz ≈ 0.35) at α = 0.05, 1–β = 0.9 requires ≈ 85 participants; we recruit 150 to accommodate attrition and missing data.

Novelty and prior art assessment
- Slow-breathing and HRV biofeedback at 0.1 Hz are established, but they do not exploit cross-modal, sub-second staggering nor respiratory/cardiac-phase gating of multisensory safety packets. Prior work documents phase-dependent modulation of perception/interoception and limbic entrainment by nasal respiration, as well as multisensory temporal binding windows; however, their integration into a timing-first, everyday multisensory calming intervention appears underexplored. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and risk management
- Measurement: PPG for HRV is robust for short windows; respiratory phase estimated from PPG-derived respiration with optional chest band in calibration. Speech features are used opportunistically and interpreted with caution given variability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12289014/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Individual differences in binding windows and odor sensitivity; mitigated by per-subject calibration and conservative odor dosing.
- Habituation: Managed via micro-jitter within TBW and rotation among familiar-safe odor notes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3711231/?utm_source=openai))

Falsifiable predictions
- A > B/C/D on RMSSD/HF-HRV during and post-session; the benefit diminishes when cues are shifted ±90° off exhalation peak or when intermodal offsets exceed the TBW. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))
- Odor pulses at inhalation onset yield larger autonomic benefit than identical pulses delivered mid-exhalation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Personalized timing policies converge to stable phase/offset parameters and maintain effects over four weeks without intensity escalation.

Milestones
- Months 0–3: hardware/software build; IRB; pilot timing accuracy (≤40 ms onset jitter; sniff-onset detection <100 ms).
- Months 4–8: lab calibration + crossover efficacy (aim 1).
- Months 9–12: personalization/generalization (aim 2–3); preregistered analyses; data release.

Impact
Proving that precise phase alignment and intermodal staggering—without altering content or intensity—can systematically lower autonomic arousal would establish time as a scalable, non-invasive mechanism for everyday emotion regulation, extend HRV biofeedback principles, and open a design space for timing-first multisensory interventions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7578229/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Cardiac-cycle-locked neck micro-mechanostimulation to preempt sympathetic escalation for everyday anxiety regulation

Integrated hypothesis–question
Can brief, noninvasive micro-mechanical pulses applied over carotid baroreceptor–adjacent skin, precisely time-locked to the cardiac cycle when baroreceptor afferents naturally fire, increase baroreflex sensitivity and transiently suppress locus coeruleus–mediated arousal, thereby intercepting the early autonomic drift that precedes conscious anxiety episodes in daily life? ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538172/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use timing, not intensity, as the control variable: deliver subthreshold-to-weak vibro/pressure “augment” pulses to the anterior–lateral neck at the carotid sinus level, phase-locked to the systolic baroreceptor burst (≈50 ms after the ECG R-peak at the sinus), to reinforce NTS→CVLM inhibition of RVLM and transiently bias parasympathetic dominance before subjective anxiety forms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7854574/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Detect precursor autonomic drift in free-living conditions.
- Build a wrist/ear wearable pipeline estimating beat-to-beat intervals and cardiac phase (PPG + inertial surrogates); track ultra‑short HF-HRV, pre‑ejection proxies, and electrodermal slope to forecast 1–10 min windows of rising sympathetic weighting and falling baroreflex sensitivity. Benchmark forecasting against self-reported anxiety probes and passive digital markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12789550/?utm_source=openai))

2) Engineer and validate cardiac‑locked neck micro‑mechanostimulation.
- Actuator: low‑amplitude, wideband vibro/impulse transducer in a soft collar, placed immediately lateral/superior to the cricoid cartilage (SCM window) to couple energy safely through superficial tissues.
- Timing: personalize R‑to‑carotid transit using initial calibration; schedule 30–80 ms pulses at early systole and brief diastolic “no‑pulse” baselines. Start at ≤0.2 g peak skin acceleration; adapt within a capped range.
- Physiological validation in-lab: randomized, within‑subject blocks comparing systolic‑locked vs diastolic‑locked vs sham pulses during quiet rest and mild stressor. Endpoints: baroreflex sensitivity (sequence/TFA), HF‑HRV, skin conductance slope, and beat‑locked bradycardic micro‑responses. Safety: exclude carotid disease/syncope history; continuous BP/SpO2 monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7854574/?utm_source=openai))

3) Test real‑world interception of anxiety drift.
- 4‑week, randomized, N‑of‑1 and crossover trial (closed‑loop vs open‑loop vs sham) in non‑clinical adults with frequent daily stressors. Primary outcomes: (a) increase in spontaneous BRS during predicted‑risk windows; (b) reduction in the proportion of predicted anxiety windows that culminate in self‑reported episodes; (c) dose–response: fewer pulses over time for same stabilization (minimum effective dose). Secondary: ecological momentary anxiety, task‑evoked arousal reactivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3327298/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and mechanistic checkpoints
- Baroreflex afferents to NTS inhibit sympathetic premotor neurons (via CVLM→RVLM), slowing HR and reducing vascular tone within fractions of a second; phasic baroreceptor activity gates cortical processing and raises pain thresholds at systole. Reinforcing the systolic afferent volley should transiently lower arousal gain. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538172/?utm_source=openai))
- LC neurons are inhibited by heartbeat‑frequency baroreceptor activation; amplifying the natural phasic inhibition offers a route to damp noradrenergic “alarm” before it scales. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0306452294904405?utm_source=openai))
- External mechanical manipulation of carotid baroreceptors is well established with neck chambers and can be synchronized to the cardiac cycle; recent data show anterior‑neck vibration alters BRS and cerebrovascular variables, supporting feasibility of a wearable mechanical approach, though not yet cardiac‑locked. This project translates lab‑grade timing (PRES) into a safe, low‑intensity, consumer‑grade actuation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7854574/?utm_source=openai))
- Physiological precursors to panic/anxiety (HR rise, CO2 shifts, reduced vagal indices) can occur minutes to an hour before awareness, enabling predictive, just‑in‑time intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3327298/?utm_source=openai))

Methods in detail
- Sensing and timing
  - Cardiac phase: ear/wrist PPG with adaptive pulse‑transit estimation; optional ECG sticker in lab. Trigger pulses ≈50 ms after detected R‑peak equivalent at carotid sinus, updated by continual transit‑time calibration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7854574/?utm_source=openai))
  - Drift detection: sliding‑window HF‑HRV (0.15–0.4 Hz) and BRS‑sequence indices; electrodermal slope; respiration proxies from PPG‑derived respiration. A Kalman filter flags divergence (falling HF‑HRV, BRS) and schedules pulse trains during risk windows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12789550/?utm_source=openai))
- Actuation parameters
  - Pulse shape: 50–100 Hz damped burst or 20–30 ms tap, amplitude‑modulated to minimize habituation; delivered for 5–10 consecutive beats, then reassess.
  - Spatial targeting: bilateral symmetry testing; explore asymmetry effects noted for carotid stimulation (left cardiac vs right pressure effects). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40385741/?utm_source=openai))
- In‑lab protocol (Aim 2)
  - Participants: healthy 18–45, n≈36, triple‑condition crossover.
  - Tasks: quiet rest; speech anticipation; Stroop.
  - Measures: beat‑to‑beat BP (Finapres), ECG/PPG, EDA, respiration; BRS (sequence, transfer function). Analysis: linear mixed models with condition×task; pre‑registered contrasts.
- Field protocol (Aim 3)
  - App‑based EMA prompts 4–6×/day for state anxiety; passive data logging; automated, blinded stimulation conditions per block.
  - Primary analysis: within‑person differences in “predicted‑risk window” conversion to episodes across arms; secondary, daily mean BRS and HF‑HRV.

Outcomes and decision criteria
- Success if systolic‑locked pulses acutely increase BRS ≥15% over diastolic‑locked and sham, and reduce predicted‑risk window conversions by ≥20% in closed‑loop vs sham, without adverse events. Dose efficiency improves over 4 weeks (≥30% reduction in pulses/day at equal or better stabilization).

Safety and ethics
- Exclusions: known carotid disease, syncope, arrhythmias, uncontrolled HTN, pregnancy.
- Limits: maximal surface acceleration, duty cycle caps, auto‑abort on bradycardia/hypotension. Medical oversight in lab sessions; adverse‑event hotline in field.

Innovation
- Prior work uses bulky neck chambers for phasic carotid stimulation and shows baroreceptor‑locked sensory gating; no consumer‑grade, cutaneous micro‑mechanical, cardiac‑locked baroreflex augmentation has been evaluated for preventive affect regulation in everyday contexts. This project operationalizes cardiac‑phase as a controllable variable to stabilize autonomic state pre‑consciously. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0301051195051791?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extension (optional)
- Compare cardiac‑locked vs respiration‑locked pulse scheduling during paced nasal breathing to test cardiorespiratory phase interactions on BRS and anxiety reactivity. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2012.00314/full?utm_source=openai))

References (key mechanistic and feasibility sources)
- Baroreflex physiology and central pathways: StatPearls; Frontiers reviews. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK538172/?utm_source=openai))
- LC inhibition by baroreceptor activation: electrophysiology. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0306452294904405?utm_source=openai))
- Cardiac‑phase sensory gating and neck‑cuff phasic stimulation: human studies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8480547/?utm_source=openai))
- Anterior‑neck vibration alters BRS/cerebrovascular measures: feasibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12551627/?utm_source=openai))
- Physiological precursors of panic/anxiety detectable before awareness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3327298/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline
- Months 0–6: device and timing calibration; IRB; Aim 2 pilot (n=12).
- Months 7–14: full Aim 2 (n=36); parameter optimization.
- Months 15–24: Aim 3 field trial; analysis; go/no‑go on larger pragmatic study based on predefined success criteria.

Title
Time-Stamped Poly(A) Tagging (TiSPAT): sequential, orthogonally photoactivated barcodes covalently written onto native mRNAs in the same live cell for single end-point, transcriptome-wide trajectory readout

Integrated hypothesis–goal
A cell’s evolving transcriptome can be captured at seven or more defined times (30 min to 24 h after a perturbation) in the very same live cell by repeatedly and selectively “writing” orthogonal molecular time-stamps onto the poly(A) tails of whatever mRNAs exist at each time. If these time-stamps are covalently attached at low occupancy and remain inert thereafter, a single end-point sequencing of each cell will decode its full, multi-timepoint trajectory with statistical power across many cells.

Atomic strategy
Invert repeated destructive sampling by converting ephemeral abundance at time ti into a durable, intracellular molecular memory: at each ti, uncage only the Ti probe so it hybridizes to poly(A) and becomes covalently crosslinked to nearby RNA, thereby appending a unique time barcode to the subset of mRNAs present at that moment. Repeat ≥7 times. At the end, lyse once, sequence once, and reconstruct per-cell trajectories from the barcode composition of each gene’s reads.

Specific aims
1) Chemistry and optics: Build a 7-color, orthogonally uncageable, low-occupancy oligo(dT)-barcode probe set bearing photo-crosslinkers that react in RNA–DNA heteroduplexes in live cells.
2) Single-cell longitudinal recording: Demonstrate ≥7 log-spaced time-stamps (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 h) in the same viable cell after a defined perturbation, and recover per-cell, per-gene trajectories from one end-point library.
3) Validation and scale: Benchmark TiSPAT trajectories against gold-standard destructive time courses, quantify distortion/perturbation bounds, and scale to thousands of cells for heterogeneity analysis.

Rationale and feasibility
- Live-cell, light-gated oligonucleotides have been delivered and activated inside single cells and intact tissues to bind endogenous mRNA (TIVA probes), establishing the feasibility of intracellular caged capture strands and 405-nm activation in viable cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4586300/?utm_source=openai))
- Orthogonal photocages enable sequential, wavelength-selective uncaging in cells (e.g., DEACM vs nitroveratryl; multi-level uncaging from 505→440→365→313 nm), supporting 7-timepoint scheduling without cross-activation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6499933/?utm_source=openai))
- Photo-crosslinkers such as diazirines and benzophenones form covalent adducts upon UV/near-UV activation and have been used on nucleic-acid probes and in RNA–DNA heteroduplex contexts, enabling stable capture of the hybridized poly(A) segment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8341421/?utm_source=openai))
- Sequential optical control of RNAs in single cells with distinct wavelengths has been demonstrated, supporting time-sliced activation in live cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32484653/?utm_source=openai))
- This approach is mechanistically distinct from ADAR-based RNA “timestamps,” which require engineered reporter transcripts and do not time-stamp the native, full transcriptome. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7956158/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1. Chemistry and optics
1.1 Probe architecture
- Seven probes Pi (i=1..7), each comprises: 12–15 nt 2′-OMe/LNA oligo(dT) capture core; unique 12–16 nt time barcode Ti; a photocage specific to λi that masks hybridization (e.g., DEACM, NV, NPP, NDBF, thio-DEACM, coumarin variants); and 2–4 diazirine/benzophenone moieties along the backbone to crosslink upon 355–365 nm pulses. Low occupancy is enforced by sub-nanomolar intracellular free concentration and short illumination windows to avoid translation/decay perturbation at poly(A). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24111849/?utm_source=openai))
- Probes are rendered cell-permeant via reversible masking (e.g., cleavable, bioreducible masking of phosphates) or by endocytosis with gentle carriers; all probes are preloaded at t<0.

1.2 Uncaging and crosslinking schedule
- At each timepoint ti: Step A, illuminate at λi (e.g., 640, 594, 561, 514, 488, 445, 405 nm; order chosen to minimize spectral bleed) for 5–15 s to remove the photocage from Pi, allowing annealing to poly(A). Step B, deliver a brief global 355–365 nm pulse (0.5–2 s, minimal dose) to activate diazirine/benzophenone and covalently fix Pi onto the poly(A)–oligo(dT) heteroduplex. Non-uncaged probes cannot anneal and thus are not crosslinked during Step B. Repeat across ≥7 log-spaced times. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32484653/?utm_source=openai))
- Illumination is widefield to process thousands of cells in parallel; power and duty cycle are tuned to remain within viability windows established by prior live-cell, light-controlled oligo methods. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4586300/?utm_source=openai))

Controls and characterization
- In vitro RNA–DNA duplex crosslink yield vs pulse energy; sequence bias assessment using synthetic poly(A) standards with controlled A-content and spike-in RNAs. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/chemlett/article/doi/10.1093/chemle/upae152/7739877?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-activation matrix: quantify unintended uncaging at off-wavelengths; accept ≤1% cross-talk per step. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24111849/?utm_source=openai))
- Phototoxicity bounds: viability, ROS, and transcriptional stress markers after 7 cycles; accept ≥90% viability and ≤10% stress-response induction by bulk RNA-seq relative to dark controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4586300/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Single-cell longitudinal recording
2.1 Biological system and perturbations
- Use adherent mammalian cells with well-characterized transcriptional responses (e.g., serum refeeding, cytokine stimulation, or a small-molecule inhibitor) at t=0. Record at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 h.

2.2 End-point library design
- At 24 h, lyse once. Use a 3′-capture library where Read 1 identifies the gene and poly(A) junction; Read 2 reads the covalently attached time-barcode cassette Ti. Because crosslinkers can block RT, incorporate short reverse-transcription conditions with strand-displacing polymerase and adapter designs that traverse the barcode flank; include a chemical deprotection step if needed to bypass adducts, as in Chem-CLIP-derived workflows. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666166724004362?utm_source=openai))
- Demultiplex per cell (cell barcode) and per time (Ti) to produce a count matrix: gene × time for each single cell.

2.3 Quantitative criteria
- Per timepoint, detect ≥1,000 genes at UMI ≥1 in ≥80% of cells; per gene, coefficient of variation across technical replicates ≤0.3; cross-time leakage of barcodes ≤2%.

2.4 Same-cell verification
- Spike-in a minority of cells preloaded with a distinct, cell-identity barcode probe that is not time-gated; verify that all Ti for a given well co-occur only with that cell-ID barcode, excluding cross-cell contamination.

Aim 3. Validation and scale
3.1 Benchmarking against destructive gold standards
- Split replicate cultures: run TiSPAT in one, and perform conventional bulk/scRNA-seq at each time in the other. Compare per-gene trajectories via dynamic time-warping and impulse-response fits; accept median Pearson r ≥0.7 per gene across time, after deconvolving the expected 3′-bias intrinsic to oligo(dT) capture.

3.2 Bias audits
- Assess 3′ UTR length, poly(A) length, and RNA half-life dependencies of tagging probability; correct with calibration curves and spike-ins to minimize systematic distortion in trajectory inference.

3.3 Throughput and heterogeneity
- Implement micro-patterned wells or microfluidic chambers for thousands of individually addressed cells per run; global illumination enables simultaneous time-stamping of all wells. Analyze inter-cell heterogeneity in response amplitude, timing, and adaptation.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Phototoxicity from repeated illumination: minimize exposure with high-quantum-yield cages, use far-red cages for early steps, confine UVA to sub-second pulses, and verify transcriptional integrity post-recording. Prior live-tissue TIVA activation supports feasibility of repeated, short 405-nm exposures when doses are constrained. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4586300/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-activation between cages: choose cages with well-separated action spectra and validate the cross-activation matrix empirically; adjust wavelength order and intensity per step. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24111849/?utm_source=openai))
- Crosslinking efficiency and RT blockage: distribute multiple diazirines/benzophenones to raise yield at low UVA dose; adapt RT and ligation steps to traverse adducts as in photoaffinity/chem-CLIP workflows. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666166724004362?utm_source=openai))
- Biological perturbation by transient poly(A) occupancy: enforce low occupancy (<5% of each mRNA species per step) and brief hybridization to limit interference with PABP-mediated processes; monitor decay/translation markers to confirm negligible global impact.

Milestones
- M1 (Months 0–6): Synthesize 7 fully orthogonal Pi; validate uncaging selectivity and heteroduplex crosslinking in vitro.
- M2 (Months 6–12): Show 7-step time-stamping and viability in cells; demonstrate end-point recovery of barcodes from ≥1,000 genes/cell.
- M3 (Months 12–18): Benchmark trajectories vs destructive time courses; deploy on ≥2 perturbations; scale to >1,000 cells and quantify heterogeneity.

Outcome and impact
TiSPAT converts dynamic, native mRNA abundance into an intracellular, multi-timepoint molecular ledger, enabling true same-cell transcriptome trajectories from a single end-point readout at scale. It is mechanistically distinct from pseudotime, metabolic labeling, lineage barcoding, few-gene reporters, Live-seq/aspiration, and ADAR-based RNA timestamping, because it time-stamps the endogenous transcriptome in situ via sequential, orthogonal photochemistry and covalent fixation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4586300/?utm_source=openai))

References (selected feasibility anchors)
- Live-cell caged oligo capture and activation (TIVA). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4586300/?utm_source=openai))
- Orthogonal wavelength-selective uncaging in cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24111849/?utm_source=openai))
- Photo-crosslinkers on nucleic-acid probes and RNA–DNA heteroduplex crosslinking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8341421/?utm_source=openai))
- Sequential optical control of RNAs with distinct wavelengths. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32484653/?utm_source=openai))
- ADAR “RNA timestamp” labels engineered transcripts, not native transcriptome. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7956158/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title: ChronoPhase: Same-cell, multi-interval transcriptome recording via age-programmed phase-partition capture with single end-point readout

Hypothesis and goal
- Hypothesis: The kinetics of material aging in an intracellular, phase-separated RNA-capture condensate can encode absolute time into the probability that newly transcribed mRNAs are sequestered during discrete windows. By presetting multiple, log-spaced partition thresholds that are crossed autonomously as the condensate ages, a single mild cue can later convert these time-encoded states into separable molecular records, enabling ≥7 time points from 30 min to 24 h in the same living cell.
- Goal: Build and validate an intracellular capture-and-encode system that (i) continuously samples polyadenylated RNA from the cytosol within defined windows after a perturbation at t=0, (ii) assigns each captured cohort a stable, sequence-readable time index, and (iii) provides either non-destructive staged release or single end-point decoding for transcriptome-wide profiling of individual-cell response trajectories.

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
- Convert time into a sequence of phase-partition boundary crossings. Engineer one condensate whose apparent affinity for mRNA-capture modules shifts in a preprogrammed, monotonic way (by intrinsic linker aging), so that “windows” open and close without external commands. One shared, late cue (e.g., salt/osmolyte shift or light) converts these embedded states into physically or chemically separable cohorts. This relies on established control of condensate assembly/disassembly and release kinetics in cells but applies it to time-encoding rather than delivery. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11582321/?utm_source=openai))

Proposed system
- Component A: Time-programmed capture condensate (TPCC)
  - A cytosolic peptide–nucleic-acid coacervate “bead” (1–3 μm) nucleated by a membrane-anchored scaffold to keep one per cell and reduce cell-to-cell variability.
  - Capture chemistry: multivalent oligo(dT)20–24 conjugated to a weak, reversible RNA-binding scaffold (PABP RRM mutants with reduced competition for translation; low expression) to sample poly(A)+ RNA broadly with limited perturbation.
  - Time encoding: a palette of orthogonal, hydrolysis-prone charge-masking linkers (e.g., thioesters, aryl esters, acetals, carbamates, and redox-labile disulfides) interspersed in the cationic peptide network. Each linker class reduces net positive charge or crosslink density with a characteristic intracellular half-life (t1/2 ≈ 0.5 h to 24 h), shifting the TPCC’s partition coefficient for poly(A)+-bound complexes at preset times.
  - Rationale: Coacervate partitioning and release are steep functions of charge density, crowding, and hydration; programmable peptide coacervates with tunable uptake/release have been demonstrated in mammalian cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11582321/?utm_source=openai))
- Component B: Time-index barcodes
  - Each TPCC is preloaded with seven short, sequence-distinct DNA barcodes (B1–B7), each masked by a kinetically distinct protective group that unmasks in the same half-life series used for partition tuning.
  - When a barcode unmasks, it can be ligated to captured mRNAs via splinted ligation using an encapsulated, low-activity ligase that functions only within the condensate microenvironment; result is stable barcode-on-mRNA adducts that survive downstream processing.
- Readout options
  1) Single end-point readout (primary path): At 24 h, gently lyse cells; isolate TPCCs on density/affinity; perform RNA-seq with pull-down of barcode–RNA conjugates to recover seven time-stamped transcriptomes per cell in one library.
  2) Non-destructive staged release (secondary path): Instead of barcoding, encode seven detachment thresholds; apply one mild osmotic/salt cue at 24 h to place the system near the transition. As the aged network crosses thresholds, bound RNPs or vesicle-bound RNA carriers are expelled in seven bursts collected from supernatant; examples of reversible EV capture/release with desthiobiotin/biotin chemistry support staged, gentle harvesting, though here used at collection surfaces ex vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7328786/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Build and calibrate TPCC materials with log-spaced aging kinetics.
  - Construct a five-chemistry library of cationic peptide scaffolds bearing distinct degradable linkers; form condensates in HEK293 and one primary-cell model.
  - Quantify charge decay and dissolution thresholds in live cells by ratiometric reporters; fit first-order kinetics to select seven linkers giving target half-lives spanning 0.5–24 h.
  - Milestone: Seven distinct inflection times (±15%) for partition shift under physiological conditions.
- Aim 2: Demonstrate time-windowed capture of endogenous poly(A)+ RNA.
  - Express low-level oligo(dT)-RRM capture modules that partition into TPCC only when the local net charge exceeds a threshold; measure capture windows by spike-in RNAs turned on at known times.
  - Validate that captured RNA mirrors whole-transcriptome proportions (allowing sampling noise) and that global translation/viability are minimally perturbed (cell growth, polysome profiling).
  - Milestone: ≥70% of captured reads map to poly(A)+ mRNA; <15% change in global translation rate vs control.
- Aim 3: Encode time indexes and perform single end-point decoding after a perturbation at t=0.
  - At t=0, administer drug/genetic perturbation; TPCC ages autonomously, opening capture windows around 0.5 h, 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, 8 h, 12 h, 24 h.
  - At 24 h, lyse and perform library prep selective for barcode–RNA adducts; demultiplex reads by barcode to recover seven transcriptomes per cell.
  - Compare reconstructed trajectories to RNA timestamping (ADAR-based) benchmarks for selected transcripts to cross-validate temporal fidelity, noting that ADAR methods infer RNA age from accumulated A→I edits rather than physical capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7956158/?utm_source=openai))
  - Milestone: Per-cell trajectories with ≥7 time bins, each with ≥2,000 genes at UMI ≥3, and consistent ordering vs ADAR-based age inference for shared reporters.

Experimental design and methods
- Materials engineering
  - Peptide scaffold: Lys/Arg-rich with periodic degradable linkers; include minor hydrophobes to tune mesh.
  - Linker palette: choose chemistries with well-separated intracellular half-lives and orthogonal sensitivities; characterize in vitro, then in cells by FRET charge sensors.
  - Condensate nucleation: membrane-tethered low-copy scaffold (e.g., GAP43 peptide) to confine a single TPCC per cell and maintain cytosolic access.
- Capture and indexing
  - Capture module: oligo(dT)20 fused to minimized RRM scaffold; low expression by weak promoter; quantify occupancy vs free mRNA by smFISH.
  - Barcodes: seven 18–22 nt sequences prehybridized to orthogonal, kinetically unmasking hairpins; splinted ligation by a thermostable ligase adapted for 37°C and enhanced within the dense phase.
- Library prep
  - Magnetic enrichment of barcode–RNA adducts; reverse transcription with template-switch; add cell barcode and UMI; standard scRNA-seq chemistry with added barcode read.
- Scaling and heterogeneity
  - Plate ≥10,000 cells/run; include spike-in time controls; model inter-cell variability in window boundaries; fit Bayesian deconvolution to correct modest window jitter.

Controls and validation
- No-TPCC and inert condensate controls to assess perturbation.
- No-barcode and scrambled-barcode controls for specificity.
- Transcriptional spike-ins driven by drug-inducible promoters at known times to calibrate time-bin boundaries.
- Orthogonal benchmark using ADAR-based RNA timestamping for a subset of transcripts (reporters) to verify time ordering. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7956158/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- Technical: Seven demultiplexed time bins per cell with distinct, non-overlapping spike-in peaks; cell viability ≥80% to 24 h; minimal global transcriptome distortion vs control.
- Biological: Perturbation-responsive pathways (e.g., immediate-early, stress, or drug-target pathways) show expected early/late kinetics with coherent single-cell heterogeneity structure.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- RNA sequestration perturbs translation: mitigate with weak-binding RRM mutants, low expression, small TPCC volume fraction; verify polysomes.
- Kinetic drift across cells: include per-cell internal standards (brief 4sU label at known times for external benchmarking) in pilot experiments; refine linker palette.
- Barcode ligation efficiency too low: enrich adducts magnetically and increase ligase local concentration within TPCC.

Novelty and relation to prior art
- Prior work established programmable coacervates with tunable uptake/release in cells and salt/redox-driven disassembly but did not record transcriptome time courses. This proposal repurposes condensate aging as an intrinsic, multi-window temporal encoder. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11582321/?utm_source=openai))
- ADAR-based RNA timestamping infers RNA age from accumulated A→I edits on engineered motifs; here, endogenous poly(A)+ RNAs are physically captured into discrete windows and barcoded, enabling whole-transcriptome, same-cell trajectories without per-transcript engineering. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7956158/?utm_source=openai))
- Reversible EV capture/release via desthiobiotin–biotin/streptavidin has been shown on devices and cell surfaces; it supports feasibility of gentle, staged release/collection should the non-destructive path be pursued, but differs mechanistically from the proposed intracellular time-encoding condensate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7328786/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- A validated TPCC construct and linker palette providing seven log-spaced capture windows from 30 min to 24 h in living cells.
- A single end-point library workflow yielding per-cell, seven-bin transcriptomes.
- Benchmark datasets comparing ChronoPhase to ADAR timestamping for shared reporters and demonstrating inter-cell response heterogeneity at transcriptome scale.
