text:
Title
Marrow-local reversible amino acid sequestration to induce a protective HSC dormancy window and lethal commitment in AML LSCs

Integrated hypothesis–question
Can a brief, spatially confined reduction of free essential amino acids (EAAs) in bone marrow—achieved by reversible, non-consumptive sequestration—push hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) into a protective integrated-stress-response (ISR) quiescent state while driving amino acid–dependent acute myeloid leukemia (AML) leukemia stem cells (LSCs) past a survival threshold, thereby reducing AML burden with minimal myelotoxicity? This question rests on two observations: HSCs tolerate nutrient stress by suppressing mTORC1/translation and maintaining quiescence, whereas AML LSCs display elevated amino acid uptake and catabolism that sustain oxidative phosphorylation and survival. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2743144/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a physical-chemistry switch—reversible sequestration of one or more EAAs within the marrow niche—to transiently lower local free amino acid activity without systemic depletion or metabolic byproducts. The trough is deep and fast enough to engage HSC ISR quiescence yet long enough to force LSCs, which maintain higher amino acid flux set-points, toward irreversible death commitment. Normal conditions are restored on demand by displacing or releasing the bound amino acids. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26543160/?dopt=Abstract&utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Engineer and validate a reversible amino acid–sequestering hydrogel (R-ASH) for marrow-local control of EAA activity.  
2) Define the “trap window” (depth × duration × recovery) that spares HSCs but commits LSCs to death in human co-culture and marrow-on-a-chip.  
3) Demonstrate in vivo efficacy and hematopoietic preservation in AML patient–derived xenografts (PDX) using intramedullary R-ASH placement with on-demand release.

Aim 1. Engineer a marrow-local reversible sequestration platform (R-ASH)
- Design: Injectable, biocompatible hydrogel microparticles bearing mixed, high-affinity reversible binding motifs for target EAAs (primary: leucine and arginine). Two chemistries will be pursued in parallel:  
  a) Molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) microgels templated against leucine/arginine to create selective binding pockets; feasibility is supported by prior amino acid–imprinted materials.  
  b) Reversible coordination/ionic capture motifs (e.g., histidine-mimetic imidazole/metal coordination matrices and carboxylate-rich sites) tuned for fast on/off kinetics at physiological pH. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25429178/?utm_source=openai))
- Localization: Intramedullary injection adjacent to endosteal surfaces creates high local binder density within diffusion-limited marrow spaces, enabling sub-millimeter depletion zones. Hydrogel mechanical properties will match soft marrow to minimize niche perturbation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40895237/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls and readouts:  
  • Equilibrium binding, selectivity, and off-rate constants for leucine/arginine vs non-target amino acids (isothermal calorimetry; microfluidic breakthrough curves).  
  • On-demand release by systemic displacer bolus (same amino acid) or local triggers (pH/thermal) validated in serum and whole marrow aspirates.  
  • Biocompatibility and cytokine neutrality in primary human mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) cultures.

Milestone: Achieve ≥70% reversible reduction of free leucine or arginine activity in marrow-mimetic media within 2–5 minutes, with ≥80% restoration within 5–10 minutes upon displacer addition; ≥10 reversible cycles without loss of capacity.

Aim 2. Define the trap window that differentially protects HSCs and eliminates LSCs
- Systems:  
  • Human CD34+ HSCs from cord blood or mobilized peripheral blood co-cultured with primary human AML LSC–enriched fractions on MSC layers and in a marrow-on-a-chip device to recapitulate diffusion constraints.  
  • Continuous microdialysis sampling to quantify interstitial amino acids and verify depletion gradients in real time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2538639/?utm_source=openai))
- Protocol: Apply R-ASH to reduce local leucine and/or arginine activity by graded depths (30–80%) for variable durations (15–180 minutes), followed by rapid restoration via displacer.  
- Mechanistic endpoints:  
  • HSC: ISR engagement (p-eIF2α, ATF4, SESN2 induction), mTORC1 suppression (p-S6, p-4EBP1), translation downshift (OPP assay), cell-cycle exit, apoptosis ≤5% at 24 h, and preservation of long-term culture–initiating cell (LTC-IC) activity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26543160/?dopt=Abstract&utm_source=openai))  
  • LSC: Loss of mitochondrial spare respiratory capacity, increased replication/proteotoxic stress markers, apoptosis/necrosis, and loss of leukemia-initiating capacity in secondary xenotransplantation assays. Prior work supports LSC dependence on elevated amino acid uptake and catabolism sustaining OXPHOS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6280965/?utm_source=openai))
- Decision rule: The trap window is defined as the minimal depletion depth and duration that preserves ≥80% HSC LTC-IC and transplantation potential while reducing LSC colony-forming units by ≥70% and leukemia-initiating frequency by ≥5-fold after recovery.

Milestone: Identify a 30–120 minute window at 50–70% local leucine/arginine reduction that meets the decision rule.

Aim 3. In vivo validation in AML PDX with hematopoietic preservation
- Model and placement: NSG mice engrafted with human AML PDX receive unilateral intramedullary R-ASH in femur. Opposite femur serves as internal control.  
- Monitoring: Dual-probe microdialysis quantifies interstitial leucine/arginine kinetics (depth, area-under-depletion, half-recovery) and correlates with tissue ISR/mTORC1 markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2538639/?utm_source=openai))  
- Intervention schedule: Two or three trap cycles per week for 2–3 weeks; each cycle comprises a 60–90 minute depletion followed by immediate systemic displacer bolus to restore amino acid levels.  
- Endpoints:  
  • Efficacy: Human AML burden (flow cytometry), LSC frequency (limiting dilution secondary transplants), survival.  
  • Hematopoietic preservation: Host HSC/progenitor frequency, competitive repopulation in secondary transplants, lineage output, and absence of cytopenias.  
  • Mechanism: Temporal sequencing of HSC ISR activation with minimal apoptosis, versus LSC loss of OXPHOS and commitment to death.

Safety and risk mitigation
- Choice of amino acid: Initial focus on leucine and arginine balances LSC metabolic vulnerabilities and ISR/mTORC1 coupling. HSCs display resilience to amino acid stress via mTORC1 downshift and ISR engagement, suggesting brief, local depletions are tolerated. If HSC stress markers exceed thresholds, reduce trough depth/duration or switch to single-amino-acid targeting with faster recovery. ([jci.org](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/89452?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target effects: Spatial confinement by intramedullary placement; rapid reversibility prevents prolonged HSC starvation, unlike systemic restriction. Continuous in situ amino acid monitoring aborts cycles if recovery lags. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2538639/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic orthogonality (optional sub-aim): Validate that outcomes arise from amino acid activity reduction, not toxic byproducts, by reproducing effects with boundary-layer transport “decoys” (tethered competitive substrates) that throttle influx at constant bulk concentrations. This tests a flux-based, target-agnostic mechanism. 

Key falsifiable predictions
- A brief, marrow-local leucine/arginine trough induces HSC ISR activation with preserved clonogenicity and transplantation capacity after rapid refeeding, whereas LSCs exhibit disproportionate loss of OXPHOS and leukemia-initiating capacity despite identical recovery. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26543160/?dopt=Abstract&utm_source=openai))  
- On-demand displacer restores interstitial amino acid levels to ≥80% baseline within minutes, and halts HSC stress signaling before apoptosis accrues. Microdialysis confirms spatial confinement and rapid reversibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2538639/?utm_source=openai))

Methods overview
- Materials: Synthesis and characterization of leucine/arginine MIP microgels (template removal confirmed by spectroscopy); parallel fabrication of imidazole/metal coordination hydrogels for reversible binding. Fast binding kinetics engineered via high surface-area microgels and short diffusion lengths. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25429178/?utm_source=openai))  
- In vitro physiology: ISR/mTORC1 readouts by immunoblot/flow; translation by O-propargyl-puromycin incorporation; mitochondrial function by Seahorse flux; survival and clonogenicity assays; LTC-IC and serial replating.  
- In vivo physiology: Intramedullary delivery under ultrasound guidance; amino acid microdialysis; serial peripheral counts; marrow histology; transplantation assays.

Rationale alignment and novelty
- Alignment: The intervention manipulates the niche’s physicochemical state (free amino acid activity) rather than discovering new molecular targets, directly leveraging HSC nutrient-stress resilience and LSC amino acid dependence. ([jci.org](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/89452?utm_source=openai))  
- Novelty: Prior AML metabolism studies emphasize systemic deprivation or enzyme-mediated degradation; reversible, marrow-local, non-consumptive sequestration to create an on/off nutrient trap has not, to our knowledge, been tested. Feasibility draws from amino acid–imprinted/binding hydrogels and real-time microdialysis monitoring. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25429178/?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If single-amino-acid sequestration is insufficient, tune binder composition to modestly co-sequester two EAAs, preserving rapid reversibility.  
- If LSC metabolic plasticity blunts killing, combine trap cycles with brief ETC inhibitors only during the trough to lower the death threshold, then withdraw at refeeding; this maintains the target-agnostic, time-locked trap logic.

Deliverables and go/no-go criteria (Year 1–2)
- Go: Demonstrated trap window ex vivo with ≥5-fold LSC frequency reduction and ≥80% HSC LTC-IC preservation; in vivo proof with significant LSC frequency drop and maintained host hematopoiesis after 2–3 weeks of trap cycles.  
- No-go: Inability to achieve rapid, reversible local amino acid control; or persistent HSC impairment despite shallow/brief troughs.

Mechanistic foundation
- HSCs maintain quiescence by suppressing mTORC1 and translation under nutrient stress; GCN2–ATF4–Sestrin2 axis sustains this suppression and survival. AML LSCs elevate amino acid uptake and catabolism to fuel OXPHOS, creating a higher flux threshold that a brief, local deprivation can breach. The R-ASH switch tests whether timing and locality—not systemic dose—can resolve HSC/LSC selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2743144/?utm_source=openai))

label: debate_bypass
text:
Title
Microbe-primed metabolic anomaly detection to eliminate dormant AML leukemic stem cells (LSC) while sparing hematopoietic stem cells (HSC)

Central hypothesis–question
Can a transient, gut-delivered microbial priming event license innate effectors to kill only those marrow-resident cells that sustain an illegitimate, energy‑demanding “pseudo‑quiescent” state—operationally defined by a composite pericellular metabolic anomaly (stable lactate–acidosis with oxygen mismatch and redox drift)—thereby eradicating dormant LSC while preserving legitimately quiescent HSC? This reframes selectivity as context gating (MAMP pulse AND metabolic DAMP anomaly) rather than discovery of new molecular markers. Plant immunity’s MAMP+DAMP coincidence inspires the gate; trained-immunity biology and engineered probiotics provide feasible implementation; AML and HSC metabolism supply the discriminant. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-phyto-082718-100146?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
License cytotoxic programs in monocytes/macrophages only when two independent conditions co-occur: (1) a time‑limited microbial-associated “training” pulse delivered safely in the gut (systemic trained-immunity program), and (2) a local, persistent pericellular anomaly around target cells, measured as a specific pattern of lactate-driven acidosis with lactate:O2 decoupling and redox drift that reflects the energetic overhead of LSC pseudo-quiescence. Legitimately dormant HSC lack this maintained anomaly and fail the gate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7186935/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale (established biology anchored to the gate)
- HSC quiescence: low ROS, glycolysis-biased metabolism in hypoxic niches; activation increases OXPHOS and ROS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9242402/?utm_source=openai))
- AML LSC: relative mitochondrial/OXPHOS and amino-acid reliance (including BCAT1/BCAA programs) with metabolic inflexibility; AML marrow shows elevated lactate that conditions macrophages via HCAR1/GPR81. ([haematologica.org](https://haematologica.org/article/view/10948?utm_source=openai))
- Immune sensing of acidity and lactate via GPCRs (GPR65/68, HCAR1) and redox-sensitive pathways can transduce micro‑gradient information to effector programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6332927/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbial cues can durably “train” innate cells and bone-marrow progenitors; engineered probiotics can deliver controlled MAMP/STING signals with clinical precedence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5766828/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims and approach

Aim 1. Define the marrow metabolic anomaly that distinguishes LSC pseudo-quiescence from HSC quiescence.
- Approach:
  - In primary human AML samples and PDX marrow, map pericellular micro-gradients at single-cell resolution using ratiometric nanoprobes and optical/electrochemical sensors: extracellular pH, lactate, and O2 to derive a lactate:O2 mismatch index; quantify extracellular redox (e.g., GSSG:GSH proxies). Co-register with single-cell transcriptional states and surface phenotypes to locate HSC vs LSC-enriched regions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343108/?utm_source=openai))
  - Test whether the anomaly is sustained (minutes–hours) near LSC clusters: temporal imaging to distinguish steady anomalies from transient fluctuations. Evaluate dependence on BCAT1/BCAA flux (stable isotope tracing, BCAT1 knockdown) and MCT1/4 transport. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24294?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria:
  - A composite anomaly signature (acidic pHe within a narrow band, elevated lactate with preserved O2, and redox drift) is significantly enriched at LSC locales but not at HSC niches in matched specimens. Buffering acidosis, inhibiting lactate export, or reducing BCAT1 activity collapses the signature.

Aim 2. Establish a safe, gut-restricted microbial “training pulse” that licenses anomaly‑gated killing without global inflammation.
- Approach:
  - Engineer a commensal E. coli Nissle 1917 strain to produce a micro‑dose STING agonist (cyclic‑di‑AMP) under a gut-confined, nutrient-sensing promoter for short pulses, incorporating biocontainment and auxotrophy. Deliver orally to mice; confirm local GALT activation with minimal systemic cytokinemia. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9378478/?utm_source=openai))
  - Readouts of trained immunity in circulating monocytes and marrow progenitors: chromatin accessibility and histone marks at glycolysis/cholesterol/redox loci; metabolic rewiring; increased responsiveness to metabolic DAMPs with unchanged baseline phagocytosis toward normal HSC targets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7186935/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria:
  - Transient marrow-homing of trained monocytes with epigenetic/metabolic signatures of training; absence of cytopenias and preserved HSC CFU/repopulating capacity.

Aim 3. Demonstrate AND‑gated selectivity ex vivo and in vivo.
- Ex vivo microphysiology:
  - Co-culture trained human monocytes with primary AML cells in microfluidic devices that impose measured LSC-like vs HSC-like gradients from Aim 1. Readouts: target‑restricted phagocytosis/ROS burst only when the anomaly pattern is present and a MAMP-trained state exists; abrogation when either input is missing (no training or gradient buffered). ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/14/14/1096?utm_source=openai))
- In vivo PDX:
  - Minimal residual disease model after cytoreduction; administer probiotic training pulses. Endpoints: LSC frequency (LRC assays, secondary transplants), relapse-free survival, and HSC preservation (LT-repopulation, lineage output). Safety: bacterial clearance, cytokine profiling, gut histology. ([haematologica.org](https://haematologica.org/article/view/10948?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria:
  - Reduction of functional LSC with stable HSC engraftment and no myelotoxicity; loss of effect when lactate export (MCT1/4) is inhibited or BCAT1 is suppressed, indicating reliance on the anomaly rather than lineage markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5669930/?utm_source=openai))

Built-in falsification and decision gates
- If Aim 1 fails to show a reproducible anomaly unique to LSC locales, ideation is invalid; abort. If training induces HSC damage or cytopenias, the gut pulse is not sufficiently confined; iterate dose/timing or abandon microbial priming. If ex vivo coincidence fails despite clear anomalies and training, the AND logic is incorrect; pivot to alternative anomaly features or different PRR biasing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9242402/?utm_source=openai))

Safety and selectivity considerations
- The proposal avoids new molecular antigen targets; discrimination is by context. The microbial pulse is gut‑restricted with clinical precedent for engineered probiotic STING agonists, minimizing systemic toxicity. Trained effector action still requires the local anomaly, reducing off‑target myelotoxicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11225568/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and metrics (18–30 months)
- Months 0–9: Map anomalies; define threshold vector separating LSC from HSC in ≥3 patient cohorts. Go/no‑go: AUC ≥0.8 for anomaly classifier. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343108/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 6–15: Validate safe microbial training pulse; document marrow trafficking and trained‑immunity epigenetic marks. Go/no‑go: preserved HSC CFU and LT‑repopulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7186935/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 12–30: Ex vivo AND‑gate demonstration and in vivo PDX efficacy with HSC sparing; dependency on lactate export/BCAT1 confirmed. Go/no‑go: ≥1‑log reduction in functional LSC with unchanged HSC repopulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5669930/?utm_source=openai))

Why this addresses the selectivity bottleneck
- HSC and LSC are not separated by stable antigens but by how they “pay” for quiescence. The proposal exploits the sustained energetic footprint of illicit dormancy plus a tunable microbial training window to create an operational, coincidence‑gated readout that aligns with known HSC and LSC metabolism, leverages feasible microbiome engineering, and is testable with clear failure modes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9242402/?utm_source=openai))

label: debate_bypass
text:
Title
Ex vivo cyclic nuclear deformation with reversible condensate toggling as a pathway-agnostic “chromatin chaos” stress test to purge AML leukemia stem cells while preserving HSC function

Integrated hypothesis–question
Do brief, repeated pulses of sublethal nuclear deformation, interleaved with fast, reversible shifts in nuclear phase separation, expose a recovery-capacity gap between adaptable HSC and relapse‑initiating AML LSC sufficient for selective ex vivo depletion without myelotoxic conditioning? This rests on two established observations: (i) HSC nuclei are unusually compliant with distinct lamin/chromatin features compared with differentiated blood cells, supporting large, recoverable excursions in nuclear organization; and (ii) forced passage through micron‑scale constrictions or rapid osmotic crowding shifts transiently ruptures the nuclear envelope, stretches chromatin, reshapes nuclear condensates, and perturbs genome‑wide transcriptional order, with survival dependent on efficient repair and re‑assembly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3839750/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single control knob—recovery kinetics of nuclear-envelope/condensate organization—by imposing short, global, pathway‑agnostic disorder bursts that HSC can repair and re‑condense rapidly, but that LSC (locked into stabilized regulatory states) cannot. The intervention is purely physical/physicochemical and ex vivo, circumventing molecular target discovery and minimizing in vivo myelotoxicity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27013428/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define a safe “disorder pulse” window that transiently increases transcriptional/noise burden yet preserves long‑term HSC function.
- Approach: Process normal human CD34+ HSPC through microfluidic channels with constrictions near nuclear size (3–5 μm). Deliver 5–15 short passes at controlled flow to trigger brief NE rupture and chromatin strain; interleave 10–60 s hyperosmotic crowding pulses (e.g., sucrose or inert PEG) with rapid return to isotonic to cross LLPS boundaries reversibly. Establish dose–response maps for deformation amplitude, cycle number, and osmotic magnitude. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568376/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts/safety rails: NE rupture/repair (lamin B1 discontinuities, CHMP7/ESCRT-III recruitment), γH2AX and 53BP1 foci kinetics, nuclear speckles/Pol II/MED1 cluster dynamics, and scRNA‑seq noise metrics (Fano factor/CV^2 burst statistics) at 0–24 h recovery; CFU‑GEMM/CFU‑GM and NSG repopulation (LTRA) non‑inferiority versus mock‑processed controls (≥90% CFU, non‑inferior LTRA). Prior data support: confined deformation elicits NE rupture with ESCRT‑III–dependent repair and transient DNA damage; hyperosmotic shifts induce rapid, reversible LLPS remodeling with minimal viability impact over multiple cycles. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27013426/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test selective vulnerability of primary AML LSC to disorder pulses versus HSC.
- Approach: Process freshly isolated AML samples (including CD34+CD38−/phenotypic LSC‑enriched fractions) alone and spiked 1:1 with healthy CD34+ HSPC under the Aim 1 “safe window.” Quantify: (i) LSC frequency by limiting‑dilution xenotransplantation; (ii) colony‑forming output; (iii) delayed recovery of NE integrity/condensate re‑assembly; and (iv) persistence of elevated transcriptional noise or replication–transcription conflict markers after recovery. Confined‑migration literature predicts survival depends on rapid NE and DNA‑damage repair; LLPS literature predicts condensates dissolve/reform with osmotic crowding on tens‑of‑seconds timescales, providing a tight, testable kinetic window for differential failure. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27013428/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism discrimination: Compare small‑pore (3–4 μm; rupture‑prone) versus large‑pore (8 μm; shear without rupture) channels; isolate contributions from LLPS toggling by running deformation‑only versus deformation+osmotic cycles. Confined migration studies show chromatin strain and condensate reshaping specifically under tight constriction, validating the pore‑size control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6232975/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Close the loop with label‑free mechanics and phase metrics to individualize pulse dosing.
- Approach: Pair processing with real‑time deformability cytometry (RT‑DC/RT‑FDC) upstream and downstream to stratify mechanical phenotypes and adapt cycle number/flow to the sample. Use nuclear speckle/Pol II cluster imaging proxies post‑pulse to titrate osmotic magnitude. RT‑DC provides scalable, label‑free mechanical phenotyping in leukemias and CD34+ cells and can guide standardized “mechanical exposure” per unit mechanical stiffness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11616701/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan and key methods
- Devices and throughput: Parallelized PDMS or thermoplastic chips with arrays of 3–5 μm constrictions; per‑run capacities in the 10^7–10^9‑cell range are practical based on existing mechanoporation and deformability‑cytometry platforms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568376/?utm_source=openai))
- Disorder pulses: One pulse = N passes through 3–5 μm constrictions at defined pressure (target peak strain sufficient for transient NLS‑cargo leakage in reporter cell lines during development), immediately followed by 10–60 s hyperosmotic crowding (e.g., +150–300 mOsm sucrose or 2–5% PEG 8k) and 2–5 min isotonic recovery. Repeat 5–15 pulses as tolerated by Aim 1 readouts. Confined deformation and osmotic crowding both rapidly perturb NE integrity and condensate material states on seconds–minutes scales. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27013428/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic endpoints: ESCRT‑III (CHMP7/CHMP4B) recruitment kinetics; cGAS foci; γH2AX/53BP1 foci appearance and resolution; nucleolar/speckle area and number; Pol II Ser5/Ser2 cluster counts; ATAC‑seq variance and TT‑seq/4sU‑seq burst‑parameter dispersion; recovery of H3K27ac super‑enhancer occupancy; scRNA‑seq noise decay half‑times.
- Functional endpoints: CFU panels; long‑term culture‑initiating cell frequency; NSG xenograft LTRA; minimal residual disease (flow, ddPCR). Selectivity is achieved if HSPC function is preserved while LSC frequency drops ≥10‑ to 100‑fold versus mock.

Predicted outcomes, decision criteria, and falsification
- Outcome supportive: HSC show rapid NE/LLPS recovery, transient noise spikes with restoration of burst kinetics, preserved CFU/LTRA; AML LSC exhibit delayed NE repair/condensate re‑assembly, sustained transcriptional noise and replication–transcription conflict, apoptotic commitment, and reduced xenograft‑initiating frequency. Confined deformation and repair dependence underpin this prediction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27013428/?utm_source=openai))
- Stop/go gates: Proceed to mixed‑graft tests only if HSC CFU ≥90% and LTRA non‑inferior after five pulses. Scale pulses if RT‑DC indicates stiffer AML subpopulations or if condensate‑recovery imaging shows incomplete HSC re‑assembly within 5–10 min.
- Falsification: If LSC recover as fast as HSC on all metrics or if HSC LTRA drops >20% at any pulse count, the atomic strategy fails; pivot to purely osmotic LLPS toggling without deformation, which is independently reversible and low‑toxicity in mammalian cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7502480/?utm_source=openai))

Controls and comparators
- Shear‑only large‑pore channels; isotonic‑only runs; osmotic‑only runs; low‑dose 1,6‑hexanediol as a positive control for condensate dissolution (toxicity‑limited, for mechanism only); RT‑FDC‑matched exposure cohorts to deconvolve mechanotype effects. Confined‑migration literature validates tight‑pore specificity for NE rupture; LLPS literature validates osmotic toggling specificity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6232975/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and safety
- Ex vivo mechanoporation and microfluidic processing preserve primary immune‑cell function and enable efficient HSPC manipulation, supporting process feasibility; osmotic LLPS toggling is fast and reversible with minimal viability loss across cycles in mammalian cells. Manufacturing‑scale, label‑free deformability phenotyping is established. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6243275/?utm_source=openai))

Translational path
- Near‑term: Apply as an add‑on ex vivo purging step for autologous or allogeneic grafts in AML/MDS after calibration on donor HSPC. Mid‑term: Pair with label‑free RT‑DC‑based lot release (mechanotype and CFU) and single‑pulse “challenge‑recovery” assays as potency metrics. Long‑term: Integrate with deformability‑based sorting to continuously bleed off mechanically/kinetically vulnerable subpopulations before/after pulses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11616701/?utm_source=openai))

Why this proposal fits the constraints
- No new molecular targets or markers; selection is based on a physical recovery‑capacity assay of nuclear and condensate organization. Ex vivo processing reduces systemic myelotoxicity by preserving HSC long‑term function while depleting LSC initiating capacity. The approach leverages conserved nuclear mechanics and LLPS physics documented across cell types, adapted here to hematopoietic graft processing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3839750/?utm_source=openai))

References supporting key premises
- HSC nuclear compliance/lamin–mechanics relation; leukocyte deformability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3839750/?utm_source=openai))
- Constriction‑induced NE rupture, DNA‑damage/repair dependence, and pore‑size effects. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27013428/?utm_source=openai))
- Condensate reshaping under confinement and reversible LLPS toggling under osmotic crowding. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11574006/?utm_source=openai))
- Ex vivo microfluidic mechanoporation/processing feasibility in primary human HSPC/immune cells; scalable label‑free mechanics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3568376/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Closed-loop, time-gated mechanical steering of pre-commitment hematopoietic trajectories to bypass LSC–HSC selectivity

Central question–hypothesis
If reversible pre-commitment windows are detected by slowed recovery after tiny, non-toxic probes, then delivering brief soft-mechanics pulses to the marrow-like niche at those moments will reduce net flux of pre-leukemic HSPC/HSC descendants into OXPHOS-dependent LSC basins while preserving long-term HSC function, thereby bypassing the conventional selectivity problem without marker targeting. This rests on three established facts: (i) AML LSCs rely on mitochondrial OXPHOS and show relative metabolic inflexibility compared with HSCs; (ii) biological systems approaching fate transitions exhibit critical slowing of recovery from small perturbations; and (iii) marrow mechanics and YAP/TAZ-linked mechanotransduction modulate hematopoietic fate. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332226003288?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use recovery-rate after a standardized micro-perturbation as the sole control signal to gate sub-minute softening/viscoelastic pulses in a mechanosensitive hydrogel niche, timed to when cells are maximally redirectable yet not committed.

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Build a steerability sensor: quantify single-cell recovery kinetics after micro-perturbations and validate that slowed recovery marks reversible pre-commitment windows in hematopoietic trajectories.
- Aim 2. Build a minimal actuator: deliver precisely timed, short-lived soft-mechanics pulses using a phototunable hydrogel niche and test whether these pulses bias ensemble trajectories away from LSC-like states and back toward HSC-like quiescence.
- Aim 3. Close the loop and quantify flux reduction: integrate the sensor and actuator in an adaptive controller and measure reduction in HSC→LSC state-flux, LSC frequency, and preservation of HSC function ex vivo.

Rationale and prior knowledge anchoring
- LSC metabolic dependency: LSCs exhibit persistent OXPHOS dependence and limited metabolic flexibility relative to HSCs, which can switch modes with state; this asymmetry offers non-cytotoxic leverage if acted on temporally rather than by static OXPHOS poisoning. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332226003288?utm_source=openai))
- Critical slowing as a proximity marker: near commitment, restoring forces weaken; recovery from small perturbations slows. This has been shown as a general principle and in cell-fate transitions. Using recovery half-time as a real-time, label-minimal index is biologically grounded. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6936706/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanical control of hematopoiesis: marrow mechanics and YAP/TAZ mechanotransduction influence hematopoietic specification and regeneration; timed changes in matrix mechanics are therefore credible actuators. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7398148/?utm_source=openai))
- Fast, reversible mechanics are feasible: phototunable hydrogels can modulate viscoelasticity/stiffness on seconds–minutes timescales in the presence of cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7334082/?utm_source=openai))
- Non-invasive readouts exist in HSCs: label-free optical redox imaging (NAD(P)H/FAD) resolves HSC metabolic status at single-cell resolution and supports real-time sensing with negligible toxicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6994633/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1. Steerability sensor
- Model system: primary human CD34+ HSPC/HSCs from healthy donors and patients with clonal hematopoiesis or early AML; low-passage AML samples enriched for stem-like fractions.
- Micro-perturbation protocol: deliver a 60–120 s oxygen or glucose micro-step or a 30 s low-magnitude shear burst within a BM-mimetic microfluidic chamber; doses calibrated below stress thresholds.
- Readout: quantify single-cell relaxation half-time back to baseline for (i) optical redox ratio FAD/(NAD(P)H) and NAD(P)H binding fraction by FLIM; (ii) traction/morphodynamic recovery on soft substrates. Validate that prolonged half-times associate with increased variance/entropy states (scRNA-seq snapshots) but remain reversible by washout. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6994633/?utm_source=openai))
- Ground-truth reversibility: immediately isolate probed cells into colony-forming unit and long-term culture–initiating cell assays; show preserved HSC function when recovery is fast and reversible trajectory shifts when recovery is slow.

Aim 2. Minimal mechanical actuator
- Hydrogel niche: marrow-mimetic, integrin-presenting PEG network with phototunable viscoelastic crosslinks enabling sub-minute, reversible softening/viscosity pulses (e.g., thioester-exchange or thiol–ene modules). Characterize pulse amplitudes (ΔG′, relaxation time τ) and recovery. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7334082/?utm_source=openai))
- Pulse design: deliver 30–180 s softening/viscous pulses at variable delays after micro-perturbation. No ligand identity change; only mechanics are modulated.
- Mechanistic readouts: track YAP/TAZ nuclear shuttling and integrin/FAK activity dynamics; monitor metabolic shifts (ORR, OCR/ECAR) to test whether pulses bias energy allocation back to maintenance/quiescence programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7398148/?utm_source=openai))
- Outcome: demonstrate that timed softening pulses following slowed recovery deflect single-cell transcriptomic/metabolic coordinates away from LSC-like clusters and toward HSC-like quiescent basins, while continuous or mistimed pulses are ineffective or detrimental.

Aim 3. Closed-loop control and flux quantification
- Controller: use recovery half-time crossing a calibrated threshold as the gating condition for issuing one or two mechanics pulses; adaptively cease pulses once recovery accelerates.
- Flux metrics: (i) committor-like probabilities to LSC-like endpoints derived from Markov-chain trajectory inference on scRNA-seq snapshots; (ii) limiting-dilution xenografts in NSG mice to quantify functional LSC frequencies; (iii) serial transplantation to assess LT-HSC function preservation. Markov models are standard for single-cell fate probability estimation; operator-theoretic Koopman approximations will be explored to forecast short-term windows but, to our knowledge, have not been applied to time physical pulses in AML—supporting novelty. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7325868/?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmarks: compare closed-loop timing versus (a) always-on soft mechanics, (b) random pulse timing, and (c) pharmacologic OXPHOS inhibition at sublethal doses.

Design details and controls
- Selectivity and safety: in parallel cultures of normal HSCs, verify maintenance of LTC-IC frequency and serial xenograft repopulation after repeated sensing+pulsing; compare with matched AML LSC-enriched samples for reduction in LSC frequency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9890038/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism discrimination: decouple photonic exposure from mechanics by sham illumination controls; confirm negligible phototoxicity at used doses (standard in phototunable hydrogel protocols). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32020346/?utm_source=openai))
- Microenvironment relevance: repeat key experiments in a BM-on-chip co-culture with stromal and endothelial compartments to test robustness under marrow-like flows and gradients. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8986554/?utm_source=openai))

Primary outcomes and go/no-go
- Primary success criterion: ≥50% reduction in estimated HSC→LSC state-flux and ≥2-fold decrease in functional LSC frequency versus controls, with no decrement in LT-HSC repopulation.
- No-go: if slowed recovery fails to enrich for reversible windows (i.e., pulses cannot redirect without harming HSC endpoints), terminate closed-loop approach.

Risks and mitigations
- Heterogeneity of AML: subtypes may exhibit variable mechano-metabolic coupling; stratify by baseline ORR and transcriptional programs, and adjust pulse parameters.
- Sensor cross-sensitivity: if redox recovery alone is insufficient, add an orthogonal, label-minimal mechanical recovery metric without introducing molecular targeting.

Innovation
- Shifts selectivity from “what to hit” to “when to nudge,” using recovery kinetics as a universal control signal and transient mechanical softening as a non-cytotoxic actuator—avoiding new molecular targets and reducing myelotoxicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9890038/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and impact
- All components—label-free HSC metabolic imaging, critical-slowing metrics, phototunable hydrogels, and standard single-cell fate inference—are available and compatible with primary hematopoietic cells, making rapid validation plausible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6994633/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Time-entrained PEMF to force early mutated HSC descendants into differentiation while sparing quiescent HSC

Integrated hypothesis-question
Can weak, phase-controlled pulsed electromagnetic fields (PEMF) entrain the intracellular Ca2+–mitochondria–redox oscillator of pre‑leukemic HSC descendants to a differentiation‑favoring regime, thereby collapsing the self‑renewal attractor before overt LSC emergence, while quiescent HSC remain functionally intact due to their glycolytic, ROSlow state and niche‑suppressed Ca2+ influx? This treats leukemogenesis as a dynamics control problem, not a molecular target problem. Quiescent HSCs favor glycolysis/ROSlow and maintain low mitochondrial workload; activation and differentiation entail increased mitochondrial activity and ROS transients. AML persistence/LSC states are comparatively OXPHOS‑dependent with higher mitochondrial mass/ΔΨm constraints. Ca2+ influx into mitochondria gates HSC division and metabolic upshifts; mitoflash frequency reports and modulates ROS/ΔΨm signaling. Low‑intensity EM fields can induce Ca2+ oscillations and mild mitochondrial ROS in stem cells without DNA damage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9242402/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use waveform timing as the therapeutic “agent”: apply subthreshold, frequency‑tuned PEMF bursts to phase‑lock pre‑LSC Ca2+–mitochondria–redox dynamics to a regime that is incompatible with self‑renewal and biased to differentiation, exploiting their narrower OXPHOS/redox setpoint and entrainment susceptibility relative to quiescent, glycolytic HSC. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define oscillator-state signatures in early mutated versus normal HSC
- Question: Do CHIP/early‑MDS/early‑AML CD34+ clones display tighter ΔΨm, higher mitoflash frequency, and more coherent Ca2+ spiking than LT‑HSC?
- Methods: Single‑cell imaging in freshly isolated human CD34+ subsets (normal cord/peripheral blood, CHIP carriers, early AML) using TMRE (ΔΨm), mitoSOX (mitoROS), Fluo‑4 (Ca2+), NADH/FAD autofluorescence. Quantify mitoflash frequency and Ca2+–ΔΨm cross‑correlation. Correlate with transcriptional pseudotime and functional assays (CFU, LTC‑IC). Outcome: a minimal dynamic biomarker panel (mitoflash frequency, ΔΨm variance, Ca2+ spike coherence) that stratifies pre‑LSC from HSC. Rationale: HSC quiescence associates with glycolysis and ROSlow; AML/persistent clones show OXPHOShigh and constrained mitochondria; mitoflash frequency is a redox/energetic reporter. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9242402/?utm_source=openai))

2) Identify PEMF entrainment windows that push pre‑LSC toward differentiation with minimal HSC impact
- Question: What PEMF frequencies/amplitudes/duty cycles phase‑lock pre‑LSC oscillators and trigger differentiation without impairing HSC function?
- Methods: Ex vivo PEMF exposure of sorted human CD34+ fractions in 3D stromal co‑culture under hypoxia (to preserve HSC phenotype). Sweep parameter grid: 5–50 Hz, 0.2–3 mT, burst length 50–500 ms, duty cycle 5–20%, sessions 10 min per hour for 6 h/day × 3 days. Readouts: (a) real‑time entrainment (phase‑locking index of Ca2+ and mitoflash events to stimulus), (b) fate bias (CD34 downshift, lineage markers, CFU skew, mitotic history), (c) maintenance of HSC function (LTC‑IC, competitive serial xenotransplant). Prior mechanistic justification: EM fields at these intensities modulate Ca2+ channel opening probability and intracellular store dynamics, generating Ca2+ oscillations and small ROS pulses linked to differentiation signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10190032/?utm_source=openai))

3) Test “entrainment‑and‑reinfusion” for pre‑emptive LSC prevention
- Question: Does ex vivo PEMF entrainment of patient CD34+ cells reduce LSC frequency and leukemia initiation potential while preserving multilineage reconstitution?
- Methods: Obtain CD34+ apheresis from individuals with high‑risk CHIP/early MDS. Randomize split samples to sham vs optimal PEMF regimen from Aim 2. Transplant equal cell doses into NSG mice. Endpoints: human engraftment, multilineage output, limiting‑dilution LSC frequency, latency to leukemia‑like disease. Safety: assess HSC fitness by long‑term repopulation and secondary transplants. Mechanistic check: do mitoflash/Ca2+ signatures shift durably post‑exposure?

Experimental design and measurements
- Cells and states: LT‑HSC (CD34+CD38−CD90+), MPP/early progenitors, CHIP‑mutant clones identified by targeted sequencing; early AML blasts for comparison.
- Live‑cell dynamics: fast confocal/2‑photon imaging for Ca2+ and mitoROS; ΔΨm with TMRE in non‑quenching mode; mitoflash detection by matrix pH/ROS reporters where feasible; confirm substrate‑dependence of mitoflash frequency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6499064/?utm_source=openai))
- Functional outputs: CFU‑GEMM/GM/E/B, LTC‑IC, cell‑cycle staging, apoptosis; xenograft readouts.
- Entrainment metrics: circular statistics for phase‑locking; frequency pulling; recovery curves after stimulus cessation.

Selectivity and myelotoxicity mitigation plan
- State‑based selectivity: Quiescent HSC are glycolytic/ROSlow with niche‑suppressed Ca2+ influx (adenosine tone), making them less responsive to weak periodic forcing than metabolically primed pre‑LSC that rely on tighter OXPHOS/ΔΨm setpoints. Exposures are brief and subthermal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9242402/?utm_source=openai))
- Operational selectivity: Ex vivo application avoids systemic toxicity; in future in vivo use, spatially focused coils over target marrow and ultralow duty cycles.
- Stopping rules: If HSC LTC‑IC or serial repopulation drops >20% versus sham, adjust field amplitude/duty cycle first, then frequency.

Success criteria and endpoints
- Aim 1: Dynamic biomarker panel separates pre‑LSC from HSC with AUROC ≥0.80.
- Aim 2: PEMF regimen achieves significant phase‑locking in pre‑LSC (Rayleigh p<0.01) with ≥2× increase in lineage commitment markers and ≥50% reduction in LTC‑IC frequency of mutant clones, while preserving ≥90% HSC LTC‑IC versus sham.
- Aim 3: ≥3‑fold reduction in functional LSC frequency and delayed/absent leukemia in xenografts, with unchanged multilineage reconstitution versus sham.

Potential pitfalls and alternatives
- Weak entrainment: If phase‑locking is insufficient, adjust burst structure (e.g., chirped bursts or intermittent resonance scanning) while keeping average energy constant. Mechanistic guardrail: keep fields within regimes known to modulate Ca2+ oscillations in stem cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10190032/?utm_source=openai))
- Readout sensitivity: If mitoflashes are hard to detect in primary human cells, use ΔΨm variance and mitoROS burst statistics as proxies linked to substrate‑dependent mitoflash modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6499064/?utm_source=openai))
- Off‑target activation: Monitor DNA damage and exhaustion markers; shorten sessions or reduce duty cycle if detected.

Why this is novel and grounded
No clinical or preclinical standard addresses early leukemogenesis by timing‑based entrainment of the Ca2+–mitochondria–redox oscillator. Prior AML metabolism work emphasizes static OXPHOS inhibition of LSC or cytotoxicity; PEMF literature in stem cells focuses on osteo/chondrogenic differentiation or protection from injury, not pre‑LSC differentiation control. This proposal unifies established HSC/AML metabolic states, Ca2+–mitochondria gating of HSC division, and mitoflash‑based redox timing with a non‑molecular, low‑toxicity actuator. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Demand-gated, adenosine-sensing immunoreprogramming at the metabolic–epidermal interface to treat obesity-associated psoriasis

Central hypothesis and integrated research question
Excess extracellular adenosine generated by hypoxia/metabolic stress in obese tissue and inflamed skin can be repurposed as an endogenous gate to localize and self-limit delivery of keratinocyte-targeted immunoreprogramming agents. Does an intradermally placed, adenosine-aptamer–gated hydrogel that releases an A2B receptor antagonist only when adenosine is pathologically elevated reprogram keratinocyte–immune signaling and attenuate psoriasiform inflammation preferentially in obese/high-adenosine skin? Extracellular adenosine accumulates under metabolic stress and hypoxia typical of obese adipose and inflamed tissues, and keratinocytes prominently signal via A2B receptors that drive IL-6 and proinflammatory programs; therefore, adenosine is both a disease-coupled cue and a mechanistic lever for site- and state-specific intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Convert metabolite overload into a brake: use adenosine itself as the gating signal for a depot that (i) opens to release an A2B antagonist when adenosine is high and (ii) passively re-sequesters adenosine as levels fall, closing release. This single control principle directly ties therapeutic flux to a core metabolic abnormality without continuous external control. Adenosine-aptamer hydrogels and phenylboronic-acid (PBA) materials already demonstrate adenosine-responsive dissolution/release and in vivo adenosine binding, enabling rapid translation to skin. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and calibrate an intradermal, adenosine-gated depot that self-limits payload release.
- Construct PEG-based microgels crosslinked with adenosine aptamer duplexes that dissociate upon adenosine binding to increase mesh size and release small-molecule payload; co-display PBA moieties to reversibly bind cis-diols on adenosine, providing sequestration and hysteresis so that release closes as adenosine normalizes. Tune aptamer sequence density and PBA:aptamer ratios to set opening thresholds within 1–100 μM adenosine, a pathophysiological range. Readouts: adenosine-titrated swelling, diffusion coefficients, and release kinetics for model fluorophores and the drug. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))
- Select payload: a selective A2B antagonist (e.g., MRS1754 or PSB-603) to blunt adenosine–A2B–EGFR–IL-6 signaling in keratinocytes. Validate target engagement in HaCaT and primary human keratinocytes by measuring IL-6 after adenosine challenge ± antagonist. ([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bpbreports/4/2/4_64/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (month 1):
- Microgel synthesis and characterization; thresholded release profile established; antagonist retains activity post-encapsulation.

Aim 2. Demonstrate keratinocyte and epidermal–immune reprogramming under obese-mimetic metabolic stress in vitro.
- Culture keratinocytes under hypoxia (1–3% O2) and with adipocyte-conditioned media to model obese microenvironments; quantify extracellular adenosine. Assess whether gated release reduces IL-6, CXCL8, CCL20, and dampens NF-κB/EGFR transactivation compared to ungated delivery at equal total dose. Co-culture with human PBMCs or IL-17–competent T cells to test reduction in Th17-skewing cues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))
- System-level validation on-chip: couple a human WAT-on-chip that recapitulates immune-competent adipose to a keratinocyte/fibroblast skin-on-chip via microfluidic perfusion. Induce adipose hypoxia/inflammation to elevate adenosine in the shared medium; test whether intraluminally placed microgels gate payload delivery and normalize keratinocyte cytokines and barrier readouts (TEER, stratification markers) only under high-adenosine flow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9218765/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (month 2):
- Dose–response curves demonstrating adenosine-thresholded suppression of keratinocyte IL-6; reduced Th17-skewing in co-culture; on-chip demonstration of state-specific gating.

Aim 3. Establish efficacy and selectivity in vivo with metabolic context.
- Use imiquimod-induced psoriasiform dermatitis in high-fat diet (HFD) mice versus lean controls to generate differential interstitial adenosine. Administer aptamer–PBA microgels by shallow intradermal microinjection within lesional skin. Endpoints (day 5–7): epidermal thickness, Munro microabscesses, Ly6G+ neutrophils, and lesional transcripts (Il6, Cxcl1/Cxcl2, Il17a, Il23a). Compare gated microgels, scrambled-aptamer microgels, and free antagonist. Expect stronger efficacy and lower off-target suppression in HFD mice due to higher adenosine-driven gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism control: topical/intradermal adenosine challenge to force gate opening in lean mice; blockade reversal with an A2B agonist to confirm pathway positioning. Keratinocyte-favored readouts supported by known A2B expression and function. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15356773?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (month 3):
- Significant improvement of psoriasiform endpoints in HFD mice with gated depot versus controls; pharmacodynamic evidence of localized A2B pathway modulation.

Experimental details and feasibility
- Materials: Adenosine aptamer sequences and hydrogel chemistries are published; adenosine-responsive dissolution and release have been shown; PBA scaffolds sequester adenosine in vivo. Synthesis and tuning can be completed rapidly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))
- Biology: Keratinocyte A2B signaling drives IL-6; extracellular adenosine rises with hypoxia/metabolic stress in obese tissue; these provide both mechanism and disease-coupled cue. ([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bpbreports/4/2/4_64/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai))
- Platforms: Immunocompetent WAT-on-chip and skin-on-chip systems support adipose–epidermis crosstalk modeling and compound testing within the project window. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9218765/?utm_source=openai))

Primary outcomes and decision points
- Outcome 1: Steep, programmable release versus adenosine concentration with built-in hysteresis (aptamer opening, PBA rebinding). Go if release ratio (pathological:physiological adenosine) ≥5 and payload remains potent.
- Outcome 2: Suppression of keratinocyte IL-6 and Th17-skewing only under high adenosine; proceed to in vivo if ≥50% reduction versus scrambled/ungated controls at equal total drug.
- Outcome 3: In vivo efficacy in HFD mice exceeding lean mice for the same total dose indicates successful demand-gating; if not, retune aptamer density or switch payload to an A2A positive allosteric modulator to bias toward immunoregulation while maintaining adenosine-gated delivery. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15356773?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and contingencies
- If adenosine levels in lesional skin are insufficient for robust gating, pre-enrich local adenosine transiently using low-dose ecto-5′-nucleotidase substrate pulses in a small area to test principle, or increase aptamer affinity via multimerization. Evidence supports adenosine surges with tissue stress, but thresholds must be empirically mapped. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))
- If A2B antagonism alone is inadequate, swap or add a low-dose A2A agonist payload within the same gate to reinforce anti-inflammatory cAMP/PKA signaling in keratinocytes and resident immune cells. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15356773?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and impact
This proposal re-architects control at the metabolic–epidermal interface by making a pathologic metabolite the real-time governor of immunoreprogramming, rather than merely a target to block. Prior art demonstrates adenosine-responsive hydrogels and in vivo adenosine-binding biomaterials, but they have not been applied to obesity-associated psoriatic inflammation or to enforce state-specific A2B pathway reprogramming in keratinocytes. If successful, this establishes a generalizable, demand-gated therapeutic paradigm for metabolically amplified skin inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Skin-first neuromodulation to normalize systemic metabolism in obesity-associated psoriasis

Integrated hypothesis–question
Does selectively collapsing nociceptor–CGRP output from psoriatic skin lower the exported signal burden that surpasses systemic disruption thresholds, thereby normalizing insulin action and lipid homeostasis in obese hosts? If yes, can we map the minimal cutaneous “setpoint” of exported factors required to restore whole-body metabolic tone? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
A single lever at the metabolic–epidermal interface: skin-restricted suppression of sensory neuron CGRP signaling at psoriatic plaques reduces IL-23/Th17 drive and collapses outbound endocrine traffic (cytokines and EV-miRNAs) below a causal threshold for systemic insulin resistance. We quantify and enforce this threshold using gradient-inversion microphysiology to define directionality and minimal effective cutaneous suppression before translation to mice. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))

Background and gap
- Psoriatic skin inflammation—especially when induced by TLR7 activation—can provoke systemic glucose intolerance and a pre-diabetic phenotype via endocrine actions of the skin secretome. Treating skin can improve metabolic readouts in some settings, but precise, skin-initiated causal levers and thresholds are undefined. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- TRPV1+ cutaneous nociceptors drive IL-23 production from dermal dendritic cells and amplify IL-23/IL-17 signaling; neuromodulation (including RTX-mediated neuron ablation) reduces this axis in the imiquimod model. Whether skin-local CGRP pathway suppression alone can restore systemic insulin action in obesity-associated psoriasis has not been directly tested. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))
- CGRP influences adipose metabolism and whole-body insulin sensitivity in obesity, yet prior work focuses on global or adipose-centric actions, not plaque-local cutaneous modulation as a metabolic therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13256775/?utm_source=openai))
- Keratinocyte-derived EV miRNAs (including miR-21/miR-155) are altered in psoriasis and circulate as potential effectors; their role as exported metabolic disruptors remains underexplored compared with adipose/liver EVs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define the outbound skin-to-metabolic organ signal threshold and dependence on CGRP using a gradient-inversion skin–adipose/liver microphysiological system.
Aim 2. Test whether plaque-restricted CGRP pathway suppression rescues systemic insulin sensitivity and lipid homeostasis in obese psoriasiform mice.
Exploratory Aim 3. Determine whether plaque therapy secondarily rewires circulating EV-miRNA cargo (miR-21/miR-155/miR-146a) and whether epidermal anti–miR delivery adds benefit.

Models
- Human skin–metabolic organ-on-a-chip (psoriatic equivalent ± TLR7 activation) linked to human adipocyte and hepatocyte microtissues (primary or iPSC-derived).
- Diet-induced obese (DIO) C57BL/6 mice with imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasiform dermatitis (back/ear). This model exhibits systemic metabolic disruption attributable to the skin secretome. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 1. Gradient-inversion mapping of actionable exported signals and setpoints
Rationale: If cutaneous outputs causally drive systemic insulin resistance, then during disease they form a directional gradient from skin→receiver tissues that collapses when the driver (skin CGRP) is suppressed. Establishing the minimal “skin-output setpoint” that restores downstream insulin signaling derisks translation.

Design
- Build a tri-compartment chip: (i) human psoriatic skin equivalent (keratinocytes + dermal fibroblasts + myeloid cells ± TRPV1+ sensory neurite co-culture); (ii) adipocyte or hepatocyte chamber; (iii) microfluidic channel with switchable flow.
- Induce psoriasiform state by topical IMQ or IL-23/IL-17A; record baseline exported factors with flow skin→metabolic organ, then invert to metabolic organ→skin.
- Intervene at the skin side with: (a) CGRP pathway suppression—CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) or CGRP-neutralizing antibody applied only to the skin chamber; (b) vehicle control.
- Readouts:
  - Directional flux: CGRP/SP, IL-6, IL-17A, IL-23 in effluents; EV counts (CD63+), EV-miRNA cargo (miR-21/miR-155/miR-146a).
  - Receiver function: insulin-stimulated pAKT in adipocytes; hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3 and insulin signaling; NF-κB reporters in macrophage co-cultures.
  - Thresholding: titrate skin-side neuromodulation intensity to define minimal reduction in exported signals that restores receiver insulin signaling ≥80% of control.
Success criteria: Demonstration that (i) disease-state export is directional (skin→receiver) and (ii) skin-side CGRP suppression collapses one or more exported factors below a quantifiable threshold that normalizes insulin signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Skin-restricted CGRP pathway suppression normalizes systemic metabolism in obese psoriasiform mice
Rationale: IMQ-induced psoriatic skin disrupts glucose homeostasis; TRPV1+ nociceptors and CGRP drive lesional IL-23/Th17. We test whether local CGRP suppression at plaques in DIO mice improves whole-body insulin sensitivity and lipid handling without systemic immunosuppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Design
- Cohorts: Male and female DIO mice (16–20 weeks on HFD). Randomize to IMQ or vehicle on shaved back skin for 5–7 days to induce psoriasiform dermatitis and metabolic stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- Interventions (plaque-restricted, contralateral vehicle control):
  1) Resiniferatoxin (RTX) microinjection into plaques (TRPV1+ nociceptor desensitization), schedule day 0 and day 3. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7583491/?utm_source=openai))
  2) CGRP receptor antagonist formulated for intradermal delivery (gepant hydrogel), daily topical/ID at plaques for 5–7 days; pharmacodynamic confirmation by lesional microdialysate CGRP reduction.
- Primary systemic endpoints (days 5–10):
  - Glucose tolerance test (GTT), insulin tolerance test (ITT); fasting insulin and HOMA-IR; hepatic triglycerides; serum triglycerides/HDL/LDL.
  - Tissue signaling: insulin-stimulated pAKT in epididymal fat and liver; hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15845623/?utm_source=openai))
- Skin and circulating endpoints:
  - Lesional IL-23/IL-17A and dendritic-cell activation; microdialysate CGRP/SP; EV abundance and EV-miRNA (miR-21/155/146a) in plasma.
Expected outcome: Local CGRP pathway suppression reduces lesional IL-23/Th17, collapses exported cytokine/EV gradients, and improves GTT/ITT and hepatic insulin signaling in DIO+IMQ mice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory Aim 3. Epidermal EV-miRNA editing as a downstream amplifier
Rationale: Psoriatic keratinocytes contribute to circulating EV-miRNAs, with miR-21/miR-155 upregulated; exosomal miRNAs can remodel insulin action in distal tissues in metabolic disease. If plaque neuromodulation only partially normalizes EV cargo, add epidermal anti–miR-21/miR-155 (LNA) via microneedles to test incremental systemic benefit. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Design
- Apply anti–miR-21/miR-155 locally to plaques (± neuromodulation). Quantify plasma EV-miRNA shifts and systemic insulin signaling as in Aim 2.
- Expected readout: Additional decrease in plasma EV miR-21/155 and increased miR-146a, correlating with improved insulin action.

Key controls and analyses
- Side-by-side lesional vs non-lesional skin treatment within the same animal to prove site specificity.
- Non-IMQ DIO controls to ensure effects require active psoriatic inflammation.
- Power calculations: n≥10 per group for 80% power to detect 20% change in AUC-GTT (alpha 0.05).
- Statistics: Mixed-effects models for repeated measures; ANCOVA for tissue signaling with lesion severity as covariate.

Milestones and 12-week timeline
- Weeks 0–3: Build/validate gradient-inversion chip; calibrate assays; complete Aim 1 threshold maps and identify minimal CGRP suppression needed.
- Weeks 3–10: Execute DIO+IMQ cohorts with RTX and gepant-ID arms; complete metabolic tests and tissue signaling.
- Weeks 8–12: Exploratory anti–miR add-on; integrate EV-miRNA analytics; finalize data synthesis.

Readouts anchoring causality
- Directionality and threshold: outbound factor gradients that invert/flatten with skin therapy (Aim 1).
- Necessity and sufficiency: local CGRP suppression reduces lesional IL-23/Th17 and rescues systemic insulin signaling (Aim 2). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))
- Generalizability: improvement observed with two distinct skin-restricted neuromodulatory modalities (RTX vs gepant).

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Risk: Gepant dermal delivery insufficient. Mitigation: prioritize RTX intervention (established in IMQ), and/or use CGRP-neutralizing antibody intradermally. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7583491/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: IL-6/STAT3 hepatic responses can be context dependent. Mitigation: prespecify hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3 and insulin-stimulated pAKT as orthogonal endpoints; incorporate adipose insulin signaling and macrophage polarization to avoid overreliance on a single hepatic pathway. ([journal-of-hepatology.eu](https://www.journal-of-hepatology.eu/article/s0168-8278%2816%2900083-0/fulltext?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: EV-miRNA shifts are modest. Mitigation: treat EV-miRNA as mechanistic secondary; focus success criteria on metabolic and signaling endpoints.

Innovation
- Skin-first neuromodulation as metabolic therapy: leverages a local neuroimmune circuit (CGRP→IL-23/Th17) to reprogram systemic insulin action in obesity-associated psoriasis. Prior CGRP–metabolism links exist, but not via plaque-restricted intervention to treat systemic metabolism. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13256775/?utm_source=openai))
- Gradient-inversion mapping to define causal, exported skin effectors and actionable thresholds before in vivo testing, reducing complexity and failure modes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- EV-miRNA reprogramming as a downstream amplifier tied to observed circulating changes in psoriasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Decision points and success criteria
- Aim 1 Go/No-Go: Demonstrate a directional export of at least one factor (CGRP/IL-6/EV-miRNA) that, when reduced by skin-side CGRP suppression, restores insulin signaling in receiver tissues on-chip by ≥80%.
- Aim 2 Success: In DIO+IMQ mice, plaque-limited CGRP suppression improves AUC-GTT and ITT by ≥20%, increases insulin-stimulated pAKT in adipose and liver by ≥30%, and reduces hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3, with concordant decreases in lesional IL-23/IL-17A and microdialysate CGRP/SP. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- Exploratory success: Plasma EV miR-21/155 decrease correlates with improved systemic insulin signaling; local anti–miR adds incremental benefit over neuromodulation alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Impact
Validating a skin-origin metabolic setpoint and demonstrating that plaque-restricted neuromodulation normalizes systemic insulin action would establish a bidirectional skin–metabolic organ axis that is therapeutically targetable without systemic immunosuppression. This reorients psoriasis comorbidity management from “treat body to fix skin” toward “treat skin to fix body,” with immediate translational paths via local neuromodulators and topical nucleic-acid therapeutics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Closed-loop, biomarker-imprinted, thresholded hydrogel niche for autonomous repair of volumetric muscle loss and critical-size bone defects

Unified hypothesis–goal
A fully resorbable, cell-free hydrogel embedding biomarker-imprinted gates and cooperative protease-threshold crosslinks can create a transient tertiary regenerative niche that: (i) recruits and organizes endogenous progenitors, immune cells, and vasculature; (ii) drives a staged inflammation→resolution→differentiation program; and (iii) self-terminates when local biochemical markers of restoration emerge. The single causal insight is to replace external timing with endogenous “restoration chemistry” as the only clock, using molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) as analyte-gated permeability switches and network percolation thresholds to enforce spatially discrete progression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4613793/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Implement epitope-imprinted, biodegradable MIP microdomains that remain collapsed/insulating until they bind stage-defining biomarkers (DAMP-low/IL-10-high for resolution; osteocalcin/collagen-I-telopeptide for bone maturation; low lactate for metabolic normalization). Biomarker binding triggers MIP swelling or crosslink scission to expose tethered ligands or open diffusion paths. Embed these MIP gates in a biodegradable hydrogel whose bulk connectivity is set above a proteolysis percolation threshold, so only sufficiently dense, protease-secreting cell collectives open “corridors” to advance. This couples local population state (cooperative proteolysis) with stage identity (MIP gating), and ties dissolution to late biomarkers for autonomous shutoff. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5223160/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Engineer biomarker-gated, biodegradable MIP microdomains that switch accessibility upon binding restoration markers.
- Design: Epitope imprinting using short, solvent-stable peptides from HMGB1 (DAMP), IL-10 (resolution), osteocalcin (OCN), and collagen I C-telopeptide. Polymer matrix: PLGA- or disulfide-crosslinked acrylate MIPs to ensure hydrolytic/bioreductive degradability. Outputs: swelling (volume fraction), pore opening, or crosslink cleavage translating to >10× change in local diffusivity or ligand exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5223160/?utm_source=openai))
- Validation: Quantify binding KD and selectivity versus scrambled epitopes; measure analyte-triggered swelling and cargo flux using FRAP/NMR diffusometry; cyclic exposure to physiological analyte ranges to confirm reversibility for early gates (HMGB1/IL-10) and irreversibility for late gates (OCN/Ctelopeptide).

Aim 2. Build a cooperative, population-thresholded hydrogel that only advances when multicellular collectives are present.
- Design: Hydrogel base (PEG-ester or elastin-like polypeptide hybrid) crosslinked by peptide linkers bearing tandem protease sites (e.g., MMP2↓X and MMP9↓Y) wired as AND gates via parallel-cleavage topology; network connectivity tuned so bulk gel collapses locally only when a critical fraction of linkers are cleaved (percolation threshold). This converts diffuse MMP fields into switch-like openings where macrophage–endothelial–progenitor clusters form. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5822735/?utm_source=openai))
- Validation: Microfluidic co-cultures producing graded MMP fluxes; map degradation fronts and corridor formation versus cell density; fit to percolation models to set linker density/kinetics needed for thresholding.

Aim 3. Encode stage progression and self-termination through MIP logic layered within the thresholded network.
- Early gate (inflammation control): HMGB1-high keeps the network “closed” to proliferation ligands; as HMGB1 falls and IL-10 rises, IL-10-imprinted MIPs swell to expose tethered chemokine-mimetic peptides (e.g., CXCR4- and CCR2-binding motifs) and heparin-mimetic captures that shape gradients, recruiting satellite cells/periosteal progenitors and monocyte-derived pro-resolving macrophages only in locally resolving zones. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6130197/?utm_source=openai))
- Mid gate (organization): In MIP-opened domains, cooperative proteolysis reaches threshold to form aligned corridors; scaffold-anchored adhesion cues (α7β1- and α5β1-selective motifs, PHSRN+RGD pairs) enforce anisotropic alignment for myofiber fusion or guide endothelial sprouting. Corridor nucleation remains spatially discrete because sub-threshold regions do not percolate. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0142961205011749?utm_source=openai))
- Late gate (maturation + autonomous shutoff): Binding of osteocalcin/collagen-I-telopeptide in bone, or metabolic normalization (low lactate) in muscle, triggers MIP collapse-to-cleavage transition (analyte-induced hydration/ion shifts accelerating ester/disulfide scission), which: (i) closes chemokine exposure; (ii) releases short-lived decoy traps that neutralize residual recruitment cues; and (iii) accelerates bulk hydrogel erosion. Material mass loss thereby tracks maturation markers, not elapsed time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13069982/?utm_source=openai))

Form factor and deployment
- Injectable paste or in situ gelling hydrogel loaded with 1–5 µm MIP microdomains and peptide crosslinkers; conforms to irregular VML or bone defects, then self-prunes as corridors are written by cells. Fully resorbable; no hardware. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4950356/?utm_source=openai))

Key readouts and success criteria
- In vitro gating fidelity: ≥10× on/off ratio in ligand exposure for each MIP gate at physiologic analyte ranges; AND-gate correctness for tandem-protease linkers; percolation-controlled corridor formation only above defined cell-density/MMP flux.
- In vivo efficacy (rat tibial critical defect; mouse tibialis anterior VML):
  - Spatiotemporal staging: early neutrophil tone reduced; macrophage polarization shift (↑CD206/Arg1), followed by progenitor recruitment (Pax7+, Sca1+) and perfused vessel ingrowth (Lectin+). Architecture: aligned myofibers with centralized-to-peripheral nucleus shift; osteoid→woven→lamellar transition with oriented osteons.
  - Function: torque recovery (muscle), torsional stiffness/ultimate load (bone) approaching contralateral limb; microCT bridging without ectopic bone; histology free of residual material by the time osteocalcin peaks (bone) or lactate normalizes (muscle).
  - Autonomy: cessation of chemokine exposure and accelerated mass loss temporally coincident with OCN/Ctelopeptide positivity (bone) or metabolic normalization (muscle), not with preset time; absence of persistent foreign-body response.
- Comparators: inert degradable gel; gel with ungated ligand display; time-programmed degradable gel. Noninferiority margin on safety; superiority on organized architecture and mechanical restoration.

Mechanistic falsification tests
- Disrupt biomarker recognition (non-imprinted controls) to test whether staging/termination fails. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37556357/?utm_source=openai))
- Flatten protease thresholds (monofunctional crosslinkers) to test loss of corridor localization and increased fibrosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7286611/?utm_source=openai))
- Replace AND with OR topology to test premature network opening and disorganized ingrowth. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5822735/?utm_source=openai))

Risk and mitigation
- Protein imprinting specificity: use epitope imprinting and surface imprinting to reduce template leaching and improve selectivity in complex fluids. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37556357/?utm_source=openai))
- Biodegradability of MIPs: use PLGA- or disulfide-crosslinked chemistries validated for degradable MIPs; confirm complete mass loss and non-toxicity of degradation products. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5223160/?utm_source=openai))
- Over/under-threshold behavior across patients: tune crosslink kinetics and network connectivity using percolation-guided design; pretest patient-relevant protease spectra ex vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7286611/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go
- Month 12: MIP gates with ≥10× analyte-switched permeability; AND-gate crosslinkers validated; cytocompatibility.
- Month 24: Corridor writing and staged cue exposure in tri-culture microtissues with functional alignment/branching.
- Month 36: Efficacy in VML and bone defect models with autonomous termination; no residual material at endpoint.

Impact
This work operationalizes endogenous restoration chemistry as the timing and termination signal, replacing preprogrammed release. The combination of analyte-imprinted gates and proteolysis-thresholded connectivity yields a self-organizing, self-pruning, cell-free niche that coordinates recruitment, patterning, and maturation while guaranteeing closed-loop shutoff upon functional restoration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4613793/?utm_source=openai))
