Title: Disappearing-ink episomal barcodes to quantify engraftment and polyclonal reconstitution after HSCT from whole-blood sampling

Unified question-hypothesis
Can non-integrating, episomal DNA barcodes delivered to donor CD34+ cells serve as a single, clinically amenable assay that both (i) confirms donor engraftment and (ii) quantifies clonal diversity and lineage-specific proliferative history over 12 months post-HSCT, by exploiting the division-dependent dilution of episomes (“disappearing ink”) and recovering barcodes from nucleated blood cells as DNA and from anucleate outputs as RNA? The core bet is that episomal vectors persist in quiescent/slow-cycling HSCs and early progenitors but are geometrically diluted with mitoses in progeny, generating informative decay kinetics per lineage measurable from peripheral blood alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835240/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Switch the clonal mark from a heritable, integrating barcode to a non-integrating episomal barcode whose copy number decays predictably with cell division. The decay itself encodes proliferative history; the barcode spectrum encodes clonal richness/evenness. This single design change converts every routine blood draw into a joint readout of engraftment status and polyclonal dynamics without bone-marrow sampling. Integrating lentiviral barcodes dominate current hematopoietic lineage tracing; leveraging integration-deficient lentiviral (IDLV) episomes as the barcode constitutes the conceptual pivot. ([ashpublications.org](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/115/13/2610/26844/Cellular-barcoding-tool-for-clonal-analysis-in-the?utm_source=openai))

Platform overview (clinical constraints addressed)
- Vector and tag: IDLV-delivered DNA barcodes (non-integrating 1-/2-LTR circles) that persist in nondividing cells, express transiently, and dilute proportionally with cell division. Barcode recovery uses targeted PCR from nucleated lineages. For erythroid/megakaryocytic coverage, include a minimal RNA barcode unit so platelets and reticulocytes, which inherit megakaryocyte/erythroid RNAs despite lacking nuclei, can be assayed by RT-PCR from plasma fractions enriched for platelets or reticulocytes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835240/?utm_source=openai))
- Sample source and logistics: Peripheral blood only; sorted leukocyte subsets, platelet-rich plasma, and reticulocyte-enriched red cell fractions at scheduled timepoints up to 1 year. Existing clinical analyzers and immunomagnetic enrichments already quantify reticulocytes and isolate their RNA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9804789/?utm_source=openai))
- Regulatory feasibility: Ex vivo manipulation with non-integrating vectors reduces genotoxicity relative to integrating marks; residual integration is measurable and monitorable. Assay is targeted PCR/NGS with turnaround on the order of days and cost comparable to small targeted sequencing panels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3751548/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Engineer and qualify an IDLV “disappearing-ink” barcode library optimized for clinical tracking.
- Design: High-complexity, noncoding barcode cassette flanked by PCR handles; include an independent minimal Pol II promoter-polyA unit that transcribes a barcode RNA (no protein ORF) to enable detection in anucleate outputs (platelets) and in reticulocytes. IDLV ensures episomal delivery; episomes are known to be transcription-competent yet progressively lost with proliferation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835240/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic rationale: In quiescent/slow-cycling LT-HSCs, episomes persist longer; in rapidly amplifying myeloid/erythroid progenitors, barcode DNA decays faster, encoding lineage-specific division histories. The same clones’ barcodes appear as RNA in platelets and reticulocytes, which inherit megakaryocyte/erythroid RNAs. ([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.78.6.2906-2920.2004?utm_source=openai))
- Distinguishing novelty: Prior hematopoietic barcoding relies on genomic integration for permanence; the deliberate use of non-integrating IDLV episomes as mitotically dilutable clonal tags for HSCT has not been the standard paradigm. Related “barcode-decay” lineage tracing with episomal libraries supports feasibility of decay-based inference, but has not been developed for clinical HSCT monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894992/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Establish a whole-blood assay to jointly measure engraftment and polyclonal diversity across all hematopoietic compartments.
- Lineage coverage:
  - Myeloid and lymphoid: Extract DNA from sorted granulocytes, monocytes, B, T, NK cells; amplify barcode DNA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894992/?utm_source=openai))
  - Erythroid: Enrich circulating reticulocytes and amplify barcode RNA by RT-PCR; reticulocytes retain RNA and are accessible from blood. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physiolgenomics.00247.2006?utm_source=openai))
  - Megakaryocytic: Isolate platelets from platelet-rich plasma and amplify barcode RNA; platelets carry megakaryocyte-derived RNAs and support RNA-seq–like measurements. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7253186/?utm_source=openai))
- Engraftment confirmation metric: Presence of any donor barcode above limit-of-detection in peripheral blood leukocytes within early post-transplant windows constitutes molecular engraftment; longitudinal increase and multilineage detection confirm hematopoietic output. Integrating methodologies (STR chimerism; TCR/BCR repertoires; integration-site analysis) serve as orthogonal comparators but are not required for the primary assay. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894992/?utm_source=openai))
- Clonal diversity metric: Within each lineage and timepoint, compute richness and evenness (Shannon/Hill numbers) from the barcode spectrum; across time, model clone-level abundance trajectories. These metrics are directly comparable to integrating-barcode studies yet derive from episomal tags. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39523608/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Calibrate and model lineage-specific episome decay to infer proliferative histories and 1-year dynamics.
- Model: Fit a geometric dilution model per lineage and clone in a state-space framework that links observed barcode counts to underlying cell numbers via division-dependent loss and sampling/assay noise. The key parameter is an effective per-division retention probability that differs by lineage due to proliferation kinetics. IDLV episomal literature supports direct proportionality of loss to mitotic activity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835240/?utm_source=openai))
- Longitudinal identifiability: Early timepoints (weeks 2–12) contain highest DNA signal in rapidly cycling outputs; later timepoints (months 3–12) retain signal predominantly in slow-cycling compartments and as RNA in platelets/reticulocytes, sustaining 1-year readouts. Platelet and reticulocyte transcriptomics are routine and stable enough to support serial quantification. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7253186/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-validation: Compare inferred proliferation parameters against known lineage turnover (e.g., granulocyte rapid turnover vs. slower lymphoid kinetics) and against any available clinical metrics (ANC recovery, reticulocyte counts). Literature on lineage tracing with integrating barcodes provides expected qualitative hierarchies for validation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894992/?utm_source=openai))

Study design and analysis plan
- Cohort: Prospective HSCT recipients with donor consent for ex vivo barcoding of a defined fraction of CD34+ cells. Non-integrating marking lowers theoretical insertional risk; perform limited integration-site surveillance to quantify any rare IDLV integration events reported in genome-editing template studies. ([iris.unisr.it](https://iris.unisr.it/retrieve/3e59c5b8-0ffd-41c8-aee8-f8750d59a0c5/PIIS1934590922003782.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Sampling cadence: Peripheral blood at dense intervals early (e.g., weekly in the first 2 months) then monthly through 12 months; isolate leukocyte subsets, platelets, and reticulocyte-enriched fractions for barcode detection as DNA (nucleated) and RNA (anucleate outputs).
- Assay: Targeted PCR/RT-PCR with unique molecular identifiers and spike-in standards to control for PCR jackpotting and extraction efficiency; small-panel NGS.
- Outcomes:
  - Primary: Concordant engraftment confirmation and polyclonal diversity indices across lineages from the same assay.
  - Secondary: Lineage-specific decay constants; between-patient heterogeneity in clonal evenness; detection of clonal skew or dominance emergence.
- Statistics: Mixed-effects models for clone trajectories; diversity rarefaction curves to standardize depth; pre-specified thresholds for engraftment positivity based on assay LOD/LOQ established in Aim 1.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Signal decay vs. 1-year horizon: Episomes dilute with proliferation; signal could fall below detection late. Mitigation: leverage RNA barcodes in platelets and reticulocytes for sustained detection of lineage output; employ sensitive targeted amplification and UMIs; focus inference on early-to-mid windows for rapidly cycling lineages and on slow-cycling/renewing compartments later. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7253186/?utm_source=openai))
- Residual integration: Although IDLVs are designed to avoid integration, rare integrations can occur. Include low-depth integration-site profiling on a subset of samples to document frequency and ensure the readout is not dominated by integrated events. ([iris.unisr.it](https://iris.unisr.it/retrieve/3e59c5b8-0ffd-41c8-aee8-f8750d59a0c5/PIIS1934590922003782.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Clinical feasibility: IDLVs have been broadly studied as safer, non-integrating delivery vehicles; ex vivo manipulation of donor HSPCs is standard in gene/cell therapy workflows. Assay relies on blood draws and targeted sequencing, aligning with clinical timelines and costs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3751548/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extension (optional, for improved identifiability)
In a parallel arm, evaluate whether adding a minimal, subthreshold S/MAR motif to a minicircle barcode (delivered by electroporation) extends episome nuclear residence without enabling robust replication, thereby creating a slower-decay tracer to complement IDLV’s faster decay for ratiometric inference. Classical S/MAR episomes replicate once per cell cycle and are mitotically stable at low copy numbers via SAF-A tethering; this arm explicitly tests whether shortened/attenuated S/MAR fragments can provide limited tethering without full replicon behavior, a property not established and thus treated as exploratory. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6789156/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and readouts for success
- Demonstrate in vitro that barcode copy number in dividing hematopoietic progenitors follows predicted geometric dilution, while remaining more stable in quiescent HSPC-enriched cultures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835240/?utm_source=openai))
- In patients, show that:
  - Engraftment is called from the first weeks post-HSCT using the same assay that later quantifies clonal diversity.
  - Myeloid lineages exhibit faster barcode DNA decay than lymphoid, while platelets/reticulocytes provide persistent RNA-barcode detection across months. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7253186/?utm_source=openai))
  - Diversity indices and decay parameters correlate with clinical course and known hematopoietic kinetics, providing actionable, lineage-resolved reconstitution maps.

Expected impact and novelty
This work reframes HSCT clonal tracking around a non-integrating, decay-informative mark, eliminating the need for bone marrow sampling and distinguishing itself from STR chimerism, TCR/BCR repertoire tracking, and retroviral integration–site or integrating-barcode approaches. It leverages established IDLV episomal biology and routine platelet/reticulocyte transcriptomics to deliver a single, blood-based assay that simultaneously answers “has engraftment occurred?” and “how diverse and dynamic is reconstitution across all lineages?” over the first post-transplant year. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2835240/?utm_source=openai))

Title: Endogenous mtDNA Haplotypes as Single-Assay Barcodes for Engraftment Confirmation and Polyclonal Reconstitution After HSCT

Hypothesis-goal (indistinguishable): A single, clinically-deployable assay that phases full-length mitochondrial genomes per cell and co-captures surface immunophenotypes can quantify donor engraftment and lineage-resolved clonal diversity across myeloid, lymphoid, erythroid-precursor, and megakaryocytic compartments, and track their dynamics over one year post-HSCT by exploiting (i) physical co-segregation of mtDNA variants as clonal barcodes and (ii) deterministic shifts in heteroplasmy shaped by sequential differentiation bottlenecks. This leverages endogenous mtDNA variation already validated for human lineage tracing and, in HSCT, avoids exogenous labeling while improving upon fragmentary short-read approaches. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6408267/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy: Treat the hematopoietic hierarchy as a signal-processing cascade that transforms stochastic mtDNA heteroplasmy in progenitors into lineage-stable, phased haplotypes. Read out those haplotypes per single cell with long-read sequencing and co-segregation analysis to define clones; assign cell types via simultaneous antibody–oligo tags to compute chimerism and diversity in one run. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6408267/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Build and analytically validate a droplet single-cell “mtDNA+ADT” assay that outputs, per cell, (a) a phased, error-corrected full-length mtDNA haplotype and (b) a lineage/state label from antibody-derived tags (ADTs). Demonstrate accurate donor–recipient assignment and clone calling across neutrophils/monocytes/NK/T/B, erythroid precursors/reticulocytes, and platelets. Note: mature RBCs lack mitochondria; reticulocytes and platelets retain mitochondria and are therefore assayable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157046/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Quantify engraftment and clonal diversity per lineage using co-segregation-defined clones and bottleneck-aware variance models; derive decision metrics (e.g., donor fraction, Shannon index, Gini) and QC thresholds.
- Aim 3: Longitudinally track clonal dynamics at prespecified timepoints through 12 months; relate shifts to clinical events and known reconstitution kinetics (early innate recovery, delayed adaptive). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3103296/?utm_source=openai))

Assay concept and workflow
- Sample schedule and coverage
  - Peripheral blood: weeks 2–6, months 3, 6, 9, 12. Platelet-rich plasma for megakaryocytic output; buffy coat for myeloid/lymphoid; reticulocyte-enriched fraction (CD71high) for erythroid output; marrow aspirate once at month 1–3 for erythroblasts if clinically indicated. Platelets and reticulocytes are included because they retain mitochondria during their functional windows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6828734/?utm_source=openai))
- Droplet chemistry (single-assay readout)
  - Cell indexing: Encapsulate single cells/platelets/reticulocytes with lysis and reverse-crosslinking buffers, a panel of oligo-tagged antibodies (TotalSeq-compatible), and barcoded primer sets. ADTs generate per-cell lineage/state readouts as in established DNA+protein droplet workflows. ([missionbio.com](https://www.missionbio.com/products/platform?utm_source=openai))
  - Full-length mtDNA capture: Perform tiled long-range PCR (e.g., 3×5.6 kb) using high-fidelity polymerase within droplets. Primers carry cell barcodes and molecule-level UMIs to enable per-cell and per-molecule consensus. Pool, clean up, and prepare long-read libraries (ONT). This enables per-molecule phasing and low-frequency heteroplasmy quantification after UMI consensus, as shown in single-cell full-length mtDNA methods (iMiGseq, Cas9-guided enrichment) adapted here for droplet-barcoded inputs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10164560/?utm_source=openai))
  - Sequencing and TAT: ONT flow cells; basecalling and demultiplexing by cell barcodes; 24–48 h turnaround in a clinical lab setting.
- Bioinformatics
  - Error suppression: Build UMI consensus per long amplicon, merge tiled fragments to reconstruct full-length, phased haplotypes per cell; eliminate strand- and homopolymer-associated artifacts by consensus and read-level filters validated for long-read UMI approaches. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19687-9?utm_source=openai))
  - Donor–recipient assignment: Compare per-cell haplotypes to donor/recipient references (buffy-coat snapshots at baseline) using multi-SNP haplotype distance, robust to heteroplasmy.
  - Clone definition by co-segregation: Construct a co-segregation matrix of phased variants across cells/timepoints; define clones as variant sets that co-occur above stability thresholds; allow nested subclones when additional variants arise. Prior single-cell studies show mtDNA variants can act as physical, heritable barcodes across hematopoietic lineages, including in HSCT with single-cell assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6408267/?utm_source=openai))
  - Bottleneck-aware analytics: Model within-lineage heteroplasmy mean/variance as a function of expected differentiation bottlenecks and proliferative bursts; deviations flag oligoclonal dominance or lineage bias during reconstitution.
  - Outputs per timepoint: For each lineage and globally—(i) donor fraction; (ii) clone count and diversity indices; (iii) largest-clone fraction; (iv) clonal turnover rate; (v) QC flags (e.g., multi-haplotype per droplet).

Validation plan
- Technical
  - Spike-in mixtures of donor/recipient leukocytes with known ratios to test assignment accuracy across heteroplasmy levels; platelet and reticulocyte controls to confirm lineage coverage.
  - Concordance with orthogonal standards in a subset: STR chimerism for donor fraction; traditional single-cell DNA+protein for immunophenotype agreement. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK608246/?utm_source=openai))
- Biological
  - Compare lineage-specific recovery curves with established HSCT kinetics (myeloid early; NK early; T/B delayed). Discrepancies trigger investigation for graft dysfunction or infection. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3103296/?utm_source=openai))

Cohort and longitudinal design
- Enroll 40 allo-HSCT recipients. Collect baseline donor/recipient gDNA for haplotypes. Sample per schedule; store excess material for confirmatory tests. Follow standard-of-care; no genetic manipulation; minimal added marrow sampling.

Clinical translation considerations
- Single-assay dual readout: chimerism and clonal diversity from the same per-cell dataset with comprehensive lineage coverage, including platelets and erythroid precursors. Mature RBCs are excluded by biology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157046/?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility: Builds on proven components—ADTs in droplet DNA workflows and full-length mtDNA long-read phasing—with adaptation to combine them. ([missionbio.com](https://www.missionbio.com/products/platform?utm_source=openai))
- TAT and cost: ONT-based, 24–48 h; panelized antibodies; scalable droplets; compatible with LDT development.
- Edge-case mitigation: If donor and recipient mtDNA haplotypes are unusually similar, add ≤20 short nuclear SNP amplicons into the same droplet reaction without changing workflow class; triggers only when haplotype distance is below pre-specified thresholds.

Milestones and success criteria
- Year 1: Analytical validation (≥99% accurate donor assignment in leukocyte spike-ins at ≥1% minor fraction; clone recall F1 ≥0.9 in mixes).
- Year 2: Prospective HSCT pilot (n=20): per-lineage donor fraction concordance with STR within ±5%; reportable diversity metrics with intra-assay CV ≤10%; detect emergent oligoclonal dominance ≥4 weeks before clinical relapse in at least two cases (signal-generation endpoint). ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK608246/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 3: Expanded validation (n=20): demonstrate clinical utility signals (association of diversity metrics with GVHD/relapse) to justify a regulated LDT.

Novelty relative to prior art
- Unlike STR chimerism or immune-receptor repertoire assays, this platform uses phased, full-length mtDNA per cell as endogenous barcodes and unites donor assignment and clonal diversity with simultaneous immunophenotyping in a single assay. Prior HSCT lineage-tracing with mtDNA has leveraged fragmentary reads from scATAC/RNA; here, per-cell long-read phasing and co-segregation enable direct clonal definitions and robust longitudinal matching, including platelets and erythroid precursors. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK608246/?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If long-amplicon efficiency in droplets is suboptimal, switch to Cas9-guided mtDNA enrichment on barcoded single-cell lysates prior to ligation and ONT sequencing; retain the same ADT co-capture and analysis stack. Feasibility of Cas9-guided full-length mtDNA enrichment has been demonstrated. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-33530-3?utm_source=openai))

Ethics and risk
- Minimal-risk, observational sampling aligned with clinical draws; single optional marrow aspirate. No exogenous genetic modification; data de-identified.

Deliverable: A clinically amenable, single-assay platform for simultaneous engraftment confirmation and polyclonal reconstitution profiling across all hematopoietic lineages, with validated longitudinal clone tracking to one year post-HSCT. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6828734/?utm_source=openai))

Title
A pre-installed, epigenetically written clonal ID and lineage ledger for single-assay, longitudinal assessment of HSCT engraftment and polyclonal reconstitution

Rationale
- DNA methylation is mitotically heritable and encodes lineage history; epimutation-based lineage inference has emerged for hematopoiesis but relies on endogenous, stochastic marks not designed for transplant readouts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11014487/?utm_source=openai))
- Programmable DNA methylation writers (ZF/TALE/dCas9–DNMT) can lay down targeted CpG methylation at defined loci, establishing durable, locally confined marks measurable by targeted sequencing. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/45/4/1703/2605790?utm_source=openai))
- cfDNA in plasma contains contributions from erythroblast and megakaryocyte progenitors, enabling access to nucleated precursors of anucleate outputs; targeted methylation assays can quantify these contributions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10662131/?utm_source=openai))
- Enzymatic methyl-seq (EM-seq) and targeted methylation sequencing provide robust, low-input clinical readouts. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1878-0261.70303?utm_source=openai))
- Error-correcting DNA barcodes derived from coding theory (e.g., Reed–Solomon-based designs) improve clone calling robustness in the face of PCR/seq errors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142223/?utm_source=openai))

Central question-hypothesis
Can a single, pre-installed synthetic genomic cassette—combining a robust error-corrected clonal ID with lineage-gated, heritable CpG “pads”—enable a one-assay measurement that simultaneously confirms donor engraftment and quantifies polyclonal, pan-lineage reconstitution over 1 year after HSCT?

Atomic strategy
Install in donor CD34+ HSPCs a compact safe-harbor cassette that:
- encodes a Reed–Solomon–redundant clonal identifier for high-fidelity engraftment and clone counting, and
- places adjacent synthetic CpG “pads” that are selectively written by a tethered de novo methyltransferase only when hematopoietic lineage programs open pad-specific access.
One targeted enzymatic methylation readout from whole blood (cells) plus plasma (cfDNA) decodes both the clonal IDs and the lineage-experience pad states at each timepoint.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Engineer and validate a synthetic clonal ID plus lineage ledger cassette (CLL-cassette) in human HSPCs.
- Design: (a) a 60–100 bp clonal ID block with an error-correcting codebook (RS-derived) to minimize barcode collisions and enable correction of substitution/indel errors; (b) 6–10 adjacent CpG-dense pads insulated by boundary elements. The DNMT writer is targeted to the cassette via high-affinity DNA-binding domains and restricted by short-range spreading to confine activity. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/45/4/1703/2605790?utm_source=openai))
- Lineage gating concept: pad accessibility is controlled by local motif architectures tuned to be preferentially occupied within myeloid, lymphoid, erythroid, or megakaryocytic transcriptional environments; when accessible, the tethered writer deposits predefined binary methylation patterns (pad on/off), which are then mitotically maintained.
- In vitro validation: differentiate engineered HSPCs toward myeloid, lymphoid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic fates; quantify pad-specific methylation states and stability through serial replating; ensure minimal off-target methylation by WGBS sampling near the cassette and at sentinel loci. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/45/4/1703/2605790?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Demonstrate single-assay engraftment confirmation and clonal diversity measurement across all lineages in vivo.
- Xenotransplant model: transplant engineered human HSPCs into NSG mice; collect monthly peripheral blood for 6–12 months. Perform one targeted EM-seq panel capturing the clonal ID block and CpG pads from leukocyte gDNA and plasma cfDNA per timepoint. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1878-0261.70303?utm_source=openai))
- Outputs: (a) Engraftment fraction (sum of valid clonal IDs / total reads) benchmarked against standard chimerism; (b) clonal abundance distribution (Shannon/Simpson indices) from RS-decoded IDs; (c) lineage engagement per clone from pad states. Confirm erythroid/megakaryocytic coverage using cfDNA, leveraging known lineage-of-origin methylation in plasma. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10662131/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Establish analytical and clinical translation parameters.
- Analytical robustness: simulate and empirically assess error profiles; verify RS decoding accuracy, pad call reproducibility, and detection limits for low-frequency clones. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142223/?utm_source=openai))
- Clinical feasibility: define blood volumes, sequencing depth, turnaround, and cost for a quarterly sampling schedule over 1 year post-HSCT; compare against STR chimerism, TCR/BCR repertoire methods, and integration-site analysis on the same specimens.

Study design and readout
- Cassette delivery: site-targeted integration into a hematopoietic safe harbor; single-copy preference to avoid multi-locus confounds.
- Writer restriction: DNMT3A/3L catalytic module tethered to the cassette to minimize genome-wide exposure; expression driven by a hematopoietic-restricted, low-level promoter with degron control. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/45/4/1703/2605790?utm_source=openai))
- Sampling: at 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months post-transplant, draw whole blood; isolate leukocyte DNA and plasma cfDNA.
- Assay: a single targeted enzymatic methylation sequencing panel amplifies the clonal ID and pad regions; identical panel applied to both leukocyte DNA and cfDNA. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1878-0261.70303?utm_source=openai))
- Decoding and quantitation: RS decoding yields per-clone counts; pad methylation called by CpG-majority within each pad. Outputs integrated into a joint clonal-lineage matrix per timepoint; temporal dynamics modeled with state-space approaches to quantify clonal stability, expansion, contraction, and lineage bias.

Key endpoints and success criteria
- Primary: concordant engraftment fraction versus clinical chimerism at all timepoints (non-inferiority margin pre-specified).
- Secondary: accurate clonal diversity metrics in leukocytes; sensitivity to detect ≥1% clone frequency; stability of pad calls across cell divisions.
- Tertiary: detection of erythroid and megakaryocytic lineage engagement from plasma cfDNA pad states, with correlation to reticulocyte counts and platelet dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10662131/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Off-target methylation risk: restrict writer localization to the cassette; include insulators; validate off-target landscape in vitro before transplantation. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/45/4/1703/2605790?utm_source=openai))
- Low cfDNA representation of the cassette: combine leukocyte DNA (robust clonality and engraftment) with cfDNA (access to erythroid/megakaryocytic progenitors); increase amplicon multiplicity for cfDNA panel to boost sensitivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10662131/?utm_source=openai))
- Editor persistence: employ self-limiting expression (degrons) or inducible shutoff after initial months once pad states are established.

Differentiation from existing methods
- Unlike STR chimerism or immune-receptor repertoire sequencing, the CLL-cassette unifies engraftment confirmation and clone-resolved, pan-lineage readouts in a single targeted methylation assay without relying on endogenous sequence polymorphisms or retroviral integration maps. It leverages designed, heritable epigenetic writing at a synthetic locus and error-corrected clonal IDs to raise quantitative reliability. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/45/4/1703/2605790?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Months 0–9: In vitro cassette engineering; writer confinement; lineage pad calibration; analytical pipeline finalized.
- Months 9–24: Xenotransplantation cohort; longitudinal sampling; cross-validation against standard clinical assays.
- Months 24–30: Pre-IND package for a prospective observational study embedding the single-assay readout alongside standard post-HSCT monitoring.

Expected impact
A compact, pre-installed clonal ID and lineage ledger read by one targeted enzymatic methylation assay can provide durable, quantitative confirmation of engraftment and high-fidelity, clone-resolved reconstitution maps across all hematopoietic lineages for up to 1 year after HSCT, using routine blood draws and plasma. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1878-0261.70303?utm_source=openai))

Title
ECC-Barcode HSCT: A single-locus, edit-then-silenced, error-corrected recombinase barcode for simultaneous donor engraftment quantification and clonal diversity tracking from peripheral blood

Central hypothesis and goal
A single-copy barcode installed at a validated safe-harbor in donor CD34+ HSPCs, stochastically resolved once ex vivo by orthogonal recombinases and then permanently silenced, will provide an invariant, heritable identifier that (i) quantifies donor chimerism and (ii) measures polyclonal reconstitution across all hematopoietic lineages via one targeted sequencing assay on longitudinal peripheral blood samples up to 1 year. Platelet and reticulocyte compartments will be captured by brief lineage-restricted barcode RNA output, enabling comprehensive lineage coverage without cell sorting. Prior work has shown recombinase-based barcoding in mice, platelet/reticulocyte RNA detectability, and clinical-grade HSPC safe-harbor editing; here we integrate these concepts into a clinically scalable, single-assay platform for HSCT. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5905670/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Replace phenotype-based cell sorting with a one-time, ex vivo recombinase resolution of a compact barcode cassette integrated at a fixed genomic locus, followed by edit-then-silence. Read the same short barcode region from: (a) genomic DNA of nucleated cells for myeloid/lymphoid lineages; (b) barcode RNA in platelets and reticulocytes for megakaryocytic/erythroid lineages, using a unified UMI-amplicon assay. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5905670/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Single-locus, error-corrected barcode: A recombinase-resolved cassette with built-in parity bits provides high diversity and on-board error detection/correction, unlike random STRs, TCR/BCR sequencing, or viral/AAV barcode libraries. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5905670/?utm_source=openai))
- Edit-then-silence: One-time ex vivo recombination; thereafter the barcode locus is transcriptionally quiescent, minimizing biological burden and drift while retaining detectability in anucleate lineages via brief, lineage-gated barcode RNAs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4797142/?utm_source=openai))
- Clinically compatible integration: Cas9 RNP targeting to CCR5 or AAVS1 with donor template delivery optimized for HSPCs; approach is aligned with ex vivo clinical gene-editing workflows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6731271/?utm_source=openai))
- Single-assay readout: One multiplexed UMI-amplicon workflow quantifies total donor chimerism and deconvolves clonal diversity across all lineages from the same blood draw, enabling year-long longitudinal tracking. Prior HDR-barcoding in HSPCs (BAR-Seq/TRACE-Seq) lacked a parity-encoded, edit-then-silenced single cassette designed for direct clinical readout including anucleate lineages. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41596-021-00529-x?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Engineer and validate the ECC-barcode safe-harbor locus in human CD34+ HSPCs.
2) Build and lock a unified clinical assay to read chimerism and clonal diversity from peripheral blood DNA/RNA.
3) Demonstrate quantitative performance, lineage coverage, and longitudinal stability in humanized mouse models and translated QC samples from clinical HSCT products.

Aim 1. Engineer and validate ECC-barcode in human CD34+ HSPCs
- Design
  - Safe-harbor targeting: Cas9 RNP to CCR5 or AAVS1; donor template (0.9–1.5 kb) with: (i) recombinase-resolvable barcode core; (ii) flanking cHS4 insulators; (iii) a 70 bp synthetic “donor-engraftment tag” adjacent to the barcode for absolute chimerism measurement. Deliver donor by rAAV6 (for kilobase-sized inserts) under GMP-like conditions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6731271/?utm_source=openai))
  - Barcode core: Interleaved loxP/lox2272 and FRT/F3 sites bracketing eight 20–24 bp “data tiles” and three 20–24 bp “parity tiles” (Hamming(11,k) scheme). A single controlled Cre/Flp pulse produces an irreversible, diverse, error-correctable genotype per HSC. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5905670/?utm_source=openai))
  - Edit-then-silence: Final cassette architecture lacks active promoters in stem/progenitor and nucleated lineages. Two ultra-minimal lineage promoters drive 80–120 nt noncoding barcode RNAs only in late megakaryocytic (PF4) and erythroid (ALAS2) stages; embedded miR-142-3p sites suppress off-lineage leakage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4797142/?utm_source=openai))
  - Transient recombinase delivery: Cre and Flp mRNA electroporation; no persistent expression.
- Experiments
  - Editing metrics: On-target HDR, allele dosage, and off-target assessment by targeted capture and high-depth sequencing; p53 activation profiling to mitigate AAV6 dose-related DDR. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1934590922003782?utm_source=openai))
  - Barcode diversity/neutrality: Clonal outgrowth assays; colony-forming units; xenotransplant limiting dilution to test long-term repopulation and multilineage output versus mock-edited controls. 
  - Cassette quiescence: RNA-seq/qPCR to confirm minimal transcription in HSPCs and nucleated progeny.

Go/no-go criteria
- ≥20% single-allele HDR in CD34+CD90+ HSPCs with ≤5% loss of repopulating capacity versus mock; no off-target events above pre-specified thresholds; stable cassette with no ongoing recombination after day 3. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-11962-8?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build and lock a unified clinical assay for simultaneous chimerism and clonal diversity
- Assay schema (one tube; two libraries)
  - DNA library (buffy coat): UMI-tagged amplicon spanning engraftment tag + barcode tiles; co-amplify a host reference locus for absolute chimerism by ratio-metric ddPCR/NGS. 
  - RNA library (platelet-rich plasma; reticulocyte-enriched fraction): RT-UMI amplicon using the same primers directed to the barcode RNA. Platelet and reticulocyte RNA presence provides megakaryocytic/erythroid coverage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3937023/?utm_source=openai))
- Error model
  - Use parity tiles for single-error correction/double-error detection; UMI consensus calling; synthetic spike-ins for limit-of-detection calibration (target 0.1–0.5% clone fraction).
- Outputs
  - Engraftment: fraction of donor-engraftment tag reads relative to host reference (primary endpoint).
  - Clonal diversity: unique corrected barcode states and their frequencies; Shannon and Hill diversity indices; lineage-specific clone contributions by comparing DNA vs barcode RNA fractions.
- Turnaround/cost
  - <72 h from draw to report; short-read sequencing of a single 300–450 bp amplicon per library; <$300/sample projected at pilot scale.

Aim 3. Demonstrate quantitative performance and longitudinal stability
- Models
  - Human CD34+ HSPC NSG xenografts with ECC-barcode; peripheral blood sampling at weeks 2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 36, 52.
  - Parallel BAR-Seq/TRACE-Seq comparators to benchmark diversity quantification and temporal stability. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41596-021-00529-x?utm_source=openai))
- Endpoints
  - Accuracy vs orthogonal standards: whole-blood STR chimerism for engraftment; concordance analysis; recovery of expected clonal structures from defined cell mixes.
  - Lineage coverage: detection of barcode RNA in platelets/reticulocytes and alignment with nucleated-cell clonal spectra.
  - Longitudinal robustness: clone gain/loss dynamics; parity-corrected error rates ≤10^-4/base per timepoint; reproducibility across sites.

Study design and analysis
- Sample size: n≥10 xenografts per arm to detect ≥20% difference in recovered clone counts with 80% power (negative binomial model).
- Bioinformatics: demultiplexing; UMI consensus; parity correction; maximum-likelihood deconvolution of clone frequencies; diversity indices with bootstrap CIs; mixed-effects models for longitudinal changes.
- Risk mitigation
  - HDR burden: optimize rAAV6 dose; consider short ssDNA donors and more compact cassettes if needed. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1934590922003782?utm_source=openai))
  - Anucleate RNA instability: stabilize barcode RNA with short circRNA scaffold or GC-balanced hairpins if sensitivity is insufficient; pre-specify fallback to megakaryocyte-derived mRNA capture only, while retaining whole-blood DNA as primary readout. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4797142/?utm_source=openai))
  - Regulatory: demonstrate absence of persistent recombinase transcripts/proteins; no constitutive transgene expression; safe-harbor integration with comprehensive off-target profiling.

Milestones
- Month 6: Cassette integrated and resolved in CD34+ HSPCs; neutrality and quiescence confirmed.
- Month 12: Locked clinical assay SOP; LOD established; external proficiency panel passed.
- Month 18: Xenograft study complete; pre-IDE package drafted with safety dossier.
- Month 24: First-in-human observational feasibility in surplus apheresis QC samples from allogeneic HSCT donors (no infusion) to demonstrate analytical validity against STR chimerism.

Expected outcomes
- Single-assay quantification of donor engraftment and clonal diversity with error-corrected barcodes across all hematopoietic lineages, including platelets and reticulocytes, using routine peripheral blood sampling up to 1 year.
- Superior robustness to sequencing/PCR errors via parity tiles and UMIs.
- Clear differentiation from STR/TCR/BCR/retroviral-integration approaches and from HDR barcoded libraries by employing a single, edit-then-silenced, error-corrected barcode cassette in a fixed safe-harbor, optimized for clinical translation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9927566/?utm_source=openai))

Comparative context and feasibility
- Recombinase barcoding is established in mouse hematopoiesis but not deployed for human HSCT tracking; safe-harbor HDR in HSPCs is clinically advancing; platelets and reticulocytes provide analyzable RNAs. The proposed convergence is novel and clinically tractable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5905670/?utm_source=openai))

Ethics and compliance
- All human cell collections under IRB-approved consent; animal studies under IACUC protocols; biosafety per institutional guidelines for ex vivo gene editing.

Deliverable
A validated, clinic-ready barcoding and analytics package (cassette design, editing and recombination SOPs, blood-based dual library kit, and analysis software) capable of simultaneous engraftment confirmation and clonal diversity assessment in HSCT without cell sorting.

Title
Physio-Temporal Demixing with Mitochondrial Anchors (PTDMA): A single-assay, clinically amenable framework to quantify engraftment and polyclonal reconstitution after HSCT from serial peripheral blood

Unified hypothesis-question
Can we noninvasively reconstruct the number, identity, and trajectories of engrafted hematopoietic clones after HSCT by treating each peripheral blood lineage as a distinct temporal filter on shared clonal production, and calibrating this demixing with endogenous mitochondrial DNA barcodes measured in serial, minimally sorted blood compartments? If so, can the same data stream also yield a robust donor–recipient engraftment readout?

Atomic strategy
Exploit known lineage-specific maturation delays and survival kinetics as orthogonal temporal filters to separate latent clonal “factory” outputs across lineages, while using naturally occurring mitochondrial variants (haplotypes and somatic heteroplasmies) detected in leukocytes and platelets as sparse genetic anchors that tie model components to real clones and provide a direct engraftment signal. Platelets and leukocytes retain mitochondria/mtDNA, reticulocytes transiently retain mitochondria before RBC maturation, and erythrocytes lack mitochondria—together enabling multilineage anchoring with predictable temporal offsets. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470328/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Build and validate a mechanistic, lineage-coupled state-space model that represents each lineage as a convolution of latent clonal production with lineage-specific impulse responses (maturation delay + survival kernel). Use expectation–maximization with Kalman filtering and Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoothing for joint inference of clone number, abundances, and kernel parameters from noisy longitudinal data. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10585354/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2. Develop a targeted, multiplex mtDNA amplicon panel and sorting-lite workflow to generate time-resolved mitochondrial haplotype/heteroplasmy profiles from granulocytes, monocytes, B, T, NK cells, platelets, and CD71+ reticulocytes (when present). Use donor–recipient mtDNA haplotype mixture as an orthogonal engraftment readout and mtDNA somatic variants as anchors linking computationally inferred components to biological clones. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6929387/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3. Prospective test in allogeneic HSCT recipients: determine agreement with standard chimerism (STR/SNP) for engraftment, and quantify resolution/accuracy of clonal diversity and dynamics across all major lineages over 12 months. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8065704/?utm_source=openai))

Study design and cohort
- Population: 30 consecutive adult allogeneic HSCT recipients (varied donors/sources) at a single center; exclude recent massive transfusion at enrollment; record transfusions prospectively.
- Sampling schedule: peripheral blood at weeks 1–12 (weekly), months 4–12 (monthly).
- Clinical readouts each timepoint: CBC with differential, absolute lymphocyte subsets by a 6–8 color panel, reticulocyte count, hemoglobin, platelets.
- Sorting-lite fractions: granulocytes, monocytes, CD3+ T, CD19+ B, CD56+ NK, platelets, CD71+ reticulocytes (early months only). Low-pressure immunomagnetic enrichment acceptable for throughput.
- Nucleic acid assays:
  - Targeted mtDNA panel (∼20–40 amplicons covering high-heteroplasmy and hypervariable regions) at ≥5,000× depth per fraction.
  - Optional shallow WGS of buffy coat at months 1, 6, 12 for benchmarking somatic mtDNA burden.
- Reference test: standard-of-care STR/SNP chimerism on whole blood and available subsets at matched visits. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8065704/?utm_source=openai))

Assay workflow and analytics
- Wet lab
  - Same-day processing; platelet isolation before leukocyte lysis to prevent cross-contamination.
  - DNA extraction optimized for low-input platelet mtDNA; UMIs to suppress sequencing/PCR error.
- Signals
  - Counts: lineage absolute counts (CBC/flow), hemoglobin, platelet count, reticulocyte percentage.
  - Genetics: mtDNA haplotype mixture in bulk fractions for donor–recipient engraftment; somatic heteroplasmy trajectories per fraction as sparse clonal anchors; acknowledge erythrocytes lack mtDNA while reticulocytes retain mitochondria only for ∼1 day after marrow egress. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK264/?report=reader&utm_source=openai))
- Forward model
  - Latent clonal production u_k(t) for clone k.
  - Lineage response h_L(t): fixed-form kernels encoding maturation lag τ_L and survival/clearance with timescale θ_L; initialize priors from literature (e.g., platelets ∼7–10 days, monocytes ∼1–2 days, neutrophils short but debated, RBC mass strongly low-pass with ∼100–120-day lifetime, reticulocytes ∼1 day). Treat lymphocyte channels with mixture of fast and slow components. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470328/?utm_source=openai))
  - Observation: y_L(t) = Σ_k (h_L * u_k)(t) + ε_L(t). A joint observation vector over lineages is fitted.
  - Constraints: non-negativity; cross-lineage lag coupling; clone-sparsity via spike-and-slab prior; lineage-specific scaling.
  - Anchoring: force a subset of components to match measured mtDNA variant allele fraction (VAF) trajectories in platelets/leukocytes/reticulocytes for clones carrying those variants; estimate mapping from VAF to cell fraction per lineage using mtDNA copy-number heuristics and learned scaling.
  - Engraftment: donor–recipient mtDNA haplotype mixture in leukocytes/platelets yields percent-donor estimate; compare to STR/SNP chimerism. Note: this is a hypothesis test; clinical validation is part of Aim 3. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4260364/?utm_source=openai))
  - Inference: extended/unscented Kalman filter + RTS smoother; model selection by Bayesian evidence to choose clone number; uncertainty via bootstrap over timepoints. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10585354/?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes
- Primary
  - Agreement of percent-donor engraftment between PTDMA mtDNA haplotype mixture and STR/SNP chimerism (concordance correlation; Bland–Altman at each time window). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8065704/?utm_source=openai))
  - Time-resolved clonal diversity (Hill/Shannon indices) and number of active clones contributing ≥5% to at least one lineage at any time.
- Secondary
  - Cross-lineage lag motifs recovered for anchored clones (e.g., myeloid/platelet early pulses, delayed erythroid mass changes) and their stability over time.
  - Early detection of clonal shifts preceding cytopenias, GVHD flares, or relapse, compared against clinical events.
  - Comparative information yield vs routine counts alone and vs genetic-only approaches (e.g., WGS-based somatic phylogenies where available). ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038%2Fs41586-024-08128-y?utm_source=openai))

Validation and benchmarking
- Simulations: generate synthetic cohorts using published lineage half-lives and stochastic clonal production; assess identifiability and error under sampling densities matching HSCT follow-up. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470328/?utm_source=openai))
- Pilot real-world: blinded analysis of 10 historical HSCT cases with archived serial samples to de-risk workflow.
- Prospective: pre-specified success if (i) engraftment concordance correlation ≥0.9 vs STR/SNP; (ii) at least 70% of clones identified by mtDNA anchors have matching demixed components; (iii) lineage-coupled model outperforms lineage-independent models in AIC/BIC and out-of-sample prediction.

Novelty and rationale
- Distinct from STR chimerism and TCR/BCR/viral integration methods: PTDMA primarily exploits physiological temporal filters and maturation lags across all lineages for demixing, using mtDNA as minimal, endogenous anchors rather than the main measurement. This leverages established biology that platelets and leukocytes contain mitochondria/mtDNA, reticulocytes transiently retain mitochondria, and erythrocytes do not, enabling a practical multilineage anchor scheme from blood alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4260364/?utm_source=openai))
- Prior dynamic models have used state-space estimation on barcoded clonal data; here we repurpose the estimator to a new identifiability regime based on lineage-specific impulse responses plus sparse mtDNA constraints. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10585354/?utm_source=openai))
- Mitochondrial variants are validated endogenous lineage-tracing barcodes in hematopoiesis and are sensitive readouts of clonal hematopoiesis burden with age, supporting feasibility for anchor definition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6469926/?utm_source=openai))

Clinical translation plan
- Sample type: peripheral blood only; ≤20 mL per visit; no marrow.
- Assay time: 48–72 h from receipt to report (counts + mtDNA panel + model).
- Cost drivers: targeted sequencing (amplicon-based), limited sorting, modest compute; amenable to CLIA workflow adaptation.
- Reporting: single, longitudinal dashboard with percent-donor engraftment, number of active clones, diversity metrics, and clone-specific lineage contributions over time.

Anticipated limitations and mitigations
- RBC compartment: absence of mitochondria prevents late genetic anchoring; mitigate by early reticulocyte anchoring and enforcing expected lagged, low-pass coupling to hemoglobin thereafter. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK264/?report=reader&utm_source=openai))
- Platelet peculiarities: platelets can release mitochondria/extracellular mtDNA; apply rigorous isolation and DNase treatment to minimize cfDNA contamination; rely on consistent within-subject trends. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4260364/?utm_source=openai))
- Neutrophil lifespan uncertainty: treat as learnable parameter within reasonable priors; sensitivity analyses across reported ranges. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5225409/?utm_source=openai))
- Donor–recipient mtDNA haplotype similarity: if haplotypes are insufficiently distinct, fall back to standard STR/SNP chimerism for engraftment benchmarking at those timepoints. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8065704/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Month 0–6: finalize panel and workflow; synthetic data validation; pilot n=10 archived cases.
- Month 6–24: enroll n=30; complete longitudinal sampling; interim analysis at 6 months for feasibility.
- Month 24–30: primary endpoint analysis; finalize assay specifications for prospective CLIA validation.

Ethics and data governance
- Genetic testing limited to mitochondrial loci; consent includes disclosure plan for incidental donor–recipient haplotype information; data de-identified; compliance with transplant society recommendations for genetic testing post-HSCT. ([astctjournal.org](https://www.astctjournal.org/article/S2666-6367%2823%2901708-6/fulltext?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
A single, minimally invasive assay and model that (i) matches or exceeds STR/SNP chimerism for engraftment tracking, and (ii) provides quantitative, lineage-resolved clonal diversity and trajectory estimates over one year post-HSCT, enabling earlier and more precise clinical interventions.

Title
Resetting danger decoding at the DRG microvasculature to treat diabetic neuropathy

Premise and open question
In diabetes, the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and its microvasculature exhibit increased permeability and structural alterations of the blood–nerve/DRG barrier, exposing neurons and satellite glia to circulating danger signals. Endothelial glycocalyx degradation and tight-junction disruption are prominent in diabetes and facilitate leukocyte adhesion and extravasation. Concurrently, macrophages and endothelial cells in and around the DRG engage pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs) such as RAGE and TLR4 in response to advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) and oxidized lipids, which sustains NF-κB signaling and neuroinflammation; DRG neurons themselves can signal via TLR4 under hyperglycemic stress. Yet, therapies rarely target the local “danger decoding” threshold at this vascular–neural interface. Can we cure the error-prone decoding rather than only blocking downstream inflammation? (Increased barrier leak in DPN; endothelial glycocalyx loss in diabetes; RAGE/TLR4 roles in neuropathy; TLR4 in DRG neurons: ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014488620300753?utm_source=openai)))

Atomic strategy
Lower effective PRR ligand occupancy at the DRG microvasculature—locally and continuously—by sequestering modified-self ligands (AGEs, oxidized lipids) on an endothelium-tethered, non-signaling multivalent decoy. This shifts endothelial and macrophage PRR inputs below activation threshold, reducing leukocyte recruitment, restoring barrier integrity, and decreasing nociceptor hyperexcitability without systemic immunosuppression.

Hypothesis–goal (merged)
Local vascular sequestration of DAMP-like modified self at the DRG resets the multi-cellular danger-decoding setpoint (endothelium, macrophages, satellite glia, DRG neurons), thereby reversing pain behavior and axonal dysfunction in diabetic neuropathy by breaking the leak→mis-recognition→inflammation positive feedback loop. (Barrier dysfunction and leukocyte adhesion amplify neuroinflammation; PRR engagement by AGEs/ox-lipids drives macrophage NF-κB: ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6339909/?utm_source=openai)))

Approach and aims
Aim 1. Build and validate a human DRG–microvasculature–immune organ-on-a-chip to quantify mis-recognition-driven neurovascular activation.
- Platform: microfluidic channel lined with human microvascular endothelium (with an engineered glycocalyx layer), upper compartment with human iPSC-derived sensory neurons plus satellite glia, and perivascular macrophages.
- Inputs: perfuse diabetic-range AGEs and oxidized lipid mixtures at clinically relevant concentrations; control shear stress.
- Readouts:
  - Endothelium: NF-κB dynamics, VE-cadherin continuity, permeability to 10–70 kDa tracers, leukocyte adhesion under flow. (Glycocalyx loss and hyperglycemia disrupt junctions and promote permeability/adhesion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768294/?utm_source=openai)))
  - Immune: macrophage transcriptional states and cytokine release.
  - Neurons: excitability, firing thresholds, immediate-early genes.
  - scRNA-seq: PRR pathway states and “tolerized” regulators (A20/IRAK-M/SOCS) across all cell types.
- Success criterion: AGEs/ox-lipid perfusion increases permeability, macrophage adhesion/activation, and neuronal hyperexcitability in the chip, recapitulating in vivo features. (Barrier leak in DPN; RAGE/TLR4 involvement. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014488620300753?utm_source=openai)))

Aim 2. Engineer and optimize a vascular-tethered, non-signaling PRR-ligand decoy that sequesters modified self at the DRG interface.
- Construct: multivalent decoy presenting high-affinity binding motifs for RAGE/TLR4 ligands (e.g., AGE- and oxidized phospholipid–binding moieties) on an inert polymer backbone equipped with endothelial glycocalyx–binding anchors to localize at the luminal surface; no cytoplasmic tail to avoid signaling. (eGCX anchors and exclusion-zone properties support luminal localization; diabetes degrades eGCX, so anchoring also functions as “glycocalyx assist.” ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768294/?utm_source=openai)))
- In-chip tests:
  - Determine decoy density required to reduce PRR occupancy (ligand–decoy vs ligand–receptor binding kinetics).
  - Measure dose–response surfaces for NF-κB suppression, permeability normalization, and leukocyte adhesion under flow.
  - Evaluate whether transient low-grade PRR stimulation subsides (no rebound hyperactivation), indicating a true threshold shift rather than exhaustion.
- Success criterion: Decoy reduces endothelial and macrophage NF-κB activation ≥50%, normalizes junctional integrity and permeability, and prevents neuronal hyperexcitability under diabetic DAMP load. (Endothelial NF-κB governs adhesion molecules; leukocyte adhesion remodels junctions. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534266/?utm_source=openai)))

Aim 3. Test in transgenic mouse models of diabetes whether targeted decoy delivery to DRG microvasculature reverses neuropathy.
- Models: STZ-induced T1D and db/db T2D mice.
- Delivery: intravenous decoy conjugated to endothelium-homing peptides; compare with endothelial PRR-deficient mice (EC-specific RAGE or TLR4 knockdown) to establish necessity/sufficiency.
- Outcomes:
  - Vascular: DRG/nerve permeability (dextran extravasation), endothelial glycocalyx integrity (plasma syndecan-1), leukocyte adhesion/infiltration.
  - Neural: DRG neuronal excitability ex vivo, intraepidermal nerve fiber density, nerve conduction.
  - Behavior: mechanical and thermal thresholds.
  - scRNA-seq of DRG vascular and immune compartments: reduced PRR target gene programs; increased negative regulators (A20/IRAK-M).
- Success criterion: Decoy phenocopies endothelial PRR knockdown in normalizing barrier function and reduces pain/allodynia with improved electrophysiology, without systemic immunosuppression. (PRR roles in DPN; barrier pathology central to dysfunction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9746912/?utm_source=openai)))

Key controls and falsification
- Specificity: a scrambled decoy lacking AGE/ox-lipid affinity controls for polymer effects.
- Off-target inflammation: monitor liver/spleen cytokines to rule out systemic immunomodulation.
- Mechanistic alternative: if benefits occur without PRR pathway suppression, re-evaluate for mechanical/junctional effects (e.g., VE-cadherin stabilization independent of PRR).

Feasibility and novelty
- Known biology supports each causal link: diabetes damages endothelial glycocalyx and increases microvascular permeability; DRG/nerve barriers become leaky in DPN; PRR engagement by modified self drives macrophage/endothelial NF-κB and leukocyte adhesion; TLR4 in DRG neurons contributes to pain. What is new is reframing DPN as a local “danger decoding” error at the DRG microvasculature and correcting it by continuously lowering effective PRR ligand availability in situ rather than broad, systemic receptor blockade. (Evidence base: ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768294/?utm_source=openai)))

Milestones
- Year 1: Chip model established; demonstration that AGEs/ox-lipids produce barrier leak, macrophage activation, and DRG hyperexcitability.
- Year 2: Decoy chemistry finalized; achieve ≥50% suppression of NF-κB and normalization of permeability on-chip.
- Year 3: In vivo delivery and efficacy; scRNA-seq confirmation of PRR-threshold reset; comparison to endothelial PRR knockdown.

Impact
Precisely reducing PRR mis-recognition at the DRG vascular interface addresses a root systems-level error that sustains neuroinflammation and excitability in diabetic neuropathy. The approach is compatible with standard-of-care glucose control and avoids global immunosuppression by acting where pathogenic decoding occurs.

text:
Title
Hepatocyte-restricted glyoxalase-1 as a systemic “metabolic sink” to prevent diabetic neuropathy

Prior art and gap
- In diabetes, methylglyoxal (MGO) arises predominantly from non-enzymatic leakage of glycolytic triose phosphates and drives sensory neuron hyperexcitability (Nav1.8/TRPA1 modification), endothelial dysfunction, and neuropathic pain; higher plasma MGO associates with worse nerve conduction and pain over time. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Detoxification of MGO is mainly via the intracellular glyoxalase system (GLO1→GLO2, GSH-dependent), which is abundant in high-flow, metabolically active organs; renal failure elevates plasma MGO, underscoring organ-level clearance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11455947/?utm_source=openai))
- GLO1 overexpression has protected kidney and heart in diabetic settings and other models, including via AAV targeted to cardiovascular tissues; however, liver-restricted AAV-GLO1 explicitly deployed as a systemic MGO sink to prevent diabetic neuropathy has not been reported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3868051/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis-question (undistinguished)
Can raising hepatocyte GLO1 capacity—without altering neural tissues—lower circulating MGO sufficiently to prevent the onset and progression of diabetic neuropathy by reducing delivery of electrophiles to dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and vasa nervorum?

Atomic strategy
Exploit hepatic mass and perfusion to create a sustained transhepatic concentration gradient for MGO: increase hepatocyte GLO1 activity to depress intrahepatic MGO toward zero, thereby accelerating plasma-to-hepatocyte influx and whole-body MGO clearance, reducing DRG and endothelial carbonyl stress.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build and validate a hepatocyte-restricted AAV-GLO1 “metabolic sink.”
- Vector: AAV8/7 with liver-specific promoter (e.g., AAT/LP1 variant). Quantify liver-specific expression and off-target transduction. ([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.1.214-224.2005?utm_source=openai))
- Biochemical endpoints: hepatic GLO1 activity, hepatic and plasma MGO (LC–MS/MS), plasma MG-H1 adducts, and D-lactate (GLO1/GLO2 product) to estimate extraction and flux. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Kinetic modeling: Fit a two-compartment mass-balance to derive hepatic MGO extraction ratio and systemic clearance change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11455947/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test neuropathy prevention in diabetic mice without altering glycemia.
- Models: Type 1 (STZ) and type 2 (db/db). Dose AAV-GLO1 pre-symptomatically; parallel AAV-GFP controls.
- Outcomes:
  - Large-fiber: motor/sensory nerve conduction velocity (MNCV/SNCV).
  - Small-fiber: intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD), thermal/mechanical thresholds.
  - DRG biology: MG-H1 adduct load, Nav1.8/TRPA1 post-translational modification, integrated stress response markers; scRNA-seq of DRG neurons, satellite glia, macrophages to quantify carbonyl-stress transcriptional signatures. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22581285/?utm_source=openai))
  - Microvascular: endothelial NO bioavailability and RAGE-pathway activation in vasa nervorum. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
  - Systemic: plasma MGO trajectory vs. nerve outcomes to test dose–response.
- Glycemia control: Document unchanged HbA1c and fasting glucose to attribute effects to detox rather than glycemic correction.

Aim 3. Human-relevant mechanistic validation in a multi-organ-on-chip.
- Assemble a perfused triad: iPSC-hepatocyte sinusoid (AAV transducible) upstream of human microvascular endothelium and human sensory neuron/DRG-like cultures. Track MGO gradients, endothelial RAGE signaling, and neuronal excitability under diabetic media; compare AAV-GLO1 vs. control. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40927767/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental approach and readouts
- Vector engineering: Select hepatotropic capsid (AAV8/7) and liver promoter (AAT/LP1); confirm liver-restricted expression by qPCR/RNA-seq and immunostaining. ([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.1.214-224.2005?utm_source=openai))
- Biochemistry: Quantify MGO (stable-isotope dilution LC–MS/MS), MG-H1 (ELISA/MS), D-lactate, hepatic GSH/GSSG, PPP flux proxies to monitor cofactor sufficiency. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Neurophysiology: Patch-clamp of small-diameter DRG neurons, Nav1.8/ TRPA1 function; behavioral assays aligned with conduction studies. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22581285/?utm_source=openai))
- Vascular: Myograph and NO assays in epineurial microvessels; RAGE/VCAM-1/ICAM-1 expression by immunostaining. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Single-cell profiling: scRNA-seq on DRG and sciatic-nerve immune/endothelial fractions to define carbonyl-stress modules and intervention reversal.

Falsifiable predictions
- If hepatocyte GLO1 elevates systemic MGO clearance, plasma MGO and MG-H1 fall with proportional rises in D-lactate; neuropathy endpoints improve despite unchanged glycemia. If neuropathy persists at low plasma MGO, MGO is not a dominant driver in this context. ([diabetesjournals.org](https://diabetesjournals.org/diabetes/article/74/Supplement_1/245-OR/158480/245-OR-Plasma-Methylglyoxal-Is-Linked-to-Nerve?utm_source=openai))

Design logic and mechanistic sufficiency
- Source chemistry: MGO formation scales with triose-phosphate pool size; lowering plasma MGO delivery reduces DRG Nav1.8/TRPA1 modification and endothelial RAGE activation that underlie hyperexcitability and hypoperfusion. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Organ leverage: Liver possesses high GLO1 capacity and blood flow; organ-level detox capacity influences circulating MGO (as mirrored by renal disease increasing plasma MGO). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0020711X78900368?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility: AAV hepatocyte targeting is mature; precedent exists for GLO1 gene delivery (cardiac/vascular), but not for liver-targeted neuropathy prevention, preserving novelty. ([journals.asm.org](https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.79.1.214-224.2005?utm_source=openai))

Key risks and mitigation
- Hepatic redox burden/GSH drain: Monitor GSH/GSSG; stop rules for hepatotoxicity. If GSH limits flux, dose-reduce or stagger vector; PPP activation will not be engineered in this first-pass atomic test to avoid confounds. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Metabolic byproduct handling: Track D-lactate; ensure renal excretion capacity; assess acid–base status. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target transduction: Use stringent liver promoters and hepatotropic capsids; quantify transgene in DRG or endothelium to confirm non-neuronal targeting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12443165?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1: >50% reduction in plasma MGO with liver-restricted expression confirmed (month 4). ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Prevention of decline in MNCV/SNCV and preservation of IENFD in STZ mice at 12 weeks post-diabetes (month 8). 
- M3: Replication in db/db mice and demonstration of reduced DRG carbonyl adducts and normalized excitability (month 12). 
- No-go: Failure to lower plasma MGO by ≥30% or lack of any neuropathy benefit despite ≥50% MGO reduction.

Translational markers
- Plasma MGO and MG-H1 as pharmacodynamic biomarkers correlate with nerve outcomes in patients; supports clinical path using circulating MGO/MG-H1 readouts in early-phase trials. ([diabetesjournals.org](https://diabetesjournals.org/diabetes/article/74/Supplement_1/245-OR/158480/245-OR-Plasma-Methylglyoxal-Is-Linked-to-Nerve?utm_source=openai))

Summary
This proposal tests a single-systems lever—hepatocyte GLO1 capacity—as a non-neuronal, non-Schwann, mechanism-centric intervention to prevent diabetic neuropathy by draining a causal electrophile before it reaches nerves and their microvessels. It is mechanistically grounded, falsifiable, and uses organ-on-chip, AAV in vivo, and scRNA-seq to connect systemic detox to neural and vascular endpoints. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
