text:
Title
H2O2-gated augmentation of the uterine Gαq “off-switch” to selectively damp stress-evoked adrenergic bursts without systemic sympatholysis

Central question/hypothesis
Can local, non-invasive delivery of a hydrogen peroxide–activatable RGS2 regulator restore the uterus’s endogenous Gαq brake only when adrenergic drive is excessive, thereby reducing pathological myometrial contractions while preserving basal sympathetic tone elsewhere? The hypothesis rests on three established facts: (i) α1-adrenergic/Gq signaling contracts human myometrium; (ii) RGS2 is an endogenous GAP that shortens Gαq signaling and is linked to uterine quiescence; and (iii) monoamine oxidase (MAO) catabolism of norepinephrine generates H2O2 near active sympathetic terminals. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6311865/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Tie brake strength to a chemical signature of excess catechol turnover: use MAO-derived H2O2 as the trigger to unmask an intracellular RGS2 Gαq-GAP, so inhibition appears only when and where adrenergic bursts occur, not at baseline. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12267328/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish that sympathetic burst activity elevates perineuroeffector H2O2 and intensifies α1/Gq-driven myometrial contractions.
2) Engineer and validate an H2O2-activatable, cell-penetrating RGS2 reagent that accelerates Gαq deactivation only under high-ROS conditions.
3) Achieve uterine-first-pass, non-invasive delivery via a mucoadhesive intravaginal hydrogel and demonstrate selective dampening of stress-evoked contractions in vivo, without systemic sympatholysis.

Rationale and innovation
- Biology: α1-ARs in human myometrium couple to Gq/PLCβ→IP3/Ca2+→MLCK to drive contraction; β2-ARs oppose via cAMP. RGS2 is a selective GAP for Gαq, upregulated in quiescent states and downregulated toward labor, positioning it as an intrinsic brake. MAO-mediated oxidative deamination of catecholamines generates H2O2 at sympathetic terminals. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6311865/?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery: Vaginal administration can enrich drug in the uterus via the uterine first-pass effect, minimizing plasma exposure and systemic impact. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Control logic: Arylboronate/borinic triggers enable H2O2-activated self-immolative cleavage to switch “on” a masked bioactive only where ROS rises; borinic acids increase reaction rates, improving biological responsiveness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))
- Novelty: No reported uterine therapy uses MAO-H2O2 to gate an RGS2-based, Gαq-targeted intracellular brake; this reframes tocolysis from receptor blockade to state- and byproduct-gated restoration of endogenous termination.

Approach

Aim 1: Map ROS–adrenergic–contractility coupling in myometrium
- Ex vivo human myometrium strips (nonpregnant hysterectomy tissue, IRB-approved). Electrical field stimulation of sympathetic varicosities and phenylephrine boluses to produce graded α1-adrenergic bursts; record force and Ca2+ transients. Measure local H2O2 with boronate-based fluorescent probes and polymeric ratiometric nanoprobes; control with catalase/peroxidase. Quantify threshold relation between H2O2 rise and suprabasal contractile gain. Expected: μM-scale phenylephrine or burst trains elevate perijunctional H2O2 and steepen α1/Gq gain; catalase blunts both readouts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3935537/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2: Engineer an H2O2-activatable RGS2-GAP that is quiescent at baseline
- Construct: Minimal RGS2 RH domain (e.g., residues ~72–203) fused to a cell-penetrating peptide (CPP). Block CPP uptake and/or RGS2–Gαq interface using an arylboronate self-immolative cage that cleaves with H2O2; evaluate faster borinic triggers to meet biological kinetics. Add an N-terminal membrane-targeting motif to enrich at the sarcolemma where Gαq operates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro biophysics: Measure GTPase acceleration on purified Gαq and off-rate on Gαq·GTP versus Gαq·GDP. Define “activity threshold” by comparing GAP activity at 0–10 μM H2O2; benchmark against uncaged RH domain. Confirm minimal activity at ≤100 nM H2O2. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Cell assays: Human myometrial smooth muscle cells. Readouts: PLCβ activity, IP3/Ca2+ spikes, and ERK under α1 stimulation. Compare basal versus burst-like agonist paradigms. Confirm that catalase suppresses activation of the construct, and that an RGS-insensitive Gαq mutant rescues signaling, verifying on-target action. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety chemistry: Quantify byproducts (phenol/boric species) and show no cytotoxicity at exposure levels; this is consistent with prior boronate prodrug literature. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Non-invasive uterine delivery and in vivo selectivity
- Formulation: Mucoadhesive, pH-tolerant intravaginal hydrogel embedding the prodrugged RGS2 construct. Optimize residence and uterine exposure using fluorescein-tagged constructs in rodents; quantify uterine/plasma ratios to confirm first-pass uterine enrichment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Models and endpoints:
  - Stress-evoked adrenergic surges: In awake rodents, use restraint/cold stress or systemic tyramine to elicit sympathetic NE release; monitor intrauterine pressure via telemetric balloons and electromyography. Test that the hydrogel reduces peak amplitude/frequency during surges but leaves basal tone unchanged. Include phenylephrine-challenge arm to standardize α1 input. Off-target guardrails: heart rate, blood pressure, pupil size to exclude systemic sympatholysis. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6311865/?utm_source=openai))
  - Mechanism confirmation: Co-administer catalase-mimetic to suppress H2O2 and abrogate efficacy; deliver an RGS2-inactive mutant control. Tissue assays for Gαq·GTP lifetime and PLCβ activity.
- Translational safety: Local irritation scores, vaginal microbiome profiles, reproductive hormone levels. Pharmacokinetics to ensure negligible systemic CPP–RGS2 in plasma.

Milestones and success criteria
- Aim 1: Demonstrate a monotonic relation between burst intensity and H2O2 with a clear threshold where contractile gain steepens; catalase flattens this slope. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24123627/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Show ≥10-fold increase in Gαq-GAP activity after H2O2 activation with ≤5% baseline activity at 0–100 nM H2O2; in myocytes, suppress burst-evoked Ca2+ peaks by ≥40% while altering basal Ca2+ <5%. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: Achieve uterine:plasma exposure ratio ≥5 after intravaginal dosing; reduce stress-evoked intrauterine pressure AUC by ≥30% with no change in resting tone and no change in systemic cardiovascular indices. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated limitations and design adaptations
- H2O2 reaction kinetics: If arylboronate cleavage is too slow at physiological H2O2, switch to borinic acid triggers or co-localize peroxidase-mimetic nanozymes within the hydrogel to raise local effective rate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8685692/?utm_source=openai))
- Variability in uterine first-pass: If uterine enrichment is suboptimal in some anatomies, restrict molecular size/charge or add uterine-tropic motifs to enhance retention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Species differences in adrenergic control: Use human tissue ex vivo for primary validation and select a second species with robust myometrial α1 biology before clinical translation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9937490/?utm_source=openai))

Clinical path (Phase 0/1 concept)
- Indication: Nonpregnant individuals with stress-exacerbated primary dysmenorrhea or uterine hyperreactivity.
- Design: Crossover, intravaginal hydrogel vs placebo. Primary endpoint: reduction in stress-provoked uterine EMG/intrauterine pressure peaks during standardized mental stress; secondary: pain scores, absence of changes in resting uterine tone and systemic sympathetic markers.

Why this meets constraints
- Non-invasive intravaginal delivery with uterine first-pass avoids systemic sympatholysis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Excess-only damping: ROS gating confines activation to adrenergic surge microdomains; basal low-ROS conditions leave signaling intact. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))
- Endogenous brake amplification: Uses RGS2’s native role to shorten Gαq signaling, not receptor blockade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Clinically translatable: Peptide/CPP cargos, mucoadhesive hydrogels, and boronate/borinic triggers have precedent in biomedical applications. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Closed-loop sacral-dermatomal afferent stimulation to attenuate bursty uterine sympathetic drive without systemic sympatholysis

Premise and rationale
- The uterus receives mixed autonomic innervation: sympathetic fibers via hypogastric pathways (predominantly T10–L1) and parasympathetic fibers via pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) coursing through the inferior hypogastric plexus. Cervical and uterovaginal afferents project to lumbosacral dorsal horn segments, enabling somato-visceral reflex interactions at the spinal level. Excess adrenergic signaling increases myometrial excitability via α-adrenergic mechanisms, whereas β-adrenergic signaling tends to relax myometrium; the balance varies with hormonal state. Segmental somatic afferent input can modulate sympathetic preganglionic neuron (SPN) activity through inhibitory interneurons and presynaptic mechanisms within the spinal cord. Noninvasive TENS reduces dysmenorrhea pain, but typical open-loop protocols have not shown consistent changes in intrauterine pressure, indicating a gap between analgesia and direct modulation of uterine efferent bursts. Cervical stretch can excite myometrial activity via the Ferguson reflex; therefore, targeting external sacral dermatomes avoids mechanically exciting cervicovaginal pathways while still engaging lumbosacral circuitry. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1472029919301134?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question (atomic strategy embedded)
Can high-pass, closed-loop activation of low-threshold sacral dermatomal afferents (S2–S4) be used as a tunable, on-demand inhibitory gain on lumbosacral sympathetic outflow to the uterus—attenuating only supra-physiological, bursty uterine activity while sparing tonic uterine and systemic sympathetic tone? The atomic strategy is to use thresholded, phasic Aβ-dominant cutaneous input as a spinal “inhibitory gain” that engages fast interneuronal and presynaptic inhibitory processes only when uterine EMG features indicate excessive adrenergic-driven activity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075457/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish that closed-loop, burst-gated sacral-dermatomal TENS (S2–S4) reduces high-frequency, high-slope components of uterine EMG during dysmenorrheic episodes without altering baseline EMG. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpcd/classification.cfm?id=OSP&utm_source=openai))
2) Demonstrate segmental specificity: show no concurrent systemic sympatholysis via heart-rate variability (HRV) indices and palmar skin conductance during stimulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10049654/?utm_source=openai))
3) Compare closed-loop versus time-matched open-loop TENS to determine the necessity of high-pass, error-triggered engagement for selective suppression. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8296814/?utm_source=openai))

Design and methods
- Population: Nonpregnant adults with primary dysmenorrhea (PD), regular cycles, no hormonal therapy changes in prior 3 months; exclude secondary causes. Two-site, randomized, double-crossover study across three menses: (A) closed-loop sacral-dermatomal TENS; (B) open-loop TENS; (C) sham. Each participant serves as own control. Safety: avoid pregnancy to preclude interference with labor-associated reflexes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12975252/?utm_source=openai))
- Sensing: Adhesive abdominal uterine EMG patch (FDA-classified uterine EMG monitor) sampling ≥500 Hz. Derived features: EMG envelope slope, phasic band power (e.g., 0.2–1 Hz), and a composite burst index via adaptive percentile thresholds calibrated during quiescent baseline on day −1. Secondary sensors: ECG-derived HRV and palmar skin conductance. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpcd/classification.cfm?id=OSP&utm_source=openai))
- Actuation (intervention): Sacral-dermatomal TENS over S2–S4 (paravertebral/posterior sacral foramina region) with large gel pads to bias Aβ recruitment (e.g., 100–200 μs pulse width; carrier 80–120 Hz; amplitude individualized to strong but comfortable sensation, below nociceptor thresholds). Stimulation is delivered in brief bursts (e.g., 1–3 s trains with fast on/off ramps), locked to detected EMG bursts with a refractory lockout (≥30 s) to prevent tonic suppression. Open-loop uses identical parameters at matched duty cycle but decoupled from EMG. Sham uses identical hardware with imperceptible subthreshold output. Safety monitoring includes skin integrity checks and adverse event logs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078521/?utm_source=openai))
- Control logic (closed-loop): High-pass controller triggers only when the composite burst index exceeds an individualized threshold, scaling stimulus amplitude by error magnitude (proportional) with anti-windup and short decay to avoid baseline bias. No integral accumulation across minutes. This implements inhibitory “gain” only during supra-physiological events. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-neuro-112723-042229?utm_source=openai))
- Outcomes:
  • Primary: Change in burst index area-under-curve (AUC) per hour versus baseline and versus open-loop/sham. 
  • Co-primary: No change in tonic EMG (median baseline power) across conditions.
  • Secondary: Pain VAS, uterine artery Doppler resistive index in a subset, HRV LF/HF and palmar skin conductance changes ≤ prespecified margins (noninferiority bounds) to confirm absence of systemic sympatholysis; rescue analgesic use. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3892726/?utm_source=openai))
- Statistics: Within-subject mixed models with condition and time as fixed effects; hierarchical false-discovery control across outcomes. Powering assumes moderate effect (Cohen’s d 0.5) on burst-AUC reduction, α=0.05, 1−β=0.8, requiring ~34 completers; inflate to 45 to allow attrition.

Mechanistic validation substudies
- Segmental mapping: Vary electrode positions rostral-caudal (L5–S1 vs S2–S4) to test segmental dependence of effects on EMG bursts. Prediction: maximal effect with S2–S4 placement. ([anatomy.ttuhscep.edu](https://anatomy.ttuhscep.edu/modules/pelvic_autonomic_module/pelvic_page11.html?utm_source=openai))
- Parameter titration: Compare Aβ-favoring settings to higher pulse widths that recruit nociceptors; prediction: nociceptor recruitment degrades selectivity and may increase sympathetic markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075457/?utm_source=openai))

Risk management and constraints compliance
- Noninvasive only: surface EMG and TENS; no intracavitary stimulation or drugs. Device parameters adhere to TENS safety norms; prior dysmenorrhea TENS trials show favorable safety. Avoid direct cervicovaginal mechanical stimulation to prevent Ferguson reflex activation. ([cochrane.org](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013331_tens-electrical-nerve-stimulation-through-skin-effective-treatment-period-pain-and-does-it-cause?utm_source=openai))
- Preserve basal and systemic sympathetic function: High-pass gating, short bursts, and refractory intervals aim to confine inhibition to phasic events; systemic markers provide stopping rules if deviations exceed bounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10049654/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and differentiators
- Prior TENS studies in PD were analgesic-focused and open-loop, with no consistent impact on intrauterine pressure; here, uterine EMG-driven, burst-gated control explicitly targets autonomic efferent dynamics rather than pain alone. Emerging closed-loop TENS wearables for PD focus on symptom relief, not physiological suppression of uterine sympathetic bursts with segmental specificity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8296814/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and translation
- All components are available: FDA-recognized uterine EMG monitors, programmable TENS, and wearable controllers for real-time closed-loop neuromodulation. Success criteria: ≥25% reduction in EMG burst-AUC versus open-loop without change in tonic EMG and without systemic sympatholysis; reproducibility across cycles. Positive results justify a pivotal trial and potential 510(k) pathway as a new intended use for TENS with closed-loop uterine EMG control. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpcd/classification.cfm?id=OSP&utm_source=openai))

Contingency
- If external sacral-dermatomal stimulation fails to achieve selectivity, pivot to optimizing segmental recruitment (electrode size/vectoring) within S2–S4 or refine burst detection features; abort criterion is failure to separate burst suppression from tonic suppression across two cycles in >60% of participants.

Title
Closed-loop, phase-targeted low-intensity focused ultrasound to desynchronize uterine sympathetic vasoconstrictor bursts while preserving basal tone

Premise and significance
- The uterus receives sympathetic efferents via the hypogastric nerves and the inferior hypogastric (uterovaginal) plexus; sympathetic fibers accompany uterine vessels and regulate vasomotor tone and smooth muscle targets. Disruption here influences uterine vascular resistance and myometrial excitability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9321487/?utm_source=openai))
- Near term, adrenergic pharmacology shifts: β-agonists classically relax myometrium and have been used as tocolytics; conversely, uterine arteries exhibit enhanced α1-mediated constriction with reduced β-mediated relaxation, increasing susceptibility of uteroplacental perfusion to sympathetic bursts. This implies that selectively attenuating high-rate vasoconstrictor drive—without global sympatholysis—could improve uteroplacental flow without abolishing basal tone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3892726/?utm_source=openai))
- Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) can noninvasively modulate peripheral autonomic pathways with reversible inhibition at intermediate intensities; neuromod effects have been demonstrated in vagus and other peripheral targets. Safety frameworks from diagnostic ultrasound (ALARA; FDA/WFUMB indices) guide exposure, especially in pregnancy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8188893/?utm_source=openai))
- Noninvasive uterine/placental sensing—surface electrohysterography (EHG) for uterine activation, uterine artery Doppler for flow, and diffuse optical/NIRS for placental oxygenation—provides real-time, local biomarkers to detect self-reinforcing sympathetic–vascular episodes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3090039/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–question
Can locally sensed, quasi-periodic uterine sympathetic vasoconstrictor bursts be identified in real time from transabdominal EHG–perfusion signatures and desynchronized on-demand by delivering brief, phase-targeted LIFU pulses to the uterovaginal branch region of the inferior hypogastric plexus, thereby reducing pathologic uterine vascular resistance while preserving basal sympathetic tone and avoiding systemic sympatholysis? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit dynamics-selectivity rather than amplitude-selectivity: detect local, coherent high-rate sympathetic burst structure (regularity, phase-locking across EHG–perfusion channels) and deliver minimally dosed, phase-shifted LIFU microbursts timed to extend refractoriness/induce spike timing jitter in the most excitable vasoconstrictor fibers, breaking synchrony (“resonance-based cancellation”) while leaving aperiodic, low-rate basal signaling and non-target pelvic sympathetic functions unaffected. Mechanistic precedent for phase-targeted cancellation and collision-based spike suppression exists in closed-loop neurostimulation and peripheral axon physiology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629558/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define a local “burst-likeness” signature of uterine sympathetic vasoconstrictor episodes.
- Combine features: EHG narrowband power/coherence (0.3–1.0 Hz), uterine artery Doppler pulsatility index surges, and placental NIRS/DOS desaturations indicating transient uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Build an online metric that rises only when these channels synchronize in a quasi-periodic pattern. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/26/15/4669?utm_source=openai))
2) Engineer a transabdominal, phase-targeted LIFU system for uterovaginal plexus region.
- Parametric LIFU pulses (frequency 0.5–3 MHz; short pulse trains with low duty cycle) are time-locked anti-phase to the detected burst fundamental, targeting parametrium adjacent to the uterine artery where sympathetic fibers concentrate. Exposures constrained under obstetric safety guidance (monitor TI/MI; ALARA). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))
3) Test selectivity: suppress pathologic bursts while preserving basal tone and systemic sympathetic function.
- Primary outcomes: (i) reduction in episodic uterine artery resistance (Doppler PI), (ii) attenuation of placental desaturation events (NIRS/DOS), (iii) minimal change in basal perfusion indices and maternal systemic autonomic markers (HRV, skin microvascular LDI outside uterine field). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9944515/?utm_source=openai))

Study design and methods
- Population and models
  - Preclinical: pregnant ewe model (uterine size and wall thickness approximating human) to validate targeting and dosing; simultaneous intra-arterial flow probes, EHG, and DOS over placentomes.
  - First-in-human feasibility: hospitalized patients with threatened preterm labor (24–34 weeks) under standard monitoring; single-session, on-demand LIFU with real-time safety gating.
- Sensing and detection
  - 8–16 channel abdominal EHG grid; uterine artery Doppler (transabdominal) for beat-to-beat PI; placental NIRS/DOS patch over placental bed for StO2; optional uterine magnetomyography (if available) to validate synchrony maps. Online phase-locked loop extracts the dominant burst phase only when EHG–perfusion coherence exceeds threshold; otherwise the system remains idle. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3090039/?utm_source=openai))
- Targeting
  - Sonographic targeting to the uterovaginal plexus region: lateral parametrium along the uterine artery course where sympathetic fibers are concentrated at the media–adventitial border. Steering minimizes fetal insonation and confines the focus to the maternal uterine wall/parametrium. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))
- Stimulation protocol
  - Phase-targeted pulses: brief LIFU microbursts delivered at a phase that maximally disrupts the detected cycle (determined during a 30–60 s calibration sweep). Closed-loop controller disengages within 1–3 cycles after coherence collapses. Exposure caps enforced by MI/TI watchdogs, with total sonication time per hour constrained below diagnostic practice norms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629558/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls
  - Sham sonication (no output) with identical targeting and timing; open-loop, non-phase-timed LIFU with matched dose to isolate the contribution of phase locking.
- Endpoints
  - Primary mechanistic: reduction in burst-likeness index; drop in uterine artery PI and concurrent recovery of placental StO2 during detected episodes versus sham/open-loop. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9944515/?utm_source=openai))
  - Physiologic selectivity: no significant change in basal uterine artery PI, placental StO2 outside episodes, maternal HR/BP, or distal skin microvascular flow.
  - Obstetric safety: no fetal heart rate abnormalities, no increase in contraction frequency/intensity on EHG, adherence to ALARA and ITRUSST thermal/MI bounds. ([acog.org](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2017/10/guidelines-for-diagnostic-imaging-during-pregnancy-and-lactation?utm_source=openai))
- Statistics and design features
  - Within-subject randomized cross-over (phase-targeted vs sham/open-loop) across multiple naturally occurring or oxytocin-provoked sympathetic–vascular episodes; mixed-effects models quantify treatment effect on PI and StO2 trajectories aligned to detection onset.
  - Powering based on paired reduction in episode-integrated placental desaturation AUC.

Mechanistic justifications
- Dynamics-selectivity: Pathologic bursts are coherent and quasi-periodic; phase-targeted perturbations preferentially disrupt synchronized activity without suppressing irregular basal firing, paralleling successful phase-cancellation paradigms in movement disorders. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629558/?utm_source=openai))
- Locality: Actuation focus is confined to uterine parametrium; sensing derives from uterus/placental bed. Systemic sympathetic outflow is not directly engaged, satisfying the no-systemic-sympatholysis constraint. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))
- Biological plausibility: Peripheral ultrasound neuromodulation can inhibit nerve conduction/non-neuronal mechanoelectrical signaling at safe intensities; late-gestation uterine arteries are particularly sensitive to α1-mediated constriction—making pathologic vasoconstrictor bursts a rational and organ-specific target. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8188893/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and translational path
- Year 1: Define and validate burst-likeness metric and safe parameter space in pregnant ewe; demonstrate on-demand reversal of induced uterine artery vasoconstriction and placental desaturations.
- Year 2: Feasibility in 20 patients with threatened preterm labor; demonstrate ≥30% reduction in episode PI peaks and ≥30% reduction in desaturation AUC versus sham without affecting basal indices.
- Year 3: Early efficacy signal—reduced progression from threatened to active preterm labor over 48–72 h adjunctive window—while monitoring obstetric safety.
- Regulatory/safety: Operate within obstetric ultrasound safety frameworks (ALARA, MI/TI monitoring) and emerging neuromodulation exposure consensus; noninvasive hardware leverages clinical ultrasound platforms with software-only closed-loop extensions. ([acog.org](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2017/10/guidelines-for-diagnostic-imaging-during-pregnancy-and-lactation?utm_source=openai))

Novelty
- No prior reports of closed-loop, phase-targeted neuromodulation of the uterine sympathetic plexus to specifically desynchronize vasoconstrictor bursts; pelvic magnetic chairs target pudendal/sacral somatic pathways for incontinence, not uterine autonomic control or frequency/phase-selective suppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9145499/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated impact
A dynamics-selective, organ-local, noninvasive neuromodulation that blunts episodic uterine sympathetic vasoconstriction without flattening basal tone offers a path to stabilize uteroplacental perfusion in high-risk pregnancies while avoiding systemic sympatholysis—meeting safety and translational constraints and opening a controllable, on-demand window for standard obstetric care. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8485361/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Topology-gated cohesin release to selectively reset pathological enhancer–promoter loops

Hypothesis/Research question
Can a 3D genome editor that couples endogenous SMC5/6 recognition of pathological DNA topology (crossings/plectonemes/supercoils) to an inducible cohesin-release effector achieve selective, reversible disruption of disease-stabilized enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops while preserving normal chromatin contacts and global topology?

Rationale
- Disease-stabilized E–P loops commonly arise within transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers enriched for Mediator/BRD4 and RNA Pol II, where multivalency increases loop residence times. These hubs provide a physical milieu that promotes persistent bridging and extrusion stalling, distinct from the short-lived contacts typical of physiological regulation. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))
- Human SMC5/6 complexes bind and respond to DNA tertiary structures with crossed helices and transcription-generated supercoils, and participate in resolving DNA junctions/catenanes. These topological signatures are predicted to accumulate at over-stabilized E–P intersections more than at transient, normal loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11379904/?utm_source=openai))
- Cohesin removal dissolves chromatin loops and domains, and acute cleavage of RAD21 has been used to reset loops rapidly; reloading restores architecture, supporting a reversible, protein-level control point. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5846482/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use SMC5/6 as a topology- and dwell-time-gated address code: when SMC5/6 accumulates at DNA crossings/supercoils indicative of persistently stabilized E–P loops, it nucleates a local, inducible cohesin-release event to reset the aberrant contact; absence of sustained topological stress leaves normal contacts untouched.

Proposed editor: TSCR (Topo-Selective Cohesin Release)
- Sensor: A DNA-junction/supercoil–binding SMC5/6 subunit-derived module that concentrates at topologically stressed chromatin (crossed helices/plectonemes).
- Effector: An inducible cohesin unloader—either a minimal WAPL-mimic that transiently opens the kleisin–SMC3 exit gate or a regulated protease that cleaves an engineered, complementation-ready RAD21 variant—configured for rapid re-sealing/reloading after action. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))
- Checkpoint logic: Effector activation requires (i) sustained SMC5/6 dwell beyond a preset threshold and (ii) an exogenous, reversible small-molecule cofactor. This implements a spindle-checkpoint–like “act only on persistent error” rule and ensures reversibility on washout.
- Optional context filter: An IDR-based partitioning tail biased to BRD4/Mediator-rich condensates to raise local TSCR concentration where pathological loops most likely occur, without triggering action absent the topology+dwell checkpoint. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Establish topological discriminants of pathological E–P loops in disease models.
Question: Do over-stabilized E–P loops exhibit enriched SMC5/6 occupancy and DNA-crossing/supercoil signatures relative to normal loops?
Plan (high-level): Compare SMC5/6 chromatin association, topological stress markers, and loop residence metrics across (i) super-enhancer–driven oncogene loci and (ii) matched physiological E–P pairs. Integrate with perturbations that weaken condensates (e.g., BET inhibition) to test whether reduced hub multivalency diminishes the topological signature without abolishing general enhancer–promoter proximity. Success criterion: a robust, quantitative separation of topological/stress features between pathological and normal loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11379904/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer and validate TSCR modules.
Question: Can SMC5/6-guided, inducible cohesin unloading reset targeted pathological E–P loops while sparing normal contacts?
Design principles:
- Sensor fidelity: Select an SMC5/6 DNA-junction–recognition element with demonstrated affinity for crossed DNA/plectonemes; tune affinity to minimize background binding at transient contacts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11379904/?utm_source=openai))
- Effector minimality: Implement a compact WAPL-mimic that opens the kleisin exit gate or a split-protease that cleaves a TEV-tagged RAD21 allele; both are established routes to acutely unload cohesin in cells and are reversible upon deactivation/re-expression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))
- Checkpointing: Encode slow assembly kinetics or multivalent reconstitution such that only prolonged SMC5/6 residence triggers effector activation; gate activity with a systemically delivered, reversible small molecule.
Readouts (conceptual): Loss of pathological loop signal with preservation of global TAD insulation and of contacts at control loci; rapid restoration after effector inactivation.

Aim 3. Evaluate functional specificity and safety.
Question: Does TSCR reduce pathological gene activation while preserving normal transcriptional programs and genome topology?
Plan (high-level): Quantify target gene output and genome-wide interaction patterns before/after transient TSCR activation; assess off-target effects at housekeeping E–P pairs and replication-associated sites where SMC5/6 also functions. Falsification: widespread TAD erosion or broad gene dysregulation would reject the selectivity premise. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5846482/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes and decision rules
- If SMC5/6 occupancy and DNA-topology markers are enriched at disease-stabilized E–P loops and TSCR selectively reduces these contacts with rapid architectural recovery post-inactivation, the hypothesis is supported.
- If TSCR causes broad loop loss akin to global cohesin depletion, the topology+dwell checkpoint is insufficient; redesign will prioritize stricter dwell thresholds or strengthened context partitioning.
- If pathological loops lack a distinct topological signature, the SMC5/6 address code is invalid in this context; pivot to a micro-environment–only filter is warranted.

Selectivity safeguards
- Layered gating (topology + sustained dwell + ligand) reduces action on transient physiological contacts.
- Optional condensate-partitioning tail limits active concentration to super-enhancer hubs without being a trigger by itself. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))
- Reversibility is intrinsic to cohesin unloading and RAD21 re-sealing/reloading; architecture should re-form on effector withdrawal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5846482/?utm_source=openai))

Delivery constraint
- ≤3 events: a single genetic payload encoding TSCR (sensor-effector fusion ± partitioning tail) and one systemic small molecule to arm the checkpoint; an optional second payload for the RAD21 complementation allele if the protease route is selected.

Innovation
This proposal reframes locus selectivity around DNA topology and dwell time rather than sequence or epigenetic state: it exploits endogenous SMC5/6 sensing of crossed/supercoiled DNA to target only persistently mis-stabilized E–P loops, and couples that sensing to a reversible cohesin-release pulse to correct 3D structure without permanent sequence alteration. While SMC5/6’s topological recognition, super-enhancer condensates, and acute cohesin unloading are each established, their integration into a topology-gated 3D genome editor aimed specifically at pathological E–P loops is, to our knowledge, untested. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11379904/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and clear no-go criteria
- Milestone 1: Demonstrate topological signature enrichment at target loops; no-go if absent despite multiple disease loci. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11379904/?utm_source=openai))
- Milestone 2: Show selective loop reset with preserved TAD insulation and rapid recovery; no-go if global loop collapse mimics RAD21 depletion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5846482/?utm_source=openai))
- Milestone 3: Show target gene normalization without broad transcriptome disruption; no-go if widespread dysregulation occurs.

Broader impact
A topology-gated, reversible 3D genome editor provides a general framework for correcting pathological chromatin contacts across diseases driven by aberrant enhancer wiring, while minimizing collateral perturbation of normal genome architecture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801379/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Kinetic partitioning of hyper-stable enhancer–promoter bridging complexes to restore 3D genome topology

Integrated hypothesis–question
Pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops arise when a subset of cohesin–coactivator assemblies attain abnormally high residence times and multivalency (e.g., under reduced WAPL activity or super‑enhancer coactivator overload), thereby stabilizing long-range contacts that bypass normal CTCF-delimited architecture. Can a nucleus-internal kinetic sink that nucleates only above a local client-density threshold and confers an ultra‑slow off‑rate selectively sequester this hyper‑stable subpopulation, lowering the effective availability of aberrant loop-forming complexes while preserving normal chromatin contacts and transcriptional neighborhoods? Cohesin processivity/dwell-time increases extend loop lengths in WAPL-deficient states, and CTCF functions as a tension-dependent barrier, indicating that kinetic and mechanical discriminants exist between normal and pathological looping; coactivator condensates concentrate clients at super‑enhancers, providing a natural threshold for selective engagement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit kinetic–valency asymmetry. Engineer an inert, extranuclear-DNA–free, nuclear scaffold that (i) remains diffuse and inert at physiological client concentrations, (ii) nucleates a condensate only when local concentrations of loop‑bridging clients exceed a preset threshold, and (iii) presents a multivalent array of Mediator/cohesin-binding modules tuned so that avidity (and hence koff) becomes extremely low only for hyper‑valent, long‑dwell assemblies. This shifts only the pathological fraction into a long‑lived, off‑pathway state without directly blocking or degrading proteins and without perturbing sequence or native anchors. Synthetic condensates can sequester endogenous factors; BET/Mediator perturbations can decouple transcriptional output from physical E–P contact, supporting the feasibility of selective kinetic diversion without collapsing topology. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41589-021-00840-4?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define biophysical signatures of pathological loop‑bridging assemblies.
- Models: (a) WAPL knockdown/auxin-degron cells to elevate cohesin residence/processivity; (b) cells with super‑enhancer–driven oncogene hijacking. Readouts: single‑particle tracking of RAD21 and Mediator subunits, FRAP/spot‑PAINT for dwell times; Micro‑C/Hi‑C for loop length/strength; ChIP‑seq for CTCF/cohesin/Mediator; nascent RNA. Expectation: a separable, long‑dwell/high‑valency client fraction emerges with extended loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build a thresholded kinetic sink (KPT) that selectively captures the pathological fraction.
- Core scaffold: a genetically encoded, nucleus‑localized condensate platform (SUMO–SIM or equivalent modular multimer) whose phase behavior is tunable. Client-binding shell: arrays of medium‑affinity binders to Mediator-tail interfaces (e.g., MED1/24/25-interacting motifs or nanobody binders raised by display) combined with cohesin-surface binders (nanobodies/monobodies to RAD21/SMC interfaces). Design principle: each individual interaction remains weak and fast-off; only high‑valency client assemblies achieve cooperative avidity for ultra‑slow dissociation. Condensation thresholding: embed weak self‑associating IDRs so that scaffold nucleates only when client valency locally exceeds a preset density, providing automatic capacity scaling and sparing of normal loci. Spatial sequestration: tether the scaffold to an inert nuclear territory (e.g., lamin‑proximal speckles) to avoid inadvertent bridging. Feasibility: endogenous protein sequestration by designer condensates is established; nuclear import and stable expression of large scaffolds are practical. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41589-021-00840-4?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test whether KPT corrects 3D topology while preserving normal contacts and transcriptional neighborhoods.
- Deploy KPT in models from Aim 1. Endpoints: (i) rescue of aberrant long‑range E–P loops (Micro‑C/Hi‑C loop strength decay vs distance); (ii) unchanged TAD boundary insulation and short‑range E–P contacts; (iii) restored radial positions of mis‑looped loci (DNA‑FISH); (iv) minimal global cohesin/CTCF redistribution (ChIP‑seq); (v) selective reduction of pathological target gene expression with preserved housekeeping transcription (PRO‑seq/GRO‑seq). Include titration series to verify threshold behavior and reversibility upon scaffold repression. Controls: inert scaffold lacking client binders; non‑thresholded scaffold to test off‑target risk.

Design and methods (concise)
- Binder discovery and calibration: yeast/phage display to generate nanobodies/monobodies against Mediator-tail epitopes and cohesin surfaces exposed in extruding/bridging states; measure KD/koff by BLI; engineer mutations to set individual KD in 1–10 µM and fast koff to enforce avidity gating. Validation: co‑IP/MS of captured clients; absence of histone capture.
- Condensate threshold tuning: vary SUMO:SIM valency, IDR composition, and client binder density; map phase diagrams in cells with optogenetic reference; set a client‑concentration midpoint above physiological and within super‑enhancer ranges; confirm nucleation only at super‑enhancer–rich foci.
- Spatial insulation: fuse mild lamina‑binding or nucleolar‑periphery tethers; confirm separation from chromatin by live‑cell imaging and CUT&RUN.
- Minimal delivery: one vector encoding KPT under an inducible promoter; optional second vector for binder variants (≤2 events total).
- Safety selectors: degron for rapid off‑switch; protease‑cleavable binder release.

Selectivity rationale and safeguards
- Kinetic discrimination: WAPL-loss and related states elevate cohesin residence/processivity; KPT captures these long‑dwell assemblies through cooperative binding, whereas normal, transient cohesin disengages before multivalent locking can occur. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Concentration/valency discrimination: super‑enhancer coactivator density crosses the nucleation threshold; physiological sites stay below, keeping KPT diffuse/inert. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801379/?utm_source=openai))
- Topology preservation: CTCF‑delimited architecture remains since KPT does not remove CTCF or deplete total cohesin, only partitions the hyper‑stable fraction; BET/Mediator perturbation studies indicate physical E–P proximity can persist despite reduced coactivator activity, arguing that selective sequestration will spare baseline contacts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801379/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and quantitative success criteria
- Year 1: Identify pathological biophysical signatures; fabricate KPT variants with tunable thresholds; demonstrate selective client capture without chromatin binding (≥5× enrichment of long‑dwell fraction in KPT co‑IP; negligible histone pull‑down).
- Year 2: In WAPL‑perturbed cells, reduce median pathological loop length and strength by ≥30% with ≤5% change in TAD insulation scores and ≤10% change in global CTCF/cohesin peak intensities. Restore E–P distances for hijacked loci by ≥25% (DNA‑FISH).
- Year 3: In disease models, downregulate hijacked oncogene expression ≥30% with minimal impact (<10%) on housekeeping gene transcription; demonstrate reversibility upon KPT shutdown.

Decision points and contingencies
- If sequestration of Mediator alone fails to correct loops (consistent with evidence that BET/Mediator loss can retain contacts), append calibrated cohesin-surface binders to KPT to engage only coactivator‑bound cohesin complexes, maintaining kinetic selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801379/?utm_source=openai))
- If unintended chromatin capture occurs, lower binder valency, increase spatial insulation, or switch to purely proteinaceous binders with no histone affinity.

Outcomes and impact
A thresholded kinetic sink offers a single, system‑level perturbation that reads out pathological kinetics and multivalency to divert only aberrant E–P bridging assemblies into an inert, long‑lived state. By avoiding DNA sequence changes and preserving normal extrusion cycles and CTCF barriers, this approach aims to correct 3D genome topology with high selectivity and minimal collateral effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
State-aware kinetic pruning of pathological enhancer–promoter loops by transient reactivation of endogenous cohesin unloading

Rationale
- 3D enhancer–promoter (E–P) communication emerges from cohesin-driven loop extrusion, halted and stabilized by CTCF and, variably, by Mediator/TF assemblies and condensates; unloading of cohesin by WAPL/PDS5 resets contacts. SMC3 acetylation and sororin antagonize WAPL, increasing cohesin residence time. These levers set E–P loop stability and re-formation rates without mutating DNA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7610352/?utm_source=openai))
- Mediator and BRD4-rich enhancer hubs contribute to E–P communication and condensate-based stabilization at identity and disease super-enhancers. However, E–P contact persistence can be decoupled from transcriptional output, implying that structural and transcriptional stabilizers are separable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10352134/?utm_source=openai))
- CTCF occupancy and barrier function are tunable via phosphorylation, providing an endogenous route to adjust barrier strength and cohesin dwell times at anchors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7030924/?utm_source=openai))
- Fresh evidence indicates that cohesin residence time gates architectural responses to chromatin hyperacetylation, highlighting kinetics as a control axis: altering loading or release (NIPBL vs. WAPL) shifts the susceptibility of loops and compartments to remodeling. ([biorxiv.org](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.01.735920v1?utm_source=openai))

Integrated problem statement (hypothesis = question)
Do cells already encode a kinetic “quality-control” rule—implemented by endogenous cohesin unloading (WAPL/PDS5) acting against insufficiently stabilized E–P encounters—such that a brief, titrated increase in cohesin turnover preferentially prunes mis-specified, disease-associated E–P loops while sparing canonical contacts that are redundantly stabilized by convergent CTCF and coherent Mediator/TF assemblies?

Atomic strategy
Raise the global probability of cohesin unloading just enough to push only under-stabilized (pathological) E–P loops below a survival threshold, relying on the higher redundancy/resilience of canonical loops to maintain or rapidly re-form. Mechanistically, this reactivates a native residence-time–based pruning program (WAPL/PDS5–dependent unloading opposed by SMC3 acetylation and strong CTCF) to achieve selective structural correction without DNA sequence change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7610352/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims and workplan

Aim 1. Quantify “stability redundancy” and endogenous pruning susceptibility across normal vs. pathological E–P pairs.
- Systems: human cell models with known pathogenic enhancer hijacking or SE-driven oncogenes (e.g., MYC, TAL1), plus matched normal lineage controls.
- Measurements:
  - Contact stability: Micro-C/Hi-C and targeted CTCF/Mediator HiChIP to define E–P loop catalogs; quantify convergent CTCF orientation, CTCF ChIP/footprinting, and Mediator/BRD4 occupancy at anchors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10352134/?utm_source=openai))
  - Kinetics: SCC1-Halo single-molecule tracking and FRAP to estimate cohesin residence times at E–P anchors before perturbation; parallel CUT&RUN for CTCF with phospho-status inference. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7030924/?utm_source=openai))
- Analysis: derive a “stability redundancy index” (SRI) per E–P pair from anchor CTCF strength/orientation, cohesin dwell time, and Mediator/TF coherence. Pre-register decision rule: loops in the bottom SRI quartile in disease but not in control are predicted-prunable.

Milestone: Demonstrate that disease-associated E–P loops occupy a lower SRI regime than canonical loops in the same cells (≥70% separation by AUROC).

Aim 2. Test selective pruning by transient reactivation of cohesin unloading.
- Perturbation: single-dose lipid nanoparticle–delivered mRNA encoding nuclear-targeted WAPL plus PDS5A minimal releasin-cofactor fragment (self-degrading via an intrinsically unstable degron; half-life ~6–12 h), to achieve a brief, system-wide increase in unloading without chronic depletion. No genome editing; no permanent integration. Delivery events ≤1 in discovery studies; ≤2 in validation (booster if needed). Mechanistic justification: WAPL/PDS5 directly catalyze cohesin exit; elevating their local availability decreases residence time globally but momentarily. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts 6–24 h post-dose:
  - Structure: Micro-C/HiChIP to assess which E–P pairs dissolve vs. persist; TAD/loop integrity at CTCF-anchored boundaries as a proxy for preserved topology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8198109/?utm_source=openai))
  - Kinetics: SCC1-Halo dwell-time shift distribution; expect modest global shortening but a bimodal outcome at E–P: preferential loss of low-SRI loops; rapid re-formation of high-SRI loops via ongoing extrusion. ([biorxiv.org](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.01.735920v1?utm_source=openai))
  - Function: nascent RNA (PRO-seq/NET-seq) to confirm selective normalization of misexpressed target genes without widespread repression.
- Controls: (i) WAPL enzymatic mutant (unloading-dead) mRNA; (ii) co-delivery of ESCO1 mRNA (SMC3 acetyltransferase) to antagonize unloading and test reversibility; (iii) phospho-mimetic CTCF transgene to reduce barrier strength and test sensitivity of canonical anchors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11427176/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria: ≥60% of predefined pathological E–P pairs dissolve; ≥80% of canonical E–P pairs maintained or restored within 12–24 h; compartment/TAD organization preserved within ±10% of baseline.

Aim 3. Map endogenous markers that predict unloading sensitivity and formalize a “state code” guiding selective dismantling.
- Multi-omic integration at pruned vs. spared E–P pairs: H3K27ac, eRNA output, RNAPII pausing indices, G4/R-loop features, Mediator/BRD4 density. Build a sparse classifier linking marker constellations to pruning outcome.
- Mechanistic cross-tests:
  - Reduce BRD4 occupancy transiently (low-dose, short-exposure BET degradation) to test whether decreasing enhancer condensate stabilization further biases pruning toward pathological SE loops without collapsing contacts broadly. Expect mixed effects; interpret cautiously given reports that enhancer–promoter proximity can persist despite BRD4 loss at many loci. Use only as a secondary probe, not as primary mechanism. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10435483/?utm_source=openai))
  - Enrich CTCF barriers at canonical anchors by transiently increasing CTCF binding competence (e.g., inhibit kinases linked to CTCF de-binding, short pulse) to test topology protection. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7030924/?utm_source=openai))

Milestone: A compact, testable “marker→pruning” rule linking internal state to unloading susceptibility that generalizes across at least two disease contexts.

Risk, falsification, and mitigation
- Risk: Global WAPL elevation could weaken essential architectural features. Falsification test: if TAD insulation and CTCF loops collapse broadly (Hi-C), model fails. Mitigation: (i) ultra-short WAPL pulses with self-degron; (ii) dose-finding guided by live cohesin kinetics to stay within a “just-enough” unloading window. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8198109/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Canonical loops may be as sensitive as pathological ones. Falsification: no SRI separation; pruning non-selective. Pivot: enrich barrier stabilization first (brief CTCF-binding enhancement) to raise canonical SRI, then repeat unloading pulse. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7030924/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Effects reflect transcriptional shutdown, not structural pruning. Control: dissociate structure from output using time-resolved Micro-C vs. PRO-seq and by using BRD4-independent loci as internal controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801379/?utm_source=openai))

Translational path (non-mutagenic, ≤3 deliveries)
- Modality: LNP-mRNA encoding WAPL±PDS5A-min, with built-in degron for automatic shutdown; 1–2 systemic doses. Optional protective pre-dose to stabilize canonical boundaries (short-acting small molecule that increases CTCF binding competence) as the third and final delivery if needed. No DNA sequence alteration.
- Biomarkers: real-time circulating eRNA panels and cfChIP for H3K27ac to monitor enhancer state; expression normalization of sentinel misexpressed genes; low-coverage Hi-C from cfDNA (exploratory).
- Indications: enhancer-hijack leukemias; SE-addicted solid tumors; developmental enhanceropathies where pathogenic E–P contacts are documented.

Decisive outcomes
- If transient unloading preferentially eliminates low-redundancy, disease E–P loops while preserving canonical topology, we have validated a state-aware kinetic-pruning program already latent in cells. This constitutes a 3D genome “editor” that corrects structure by briefly rebalancing cohesin residence time via native releasin activity—precise, reversible, and non-mutagenic. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7610352/?utm_source=openai))

References (selected, load-bearing)
- WAPL/PDS5 regulate cohesin unloading and 3D architecture; dynamic cycle needed for distal regulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7610352/?utm_source=openai))
- Cohesin residence time gates architectural responses to hyperacetylation. ([biorxiv.org](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.01.735920v1?utm_source=openai))
- SMC3 acetylation antagonizes unloading; sororin locks exit gate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11427176/?utm_source=openai))
- Mediator and BRD4 in enhancer function/condensates and their separability from E–P contact maintenance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10352134/?utm_source=openai))
- CTCF phosphorylation diminishes DNA binding, offering a tunable barrier axis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7030924/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Activity-gated local cohesin release at hyperacetylated enhancer anchors to collapse pathological enhancer–promoter loops

Hypothesis–Question
Can a chromatin reader that senses super-enhancer byproducts (high H3K27ac density and BRD4/Mediator condensates) and, only above a multivalent avidity threshold, recruit a cohesin-unloading effector locally at the enhancer anchor, selectively collapse pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops while preserving canonical CTCF/cohesin topology and normal contacts? Pathological loops in cancer often arise from enhancer hijacking or super-enhancer amplification and are sustained by cohesin loop extrusion stalling near hyperactive enhancer condensates; targeted enhancement of cohesin release at those anchors should shorten contact dwell time and reduce oncogene transcription. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-026-01748-6?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Convert enhancer overactivity into its own inhibitory signal: multivalent detection of enhancer byproducts triggers local recruitment of an unloading bias (PDS5/WAPL axis) to tilt the cohesin load–extrude–release cycle toward release specifically at pathological enhancer anchors. This exploits: (i) hyperacetylation/BRD4–Mediator condensates as inputs; (ii) WAPL/PDS5 control of cohesin release as the actuator. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10527203/?utm_source=openai))

Tool concept
- Reader layer (density-gated): a modular multivalent H3K27ac reader scaffold (e.g., engineered chromatin readers with tandem acetyl-lysine binding domains) plus a low-affinity BRD4/Mediator-IDR–interacting peptide. The scaffold assembles stably only where acetylation density and cofactor crowding exceed a threshold (super-enhancers), implementing avidity-based selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7289633/?utm_source=openai))
- Effector layer (structural first): a minimal PDS5-recruiting module that locally increases PDS5/WAPL activity and/or competes with NIPBL for cohesin binding, biasing toward cohesin unloading at the engaged enhancer anchor. Secondary, reversible epigenetic repression (KRAB or DNMT3A catalytic fragment) can be conditionally co-recruited as a transient brake. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/15/1/51?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims and workplan

Aim 1. Validate the recognition threshold: does the multivalent reader discriminate pathological from normal enhancers?
- Build a panel of reader constructs with increasing numbers/arrangements of acetyl-lysine binding repeats and weak BRD4/MED1-IDR–interacting motifs.
- Calibrate binding/dwell using live-cell FRAP and CUT&Tag across: (a) cancer cell models with hijacked/super-enhancer-driven oncogenes (e.g., MYC, TERT), (b) matched normal cells. Expect preferential accumulation at hyperacetylated enhancer condensates. Benchmark against H3K27ac and BRD4/Mediator profiles. Success criterion: ≥5–10× enrichment at pathological super-enhancers relative to typical enhancers; negligible occupancy at CTCF boundary sites. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-026-01748-6?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer and benchmark the unloading actuator: can localized PDS5/WAPL recruitment collapse pathological E–P loops without disturbing TAD boundaries?
- Effector designs:
  - E1: PDS5-recruiting peptide(s) mapped from known cohesin–PDS5 interfaces to enhance local PDS5 occupancy.
  - E2: WAPL-recruiting adaptor (peptidic binder to WAPL or PDS5–WAPL surface) to increase unloading locally.
  - E3: NIPBL-competitive peptide to reduce local loading.
- Quantify loop disruption with targeted Micro-C/HiChIP for the oncogene locus; measure insulation scores at nearby CTCF sites to ensure boundary preservation. Prediction: reduced enhancer–promoter contact frequency/dwell and shorter loop lengths at targeted anchors; unchanged CTCF-anchored TADs. Rationale: WAPL/PDS5 promote cohesin release; global WAPL loss extends loops, so focal increase should shorten them locally. Success criterion: ≥50% reduction in pathogenic E–P contact frequency with <10% change in neighboring CTCF–CTCF loop insulation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22063?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate functional selectivity and reversibility at disease loci.
- Transcriptional outcomes: nascent transcription (PRO-seq) and steady-state RNA-seq for oncogene(s) versus housekeeping genes.
- 3D genome integrity: in situ Hi-C genome-wide to confirm minimal off-target architectural changes.
- Reversibility: inducible expression/off-switch to verify that withdrawal restores enhancer activity/contacts; optional co-recruitment of a low-dose KRAB/DNMT module to transiently stabilize silencing without sequence change. Success criteria: selective downregulation of oncogene(s) with minimal transcriptome-wide impact; restoration upon withdrawal. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41388-021-01793-7?utm_source=openai))

Key design and feasibility justifications
- Target definition by pathology outputs: Super-enhancers exhibit dense H3K27ac and BRD4/Mediator condensates; multivalency sharpens discrimination at high PTM density. This reduces activation at normal enhancers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10527203/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary structural mechanism: Cohesin positioning and loop length are governed by the balance of NIPBL-mediated loading and WAPL/PDS5-mediated release; modulating this locally is expected to alter E–P loop dwell without global disruption. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/13/22/1896?utm_source=openai))
- Novelty check: We found no reports of activity-gated, mark-density–sensing recruitment of WAPL/PDS5 to specific enhancer anchors; prior manipulations of WAPL are global or inducible-degradation based rather than locus-restricted, and CRISPR-based looping tools primarily target loading or tethering rather than selective unloading at hyperacetylated enhancers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7610352/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental models and assays
- Models: cancer lines with defined enhancer hijacking/super-enhancers driving MYC, TERT, CCND1, ERBB2; normal counterparts for selectivity controls. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-026-01748-6?utm_source=openai))
- Chromatin assays: CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for H3K27ac, BRD4, MED1; Micro-C/HiChIP for local contacts; in situ Hi-C for global architecture.
- Transcriptional assays: eRNA GRO-seq, PRO-seq, RNA-seq.
- Live-cell imaging: reader/effector dwell times; cohesin (RAD21) dynamics with Halo-tags.
- Safety/containment: inducible expression; degron-based kill-switch for the effector.

Controls
- Reader-dead mutants (acetyl-lysine pocket mutations).
- Effector-dead mutants (PDS5/WAPL binding–deficient).
- Swapped reader with H3K4me3 reader to confirm enhancer-selective gating.
- Untargeted global WAPL perturbation as positive control for loop-length sensitivity.

Milestones and quantitative success criteria
- M1 (month 6): Reader achieves ≥10× enrichment at pathological vs. typical enhancers; negligible CTCF boundary occupancy.
- M2 (month 12): E–P contact frequency at targeted loci reduced ≥50% with <10% change in adjacent CTCF insulation.
- M3 (month 18): Oncogene expression reduced ≥60% with ≤5% genome-wide differential genes (FDR <0.05); reversal upon withdrawal within 72 h.
- M4 (month 24): In vivo xenograft proof-of-concept: tumor growth delay with preserved normal tissue transcriptional profiles.

Risk assessment and alternatives
- Risk: Effector potency too low for measurable loop collapse. Mitigation: increase local concentration via SunTag/OLIG repeats on reader; test E1–E3 variants; modest optogenetic clustering limited to reader-engaged sites to avoid global effects.
- Risk: Off-target binding at highly acetylated promoters. Mitigation: require dual input (H3K27ac density + BRD4/Mediator-IDR proximity) and tune valency to exceed typical promoter PTM densities. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10527203/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Boundary leakage. Mitigation: explicitly exclude CTCF-bound DNA by including a CTCF-contact–disrupting mask on the reader; monitor insulation in real time.

Deliverables
- A validated, single-vector, avidity-gated cohesin-release tool that selectively collapses pathological E–P loops without altering DNA sequence.
- Quantitative datasets linking enhancer PTM density/condensates to local cohesin turnover and loop dwell.
- Reagents (plasmids, reader/effector variants) and protocols for community use.

Impact
If successful, this establishes an activity-coupled, topology-preserving “3D genome editor” that treats enhancer hyperactivity as the targeting signal, uses structural protein control as the primary lever, and leaves the canonical chromatin architecture intact. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/13/22/1896?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Tension-adaptive cohesin: a mechanically gated kleisin “fuse” that unloads overstressed enhancer–promoter loops while preserving normal 3D genome topology

Central hypothesis–question
Can we bias cohesin’s endogenous WAPL/PDS5 unloading gate so that it opens only when an enhancer–promoter (E–P) loop exhibits a pathological mechanical signature (sustained, oriented axial tension above the physiological duty cycle), thereby dissolving aberrant loops while leaving normal contacts intact? This asks whether sub-piconewton-to-piconewton DNA tensions that regulate loop extrusion and CTCF stalling can be transduced into a local increase in WAPL-dependent gate opening specifically at overstressed anchors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10132984/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Transduce elevated, persistent axial tension at a cohesin–CTCF–Mediator E–P anchor into allosteric facilitation of cohesin’s DNA exit gate (RAD21–SMC3) by grafting a mechanically labile helix “fuse” that flips under calibrated load to unmask a short WAPL/PDS5 docking motif. The load threshold is set just above the physiological regime at which CTCF arrests extrusion (~0.14–0.15 pN) and below forces generated during pathologic stalling/hijacking, ensuring selective unloading of overstressed loops. The design borrows the gating logic of mechanosensitive channels’ tension-coupled helices but is implemented with low-force, genetically encoded coiled-coil elements to match nuclear force scales. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10132984/?utm_source=openai))

Background and rationale (concise)
- Cohesin extrudes DNA loops and stalls at CTCF in an orientation- and DNA-tension–dependent manner; stall forces for SMC loop extrusion are sub-pN–to–low-pN. WAPL/PDS5 opens the DNA exit gate at the RAD21–SMC3 interface to unload cohesin. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))
- Stabilizing cohesin (e.g., WAPL loss) abnormally extends loops and perturbs distal gene regulation; structural variations can hijack enhancers to form oncogenic E–P loops. These create loops with abnormally long lifetimes and persistent anchor load. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanosensitive helix gating is a proven principle in MscL/MscS; genetically encoded coiled-coil tension elements provide tunable thresholds in the pN range, suited to nuclear mechanics. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18310324/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- A first, mechanically gated cohesin variant that converts loop-anchored tension history into selective WAPL recruitment and ring opening.
- Thresholds are matched to chromatin mechanics rather than sequence, distinguishing pathological from physiological E–P loops without editing DNA.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define the mechanical duty cycle that distinguishes pathological from physiological E–P loops.
- Model systems: (i) WAPL-auxin degron mESCs to create hyper-stable loops; (ii) an enhancer-hijacking cancer line (e.g., MYC hijack). Compare to matched controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: Micro-C/HiChIP for E–P contacts; live-cell cohesin residence tracking; polymer modeling to infer axial tension distributions; integrate with published stall-force regimes. Success criterion: a quantitative duty-cycle threshold (fraction of time above ~0.15 pN equivalent inferred tension) that maximally separates pathological from normal loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7316503/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer a tension-adaptive kleisin fuse (TAK-fuse) that opens cohesin’s exit gate only under pathological load.
- Construct: Insert a calibrated, low-force coiled-coil hairpin (threshold 0.2–1 pN) into a permissive surface loop of human RAD21 near the SMC3-binding region; fuse a cryptic WAPL/PDS5 short linear motif (SLiM) to the hairpin such that hairpin opening unmasks the SLiM. The design borrows the MscL helix gating logic (tension tilts a helix equilibrium to open a downstream gate) but implemented with a cytosolic/nuclear-compatible coiled-coil sensor. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39805005/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro calibration: Reconstitute cohesin–NIPBL on DNA curtains; apply defined forces; measure unload probability vs force with and without the TAK-fuse. Benchmark against wild-type and WAPL/PDS5 addition. Success criterion: a ≥3-fold increase in unload probability only above the calibrated threshold, with ≤10% impact below threshold. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_curtain?utm_source=openai))
- In cells: Replace endogenous RAD21 with TAK-fuse RAD21 via AAV-HDR or PiggyBac in inducible systems. Measure: cohesin chromatin residence (FRAP/single-molecule), global TAD/loop architecture (Micro-C), and targeted E–P loops at disease loci. Success criterion: selective weakening of pathological E–P loops with preservation (±5–10%) of aggregate TAD insulation and normal E–P contact frequencies.

Aim 3. Test anchor-geometry selectivity and reversibility; compare to a catch-bond–inspired variant.
- Geometry/orientation: Direct the TAK-fuse axis along the expected DNA tension vector (RAD21–SMC3–CTCF N-terminus line). Perturb orientation by swapping linkers to test anisotropy.
- Reversibility/self-termination: After unloading, force dissipates; masked SLiM re-forms; verify rapid reloading and restoration of normal loops.
- Comparative construct: A catch-bond–inspired “latch” at the CTCF–cohesin interface engineered to expose a WAPL-docking SLiM under persistent load; evaluate feasibility given higher typical catch-bond force scales. Down-select based on on-target/off-target trade-offs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10132984/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan and methods (key steps)
- Sensor selection and tuning: Use published coiled-coil GETS libraries to choose modules with 0.2–1 pN thresholds; validate folding/unfolding in vitro by magnetic tweezers optical trapping on fusion peptides. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39805005/?utm_source=openai))
- Gate coupling: Map RAD21–SMC3 contact by leveraging structural reviews of the exit gate; place the hairpin to allosterically destabilize the interface upon opening and to unmask a minimal WAPL/PDS5 SLiM. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28220956/?utm_source=openai))
- Quantifying selectivity: In WAPL-depleted and enhancer-hijack models, measure differential changes in (i) loop strength at disease E–P pairs versus housekeeping E–P pairs, (ii) genome-wide insulation scores, and (iii) transcriptional outputs at target vs non-target genes (PRO-seq/RNA-seq).
- Minimal delivery regime: Single vector for RAD21-TAK-fuse knock-in or stable complementation; optional second event for inducible expression control. Total delivery events ≤2.

Risk analysis and contingencies
- Force-scale mismatch: If sub-pN loads are insufficient, raise sensitivity by (i) lowering coiled-coil stability or (ii) multimerizing weak SLiMs to increase avidity only when the hairpin opens; avoid global WAPL recruitment by restricting SLiM affinity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39805005/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target unloading: Limit WAPL docking affinity; include degron-insensitive control; monitor TAD integrity. If needed, gate the SLiM behind a protease site activated by local Mediator tether strain to add a second specificity layer. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6114138/?utm_source=openai))
- Cohesin function impairment: Use heterozygous expression with endogenous backup during calibration; shift to full replacement only after demonstrating preserved global architecture.

Milestones and success criteria
- Year 1: Mechanical duty-cycle map distinguishing pathological from normal E–P loops; in vitro TAK-fuse showing thresholded unloading. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7316503/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: In-cell demonstration that TAK-fuse selectively weakens hijacked or WAPL-stabilized E–P loops while maintaining TAD insulation and normal E–P contacts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 3: Generalization across loci; comparative assessment with catch-bond–inspired variant; dossier on safety/selectivity for translation.

Expected outcomes and impact
This work should establish a 3D genome editor that operates by tension history rather than sequence or histone state, dissolving only aberrant E–P loops and preserving normal topology. It leverages endogenous cohesin unloading machinery and matches chromatin force scales, addressing a key gap between polymer physics of loop extrusion and practical correction of pathological 3D genome wiring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))
