Title
Geometry-gated decoys that selectively dissolve pathological enhancer–promoter loops by siphoning disease‑biased cohesin/CTCF assemblies

Hypothesis–Question
Do disease-biased cohesin/CTCF assemblies occupy a mesoscale geometric and kinetic state (anchor spacing, orientation, dwell-time) that can be selectively neutralized by an intranuclear, geometry‑matched, low‑affinity multivalent scaffold, thereby collapsing pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops while sparing normal 3D genome topology?

Atomic strategy
Treat “geometry” as the epitope. Build a soluble nuclear decoy that presents a constellation of weak, orthogonal interaction modules arranged at nanometer-scale distances and angles matched to the disease-biased cohesin/CTCF assembly. Only complexes adopting the pathological geometry achieve cooperative multivalent engagement and long-lived sequestration; normal complexes (different geometry/shorter residence times) fail to reach the avidity threshold and release rapidly.

Rationale and prior evidence (condensed)
- Cohesin extrudes loops and is halted/retained by CTCF; residence-time control by WAPL/PDS5/NIPBL tunes loop stability and topology. Dysregulation alters dwell times and loop landscapes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5730888/?utm_source=openai))
- Synthetic multivalent scaffolds and condensates can be programmed to recruit specific clients in nuclei via weak multivalent interactions, enabling selective, reversible sequestration. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27374333/?utm_source=openai))
- Programmable nuclear nanostructures (e.g., DNA/protein scaffolds) can be delivered to and function within mammalian nuclei. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9999407/?utm_source=openai))
- Existing 3D-genome engineering tools reposition or enforce contacts (CRISPR-GO/CLOuD9/OptoLoop) but do not use geometry-gated decoy sequestration to selectively erase pathological loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13005720/?utm_source=openai))

Proposed tool
GEO-TRAP: A nucleus-localized, inert protein/DNA hybrid scaffold displaying a programmable array of low-affinity binders (peptide/mini-aptamer modules that recognize shallow, non-PTM-specific surfaces on cohesin/CTCF/Mediator). Modules are arranged on a rigidizable framework to match pathological loop geometry (effective anchor-to-anchor distance, orientation, and curvature). Cooperative capture forms a non-productive complex that is rapidly reversible upon scaffold withdrawal; normal assemblies fail geometric and kinetic thresholds.

Scope and system
- Disease models: (a) WAPL/PDS5 perturbation and cohesinopathy-like states with prolonged cohesin residence; (b) cancer lines with cohesin/CTCF axis alterations (e.g., STAG2 loss) that show ectopic E–P contacts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5730888/?utm_source=openai))
- Target complexes: cohesin–CTCF–cofactors that stabilize disease E–P loops.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define disease‑biased geometric/kinetic signatures of pathological E–P loops.
- Question: What mesoscale distances/orientations and dwell-time distributions distinguish pathological from normal E–P loops?
- Plan: Integrate Micro-C/HiChIP(CTCF/cohesin) with polymer modeling to infer anchor spacing/orientation; pair with live-cell single-molecule tracking of cohesin to quantify residence-time shifts in disease vs reference states. Use these parameters to specify a narrow geometric/kinetic acceptance window for decoy design. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Reproducible geometric ranges (nm-scale) and ≥2-fold dwell-time increase unique to disease state; parameterizable into scaffold CAD.

Aim 2. Engineer GEO-TRAP scaffolds that encode geometry as specificity.
- Question: Can a multivalent array of weak, orthogonal binders arranged to the pathological geometry achieve superselective capture only under disease-state kinetics?
- Plan: Construct two scaffold families:
  - Rigidizable protein nanorods/cages bearing k copies of binder A (cohesin surface) and l copies of binder B (CTCF surface) with fixed intersite distances/angles; and
  - DNA-based nanocalipers with base‑paired struts that set inter-binder spacing and can be nucleo-imported.
  Binder chemistries are tuned for KD in the high‑µM to mM range individually; only multivalent co-engagement yields low apparent off-rates (avidity). Optimize array stoichiometry and spacing against Aim‑1 parameters to create a steep superselectivity curve (binding only when both geometry and dwell-time match). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10107566/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: In‑nucleus FRAP/FLIM-FRET to quantify GEO-TRAP:cohesin/CTCF residence times; depletion of target complexes from pathological anchors by ChIP-seq/CUT&RUN; minimal effect at physiological loops.
- Success criteria: ≥50% reduction of disease-anchor occupancy with ≤10% change at normal anchors; target residence-time increase on scaffold with no global condensate formation.

Aim 3. Test correction of 3D topology and transcription with preservation of normal architecture.
- Question: Does GEO-TRAP erase pathological loops while maintaining baseline TADs/loops and gene expression?
- Plan: Measure changes in contact maps (Micro-C/Hi-C) and E–P contacts (HiChIP/Micro-C capture) pre/post scaffold induction; quantify transcriptional rescue at disease‑upregulated loci while monitoring global expression stability. Benchmark against CRISPR‑GO/CLOuD9 perturbations to confirm orthogonality and selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13005720/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Collapse of predefined pathological loops; preservation of TAD insulation/stripe strength and loop landscapes within ±10% of baseline; targeted transcript normalization with minimal genome‑wide expression drift.

Design constraints and operating principles
- Selectivity: Encoded by geometry (spacing/orientation) and weak‑to‑strong avidity transition only at disease‑state dwell-times; avoids reliance on specific PTMs.
- Reversibility: No DNA sequence change. Upon scaffold withdrawal (transcriptional shutoff or degradation tag), pathological loops can re-form, providing internal control.
- Preservation of normal topology: Normal loops do not match the decoy’s spatial constellation and thus remain unperturbed.
- Delivery ≤3 events: (1) Single transduction/transfection of GEO‑TRAP expression cassette (NLS-tagged); (2) optional small‑molecule conformational stiffener to “lock” scaffolds during evaluation; (3) optional light pulse for inducible deployment window (if an opto-stiffening module is used). Total events ≤3.

Validation logic and metrics
- Mechanism: Demonstrate that cooperativity requires both geometry and co-engagement (loss of function upon scrambling intersite spacing or deleting one binder type).
- Off-target assessment: Global chromatin compaction (ATAC-seq), replication timing, and cell-cycle progression remain within control ranges.
- Functional rescue: Disease-relevant phenotypes (e.g., proliferation dependence on pathological E–P loops) revert toward baseline upon GEO‑TRAP induction.

Risk analysis and contingencies
- If nuclear delivery of DNA nanocalipers is suboptimal, pivot to rigidizable protein scaffolds with genetically encoded inter-binder spacers; preserve the same geometric logic. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36601-1?utm_source=openai))
- If individual binder modules are too weak, increase valency while keeping geometry fixed; if off-target sequestration occurs, lower valency and tighten spacing tolerances to sharpen the superselective window.
- If dwell-time differences are insufficient in a given model, select alternative disease contexts with documented cohesin residence-time shifts (e.g., WAPL perturbations). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5730888/?utm_source=openai))

Outcome
A reversible, geometry‑gated decoy that preferentially siphons disease‑biased cohesin/CTCF assemblies, dissolving pathological E–P loops while preserving normal 3D genome topology. This advances 3D genome “editing” beyond locus tethering toward state‑selective, non-mutational topology correction via encoded mesoscale geometry.

text:
Title
Epigenetic-cue-gated cohesin loading to lock normal enhancer–promoter loops followed by transient endogenous NIPBL downshift to clear cancer-specific contacts

Hypothesis-question
Can a multivalent, epigenetic-cue-gated cohesin loader that selectively stabilizes developmentally licensed enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops render those normal contacts resilient to a brief, partial reduction of endogenous NIPBL activity, thereby causing preferential collapse of unlicensed, cancer-specific E–P contacts without altering DNA sequence?

Atomic strategy
License before purge: boost cohesin loading and dwell time only at pre-licensed E–P pairs using a loader that requires coincident enhancer H3K27ac, promoter H3K4me3, and convergent CTCF occupancy; then apply a short, global endogenous NIPBL downshift to weaken all loops. Licensed normal loops persist because they retain local loader activity; unlicensed pathological loops lack sufficient cues to recruit the loader and collapse when endogenous loading dips. This exploits core features of cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and CTCF/WAPL governance and avoids permanent sequence edits. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22063?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build and calibrate an epigenetic-cue-gated cohesin loader (ECGL)
- Architecture: a minimal NIPBL/MAU2 loading core fused to a multivalent reader hub (low-affinity tandem bromodomains for H3K27ac, a PHD for H3K4me3, and a peptide that detects the DNA-bound conformation of CTCF) plus a weak Mediator-interacting motif to bias protection at active regulatory hubs; include a negative selector (e.g., HP1 chromodomain) to autoinhibit in H3K9me3 neighborhoods.
- Nuclear context gate: incorporate an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) composition tuned to enrich in transcriptionally active, speckle-proximal microenvironments while avoiding hypervalent super-enhancer condensates, increasing selectivity for normal promoter hubs. Partitioning rules and BRD4/MED1 condensate properties guide IDR design. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))
- Calibration: tune module affinities so no single interaction is sufficient; protection emerges only from coincident cues within authentic E–P assemblies.

2) Demonstrate protect-then-clear topology editing in oncogene hijacking models
- Models: isogenic cell systems with well-mapped hijacked E–P contacts.
- Protect: express ECGL (stable or mRNA) to clamp licensed E–P loops.
- Clear: transiently downshift endogenous NIPBL (12–24 h) using siRNA/ASO or degron-based genetics in vitro (research setting), then allow recovery.
- Readouts: Micro-C/HiChIP for RAD21 to quantify loop retention vs loss; CUT&Tag for H3K27ac/H3K4me3; live-cell cohesin imaging; compare normal vs oncogenic E–P contacts and TAD integrity pre/post pulse.
- Success criterion: normal E–P contacts preserved while cancer-specific E–P contacts and associated hubs preferentially collapse; global TAD architecture recovers.

3) Test functional rescue without sequence edits
- Measure transcriptional outputs (PRO-seq/RNA-seq) and enhancer activity (eRNA) at identity genes and oncogenic drivers before, during, and after the pulse.
- Assess selectivity and safety: proliferation, DNA damage markers, mitotic progression, and off-target compaction.

Key justifications and feasibility
- Cohesin loop extrusion organizes interphase genomes; CTCF orientation and WAPL-controlled release specify and limit loop growth, anchoring many E–P interactions at CTCF sites. Thus, targeted modulation of cohesin loading/dwell time is a direct handle on E–P topology. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22063?utm_source=openai))
- Targeted cohesin loading is sufficient to induce defined loop trajectories in living cells, establishing the practicality of loader-centric interventions; however, prior work tethered loader subunits to engineered arrays rather than using native multi-cue gating for selective protection. Our proposal extends this principle to endogenous, developmentally licensed E–P contacts. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41102415/))
- Endogenous NIPBL downshift reduces loop formation genome-wide; by providing an exogenous, cue-gated loader only at licensed sites, protected loops maintain local loading during the pulse while unlicensed loops lack compensatory loading and collapse. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12207409/?utm_source=openai))
- Developmental recruitment of NIPBL by pioneer factors (for example FOXA1) shows that chromatin-context-dependent cohesin loading is a native mechanism, supporting the plausibility of a multivalent reader hub that “listens” to enhancer–promoter chromatin states. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-026-02688-7?utm_source=openai))
- Partitioning into transcriptional condensates is sequence-composition dependent and tunable via IDR design, enabling a nuclear-context gate that enriches ECGL where normal promoter hubs reside and disfavors SE-like oncogenic hubs. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-73800-y?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1: ECGL construction and in situ biophysics
- Modular library: systematically vary reader stoichiometry and affinities; build IDR variants spanning charge/aromaticity grids.
- Single-molecule and FRAP: quantify ECGL residence times at promoters/enhancers vs SE hubs; measure partition coefficients relative to BRD4/MED1 foci.
- ChIP/CUT&RUN: confirm local enrichment of NIPBL/MAU2 and cohesin at licensed E–P pairs; quantify RAD21 dwell change.
- Controls: catalytically inactive loader core; reader-deficient variants; TACL-like tethering as a sufficiency positive control for local loading. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41102415/))

Aim 2: Protect-then-clear topology editing
- Protect phase: express best ECGL variant; map loop landscapes by Micro-C and promoter capture Hi-C.
- Clear pulse: transient NIPBL downshift (siRNA/ASO or degron line for research proof) for 12–24 h; washout; remap loops at 6, 24, and 72 h.
- Selectivity metrics: fraction of normal E–P loops retained vs cancer-specific loops lost; TAD boundary strength recovery; cohesin occupancy redistribution.
- Mechanistic probes: manipulate WAPL levels modestly to test sensitivity of protected vs unprotected loops to increased release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Functional outcomes and reversibility
- Transcriptome: PRO‑seq/RNA‑seq to test rescue of lineage programs and reduction of oncogenic expression; eRNA changes at protected vs cleared sites.
- Epigenome stability: H3K27ac/H3K4me3 CUT&Tag to monitor enhancer/promoter states during and after editing.
- Reversibility: small‑molecule degron on ECGL for off-switch; confirm return to baseline dynamics within 3–7 days.

Delivery and triggers (≤3 events)
- Event 1: ECGL expression (viral or mRNA).
- Event 2: Transient NIPBL downshift (siRNA/ASO; in vitro may use degron genetics).
- Optional Event 3: ECGL degradation pulse to fully restore native dynamics after recovery.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: ECGL enriches at licensed E–P pairs with ≥2× cohesin dwell increase and negligible occupancy at SE-like hubs.
- M2: Following NIPBL downshift, ≥60% of mapped cancer-specific E–P contacts collapse while ≥80% of normal E–P contacts persist and recover after washout.
- M3: Identity gene programs are preserved or improved; oncogenic drivers decrease without genome-wide TAD disruption.

Risk and mitigation
- Overstabilization may impede transcription near protected sites; TACL shows activated extrusion can suppress local transcription and alter H3K27ac, so enforce low-affinity, time-limited clamping and include an off-switch. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41102415/))
- Chromatin mimicry by cancer enhancers: add negative selectors (e.g., H3K9me3, nonconvergent CTCF geometry sensors) and IDR gating to sharpen context dependence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22063?utm_source=openai))
- Global NIPBL downshift toxicity: minimize duration and degree; test partial knockdown kinetics; monitor cell-cycle and genome integrity.

Expected outcome and impact
A reversible 3D genome editor that first secures normal E–P wiring, then selectively clears unlicensed pathological contacts by exploiting endogenous rules of cohesin loading, CTCF gating, and nuclear partitioning. This establishes a protect-then-clear paradigm for topology-level correction without DNA sequence changes, with strong mechanistic grounding and a clear translational path. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22063?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Force-gated CTCF to selectively dissolve low-tension enhancer–promoter loops while preserving architectural genome topology

Integrated hypothesis–question
Can embedding a tunable mechanosensitive linker within CTCF convert local chromatin tension into a kinetic discriminator that shortens lifetimes of weak, pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops while preserving high-tension, CTCF-anchored architectural contacts, thereby correcting 3D wiring without sequence edits? This rests on two grounded premises: (i) cohesin-driven loop extrusion operates in the piconewton force regime and stalls at CTCF barriers; (ii) CTCF barrier activity is DNA-tension dependent, implying that anchor lifetimes can be modulated by force-sensitive off-rates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Mechanically gate CTCF off-rate. Engineer a CTCF variant (FG-CTCF) whose DNA-binding lifetime increases under higher chromatin tension and decreases under low tension. This converts local mechanical load—high at stable, convergent CTCF boundaries; low at aberrant E–P tethers—into a self-selecting filter on loop persistence, without predefining disease-specific sequences. Force-dependent off-rate control is a well-established physical principle for protein–ligand and protein–DNA bonds. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19491034.2020.1782024?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Engineer FG-CTCF variants with tunable force-dependent off-rates and validate barrier behavior under defined DNA tensions in vitro.
- Aim 2. Replace endogenous CTCF with FG-CTCF in cells and test whether weak, pathological E–P loops are selectively destabilized while TAD boundaries and canonical CTCF loops are preserved.
- Aim 3. Escalation path (if needed): co-express a low-potency RAD21 ring-destabilizing variant to bias cohesin unloading at weak anchors, preserving robust barriers stabilized by STAG–CTCF interactions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))

Design and rationale

1) Protein design: FG-CTCF
- Scaffold: Human CTCF with intact 11 zinc fingers (ZF1–ZF11).
- Mechanosensitive linker insertion: Introduce an elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) segment between central ZF clusters (e.g., between ZF5–ZF6) to create a compliant hinge that exhibits extensible mechanics under pN forces. ELP linkers are genetically encodable, mechanically well-characterized, and tunable in contour length and stiffness. The design goal is a slip-to-stabilized response: at low force (weak loops), the hinge geometry penalizes multizinc-finger engagement (higher off-rate); at elevated force (extrusion stall at strong anchors), extension aligns ZFs to lower the off-rate. A panel of ELP lengths/compositions will be screened to set thresholds within the 0.1–1 pN regime relevant for SMC extrusion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

- Barrier function under load: Test whether FG-CTCF increases cohesin stall probability and dwell under higher DNA tension, consistent with CTCF’s tension-dependent barrier behavior, and allows rapid dissociation at low tension. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05961-5.pdf?utm_source=openai))

2) Optional synergy: RAD21 ring-destabilizing variant (low-potency)
- Rationale: Cohesin release occurs via opening of the SMC3–RAD21 exit gate, promoted by WAPL/PDS5. A mild reduction in RAD21 interface stability should preferentially increase unloading where anchors are not reinforced (weak E–P), leaving high-tension, STAG/CTCF-stabilized barriers largely unaffected. This creates an orthogonal kinetic filter on weak loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1. Biophysical engineering and validation
- A1.1 Construct panel: Generate 12 FG-CTCF variants with ELP linkers (varying repeats and guest residues) inserted between ZF5–ZF6 (and two alternatives: ZF4–ZF5, ZF6–ZF7). Purify proteins.
- A1.2 Single-molecule DNA–protein kinetics under force: Use magnetic/optical tweezers with DNA tethers harboring high-affinity CTCF motifs; measure koff(F) for WT- and FG-CTCF at 0.05–1.0 pN. Target behavior: FG-CTCF koff reduced relative to WT at ≥0.3–0.6 pN and increased at ≤0.1–0.2 pN, consistent with load-sensitive barrier formation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))
- A1.3 Reconstituted extrusion barrier assay: With human cohesin and NIPBL, quantify loop-extrusion stall frequency and dwell at CTCF sites under controlled tension in DNA curtains/tweezers. Benchmark against WT-CTCF. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))
- Success metric: A variant exhibiting ≥2-fold off-rate decrease at ≥0.3 pN and ≥2-fold increase at ≤0.1 pN vs WT; corresponding ≥1.5-fold increase in cohesin stall probability under high tension.

Aim 2. Cellular selectivity and topology preservation
- A2.1 Controlled replacement: Deliver a single vector encoding FG-CTCF and an shRNA that knocks down endogenous CTCF; include an auxin- or dTAG-degron on endogenous CTCF if a degron line is available. Inducible expression to gate timing.
- A2.2 Assay weak vs strong loops: Identify E–P loops with lower CTCF occupancy/valency (e.g., nonconvergent sites, suboptimal motifs) versus canonical convergent boundary loops. Use Hi-C/HiChIP for CTCF/cohesin to quantify loop strength, aggregate peak analysis, and insulation scores pre/post FG-CTCF induction. Preserve: boundary insulation and convergent CTCF loops; Reduce: low-occupancy E–P loops and hijacked enhancer connections.
- A2.3 Functional outcomes: RNA-seq to test normalization of misexpressed genes linked to weak E–P contacts; ChIP-seq CUT&RUN for CTCF, STAG1/2, RAD21 to confirm anchor-specific occupancy changes. STAG–CTCF interaction is expected to reinforce high-tension sites. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))
- A2.4 Off-target topology guardrails: Quantify global TAD insulation and compartment strength; criterion for preservation: median boundary insulation change <10% and compartment eigenvector correlation >0.9 relative to WT.

Aim 3. Escalation with RAD21 variant (only if Aim 2 shows residual pathological loops)
- A3.1 Co-deliver a bicistronic vector encoding a mild RAD21 variant with reduced stability at the SMC3–RAD21 exit interface (tuned in vitro to increase WAPL-facilitated unloading ≤1.5× WT). Validate no global loss of cohesin at strong CTCF/STAG-enriched barriers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))
- A3.2 Reassess loop selectivity as in Aim 2; proceed only if boundary insulation remains within preservation criteria.

Mechanistic falsification and decision gates
- F1. If FG-CTCF fails to show force-dependent koff in Aim 1 despite ELP tuning, reject the atomic strategy (“ideation failed”) and do not proceed in cells.
- F2. If FG-CTCF reduces insulation at strong CTCF boundaries by >15% in Hi-C or broadly reduces cohesin occupancy at STAG-enriched barriers, terminate and revert to WT-CTCF controls. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))
- F3. If adding RAD21 variant causes widespread cohesin loss (HiChIP RAD21 reduction across boundaries) or global gene-expression drift (RNA-seq PC1 shift), discontinue Aim 3. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-70484-2?utm_source=openai))

Readouts, statistics, and controls
- Single-molecule: Fit koff(F) to Bell–Evans models; compare FG-CTCF vs WT via ANCOVA on log(koff) vs F. Include control ELP insertions at noncritical CTCF loops (e.g., N-terminus) to rule out generic destabilization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7007008/?utm_source=openai))
- Chromatin topology: Perform 3 biological replicates per condition; use insulation score delta distributions and aggregate peak analysis for loop classes; FDR control for RNA-seq differential expression.
- Functional controls: WT-CTCF rescue; catalytically neutral cohesin ATPase mutant to verify extrusion dependence; STAG2 knockdown to test predicted reinforcement role at strong barriers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))

Delivery plan (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Single vector expressing FG-CTCF (inducible) plus CTCF shRNA and fluorescent reporter.
- Event 2 (only if Aim 3 triggered): Bicistronic vector for low-potency RAD21 variant (inducible).
- Event 3: Not used; kept in reserve for safety degron or reporter swap if required.

Safety and non-permanence
- No DNA sequence modification of genomic anchors. All interventions are protein-level and reversible via induction/degradation. Cohesin unloading leverages the native WAPL exit gate mechanics without genome edits. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and impact
- A validated FG-CTCF that stabilizes high-tension, convergent CTCF boundaries while preferentially destabilizing weak, pathological E–P loops, restoring normal enhancer wiring without requiring locus catalogs. This exploits established physics of loop extrusion forces and force-dependent barrier activity, translated into a selective, self-tuning 3D genome editor. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If ELP linkers perturb DNA specificity, shift insertion site among ZF interdomains or modulate ELP composition to tune mechanical response.
- If force thresholds mismatch physiological ranges, calibrate via in situ tension reporters or adjust ELP length to match 0.1–1 pN regime measured for SMC complexes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- M1 (Months 0–6): Identify at least one FG-CTCF with desired koff(F) profile in vitro.
- M2 (Months 6–12): Demonstrate selective weakening of weak E–P loops with preserved boundary insulation in cells.
- M3 (Months 12–18): Optional RAD21 co-tuning achieves further reduction of residual weak loops without boundary loss. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-70484-2?utm_source=openai))

Title: KineLoop — Kinetic biasing of 3D genome reassembly to extinguish pathological enhancer–promoter loops

Hypothesis/Goal
Reversible, global collapse of architectural loops followed by controlled, temporal re-entry of loop-forming machinery will bias a limited pool of cohesin/Mediator toward bona fide enhancer–promoter (E–P) anchors, allowing normal 3D topology to self-reconstitute while deprioritizing re-formation of pathological E–P loops. The atomic strategy is time-ordering: seed early nucleation only at legitimate anchors before bulk reassembly, exploiting factor limitation and nonequilibrium assembly of loop extrusion and transcriptional bridging. This operates without DNA sequence mutation and primarily manipulates structural proteins; it can be reinforced locally by transient, site-specific torsional fences at pathological loci during the reassembly window. Cohesin/CTCF/Mediator underpin TADs and E–P proximity through loop extrusion and bridging; WAPL and NIPBL tune residence and loading; DNA torsion modulates cohesin engagement and extrusion efficiency. ([biorxiv.org](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.08.14.667581v2.full?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Converts 3D genome “editing” into kinetic control of reassembly order after a reversible global reset, rather than sequence alteration or forced tethering of loci. Prior methods engineer static loops (CLOuD9, LADL/OptoLoop) or delete/flip CTCF sites; none intentionally bias genome-wide reassembly kinetics to select against pathological loops. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15993?utm_source=openai))
- Uses transient, anchor-first nucleation and optional locus-specific torsional barriers to reshape the energy landscape that loop extrusion and Mediator/BRD4 bridging explore during recovery, leveraging known sensitivities of cohesin loading, residence time, and DNA supercoiling. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims
Aim 1. Build anchor-first nucleation seeds to front-load cohesin/Mediator at bona fide E–P anchors prior to bulk reassembly.
- Design: A catalytically inactive dCas9 “seed” targeted to validated normal anchors (convergent CTCF/promoter sites) fused to minimal NIPBL segments that stimulate cohesin ATPase/loading (MINI-NIPBL) and/or a Mediator tail peptide that increases Mediator clustering. Seeds are expressed 2–4 h before global restoration of architectural proteins after acute depletion. Rationale: NIPBL/Mediator accumulate near promoters/enhancers and facilitate cohesin loading/activation; early nucleation at high-affinity native anchors should capture limiting cohesin and establish long-residence loops if WAPL release is temporarily dampened at those sites. Metrics: on-rate and residence of RAD21 at seeded anchors (ChIP-seq/FRAP), early loop re-appearance (Micro-C/Hi-C). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Implement sequential kinetic gating of the global reassembly program in degron-enabled cell systems and quantify topology/selectivity.
- System: Human cells with auxin/dTAG-degradable RAD21 (cohesin), CTCF, and a Mediator subunit to acutely erase loops, then rescue by timed washout/re-expression. Rationale: Eliminating CTCF/cohesin erases loops; reintroduction restores them with characteristic kinetics that can be biased by prior anchor nucleation and transiently reduced WAPL activity. Assays: time-resolved Micro-C/Hi-C, cohesin/CTCF/Mediator CUT&Tag, and allele-resolved HiChIP at disease loci (e.g., enhancer hijacks). Outcome: selective restoration of normal E–P loops and suppression of pathological contacts, with preserved TADs/compartments. Controls: seeds at scrambled sites; reassembly without seeds; WAPL modulation off. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867417305317?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3 (optional reinforcement). Apply transient, locus-specific torsional fences at pathological enhancers/promoters during reassembly, then remove.
- Design: A dCas9 topological clamp (dual gRNAs spanning 100–300 bp) plus recruitment of a Topo1-activity dampening peptide or steric swiveling constraint for 6–12 h post-rescue to accumulate local positive supercoils and reduce cohesin loading/extrusion efficiency at the pathological site; fence is removed after normal anchors are stabilized. Rationale: Cohesin extrusion and loop length are sensitive to torsion; Topo1 inhibition or impaired relaxation shortens loops in cells; modulating supercoiling locally should raise the energy barrier for re-forming the pathological loop without altering sequence. Metrics: reduced cohesin/Mediator residence and contact frequency at the pathological pair during the window, with recovery after fence removal. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124725006278?utm_source=openai))

Experimental Design and Methods
1) Model loci and pathologies
- Select two validated enhancer-hijack models (e.g., oncogenic super-enhancer miswiring) with known pathological E–P loops and normal counterpart contacts for benchmarking; design seed gRNAs to legitimate anchors and clamp gRNAs to pathological anchors.

2) Global disruption and staged rescue
- Deplete RAD21 and CTCF (± Mediator subunit) using AID/dTAG for 4–8 h to remove TAD loops, confirmed by Micro-C and loss of CTCF/Cohesin peaks. Reintroduce seed constructs first; 2–4 h later, washout degron ligands to allow bulk cohesin/CTCF/Mediator return; optionally reduce WAPL activity transiently (chemical degron or RNAi) for 6–12 h to extend residence of early-formed loops. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867417305317?utm_source=openai))

3) Readouts
- Structure: time series Micro-C/Hi-C at 0, 2, 6, 12, 24, 48 h post-rescue; loop callers quantify E–P contacts and insulation scores.
- Protein dynamics: RAD21/CTCF/Mediator CUT&Tag and live-cell single-molecule tracking to derive on/off rates and residence.
- Transcription: PRO-seq and nascent RNA at target genes to test restoration of physiological expression.
- Supercoiling state (optional Aim 3): topo-sensitive psoralen-seq or supercoil-trap assays at targeted loci.

4) Selectivity criteria
- Pathological E–P loop frequency reduced ≥50% relative to no-seed rescue while normal E–P loops return to ≥80% of baseline; TAD insulation and A/B compartments comparable to pre-disruption state.

5) Delivery constraints (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Transduce seed/clamp constructs (single vector with multiplexed gRNAs) and optional WAPL-tuner.
- Event 2: Small-molecule degron treatment to deplete, then scheduled washout to rescue structural proteins.
- Event 3: Induce seed/clamp clearance (degron/antisense) after topology stabilizes.

Risk Assessment and Alternatives
- Risk: Seeds mis-target or nucleate at low-affinity/non-native sites. Mitigation: require convergent CTCF motif proximity and promoter histone marks for gRNA design; include seed variants that require TF co-binding domains to limit off-target anchoring.
- Risk: Global disruption harms viability. Mitigation: use short pulses and partial depletion; focus on loci-specific readouts; verify recovery of compartments.
- Risk: Torsional fences perturb local transcription excessively. Mitigation: limit window; measure recovery; deploy only if Aim 1–2 insufficient. The mechanistic link between torsion and extrusion justifies a transient fence as a physical barrier. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124725006278?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and Success Criteria
- M1: Demonstrate that anchor-first seeding advances the timing of cohesin/Mediator accumulation at legitimate anchors by ≥2 h versus bulk rescue alone and increases residence time locally. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Show selective suppression of pathological E–P loops with restoration of normal loops and TAD insulation within 24–48 h post-rescue.
- M3 (optional): Show that a 6–12 h torsional fence further decreases pathological loop re-formation without long-term transcriptional penalty.

Why it will work
Loop extrusion is sensitive to loading sites (NIPBL), residence time (WAPL), CTCF orientation/barriers, and DNA torsion; all are kinetically and mechanically tunable. Early capture at legitimate anchors consumes limited cohesin and sets long-lived loops, while temporary torsional penalties at pathological sites raise their assembly barrier during the critical window. Together, this reweights reassembly trajectories toward physiological topology without altering sequence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))

Title
Mechanosensitive unloading of diseased enhancer–promoter loops via conformation-selective intrabodies that recruit WAPL/PDS5

Background and novelty assessment
- Mechanistic ground truth: Mammalian chromatin architecture emerges from cohesin-driven loop extrusion constrained by CTCF orientation; residence time and anchor composition modulate enhancer–promoter (E–P) contact frequency and duration. WAPL–PDS5 catalyzes cohesin unloading by opening the Smc3–RAD21 gate, thereby limiting loop extension and enforcing directionality rules. Mediator/BRD4-enriched enhancers can stall cohesin and stabilize contacts. These points are consistently supported by recent syntheses and primary studies. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-024-00795-x?utm_source=openai))
- Disease relevance: Structural variants, boundary erosion, and enhancer hijacking pathologically rewire E–P pairing, often yielding longer-lived contacts and aberrant anchor usage; this is established across genetic disorders and cancers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25959774/?utm_source=openai))
- Gap: Available 3D-genome engineering tools can force loops (e.g., CLOuD9, LADL) or globally alter cohesin dynamics (WAPL depletion) but do not selectively dismantle only aberrant loops based on their physical state. No reports were found of conformation- or tension-state–selective intrabodies against cohesin/CTCF that locally recruit WAPL/PDS5, nor geometry-gated small molecules used as inter-anchor “distance readers” in nuclei. PROTAC selectivity via linker geometry is known, but has not been applied to sense 3D chromatin anchor spacing; targeted WAPL tethering to individual anchors was not identified. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15993?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility cues: Cohesin exhibits ATPase-coupled conformational states and interface plasticity (including Smc3–RAD21 and kleisin–STAG surfaces) that plausibly expose strain-dependent epitopes; computational and display-based discovery of epitope-specific nanobodies is tractable. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–goal (deliberately inseparable)
Abnormally stabilized E–P loops impose a distinct mechanical/conformational state on CTCF–cohesin–cofactors at their anchors (greater dwell time, altered interface angles, and stalled extrusion). A conformation-selective intrabody that recognizes a tension-exposed cohesin/CTCF neo-epitope and recruits a minimal WAPL/PDS5 unloading module will preferentially disassemble these pathological loops while sparing normal contacts and preserving global topology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit disease-imposed mechanics as the actuator: bind only to a mechanically strained conformer at E–P anchors and, upon binding, locally bias cohesin’s release reaction via WAPL/PDS5—self-terminating as soon as the aberrant loop opens (epitope relaxes).

Operational design (conceptual; non-procedural)
- Effector architecture: A low-affinity, conformation-specific intrabody (“ms-iBody”) fused to a minimal WAPL/PDS5-interacting peptide. Binding requires a strain-exposed epitope on cohesin/CTCF observed at long-lived, misassembled anchors; in relaxed/healthy states, affinity is insufficient to engage. Primary mechanism: structural protein manipulation of the cohesin cycle; no DNA sequence alteration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Selectivity guards:
  - Force-state gating: epitope exposed only under stalled extrusion/anchor torque. Cohesin state plasticity supports this assumption. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))
  - Context gating: an auxiliary weak binder to a Mediator/BRD4 surface increases avidity only at hyperacetylated, condensate-like enhancers known to stall cohesin, sharpening specificity for disease super-enhancers. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00018-024-05559-8?utm_source=openai))
  - Self-limitation: after unloading, the strained conformation dissipates and ms-iBody disengages.

Model systems and mapping of discriminants (Aim 1)
- Define “pathologic anchor” signatures at exemplar loci with enhancer hijacking or boundary erosion (e.g., PDGFRA boundary loss in IDH-mutant glioma; oncogenic super-enhancer–MYC modules). Readouts: local cohesin/CTCF/Mediator occupancy, contact dwell-time proxies, and extrusion stall patterns; ensure normal E–P pairs in the same cells serve as internal controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4880504/?utm_source=openai))
- Outcome: a panel of loci with quantifiable differences in residence/geometry that will be used to benchmark selectivity.

Binder discovery and validation (Aim 2)
- Identify strain- or state-specific epitopes on cohesin/CTCF interfaces implicated in unloading control (e.g., Smc3–RAD21/kleisin–STAG regions). Combine structure-guided in silico designs with display selections against state-biased antigens; screen for intrabodies that bind strongly to the “stalled” conformer and weakly to the “relaxed” conformer. Reference states derive from structural and biochemical knowledge of cohesin’s ATPase cycle and gate opening by WAPL–PDS5. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmarks: (i) state selectivity in cell-free binding; (ii) negligible binding at fast-turnover/healthy anchors; (iii) loss of binding upon global relaxation of cohesin dynamics.

Mechanism-of-action build (Aim 3)
- Fuse ms-iBody to a minimal WAPL/PDS5-recruitment cassette; confirm that ms-iBody engagement raises local cohesin unloading probability without globally altering TAD organization or anchor usage. Global loop extrusion roles of WAPL/PDS5 and their impact on loop networks provide quantitative expectations for “what not to see” system-wide. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5730888/?utm_source=openai))
- Optional transient chromatin “friction”: a weak, reversible writer/reader (e.g., short-lived deacetylase recruitment) appended to ms-iBody reduces immediate re-stabilization at hyperacetylated enhancers; include washout designs to ensure reversibility and avoid persistent marks. Mediator/BRD4-rich super-enhancers correlate with high contact propensity but are not strictly required for looping, supporting a nudge-only role. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9659172/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts and success criteria
- Topology: restoration of local contact maps toward healthy baselines at target loci with minimal perturbation of non-targeted neighborhoods and global TAD structure. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-024-00795-x?utm_source=openai))
- Kinetics: reduced contact dwell time specifically at pathological E–P pairs; normal short-lived E–P “kisses” retained. Recent live-imaging and synthesis pieces estimate loop lifetimes on the order of minutes, providing quantitative priors. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/docserver/fulltext/cellbio/41/1/annurev-cellbio-111822-122324.pdf?accname=guest&checksum=A59DC90DF46E50983E408271E0A524F1&expires=1781441214&id=id&utm_source=openai))
- Transcription: normalization of misexpressed target genes without widespread transcriptional collapse characteristic of global cohesin or BET perturbation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-targets: genome-wide assessment shows low-rate incidental unloading at healthy anchors; no emergence of ectopic long loops or loop networks linked to WAPL loss. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Comparative arm (orthogonal validation)
- A proximity-activated split-WAPL recruiter (half-modules targeted to enhancer vs promoter anchors via modest-affinity readers) used as an AND-gate control for dwell/orientation dependence. Reconstitution should require prolonged, disease-like proximity; normal fleeting contacts fail to assemble. This tests the necessity and sufficiency of pathological dwell/orientation independent of force-state epitopes. (Background supports the logic that looped proximity increases E–P contact probability but is often transient in healthy cells.) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))

Delivery and deployment
- One delivery event: a single vector expressing ms-iBody–WAPL/PDS5-recruiter (bicistronic inclusion of the optional BRD4/Mediator microbinder permissible within the same event). No DNA sequence editing; effects remain at the level of structural cycling of cohesin.

Key risks and falsification tests
- Risk: disease anchors might not expose unique epitopes. Falsification: if binders cannot discriminate stalled vs relaxed states in vitro and in cells despite adequate search space, the atomic strategy fails.
- Risk: unloading at diseased anchors could trigger compensatory rewiring. Counter-readout: emergence of alternative pathogenic loops in the same domain indicates a need to couple unloading to a transient anti-stabilization nudge at the enhancer surface; the optional module directly tests this.
- Alternative outcome: if mechanics are insufficiently distinct, the split-recruiter AND-gate should still selectively act on long-dwell contacts, providing an independent route to selectivity.

Why this will not collapse global topology
- The trigger is a local conformer plus context avidity (stalled/mechanically strained anchor within a Mediator/BRD4-rich enhancer). WAPL/PDS5 recruitment is transient and spatially constrained; global extrusion remains intact, consistent with known consequences of localized vs global WAPL modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Map discriminants at chosen disease loci; identify state-biased epitopes and initial ms-iBody hits. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Build ms-iBody–WAPL/PDS5 prototypes; demonstrate selective loop relaxation and transcriptional correction at ≥2 pathological loci with preserved global topology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 3: Generalize to additional pathologies (SV-driven enhancer hijacking and methylation-driven boundary erosion) and benchmark safety/selectivity windows. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959437X24000480?utm_source=openai))

Decision rule
If ms-iBody–mediated unloading normalizes pathogenic contact topology and expression at target loci while leaving healthy E–P contacts and TAD structure statistically unchanged, the hypothesis stands; if not, the mechanics-as-trigger premise is rejected in favor of dwell/orientation–gated proximity approaches.

text:
Title
AND-gated, sPLA2/pH-triggered T cell and monocyte “backpacks” for site-selective, extracellular drug release in tumors and inflamed tissues

Central hypothesis (question and claim as one)
Can we exploit extracellular secretory phospholipase A2 (sPLA2) that is elevated in many tumors and inflamed sites, together with local acidosis, to achieve coincidence-gated, extracellular payload release from immune-cell-tethered liposomes that do not perturb leukocyte homing and function? If sPLA2 access to a tethered vesicle is sterically masked at blood pH and unmasked only at pathologic pH, then release should occur almost exclusively where both cues co-occur, while receptor mobility and chemotaxis of the carrier cell remain intact. Elevated sPLA2 in multiple cancers/inflammation and extensive prior art on sPLA2-sensitive liposomes support feasibility of the trigger, while cell-surface “backpack” anchoring via CD45 has shown non-internalizing, stable residence on leukocytes ex vivo and in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3579817/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Move the trigger to the environment and the carrier to the cell, but keep them decoupled: a liposome engineered to be both pH-unmasked and sPLA2-degradable is tethered to leukocyte surface territories that avoid endocytic capture (CD45 domains), so the cell remains a navigator and the liposome remains an extracellular, enzyme-addressable depot. Coincidence (pH AND sPLA2) acts as the sole release logic.

Specific aims
1) Build an AND-gated, immune-cell-tethered liposome that releases cargo only when extracellular pH is low and sPLA2 is present.
2) Dock the liposome to leukocytes via non-internalizing CD45 territories without impairing rolling, arrest, diapedesis, or chemotaxis.
3) Demonstrate site-selective drug release and efficacy with safety margins in murine models of inflammation and solid tumors.

Design overview
- Carrier: 80–120 nm liposomes with composition tuned for sPLA2 susceptibility (PC/CHOL with anionic lipid such as PG; low DSPE-PEG to control corona). sPLA2 hydrolyzes sn-2 acyl chains and destabilizes anionic/PEGylated bilayers, enabling extracellular release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5509414/?utm_source=openai))
- Gate 1 (mask): pH-labile PEG shell (hydrazone- or orthoester-linked PEG brush) that sterically blocks sPLA2 access at pH 7.4 and sheds at pH 6.3–6.8 typical of tumors/inflamed sites. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8008067/?utm_source=openai))
- Gate 2 (trigger): exposed bilayer becomes susceptible to local sPLA2 (notably group IIA) to permeabilize/rupture the tethered liposome and release cargo extracellularly. sPLA2 elevation is reported in multiple cancers and inflammatory states. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7988039/?utm_source=openai))
- Tethering to cells: anti-CD45 Fab (low valency) conjugated to a flexible PEG-cholesterol insert or to a small amphiphile, positioning the vesicle in CD45-rich, glycocalyx-dense territories known to support stable “backpack” residence on T cells and monocytes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6078803/?utm_source=openai))
- Functional payloads: small molecules (e.g., doxorubicin, cisplatin analogs), cytokines-inhibitors, or checkpoint peptides; choice matched to indication. sPLA2-responsive liposomes have been shown to release multiple classes of agents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5509414/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety hedge: prior reports of in vivo toxicity from untargeted sPLA2-sensitive liposomes motivate coincidence gating and low surface density per cell; we include dose de-escalation and off-target activation checks. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016836591730740X?utm_source=openai))

Aim 1. Chemistry, build, and bench characterization
- 1.1 Synthesize pH-masked, sPLA2-sensitive liposomes
  - Lipid mix: DSPC:CHOL:DSPG:DSPE-PEG2000 (molar 55:35:8:2) as baseline; vary anionic fraction (0–15 mol%) to tune sPLA2 kinetics. Load calcein/SRB for release assays; later, model drugs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8008067/?utm_source=openai))
  - Mask: 5–10 mol% pH-labile PEG brush via hydrazone-linked PEG-lipid; quantify mask shedding t1/2 at pH 7.4, 6.8, 6.5.
- 1.2 Release logic validation (coincidence detection)
  - Matrix: four conditions—pH 7.4/−sPLA2; pH 6.6/−sPLA2; pH 7.4/+sPLA2; pH 6.6/+sPLA2 (human/murine sPLA2-IIA 1–100 nM with Ca2+). Expect near-zero release unless both cues present; quantify krelease and fractional release at 2 h and 24 h. Reviews and primary data show sPLA2-driven release from anionic/PEGylated liposomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5509414/?utm_source=openai))
  - Protein corona effect: measure with/without 50% serum; PEG and charge modulate sPLA2 access; optimize PEG length/density accordingly. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378517315302556?utm_source=openai))
- Milestones
  - AND selectivity index ≥10 (releasefraction pH6.6/+sPLA2 divided by each single-cue condition) and ≥100 vs pH7.4/−sPLA2.
  - No fusion with leukocyte membranes in supported bilayer assays.

Aim 2. Ex vivo leukocyte docking and function preservation
- 2.1 Tethering strategy
  - Conjugate anti-CD45 Fab to PEG-cholesterol anchors; incubate with human/mouse T cells and monocytes to display 1–5 liposomes/cell. Prior work shows anti-CD45 nanogels/backpacks stably reside on T cells/monocytes without loss of function. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6078803/?utm_source=openai))
- 2.2 Non-internalization and lateral mobility
  - Confocal and TIRF to confirm surface localization 0–48 h; measure FRAP of LFA-1/CCR7/CXCR4 with and without backpacks to ensure diffusion coefficients within 90% of baseline.
- 2.3 Leukocyte biomechanics and trafficking
  - Microfluidic flow chambers (P-selectin/ICAM-1) to quantify rolling velocity, arrest fraction, and firm adhesion.
  - Transwell and microchannel chemotaxis to CXCL12/CCL2 gradients; acceptance: chemotactic index and velocity within 85–100% of untreated cells.
- 2.4 Off-target release control
  - Whole blood shear (10–30 dyn/cm2) with physiologic pH/sPLA2; verify negligible release. Introduce pH 6.6 only or sPLA2 only as single-cue controls; expect low release.

Aim 3. In vivo coincidence-gated release, efficacy, and safety
- 3.1 Models
  - Inflammation: LPS-induced lung or arthritis models (elevated sPLA2, low pH).
  - Cancer: sPLA2-high syngeneic tumors (e.g., CT26/MC38); confirm sPLA2 activity in tumor interstitial fluid before dosing. Elevated sPLA2 reported in multiple cancers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3579817/?utm_source=openai))
- 3.2 Dosing
  - Adoptively transfer autologous or syngeneic T cells/monocytes bearing backpacks; track with near-IR fluorophores.
- 3.3 Readouts
  - On-target release: FRET dequenching on liposome cargo; microdialysis or MALDI imaging of drug in tumor/inflamed tissue vs healthy organs.
  - Efficacy: tumor growth delay or inflammatory score reduction vs free drug and non-gated controls.
  - Safety: cytokines, complement activation, liver/kidney histology; monitor systemic leakage acknowledging toxicity observed with ungated sPLA2 liposomes. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016836591730740X?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria
  - ≥5× higher drug AUC in lesion vs matched healthy tissue.
  - Equal or better efficacy at ≤50% systemic drug dose compared to free drug.

Manufacturing and translational plan
- Cell processing: closed-system incubation (5–15 min) to decorate cells; wash and formulate for infusion. Components (lipids, PEGs, Fabs) have clinical precedent; anchoring and liposome assembly align with liposomal GMP workflows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5509414/?utm_source=openai))
- Release and QC: particle size/PDI, mask shedding kinetics, sPLA2-triggered release rate, per-cell liposome count, absence of Fc-mediated activation (Fab only).
- Regulatory posture: ex vivo–modified autologous cells with non-genetic, non-covalent surface attachments; payload in a well-characterized liposome; prior art supports both sPLA2-responsiveness and CD45-anchored backpacks, but their coincidence-gated combination on living immune couriers is not established. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16305438/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and contingencies
- Variability of sPLA2 across indications: pre-screen lesions for sPLA2 activity; if low, pivot second cue to protease (MMP2/9) while retaining pH masking architecture. Dual-responsive liposomes to MMP/pH are established. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.biomac.8b01510?utm_source=openai))
- Enzyme access in dense matrices: tune anionic lipid fraction and PEG shedding threshold to increase sPLA2 binding.
- Potential immunogenicity/toxicity: limit per-cell backpack density; include dose-escalation and stopping rules referencing prior toxicity signals in ungated systems. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016836591730740X?utm_source=openai))

Claims of novelty relative to art
- sPLA2-sensitive liposomes and pH-responsive masks are known, and CD45-anchored backpacks on leukocytes are reported. The new combination is: an immune-cell-tethered, AND-gated (pH-unmasking plus sPLA2-trigger) extracellular release system that preserves leukocyte migration while confining drug liberation to lesions. Literature does not document PLA2-gated release from cell-tethered carriers with environmental coincidence logic. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16305438/?utm_source=openai))

Go/no-go gates
- Bench: AND selectivity index ≥10 and release t1/2 ≤2 h under dual-cue.
- Ex vivo: migration and adhesion metrics within 85–100% of unmodified cells.
- In vivo: ≥5× lesion:healthy drug AUC and significant efficacy vs controls without systemic toxicity.

Milestones and timeline (12–18 months)
- Months 0–4: Chemistry optimization and AND gating quantification (Aim 1).
- Months 4–8: Ex vivo leukocyte docking and function validation (Aim 2).
- Months 8–18: In vivo pharmacology, efficacy, and safety; manufacturability assessment (Aim 3).

Anticipated impact
A cell-mediated, coincidence-gated, extracellular drug release platform that uses native leukocyte homing while minimizing off-target exposure, with a parts list compatible with clinical translation and room for IP around the gating architecture and cell-docking geometry. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16305438/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Orthogonal marrow niche rewiring with localized immune polarity inversion to eradicate LSCs under non‑genotoxic allo‑HSCT conditioning

Central question/hypothesis
Can we convert the bone marrow into a privileged survival niche for donor HSCs that LSCs cannot use, and simultaneously localize multi‑axis immune pressure (anti‑PD‑1/PD‑L1, anti‑CD47, NK recruitment) within the marrow, so that reduced‑intensity allo‑HSCT achieves relapse control comparable to or better than MAC without systemic genotoxicity or excess GVHD? The hypothesis rests on: (i) LSC retention and quiescence via CXCL12/CXCR4, VLA‑4/VCAM‑1, E‑selectin and trophic inputs including SCF/c‑KIT, THPO/MPL, and Ang‑1/Tie2; (ii) immune escape after allo‑HCT via HLA loss/downregulation and checkpoint upregulation; and (iii) the capacity of NK effectors to mediate GVL with relatively low GVHD risk. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai)) ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18371409/?utm_source=openai)) ([ashpublications.org](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/133/12/1290/260469/Mechanisms-of-immune-escape-after-allogeneic?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12482124/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Recode niche compatibility: provide donor HSCs with an orthogonal trophic axis (engineered receptor–ligand pairs) that is unavailable to LSCs, while locally suppressing native SCF/THPO/Ang‑1 signals and inverting immune signaling polarity in the marrow (recruit effectors and neutralize evasion cues in situ). This single change of “who can read the niche signals” forces LSCs off their survival supports and exposes them to localized, multi‑mechanism immune killing, compensating for the loss of MAC cytotoxicity. Orthogonal cytokine–receptor pairs are clinically plausible from prior IL‑2/IL‑2R work and can be adapted conceptually to hematopoietic trophic axes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build an orthogonal trophic channel for donor HSCs and withdraw native trophic support from LSCs within marrow.
- Engineer donor HSCs ex vivo to express orthogonal variants of key trophic receptors (prototype: MPL*, KIT*), and deliver marrow‑anchored orthogonal ligands (THPO*, SCF*) via ECM‑binding fusions to confine activity to bone marrow. As a counter‑field, locally neutralize native THPO/SCF/Ang‑1 signals with marrow‑anchored decoys/aptamers activated by leukemia‑associated proteases. Readouts: donor HSC engraftment/lineage reconstitution; loss of LSC quiescence, detachment from niche, and apoptosis/clearance; preservation of host stromal integrity.
- Rationale: THPO/MPL, SCF/c‑KIT and Ang‑1/Tie2 sustain HSC quiescence and are co‑opted by AML/LSCs; depriving native inputs selectively stresses LSCs, while orthogonal ligands maintain donor HSC fitness. Engineered ligand biasing of c‑KIT signaling and orthogonal IL‑2/IL‑2R precedents support feasibility of selective trophic wiring. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18371409/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5526607/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Create a bone‑marrow–anchored “polarity inversion” field that co‑recruits effectors and disables evasion locally.
- Construct a marrow‑retained chemo‑immunologic scaffold that: (i) displays ECM‑tethered chemokines (e.g., CXCL9/10 motifs) to recruit CXCR3+ donor NK/T effectors; (ii) presents protease‑activated PD‑L1 “Probody” traps and SIRPα decoys to neutralize PD‑1/PD‑L1 and CD47 “don’t‑eat‑me” signals where leukemia remodeling is highest; and (iii) includes collagen‑binding cytokine modules (e.g., IL‑15/IL‑12 analogs) to sustain NK cytotoxicity without systemic exposure. Readouts: spatial drug activation, local checkpoint consumption, NK recruitment/activation, phagocytosis, minimal systemic cytokinemia, and GVHD indices.
- Rationale: Protease‑activatable anti‑PD‑L1 agents demonstrate intratumoral activation; collagen‑anchored immunocytokines increase local bioavailability and reduce systemic toxicity; SIRPα decoys trigger macrophage phagocytosis and can aid NK activity. Bone/marrow anchoring can be achieved through ECM‑binding domains and/or bisphosphonate‑based hydroxyapatite targeting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8311335/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7811803/?utm_source=openai)) ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/27/8/2190/672069/Phase-I-Study-of-the-CD47-Blocker-TTI-621-in?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9195145/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test temporal uncoupling: transiently dismantle physical retention before delivering a short‑lived donor NK pulse.
- Evaluate marrow‑localized CXCR4 and/or E‑selectin antagonism to transiently release LSCs from protective contacts, followed by a brief infusion of donor NK or CAR‑NK cells targeting an LSC‑restricted antigen (e.g., CLEC12A) with built‑in safety off‑switch. Readouts: LSC mobilization kinetics, niche occupancy changes, NK infiltration and kill, MRD clearance, and GVHD safety.
- Rationale: CXCR4/E‑selectin antagonists mobilize AML cells and have been combined with therapy; allo‑NKs can target HLA‑loss clones with lower GVHD liability than T cells, complementing localized checkpoint/CD47 blockade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7499473/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12482124/?utm_source=openai))

Study design overview
- Platform: RIC/NMA allo‑HSCT in preclinical humanized AML models and an early‑phase clinical pilot in high‑risk AML candidates for RIC allo‑HCT. No genotoxic conditioning beyond standard RIC/NMA backbones; exclude busulfan/TBI per constraint.
- Modules and sequence: (1) Orthogonal donor HSCs + marrow‑anchored orthogonal ligands (engraftment privilege); (2) marrow‑anchored polarity inversion scaffold (checkpoint/CD47 traps + chemokine/cytokine recruitment); (3) timed, short‑persistence donor NK/CAR‑NK pulse post‑displacement.
- Controls: matched RIC allo‑HSCT alone; RIC + NK without niche rewiring; and, where ethical, MAC historical benchmarks for relapse. Co‑primary endpoints: 1‑year relapse incidence and GVHD grade II–IV. Key secondary endpoints: MRD negativity at day +100, donor chimerism, time to neutrophil/platelet engraftment, non‑relapse mortality, and immune biomarker spatial gradients.

Mechanistic validation and readouts
- Niche compatibility switch: single‑cell RNA/ATAC and phospho‑signaling of donor HSCs and LSCs under native vs orthogonal trophic inputs; in situ proximity ligation to confirm orthogonal receptor engagement only on donor HSCs; functional readouts of quiescence exit/apoptosis in LSCs.
- Polarity inversion: spatial proteomics to quantify PD‑L1 trap activation and CD47 blockade in marrow; intravital microscopy for NK recruitment and phagocyte synapse formation; systemic cytokine profiling for off‑target activation.
- Temporal uncoupling: live‑tracking of LSC mobilization vs NK arrival; kill efficiency vs simultaneous delivery.

Statistical/scientific milestones
- Go/no‑go 1: donor engraftment non‑inferior to RIC controls with reduced LSC markers in marrow niches (power for 20–30% relative reduction). 
- Go/no‑go 2: localized checkpoint/CD47 target occupancy ≥ predefined intramarrow threshold with minimal systemic engagement; absence of excess acute GVHD vs RIC.
- Go/no‑go 3: composite relapse endpoint at 12 months non‑inferior to MAC historical rates with equal or lower grade III–IV GVHD.

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Orthogonal axis specificity: risk of cross‑talk with native receptors. Mitigation: use validated orthogonal design principles (loss‑of‑function in native binding interface plus gain‑of‑function complementary mutations) and marrow‑anchored ligands to confine exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))
- LSC trophic heterogeneity: some clones may be less dependent on THPO/SCF/Tie2. Mitigation: combine trophic withdrawal with polarity inversion and NK pulse; stratify by MPL/Tie2/KIT expression and CXCR4/VLA‑4/E‑selectin levels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9820412/?utm_source=openai))
- Checkpoint/CD47 blockade toxicity: anemia/thrombocytopenia and systemic inflammation. Mitigation: marrow anchoring and protease‑activated traps to limit peripheral exposure; select SIRPα decoy formats with minimal erythrocyte binding. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/23/4/1068/122917/TTI-621-SIRP-Fc-A-CD47-Blocking-Innate-Immune?utm_source=openai))
- Mobilization‑related leukostasis: employ local marrow‑retained antagonists and monitor mobilization kinetics; sequence NK infusion after transient displacement window based on biomarker timing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7499473/?utm_source=openai))
- NK persistence/efficacy: insufficient dwell time. Mitigation: local IL‑15/12 support via collagen‑anchored modules; CAR specificity to CLEC12A where appropriate; preserve safety with short‑lived products/suicide switches. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11292205/?utm_source=openai))

Why this fulfills the constraints
- Compensates for lost MAC cytotoxicity by removing LSC trophic supports and adding localized, multi‑axis immune pressure without systemic genotoxic injury. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai))
- Excludes busulfan/TBI; interventions are signaling/microenvironmental and spatially confined.
- LSC‑selectivity with preserved HSC engraftment via orthogonal niche privilege. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))
- Overcomes marrow sanctuary: dismantles adhesion (temporal uncoupling) and replaces survival cues LSCs rely on, while recruiting effectors into those microdomains. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai))
- Counters immune evasion in parallel: HLA‑loss addressed by NK; PD‑L1 and CD47 neutralized locally. ([ashpublications.org](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/133/12/1290/260469/Mechanisms-of-immune-escape-after-allogeneic?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8311335/?utm_source=openai))
- Enhances GVL without exacerbating GVHD by marrow localization and NK‑favored biology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12482124/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated impact
If successful, this program establishes niche‑level compatibility engineering plus localized polarity inversion as a generalizable, non‑genotoxic path to eradicate LSCs in RIC/NMA allo‑HSCT, matching or surpassing MAC relapse control while reducing systemic toxicity and GVHD.
