Title
Adenosine-integrated lifetime control to autoregulate sleep–wake by biasing locus coeruleus excitability

Rationale
Sleep homeostasis (Process S) is encoded in part by activity-dependent accumulation and clearance of extracellular adenosine, which promotes sleep by inhibiting arousal systems (e.g., noradrenergic locus coeruleus, LC) predominantly via A1 receptors; A2A actions in select basal ganglia/preoptic circuits also increase sleep probability. Ectonucleotidases CD39/CD73 generate extracellular adenosine from ATP/ADP, and equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENTs), especially ENT1, shape extracellular adenosine dynamics and sleep homeostatic markers. The sleep–wake flip‑flop is stabilized by orexin and reciprocal inhibition between sleep- and wake-active nodes, but homeostatic bias toward sleep after sustained wake is widely attributed to adenosine tone. Thus, a controller that converts local A1R engagement into a tunable protein half-life can, in principle, integrate sleep pressure and bias LC output without chronic receptor stimulation or external commands. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13149043/?utm_source=openai))

Central hypothesis-question
Can we implement a thermostat-like homeostat for arousal by coupling the lifetime of an intracellular controller molecule directly to endogenous adenosine receptor activation, so that accumulated “sleep-pressure time” stabilizes a hyperpolarizing bias in LC neurons and, as adenosine dissipates during sleep, the bias decays—yielding bidirectional, repeatable, low-tolerance control of wakefulness?

Atomic strategy
Encode Process S as protein persistence: make the degradation rate of a membrane excitability modulator the direct readout of local A1R–β‑arrestin recruitment. High adenosine (sustained wake) stabilizes the modulator; falling adenosine (sleep) re-exposes a degron for rapid clearance. This uses degradation-rate modulation for fast, reversible control and stores “sleep debt” in the controller’s concentration rather than in dedicated memory circuitry. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-genet-120116-024656?utm_source=openai))

Design overview
- Sensing-to-lifetime coupling: Adapt a Tango-like A1R–β‑arrestin TEV proximity system so that endogenous A1R activation recruits TEV to cleave a degron from an intracellular effector, converting receptor occupancy into proteolytic stabilization rather than transcriptional reporting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4424118/?utm_source=openai))
- Effector: A modest-conductance leak K+ channel (e.g., TASK-3/TREK-1 chimera with reduced unitary conductance) or a membrane-tethered K+ conductance booster, fused N‑terminally to a fast degron (PEST/CL1) separated by a TEV site. Stabilization increases leak, suppressing LC firing and promoting sleep; loss of stabilization restores firing for wake. Adenosine’s known A1R‑GIRK/HCN effects in chemosensitive and LC-like neurons support the directionality. ([eneuro.org](https://www.eneuro.org/content/5/6/ENEURO.0404-18.2018?utm_source=openai))
- Cell targeting: TH-Cre–restricted AAV delivery to LC in mice (plus off-target controls). Circuit choice prioritizes safety: LC down-bias reduces arousal without overriding circadian gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3961294/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 1: Build and calibrate an adenosine-to-lifetime integrator (Ado-LI)
- Construct: A1R-TEVcs-cargo and β‑arrestin2–TEV protease (or split‑TEV) + effector bearing TEVcs–degron. In HEK293 cells, quantify stabilization kinetics versus adenosine or A1R agonist/antagonist, then in LC-like neuronal culture with endogenous adenosine manipulation (CD39/CD73 ectoenzyme and ENT pharmacology). Metrics: effector half-life, dynamic range, and time constant versus receptor activation history. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4424118/?utm_source=openai))
- Acceptance criteria: ≥5-fold change in effector half-life between high and low A1R activation; response halftime ≤30–60 min; negligible basal stabilization without A1R activation.

Specific Aim 2: Demonstrate closed-loop sleep–wake bias in LC
- Acute slice physiology (LC): Record membrane potential/firing under endogenous adenosine manipulation; test whether sustained adenosine exposure stabilizes effector and reduces firing; washout should restore firing as effector is re-degraded. Controls: inactive TEV, scrambled TEV site, degronless effector.
- In vivo (EEG/EMG + LC fiber photometry): In TH‑Cre mice injected bilaterally in LC, test whether after enforced wake (sleep deprivation) the system increases NREM/SWS bout probability and reduces sleep latency; after recovery sleep, reduced leak (due to degron exposure) should increase wake propensity on the subsequent light phase. Endpoints: NREM time, bout length, spectral slow‑wave activity (SWA), sleep latency, and LC NE dynamics. Safety: absence of cataplexy‑like episodes; preserved circadian phase. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13149043/?utm_source=openai))
- Acceptance criteria: Significant buffering of sleep debt expression (shorter sleep latency, increased early‑recovery NREM) after deprivation and symmetric return toward baseline after recovery without pharmacological inputs.

Specific Aim 3: Quantify thermostat properties and tolerance resistance
- Integral behavior: Fit a leaky-integrator model linking time‑integrated A1R activation to effector abundance and to arousal metrics. Compare to transcriptional control surrogates to test whether degradation‑rate control yields faster setpoint adjustments at matched protein copy numbers. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-genet-120116-024656?utm_source=openai))
- Repeatability/tolerance: Challenge with repeated deprivation/recovery cycles over weeks; monitor stable efficacy, receptor signaling (A1R levels/desensitization), and absence of compensatory hyperexcitability.

Key controls and comparators
- Genetic: TEV-dead, TEVcs-mutant, degronless effector, and receptor-only arms.
- Pharmacologic: A1R antagonism (caffeine-like) to flatten stabilization curve; ENT1 inhibitor to elevate extracellular adenosine and test sensitivity to transport-governed tone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4532636/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target safety: Whole-brain c-Fos mapping; cardiorespiratory monitoring to exclude brainstem autonomic disruption.

Why this satisfies constraints
- Safety: No exogenous actuating drugs; effects capped by stoichiometric effector abundance; cell-type targeting; limited gain (leak K+ bias rather than hard inhibition). Adenosine pathway alignment reduces off-target chemistry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13149043/?utm_source=openai))
- No tolerance: The system does not chronically agonize receptors; it converts native receptor occupancy into protein persistence, minimizing receptor desensitization risks. Continuous turnover prevents saturation drift. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev-genet-120116-024656?utm_source=openai))
- Repeatability: Proteostasis-based actuation renews each cycle; TEV site is sequence‑specific; Tango-like proximity logic is robust across GPCRs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4424118/?utm_source=openai))
- Bidirectionality: High adenosine stabilizes hyperpolarizing bias to promote sleep; low adenosine re-exposes degron to promote wake—both directions emerge from the same lifetime coupling.

Exploratory extension (optional)
- Mutual sequestration threshold: Add a low-level, constitutive wake‑biasing scaffold (W) that is stoichiometrically neutralized by stabilized S (the effector). The free fraction sets a soft threshold, providing sharper, mass‑limited switching without enzymatic amplification. Bench-top validation in HEK cells with heterodimeric S–W pairs will test titration ultrasensitivity and setpoint tuning. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2694680/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success metrics (12–24 months)
- M6: HEK calibration of Ado‑LI (≥5× lifetime shift; EC50 within physiological adenosine range inferred from A1R tone). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13149043/?utm_source=openai))
- M12: LC slice proof that sustained adenosine stabilizes effector and reduces firing; reversibility on washout.
- M18: In vivo demonstration of buffered sleep homeostasis after deprivation and symmetric release after recovery, with preserved circadian phase.
- M24: Week‑scale cycling with stable efficacy, no adverse phenotypes; optional S–W threshold validation.

Go/no‑go
- No‑go if effector stabilization cannot be driven by endogenous adenosine (i.e., requires supraphysiologic A1R activation) or if LC bias induces instability (fragmented sleep or autonomic side effects).
- Pivot options: switch to A2A‑gated integration in nucleus accumbens/preoptic nodes; or replace protease logic with ligand‑stabilized degrons once endogenous‑metabolite‑responsive domains become available.

Anticipated impact
This project tests an intrinsic, biocompatible “thermostat” that encodes sleep pressure directly in protein lifetime to continuously and reversibly bias arousal without external commands, drug dependence, or high‑gain cascades—an operational route to safe, tolerance‑resistant regulation of human sleep induction and wake promotion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13149043/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Programmable phase-targeted skin thermal pulses for safe, repeatable, bidirectional control of human sleep induction and wake promotion

Background and rationale
In humans, retinal melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to entrain the circadian clock; ipRGC activity is indexed noninvasively by the post-illumination pupil response (PIPR). Light timing relative to internal phase determines advance versus delay responses. These are established properties that allow objective readouts of circadian photic sensitivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6395400/?utm_source=openai))
Peripheral and central clocks are partially dissociable: feeding schedules and physiologic temperature cycles entrain peripheral tissues (e.g., liver, lung), whereas the adult SCN is comparatively resistant to direct temperature resetting. Controlled misalignment can therefore be created and resolved with appropriately timed nonphotic cues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC317100/?utm_source=openai))
Skin temperature and distal–proximal heat distribution acutely gate sleep: distal warming increases heat loss, shortens sleep onset latency, and predicts sleep initiation. These thermoregulatory effects provide a safe, nonchemical lever for sleep induction. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17078772/?utm_source=openai))
Core body temperature minimum (CBTmin) is a validated phase marker that correlates with dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) and with modeled circadian phase from ambulatory data, enabling lower-burden phase tracking in field studies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5476188/?utm_source=openai))

Working hypothesis (inseparable from the research question)
Can minimal-dose, phase-targeted skin thermal pulses—scheduled at moments of maximal individual thermal sensitivity estimated in real time—safely and repeatably induce sleep when desired and promote wake when required, while achieving predictable circadian phase shifts with lower photic dose than standard light therapy?

Atomic strategy
Exploit temperature’s differential leverage on peripheral oscillators and thermoregulatory sleep gating by:
- estimating an individual’s local temperature phase-response derivative using brief micro‑pulses and fast biomarkers (distal–proximal temperature gradient, DPG) to identify high-gain phases; then
- delivering minimal-energy, site-specific thermal pulses (distal warming for sleep induction; proximal or neutral thermal scheduling paired with morning/evening light for wake promotion and phase steering), while constraining transient SCN–peripheral offsets to safe bounds. This is a single causal lever: time-optimized thermal input tuned to individual sensitivity.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Identify individual thermal PRCs and high-gain windows.
- Question: What are the advance and delay lobes of each participant’s thermal PRC, and how stable are the local gains over weeks?
- Approach: Over two weeks, deliver 60–180 s thermal micro‑pulses (±2–3°C from baseline) at quasi-random internal phases. Read out immediate responses: DPG change (sleep-gating proxy) and actigraphy micro-adjustments. Validate entrainment effects by measuring next-day phase (DLMO in-lab 1×/week; daily CBTmin from wearable sensors). Masking-versus-entrainment separation uses the ratio of acute DPG change to next-day CBTmin/DLMO shift. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17078772/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Closed-loop minimal-dose thermal control for phase shifts with and without light.
- Question: Does personalized, closed-loop thermal scheduling reduce total light dose needed to produce target phase shifts compared with state-of-the-art light-only protocols?
- Design: Randomized three-period crossover (N=60): (i) closed-loop thermal-only; (ii) closed-loop thermal+light; (iii) standard fixed-schedule light. Targets: +1.5 h advance (eastward model week) and −1.5 h delay (westward model week). Controller selects pulse timing and site (distal vs proximal) from the estimated PRC and enforces constraints on cumulative thermal energy and allowable central–peripheral lead/lag (≤2 h, ≤72 h). Outcomes: phase shift magnitude (DLMO/CBTmin), variance, total photopic melanopic dose. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3625727/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Bidirectional behavioral control: sleep induction and wake promotion under operational constraints.
- Question: Can the same individualized thermal schedule reliably shorten sleep onset and improve pre-dawn wake performance without tolerance across eight weeks?
- Tasks: 
  - Sleep induction: distal warming pulses during the 90 min pre‑bed window aligned to high-gain delay/advance lobes as needed; primary endpoint: sleep onset latency by in‑home PSG subset and actigraphy. 
  - Wake promotion: pre-dawn proximal neutral-to-slight-warming pulses plus time‑appropriate light when advancing; endpoint: Psychomotor Vigilance Task and subjective sleepiness. 
  - Tolerance monitoring: weekly re‑probing with micro‑pulses; declining response slope triggers dose rotation (site alternation, pulse pattern change). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17078772/?utm_source=openai))

Methods overview
Participants
- Healthy adults (18–55), regular sleep schedules; second cohort: rotating shift workers (n=40) for external validity.

Interventions
- Wearable thermoelectric patches (Peltier) at distal (hands/feet) and proximal (clavicle/upper arm) sites with closed-loop temperature control and skin safety sensors.
- Timed light exposure (melanopsin-weighted, centered near 480 nm) as comparator/adjunct; ipRGC function tracked by PIPR pupillometry to index photic sensitivity day to day. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4993463/?utm_source=openai))

Sensing and phase estimation
- Continuous wrist/skin temperature, heart rate, activity; daily CBTmin estimation from multimodal wearables and weekly salivary DLMO. Analytical pipeline uses established relationships between CBTmin and DLMO for phase inference, with masking-aware demixing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5476188/?utm_source=openai))

Control policy
- Initialization: two-week micro‑perturbation mapping builds an individualized thermal PRC.
- Online update: each session begins with a 60–120 s test pulse; acute DPG slope updates local gain; the controller then schedules the main pulse at the predicted optimal phase with minimal amplitude/duration.
- Safety and habituation constraints: per-night thermal energy cap; alternating anatomical sites; randomized micro‑pulse timing within the sensitive phase band to prevent predictable adaptation.

Endpoints and analyses
Primary
- Magnitude and variance of phase shifts (DLMO, CBTmin) for advance and delay weeks; noninferiority margin versus standard light for magnitude, superiority for reduced light dose in combined arm. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/074873040001500609?utm_source=openai))
Secondary
- Sleep onset latency and sleep efficiency; pre‑dawn vigilance; adverse events; habituation indices (change in micro‑pulse response slope over time).
Mechanistic
- Individual PRC parameters (advance/delay lobe width, peak, curvature); correlation of acute DPG changes with next‑day phase changes to quantify masking/entrainment separation.

Safety
- Skin temperature excursions limited to ±3°C from baseline; maximum continuous pulse ≤5 min; total nightly “thermal dose” cap; automatic abort on abnormal skin thermistor/impedance readings. Distal warming dosed within ranges shown to facilitate sleep onset in controlled studies. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17078772/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and feasibility
- Temperature entrainment of peripheral clocks and the SCN’s relative resistance are well established in mammals, supporting selective leverage of thermal cues; however, to our knowledge there are no human trials that use programmable, closed‑loop skin thermal pulses to map individual temperature PRCs and drive circadian phase as a primary endpoint. Our preliminary review found no reports of Peltier‑based wearable thermal entrainment protocols in humans. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3625727/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria and milestones
- By Month 6: Demonstrate reliable estimation of individual thermal PRCs (bootstrap CI width <30 min for peak timing).
- By Month 12: Closed‑loop thermal+light arm achieves ≥1.5 h mean advance with ≥30% lower melanopic dose versus standard light; noninferiority of thermal-only arm for ±1.0 h targets.
- By Month 18: Sustained bidirectional behavioral control with no decline (>10%) in micro‑pulse sensitivity, indicating tolerance prevention.

Risks and mitigations
- Weak thermal entrainment: pre‑specify combined thermal+light fallback and cap SCN–peripheral offsets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3625727/?utm_source=openai))
- Misclassification of masking as entrainment: enforce biomarker separation (acute DPG/PIPR vs next‑day CBTmin/DLMO) and require concordance for phase updates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6395400/?utm_source=openai))

Impact
A single, low-risk, nonchemical actuator—phase-targeted skin thermal pulses—tested with objective phase markers, offers a path to safe, repeatable, bidirectional sleep induction and wake promotion with reduced reliance on pharmacology and high-dose light. The approach operationalizes individual sensitivity mapping and bounded central–peripheral counter‑steering into a practical, wearable therapeutic framework. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC317100/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Phase-locked interoceptive conditioning for bidirectional control of sleep–wake transitions via respiration-timed distal microthermal cues

Summary
Goal: Establish a drug-free, conditioning-based interface that reliably induces sleep and promotes wakefulness by timing sub-perceptual distal thermal micro-pulses to endogenous respiratory phase and thermoregulatory dynamics. The central bet is that precise timing—not stimulus intensity—lets gentle interoceptive cues acquire control over the sleep–wake flip-flop, yielding durable, low-tolerance effects.

Rationale
- Sleep onset is favored when vasodilation raises distal skin temperature relative to proximal (distal–proximal gradient, DPG), accelerating heat loss; DPG robustly predicts reduced sleep onset latency (SOL), and distal/periocular warming improves SOL in controlled trials. These thermoregulatory changes interface with preoptic warm-sensitive neurons that bias the VLPO–arousal “flip-flop” toward sleep. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/43366.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Respiration entrains autonomic and arousal circuits; preBötzinger-complex neurons project to and excite locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic neurons (arousal), and baroreceptor input modulates LC activity. Exhalation generally favors vagal dominance; brief, phase-locked inputs can therefore exploit windows of lowered arousal gain, or conversely reinforce arousal on inhalation. Slow-breathing meta-analyses confirm increased vagally mediated HRV. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5505554/?utm_source=openai))
- The hypothalamic flip‑flop architecture provides a thresholded, rapidly reconfiguring switch; precise, phase- and threshold-aligned cues should bias transition probability with minimal energy and minimal adaptation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04284?utm_source=openai))

Central hypothesis (indivisible question-insight)
Can sub-perceptual, bidirectional thermal micro-pulses, precisely timed to respiratory phase and impending DPG shifts, be conditioned to function as a reliable “on/off” control for sleep–wake transitions?

Specific aims
Aim 1. Demonstrate acute, closed-loop sleep induction by timing distal micro-warming to end‑exhalation during rising DPG.
Aim 2. Demonstrate wake promotion by timing distal micro-cooling to early‑inhalation during stable wake or drowsy N1.
Aim 3. Establish conditioning: after multi-night pairing with the appropriate internal states, test whether the timed thermal cues alone (without concurrent DPG rise/fall) can elicit faster sleep onset or sustained wake, respectively, without increasing stimulus intensity (tolerance prevention).

Atomic strategy
Exploit the endogenous slope/phase of internal signals (respiratory phase; DPG trajectory) as the unconditioned temporal structure. Pair minimal, sign-symmetric distal thermal pulses with these windows to create conditioned interoceptive triggers for the sleep–wake switch. The mechanism is timing-gated disinhibition of VLPO (warming at exhalation) versus facilitation of LC/arousal (cooling at inhalation). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/43366.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Methods

Population and design
- N=60 adults (18–55), mixed sleepers including subclinical sleep complaints; randomized, within-subject, counterbalanced crossover.
- Four in-lab overnights plus 14-day home phase.
  1) Baseline (no stimulation).
  2) Sleep-induction test: closed-loop end-exhalation micro-warming vs yoked sham (randomized blocks).
  3) Wake-promotion test: closed-loop early-inhalation micro-cooling vs yoked sham during scheduled early-morning awakenings and afternoon quiet wake.
  4) Conditioning probe: cues delivered without favorable internal state (e.g., earlier bedtime with attenuated DPG rise; mid-day quiet rest for wake), to test learned control.
- Home phase: nightly training with closed-loop pairing; daytime wake-promotion practice. Daily micro-randomized trials estimate persistence and tolerance.

Sensing and state estimation
- Respiration phase: nasal cannula pressure or PPG-derived respiratory waveform; Hilbert-phase estimate with beat-to-beat correction.
- Distal and proximal skin temperature: dorsal wrist/hand and infraclavicular patches; compute DPG in real time.
- Autonomic markers: PPG HRV (HF power, RMSSD) and skin conductance for secondary analyses.
- Sleep staging: ear‑EEG or validated headband for N1/N2 detection during in‑lab nights; actigraphy at home.
- Safety interlocks: skin thermistors over actuators; absolute temperature and rate-of-change limits; abort on arousals.

Actuation
- Distal micro-warming: resistive film on dorsal wrists/hands; 0.1–0.2°C step, 6–10 s at end‑exhalation epochs, duty-cycled 1:3, capped cumulative thermal dose.
- Distal micro-cooling: Peltier microblips or conductive contact with room-temp mass; 0.1–0.2°C drop, 3–6 s at early-inhalation epochs, similar duty cycle.
- Amplitudes are below conscious detection thresholds for most users, avoiding exteroceptive confounds.

Control policy
- Event-triggered, phase-locked delivery with adaptive thresholds:
  - Sleep induction: trigger only when DPG slope > setpoint and HRV HF rising; deliver end-exhalation warming micro-pulse.
  - Wake promotion: trigger when DPG slope ≤ 0 and HRV HF falling (or alpha increase) during drowsy wake; deliver early-inhalation cooling pulse.
- Minimal-gain proportional correction; no integral term during conditioning to prevent escalation; randomized micro-variability to reduce habituation.

Primary outcomes
- Aim 1: SOL to N2 (PSG-defined) versus sham; effect size Cohen’s d; within-subject mixed models. Secondary: DPG trajectories, HRV changes.
- Aim 2: Time to sustained wake (≥5 min EEG/behavioral) from drowsy N1/quiet wake; morning psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) lapses after nocturnal awakenings versus sham.
- Aim 3: ΔSOL and Δtime-to-wake when cues are presented without favorable internal state, compared with baseline and with concurrent-state sessions; retention at 2-week follow-up.

Statistical plan and power
- For SOL reduction of 20% (SD 30%) within-subject, α=0.05, power 0.8 → n≈40; recruit 60 to account for attrition and subgroup analyses.
- Linear mixed-effects with subject random intercepts; fixed effects: condition, night order, circadian phase; interaction of condition × (respiratory phase accuracy; DPG slope).

Mechanistic assays (subset, n=20)
- Pupillometry during controlled dim-light wake sessions to index LC-linked arousal responsiveness after conditioning (morning). 
- Breath-pacing blocks (6 vs 12 breaths/min) to probe interaction of slow breathing with cue efficacy. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763422002007?utm_source=openai))

Safety and constraints adherence
- Side effects minimized by low-amplitude, short-duration, skin-safe thermal pulses with locked upper bounds; continuous skin temp monitoring.
- Tolerance prevention: learning relies on contingency and timing; amplitudes do not escalate; randomized schedules and sparse delivery guard against habituation.
- Repeatability: closed-loop gating by endogenous phase/slope anchors stimuli to physiological context, reducing drift across nights and individuals.
- Bidirectionality: same sensory channel (distal thermal) with opposite sign and phase for wake versus sleep.

Contingencies and falsification
- If end-exhalation timing does not outperform non-phase-locked warming, the hypothesis that timing windows carry unique leverage is weakened; we will test alternative phases and coupling to HRV maxima/minima.
- If conditioning fails (cues ineffective without favorable state), then internal-state predictive structure is necessary but not sufficient; we will quantify required baseline DPG slope to define operational limits of control.
- If micro-cooling fails for wake, we will test coupling to early-inhalation plus brief posture change to increase baroreflex unloading; analysis will adjudicate whether arousal gain modulation requires multimodal input. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0306452294904405?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Introduces phase-locked interoceptive conditioning: using endogenous respiratory phase and thermoregulatory slope as the “teacher signal” to endow minimal thermal microcues with state-switching efficacy.
- To our knowledge, no prior system delivers respiration-phase-locked, bidirectional distal thermal micro-pulses to control sleep–wake transitions; existing approaches use bulk warming/cooling or exteroceptive stimuli without leveraging internal timing windows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7683599/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility anchors
- DPG is a robust predictor of SOL and is modifiable by mild peripheral/periocular warming. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/43366.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Respiratory networks drive LC arousal neurons; baroreceptor–LC coupling offers a mechanistic port for phase-locked arousal modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5505554/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Month 6: Hardware/algorithms validated on bench and in 10 pilot nights (tracking accuracy ≥90% for respiratory phase; skin ΔT command following ≤0.05°C RMS error).
- Month 12: Complete Aim 1 crossover; report SOL effect size and safety.
- Month 18: Complete Aim 2 and conditioning probes; report bidirectional control and retention.
- Month 24: Home-phase analyses on tolerance and generalization.

Expected outcome and impact
If successful, the work yields a compact, safe, and enduring method to train a reliable mental “on/off” switch for sleep using the body’s own timing architecture. It operationalizes a conditioning framework that is mechanistically grounded in thermoregulatory gating of VLPO and respiratory coupling of LC, meeting safety, tolerance, repeatability, and bidirectionality constraints without pharmacology. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04284?utm_source=openai))

Title
Hemodynamic readiness–gated micro‑thermal nudging for bidirectional regulation of human sleep induction and wake promotion

Central hypothesis–question
Can a real‑time “readiness index” derived from fast prefrontal fNIRS signatures of neurovascular–metabolic change predict imminent sleep–wake transitions within a seconds‑to‑tens‑of‑seconds horizon, and can sparse, state‑concordant micro‑thermal pulses delivered only at these permissive windows reliably shorten sleep onset and facilitate wakefulness without tolerance or side effects? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7710901/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit the metastability of sleep–wake switching: detect approach‑to‑transition by the sign and dynamics of sub‑minute prefrontal hemoglobin transients and pulse‑synchronized features (fast fNIRS), then apply minimal, brief skin‑temperature nudges aligned with the intrinsic direction of change—distal/periocular warming to amplify ongoing descent into NREM; supraclavicular/forehead mild cooling to amplify spontaneous ascent toward wake. This cooperates with endogenous control rather than forcing continuous stimulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7710901/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and prior evidence (mechanism audit)
- fNIRS around sleep onset and offset: frontal oxyhemoglobin (HbO) and total hemoglobin (tHb) decrease at sleep onset and increase at sleep offset; short‑lived, parallel HbO/HbR shifts occur in the immediate transition window. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10825508/?utm_source=openai))
- NREM micro‑architecture contains local down‑states (K‑complexes) and regionally confined ON/OFF periods that nucleate global change; K‑complex is an isolated cortical down‑state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3715654/?utm_source=openai))
- fNIRS at ≥10 Hz captures fast hemoglobin dynamics and cardiac/respiratory oscillations that reflect cerebrovascular tone and autonomic state; these components change across vigilance and drowsiness. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00742/full?utm_source=openai))
- Thermal manipulation causally modulates transitions: mild distal/periocular or proximal skin warming shortens sleep‑onset latency and deepens early sleep; conversely, mild skin cooling increases vigilance and wake maintenance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7683599/?utm_source=openai))
- Closed‑loop auditory stimulation reliably modulates ongoing slow oscillations but is most effective once stable NREM exists; effects on initiation are mixed, underscoring the need to target the true transition window. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2012.01039.x?utm_source=openai))
- Sleep onset exhibits bifurcation‑like tipping behavior, supporting a hazard‑based, readiness‑triggered control policy rather than continuous forcing. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-025-02091-1.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Innovation (novelty and constraint fit)
- Use fNIRS‑derived energetic/vascular derivatives (not EEG) as the primary, noninvasive trigger for closed‑loop, bidirectional control—an underexplored sensing modality for sleep transitions. Prior work has used fNIRS to characterize transitions and drowsiness, but not to drive closed‑loop intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7710901/?utm_source=openai))
- Deliver ultra‑brief, state‑concordant thermal nudges at detected transition “saddles,” minimizing total stimulus dose and habituation risk while preserving safety and repeatability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7683599/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Derive and validate a fNIRS‑based Sleep–Wake Transition Readiness Index (SWTRI).
- Sensing: Multi‑distance prefrontal fNIRS (sampling ≥20 Hz) with short‑separation channels for scalp regression.
- Features: (i) first and second derivatives of HbO, HbR, tHb; (ii) HbO–HbR phase and coherence; (iii) amplitude/phase of cardiac‑synchronized oscillations; (iv) very‑low‑frequency (0.01–0.1 Hz) power and cross‑site synchrony.
- Model: A time‑varying proportional hazards model that estimates the instantaneous probability of transition (wake→N1/N2; NREM→wake) within 5–30 s.
- Validation: Polysomnography (AASM rules) as reference; AUC for 10‑s forecast horizon; calibration (Brier score); external validation night. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7710901/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test readiness‑gated micro‑thermal nudging for sleep induction and wake promotion.
- Interventions:
  - Sleep induction: 30–90 s periocular warming (≈40–42°C surface device; Δskin ≤+2°C) or distal warming socks/pads, triggered when SWTRI(sleep) exceeds threshold and HbO′ is negative. Primary endpoint: sleep‑onset latency (SOL) to N2. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7683599/?utm_source=openai))
  - Wake promotion (final sleep cycle): 10–30 s mild cooling of supraclavicular/forehead skin (target 18–20°C surface; Δskin ≤−2°C) triggered when SWTRI(wake) exceeds threshold and HbO′ is positive. Primary endpoints: probability of awakening within 3 min of scheduled time without alarm and Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT) at +30 min. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3256315/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: yoked‑timing thermal stimuli (same dose, randomized off‑window), and sham (device contact, no temperature change).
- Outcomes: SOL, arousal count, N2 stabilization time, wake‑after‑sleep‑onset, subjective sleep quality, next‑day alertness, and adaptation across 4 weeks (slope of effect size vs. night).

Aim 3. Safety, tolerance, and mechanistic mediation.
- Safety: skin integrity checks, thermal comfort VAS, awakenings from stimuli, adverse events.
- Tolerance: stability of effect across nights; absence of stimulus‑evoked spectral signatures outside target windows.
- Mediation: test whether stimulus efficacy depends on SWTRI level at delivery; verify reduction of total stimulus dose vs. open‑loop schedules.

Study design
- Phase 1 (n=40, lab): model derivation and within‑night validation (Aim 1).
- Phase 2 (n=60, lab, randomized crossover): three conditions over non‑consecutive nights—closed‑loop thermal nudging, yoked control, sham (Aim 2).
- Phase 3 (n=80, home, 4 weeks): pragmatic assessment of long‑term efficacy, safety, and tolerance with remote fNIRS and thermo‑actuators (Aims 2–3).

Technical implementation
- fNIRS: prefrontal montage with 3–3.5 cm source‑detector pairs and 8–10 mm short‑separation channels; dual wavelengths; 20–30 Hz sampling; online motion and cardiac component separation.
- Online analytics: sliding‑window feature extraction (1–8 s), SWTRI inference at 2 Hz, refractory periods to prevent overstimulation, and adaptive thresholds per circadian phase.
- Thermal actuators: medical‑grade, Peltier‑based periocular band and supraclavicular pad with closed‑loop skin thermistors; ramps ≤0.3°C/s to avoid startle; automatic abort if micro‑arousal detected.

Primary endpoints and statistics
- Aim 1: SWTRI AUC≥0.80 for 10‑s horizon; time‑to‑event concordance; decision‑curve analysis for trigger utility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7710901/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Within‑subject SOL reduction ≥20% vs. sham; awakening probability increase ≥20% vs. sham in final cycle; mixed‑effects models with participant as random effect; Holm‑Bonferroni correction.
- Aim 3: Non‑inferiority in arousal rate vs. sham; flat or improving effect over weeks (no tolerance).

Risk management and ethical safeguards
- Thermal ranges constrained to thermoneutral comfort; automatic cut‑outs; exclusion of severe dermatologic or thermoregulatory disorders.
- Sparse, window‑locked stimuli minimize exposure and chance of habituation relative to continuous methods. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2012.01039.x?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory analyses
- Compare SWTRI‑triggered thermal nudging to a minimalist closed‑loop auditory condition during verified NREM (two 50‑ms pink‑noise clicks phase‑locked to endogenous slow‑oscillation upstate) to benchmark effect sizes and confirm state dependence. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23583623/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and expected outcomes
- fNIRS reliably captures transition‑related hemodynamics and fast pulsatile components; thermal nudging has established causal leverage on SOL and vigilance. Combining these in a readiness‑gated, bidirectional controller should reduce SOL, stabilize early N2, and increase on‑schedule awakening probability with minimal dose and side effects, while avoiding tolerance through sparse, state‑contingent delivery. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10825508/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- M6: Validated SWTRI algorithm and open dataset.
- M12: Phase‑2 crossover complete; predefined clinical effect achieved or design iterated.
- M24: Home trial complete; safety/tolerance confirmed; protocol and software released.

Interpretation criteria (falsification)
- If SWTRI fails to predict transitions above chance (AUC≤0.6), the energetic/vascular proxy is insufficient.
- If closed‑loop thermal nudging at readiness peaks does not outperform yoked/sham with equivalent dose, the metastability‑nudge premise is falsified.
- If arousal rates or discomfort exceed sham, the approach violates safety constraints and should not be advanced.

Key references (indicative)
- fNIRS at transitions and offsets; discrete HbO/HbR events at onset. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10825508/?utm_source=openai))
- Local down‑state (K‑complex) as nucleation element. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3715654/?utm_source=openai))
- Fast optical components and cardiac oscillations in fNIRS. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK20223/?utm_source=openai))
- Thermal modulation of SOL and vigilance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7683599/?utm_source=openai))
- Closed‑loop auditory stimulation is state‑dependent (benchmark, not primary). ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2012.01039.x?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- Open‑source SWTRI algorithm and de‑identified datasets.
- Wearable reference design for prefrontal fast fNIRS and safe micro‑thermal actuators.
- Clinical evidence package supporting a low‑risk, repeatable, bidirectional sleep–wake regulator that minimizes tolerance by aligning with natural transition dynamics.

Title
Phase-targeted auricular vagus nerve stimulation at N2→N3 transitions to jointly deepen slow-wave sleep and bias circadian timing

Rationale
- Process S: Sleep pressure rises with wake via astrocyte–neuronal metabolism and adenosine build-up; it dissipates when cortical slow oscillations dominate NREM, reflected in slow-wave activity (SWA). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5523826/?utm_source=openai))
- State transitions expose labile set-points: brief, coordinated swings in extracellular K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and neuromodulators accompany sleep–wake and NREM microstate changes; these shifts are sufficient to toggle network state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5441687/?utm_source=openai))
- Locus coeruleus (LC–NE) dynamics gate sleep microarchitecture and NREM→REM cycling in infraslow bands; LC activity is low in NREM, near-silent in REM, and phasic modulation biases microarousals and transitions. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-024-01822-0?utm_source=openai))
- Transcutaneous auricular VNS (taVNS) afferents engage NTS→LC and related brainstem–hypothalamic circuits; short trains can increase LC-linked markers (pupil, fMRI LC signal) with parameter dependence, though some marker findings are inconsistent across protocols. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/jn.00008.2026?doi=10.1152%2Fjn.00008.2026&utm_source=openai))
- taVNS improves insomnia symptoms in randomized, sham-controlled trials, supporting safety and relevance to sleep regulation, but timing has been open-loop and not transition-locked. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question
Can brief, closed-loop taVNS bursts delivered precisely at endogenous N2→N3 transition windows amplify SWA (reducing Process S) and, when scheduled near habitual wake, also bias circadian phase markers—thereby realigning homeostatic and circadian processes with minimal dose?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the system’s high gain at thalamocortical/neuromodulatory/ionic “handshake” moments: deliver peripheral, low-dose, phase-locked taVNS pulses at N2→N3 boundaries to stabilize slow oscillations (S) while phasically engaging LC–NTS–hypothalamic relays that convey time-of-day signals (C). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5441687/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Detect the N2→N3 transition in real time and characterize its electrophysiological and autonomic signatures in humans.
2) Test whether N2→N3-locked taVNS increases SWA and accelerates the overnight decline in delta power versus sham and versus asynchronous taVNS.
3) Test whether late-sleep, pre-wake taVNS micro-bursts bias circadian phase (ΔDLMO; ΔCBTmin) over two weeks compared with sham.

Study design
Phase I (in-lab, mechanistic crossover; n=40 adults with insomnia disorder, ISI≥15):
- Nights: (A) sham, (B) asynchronous taVNS (random N2/N3 delivery), (C) transition-locked taVNS.
- Washout ≥48 h between nights; order counterbalanced.

Phase II (home, parallel-group; n=80; 2-week intervention):
- Groups: transition-locked “SWA-deepen” protocol during first NREM cycles; “pre-wake” protocol in last sleep cycle; matched sham.
- Primary circadian endpoint collected in-lab at baseline and day 15.

Closed-loop detection and stimulation
- Detection: single-lead frontal EEG + EOG + thoracic respiration; real-time algorithm flags N2→N3 boundary using increasing delta power, spindle–delta cross-frequency coupling shift, K-complex-to-slow-oscillation succession, and respiratory slowing. Acoustic closed-loop work validates that phase-locked delivery at SO up-states can reliably enhance SWA; we adopt similar latency constraints. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23583623/?utm_source=openai))
- Actuator: taVNS at left cymba conchae (gold-cup clip); constant-current, charge-balanced biphasic pulses; per-consensus reporting standards. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8040977/?utm_source=openai))

Stimulation protocols (dose-minimizing, parameter-bifurcated)
- SWA-deepen (N2→N3-locked): 1–10 Hz trains, 500 µs pulse width, 1–2 s train at exhalation onset, intensity set to just-perceptible threshold then −10% to ensure sleep compatibility; deliver only on detector-confirmed N2→N3 windows, max 6 trains per cycle, 2 cycles/night.
- Pre-wake arousal/phase-bias (last NREM cycle, ~90 min before habitual wake): burst protocol of 5 pulses at 25 Hz repeated every 1 s for 10 s, two blocks separated by 2 min; low duty cycle to avoid sleep fragmentation; scheduled relative to predicted CBT nadir across nights. Parameter choices reflect human taVNS autonomic effects of higher frequency/energy density and short-train feasibility. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29716843/?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes
Phase I primary:
- Change in SWA (0.5–4 Hz) across NREM relative to sham; and steeper overnight delta power decline slope (indexing Process S dissipation). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7891187/?utm_source=openai))
Phase I secondary:
- N3 minutes; arousal index; spindle–SO coupling metrics; HRV (SDNN/RMSSD); morning salivary alpha-amylase (LC-NE proxy). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11487125/?utm_source=openai))

Phase II primary:
- Circadian phase shift: ΔDLMO and ΔCBTmin from baseline to day 15. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519507/?utm_source=openai))
Phase II secondary:
- Sleep timing regularity (actigraphy), ISI/PSQI change; Montreal Cognitive Assessment attention subscore (daytime alertness proxy).

Mechanistic assays (subsample n=20)
- Pupillometry during controlled pre-sleep tVNS trains to calibrate LC-linked responsiveness (daytime session). ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/jn.00008.2026?doi=10.1152%2Fjn.00008.2026&utm_source=openai))
- Salivary melatonin profiles (DLMO) and cortisol AM/PM ratio.

Controls for confounds
- Light exposure logging and standardization on test days.
- Fixed caffeine/alcohol abstinence windows.
- Randomization stratified by chronotype (MEQ).

Statistical plan
- Phase I: Linear mixed models with condition (sham/asynchronous/locked) as fixed factor; subject random intercepts; primary endpoint family-wise error controlled (Holm). Power: Detect 0.25–0.30 SD increase in SWA with 80% power at α=0.05 (within-subject).
- Phase II: ANCOVA on ΔDLMO with baseline DLMO covariate; target detectable shift ≥30 min vs sham. Missing data by multiple imputation.

Safety and tolerance management
- Adverse event monitoring per taVNS safety meta-analysis; nightly cap on delivered pulses; automatic lockout on arousal detection; intensity titrated below sensory threshold during sleep. The literature supports overall favorable safety of taVNS across trials. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-25864-1?utm_source=openai))
- Anti-tolerance: event-triggered micro-dosing only at transitions; stochastic micro-jitter of inter-train intervals; no nightly escalation.

Feasibility and novelty
- taVNS improves insomnia symptoms in RCTs, establishing relevance to sleep but prior work is open-loop; no studies have delivered taVNS time-locked to N2→N3 transitions to co-target SWA and circadian markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))
- The transition-locked principle is grounded in ionic and LC–NE lability and leverages closed-loop methods proven in acoustic stimulation to modulate SOs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5441687/?utm_source=openai))

Falsification and decision points
- If transition-locked taVNS does not exceed asynchronous taVNS on SWA or delta-slope, reject the high-gain window premise for peripheral vagal input.
- If pre-wake protocol fails to shift ΔDLMO/ΔCBTmin despite preserved sleep, pivot to pairing with bright light or melatonin to test additivity of a non-photic cue with established zeitgebers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16263827/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- M1 (months 0–6): Validate detector; demonstrate <150 ms latency and >85% precision for N2→N3 boundary in-lab relative to manual PSG.
- M2 (months 6–12): Show ≥10% SWA increase and steeper delta-slope versus sham in crossover.
- M3 (months 12–18): Demonstrate ≥20–30 min mean phase advance or delay (direction per schedule) versus sham without increased arousals.
- Go/No-go: Achieve M2 and either a significant ΔDLMO or ΔCBTmin shift to proceed to a longer outpatient trial.

Impact
A minimal-dose, transition-locked taVNS protocol could synchronously reduce homeostatic sleep pressure and nudge circadian timing, addressing insomnia and misalignment with a single peripheral actuator under strong safety constraints. The proposal explicitly tests whether leveraging endogenous handshake windows yields superior, durable control over sleep induction and wake promotion compared with traditional continuous stimulation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-25864-1?utm_source=openai))

Title
Sparse, phase-targeted electrical nudges at separatrix crossings to bidirectionally control human sleep depth

Background and rationale
- NREM slow oscillations (<1 Hz) reflect alternating cortical UP (depolarized) and DOWN (hyperpolarized/silent) states, coordinated with thalamocortical dynamics and expressed as traveling waves across cortex; neuromodulatory tone biases the system between desynchronized wake and synchronized NREM modes. These dynamics exhibit multistability/metastability, with transitions that can be precipitated by brief perturbations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4712264/?utm_source=openai))
- Closed-loop, phase-targeted stimulation can modulate brain rhythms: auditory pulses at the slow-wave UP phase boost slow-wave activity and spindle coupling; closed-loop tES/tACS has also been used to align stimulation to endogenous sleep slow waves. However, low‑frequency tES entrainment during sleep is debated based on intracranial recordings, motivating strategies that exploit timing rather than forceful continuous drive. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
- Traveling‑wave tACS using phase‑shifted multielectrode drive can impose spatial phase gradients in humans and nonhuman primates, offering a handle on network propagation with low currents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13167727/?utm_source=openai))
- Real‑time phase estimation with Kalman‑filter approaches has been demonstrated for closed‑loop EEG stimulation, establishing feasibility for predictive, low‑latency interventions. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–question
Can brief, sub‑threshold, closed‑loop electrical nudges delivered at predicted separatrix crossings of the cortical slow oscillation bidirectionally shift global brain state—toward deeper NREM (sleep induction) or toward desynchrony (wake promotion)—more efficiently and safely than continuous entrainment?

Atomic strategy
Exploit metastability: identify imminent UP→DOWN or DOWN→UP transitions with a predictive state estimator and deliver millisecond‑timed, low‑dose electrical pulses that respectively increase or decrease the probability of the transition completing, thus flipping the network between slow‑wave–dominated and desynchronized regimes. PRC theory and empirical phase‑resetting results justify strong phase dependence; traveling‑wave field patterns refine which subnetworks participate without higher currents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4079848/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build and validate a real‑time estimator of slow‑wave phase, amplitude, traveling‑wave direction, and a latent arousal state from frontal EEG, using an extended Kalman filter with artifact-aware updates. Benchmark phase prediction error and transition‑timing forecasts against polysomnography labels. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))
2) Sleep induction: test whether late‑UP–timed, 100–200 ms sub‑Hz pulse bursts increase DOWN‑state probability, amplify slow‑wave activity (SWA), and reduce sleep latency relative to sham and continuous tACS. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
3) Wake promotion: test whether early‑DOWN–timed, brief broadband/high‑beta jittered bursts abort imminent DOWN states, reduce SWA, and shorten time‑to‑wake at scheduled awakenings; contrast with down‑phase–targeted auditory stimulation literature indicating depth reduction. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389945725005052?utm_source=openai))
4) Long‑term use: quantify adaptation/tolerance over 4 weeks under sparse, variable‑timing policies versus periodic entrainment.

Methods

Participants
- N=36 healthy adults, randomized, within‑subject crossover across stimulation policies; overnight lab studies plus morning wake‑assistance sessions.

Hardware
- 8‑channel EEG (Fz, F3/F4, Cz, Pz, mastoids) plus 4‑electrode tES (two frontal, two parietal) enabling phase‑shifted multi‑site pulses to create low‑amplitude traveling fields; current ≤1 mA per channel, total injected current ≤2 mA, duty cycle <5%. Traveling‑wave phase gradients 10–40 ms anterior→posterior when used. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6561925/?utm_source=openai))

Closed‑loop controller
- Estimator: EKF tracking of latent oscillators for SO (0.5–1 Hz), spindle (12–15 Hz), and alpha/beta (8–25 Hz) plus a slow arousal state; prediction horizon 150–300 ms to schedule pulses at extrema/zero‑crossings with confidence gating. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))
- Tipping‑point detection: rising SO amplitude and slope, spindle probability changes, and increasing spatial phase alignment flag imminent UP→DOWN; the reverse pattern flags DOWN→UP; state uncertainty aborts stimulation. Grounded in slow‑oscillation and thalamocortical timing literature. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4712264/?utm_source=openai))
- Stimulation policies:
  • Sleep‑induction policy: on predicted late‑UP→early‑DOWN, deliver 1–2 cycles of sub‑Hz monophasic/biphasic burst (100–200 ms envelope), optionally with a brief 12–15 Hz packet nested in early UP to promote spindle coupling. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
  • Wake‑promotion policy: on predicted early‑DOWN, deliver a 100 ms broadband, non‑sinusoidal transient or a short 18–22 Hz packet with 10–20 ms interelectrode phase offsets to desynchronize and oppose frontal slow‑wave initiation; jitter timing ±20–40 ms to prevent adaptation. Down‑phase–targeted auditory studies motivate depth‑reduction feasibility; here translated to electrical nudges. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389945725005052?utm_source=openai))
- Optional spatial steering: when estimator detects anterior→posterior SO propagation, apply matching phase‑lead to reinforce sleep; invert/orthogonalize gradients for wake promotion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13167727/?utm_source=openai))

Controls
- Sham (ramp‑in/out only), open‑loop periodic tACS at SO frequency, and closed‑loop auditory UP‑phase tones as an active comparator for sleep induction. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes
- Primary (sleep induction): latency to N2; SWA power (0.5–4 Hz) over first 20 min; spindle–SO coupling metrics; subjective sleep latency on KSS. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
- Primary (wake promotion): time‑to‑sustained wake after a cue at the end of the last NREM cycle; reduction in SWA and increase in alpha/beta during the 2‑min window; psychomotor vigilance within 5 min of wake. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389945725005052?utm_source=openai))
- Secondary: phase‑locking value between stimulation and SO; transition hazard modulation; adverse events per NIBS guidelines. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2025.1682450/pdf?utm_source=openai))

Analysis
- Mixed‑effects models comparing policies; permutation tests for transition hazards; estimator performance as circular error between predicted and observed extrema. Power analysis assumes medium effect (d=0.5) for sleep latency reduction with closed‑loop auditory comparator benchmarks. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))

Safety, feasibility, and tolerance mitigation
- Current densities within established tES practice; automatic caps on total charge/day; ≥20 s refractory after any arousal; real‑time impedance and skin monitoring; nightly AE logs. Sparse dosing and phase‑jittered policies minimize habituation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2025.1682450/pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Recognized uncertainty: intracranial data question robust slow‑wave entrainment by low‑frequency tES; this protocol tests an alternative, timing‑leveraged, minimal‑energy mechanism rather than continuous 1:1 forcing. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-01045-x?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision points
- M1: EKF achieves mean phase error <20° at SO peak and predicts UP→DOWN within ±100 ms.
- M2: Sleep‑induction policy reduces N2 latency by ≥15% vs sham and ≥10% vs periodic tACS; increases SWA by ≥10% without increasing arousals.
- M3: Wake‑promotion policy reduces time‑to‑wake by ≥20% vs sham with sustained alpha/beta increase and no excess post‑wake sleep inertia.
- M4: Over 4 weeks, no decrement (>5%) in efficacy metrics; AE rate non‑inferior to comparators.

Novelty and impact
- Shifts the control objective from continuous entrainment to separatrix‑triggered regime switching, tested bidirectionally in humans; integrates traveling‑wave field shaping only as needed, and leverages proven closed‑loop estimation to achieve sparse, safer, and potentially tolerance‑resistant control of sleep depth. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))

Data and code
- Pre‑registered protocol; open release of anonymized EEG/stimulation logs and EKF code after publication.

Title
Phase-locked, low-duty-cycle auricular vagus stimulation during controlled partial sleep restriction to amplify homeostatic rebound sleep and next-day alertness

Background and gap
- Human sleep timing and depth are governed by a homeostatic process S and a circadian process C; NREM slow-wave activity (SWA, 0.5–4.5 Hz) indexes S and increases after extended wake, then dissipates during sleep. Adenosine accumulates with wake and promotes sleep via A1/A2A receptors. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1111/jsr.12371?utm_source=openai))
- Adenosine directly inhibits orexin (hypocretin) neurons in lateral hypothalamus via A1 receptors, reducing arousal drive; orexin neurons project to locus coeruleus (LC) to stabilize wakefulness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1783688/?utm_source=openai))
- Partial sleep restriction (PSR) can elicit SWA increases and recovery dynamics, but effects vary by dose and timing; clean, repeatable augmentation of rebound sleep without pharmacology remains unsolved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4747841/?utm_source=openai))
- Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) can modulate central arousal/autonomic circuits and improves insomnia in randomized trials with favorable safety, but LC engagement markers are debated; timing relative to homeostatic/circadian phase is largely unexplored. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))
- Theory predicts diversity-/phase-resonance phenomena in orexin-based sleep-wake models, suggesting that small, phase-locked inputs can amplify stable oscillations. Translation of this to human state control has not been tested. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3426568/?utm_source=openai))

Research question (hypothesis-as-question)
Can brief, morning, phase-locked taVNS bursts delivered during a week of mild, controlled partial sleep restriction increase the amplitude of the sleep–wake cycle—manifested as larger nocturnal SWA and improved next-day vigilance—without tolerance or safety liabilities?

Atomic strategy
Exploit resonance locking: apply minimal, phase-accurate taVNS pulses near the ascending limb of circadian wake (shortly after habitual wake time) during PSR days to add energy to the wake node (LC–orexin network) while withholding stimulation in the evening so accumulated adenosine can dominate, producing stronger rebound SWA. The causal chain is single-step: precise phase addition to arousal → larger daytime arousal amplitude without continuous drive → larger homeostatic pressure and cleaner nocturnal dissipation.

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Determine whether phase-locked morning taVNS during PSR increases nocturnal SWA and reduces sleep latency versus sham and mistimed taVNS.
- Aim 2: Test whether controlled, bounded variability in taVNS intensity/pulse structure prevents tolerance across 6 weeks while maintaining efficacy.
- Aim 3: Quantify mechanistic engagement of LC–arousal using pupillometry during stimulation and relate it to SWA rebound; explicitly assess mixed prior findings by intensity titration.

Design
- Population: Healthy adults, age 18–40, habitual 7–9 h sleepers; exclude sleep/circadian disorders and medications affecting sleep.
- Design: Randomized, double-blind, 3-condition crossover with ≥14-day washouts: (A) PSR + phase-locked taVNS; (B) PSR + sham; (C) PSR + taVNS mistimed to the descending circadian phase (late afternoon).
- Partial sleep restriction: Time-in-bed curtailed by 90 min for 5 consecutive nights per condition, anchored to habitual schedule to avoid circadian drift.
- Phase targeting: Phase-locked sessions start 45–75 min after habitual wake time (ascending circadian wake); mistimed control at circadian wake decline.

Intervention
- Device/placement: Auricular concha cymba/tragus montage (taVNS).
- Parameters (dose windowed to sensory threshold): 20–25 Hz, 200–300 μs pulse width, 30 s on/30 s off for 15 min; intensity titrated to strong-but-comfortable sensation. Include day-to-day micro-variability of ±10–15% in current and burst duty (Aim 2) to reduce adaptation while keeping mean dose constant. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32831871/?utm_source=openai))
- Evening: No stimulation to avoid counteracting adenosine/VLPO expression.

Outcomes
- Primary: Change in whole-night NREM SWA (0.5–4.5 Hz) on Nights 1 and 5 of PSR (PSG), vs. sham and mistimed.
- Secondary: Sleep latency and efficiency (PSG), next-day psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) lapses, subjective sleepiness, and alertness.
- Mechanistic biomarkers: Pupil dilation during/after taVNS as LC proxy with intensity titration; heart rate variability; evening salivary melatonin to confirm stable circadian phase; exploratory correlation between morning pupil response magnitude and same-night SWA gain. Mixed prior reports on taVNS–pupil coupling will be explicitly tested with individual thresholding. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32050095/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: Adverse events, skin integrity, bradyarrhythmia screening. Reported taVNS trials in insomnia show benefit with few serious AEs; we monitor continuously. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic justification
- PSR increases adenosine tone and SWA rebound; orexin neurons are directly inhibited by adenosine via A1 receptors, while orexin–LC connectivity supports arousal. Phase-locked morning taVNS is expected to transiently raise arousal network output (via NTS→LC and broader CAN) without flattening S accumulation; evening withdrawal allows adenosine/VLPO dominance, deepening SWA. This tests oscillator-phase addition rather than continuous drive. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4747841/?utm_source=openai))

Analysis
- Linear mixed-effects models with condition, day (1 vs 5), and sequence as fixed effects; participant as random intercept.
- Equivalence and superiority testing for SWA change (A vs B primary; A vs C mechanistic control).
- Mediation: Does pupil response area during morning stimulation predict same-night SWA increase?

Tolerance and repeatability (Aim 2 extension)
- Six-week parallel extension in a subset: compare fixed-parameter vs micro-variable parameter schedules on weekly SWA gain and PVT; test slope of effect decay. Diversity-induced resonance theory motivates bounded variability to maintain network gain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3426568/?utm_source=openai))

Power
- Assuming a conservative 10–15% SWA increase with PSR+taVNS over sham on Night 5 (within-subject SD 12%), N=36 completers yields >80% power (α=0.05, two-sided). Interim futility after 18.

Milestones and go/no‑go
- Go: Night‑5 SWA increase ≥10% vs sham with no safety signal; pupil–SWA correlation present.
- No‑go: Null SWA effect with tight CIs or adverse event rate >10% moderate AEs related to device.

Innovation
- Tests a phase-resonant, low-duty, non-pharmacologic actuator to train the endogenous adenosine–orexin–LC axis; leverages PSR to probe and amplify homeostatic dynamics while minimizing desensitization via micro-variability. Prior taVNS sleep trials did not target homeostatic/circadian phase or adaptation explicitly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))

Potential outcomes and interpretations
- Positive: Larger SWA and better vigilance with phase-locked taVNS than sham/mistimed → supports resonance-locking of arousal to amplify the natural sleep–wake oscillation.
- Mixed: SWA gain without vigilance benefit → refine dose or phase; consider adding objective circadian phase markers.
- Negative: No differences → falsifies phase-addition premise under these parameters; proceed to parameter sweep or alternative actuators.

References (representative)
- Two-process and adenosine homeostasis: Borbély et al., 2016/2022; recent A1/A2A review. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1111/jsr.12371?utm_source=openai))
- Adenosine inhibition of orexin neurons; orexin–LC arousal pathway. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1783688/?utm_source=openai))
- PSR and SWA rebound dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4747841/?utm_source=openai))
- taVNS efficacy/safety in insomnia; LC engagement debates and pupil markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))
- Diversity-induced resonance in orexin model. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3426568/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Prestress-encoded ENS timing as a durable gut-origin signal that suppresses hypothalamic hunger drive via spinal pathways

Background and prior art check
- After weight loss, AgRP/NPY neurons exhibit persistent hyperexcitability and biased responsiveness that promote weight regain. This central plasticity outlasts normalization of diet, making peripheral inputs less effective unless they carry high salience or non-adapting codes. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41574-020-00407-8?utm_source=openai))
- Enterochromaffin/enteroendocrine cells are mechanosensitive; Piezo2 transduces epithelial strain into depolarization and transmitter release. Mechanical state is therefore a legitimate peripheral variable that can be written into epithelial–ENS activity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6094143/?utm_source=openai))
- The ENS supports electrical coupling: connexin-36–dependent gap junctions form functional electrical synapses between nitrergic (nNOS+) enteric neurons; coupling shapes network dynamics and gut motor output. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4043341/?utm_source=openai))
- Enteric glia signal via connexin-43 hemichannels; Cx43-dependent gliotransmission modulates neuronal activity and colonic transit, demonstrating that non-synaptic, field-like network control is native to the ENS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3935238/?utm_source=openai))
- Non-vagal spinal afferents convey gut information to hindbrain/hypothalamus and participate in satiation and energy balance; this pathway is underexplored relative to vagal circuits and provides an alternative conduit to feeding centers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11583444/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty/limits clarified
- No prior reports were found of using persistent tissue prestress to store a satiety “memory” in gut circuits, nor of encoding satiety as a low-frequency timing signature in ENS that biases spinal afferent processing. This proposal leverages established mechanosensitivity and ENS electrical/glial coupling but repurposes them to write and read a durable, non-hormonal, non-vagal code.

Integrated hypothesis-question
Can a controlled, sub-nociceptive prestress applied to distal gut epithelium reset the operating point of ENS microcircuits and entrain a low-frequency, phase-stable inhibitory timing signature that ascends via spinal pathways to suppress hypothalamic hunger drive and prevent weight regain after dieting?

Atomic strategy
Map a mechanical state variable (chronic, gentle mucosal/circumferential prestress) onto ENS network timing—rather than firing rate—so that the “signal” is a persistent phase/synchrony pattern that resists central rate desensitization and recruits spinal satiation relays.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and validate a distal-gut prestress device that writes a persistent ENS timing state without pain or obstruction.
- Device: mucoadhesive, compliant microstructured ring/patch for sigmoid/rectal segment to impose 3–5% circumferential prestress (below nociceptive thresholds; chosen region minimizes vagal fibers and favors pelvic/splanchnic afferents).
- Readouts ex vivo (mouse colon preparations): calcium imaging and patch clamp of myenteric/submucosal circuits to quantify (i) shifts in resting potential and rheobase of nNOS+ vs cholinergic neurons; (ii) emergence of coherent 0.1–2 Hz inhibitory network oscillations; (iii) Cx36 dependence of timing coherence using Cx36−/− tissue or gap-junction blockers; (iv) Cx43 hemichannel contribution to network entrainment via 43Gap26.
- Epithelial requirement: repeat with EC/EEC Piezo2-deficient mice to test whether epithelium-to-ENS mechanotransduction is necessary for state writing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6094143/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: quantify motility indices and visceral nociception markers (spinal c-Fos in lamina I/II; visceromotor response) to confirm sub-nociceptive operation.

Aim 2. Test whether prestress-encoded ENS timing engages spinal assemblies and suppresses feeding after weight loss.
- Model: diet-induced obese mice undergo 15–20% weight loss; then randomized to prestress vs sham.
- Circuit assays in vivo:
  - Multisite electrophysiology/fiber photometry: lumbosacral dorsal horn and lateral parabrachial CGRP neurons during meals to detect low-frequency coherence increases under prestress; confirm pathway specificity by transient spinal deafferentation (chemogenetic silencing of lumbosacral DRG) while leaving vagus intact. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11583444/?utm_source=openai))
  - Hypothalamic readouts: AgRP and PVH neuron activity (fiber photometry/Miniscope) during refeeding.
- Behavior/physiology endpoints: cumulative intake, meal size/termination latency, and body-weight trajectory over 6–8 weeks post-diet compared to sham. Primary outcome: reduced weight regain slope in prestressed animals relative to sham, with preserved effect under intact spinal but not when spinal afferents are silenced. Secondary: unchanged outcome under subdiaphragmatic vagotomy (non-vagal mechanism control).

Aim 3. Determine durability, plasticity, and “off-device” persistence of the prestress code.
- Chronicity: maintain prestress for 4 weeks, then remove device. Track (i) persistence of ENS timing signature; (ii) sustained feeding suppression and weight maintenance for ≥4 additional weeks.
- Mechanism of persistence: assess ECM remodeling and changes in network coupling (Cx36 puncta density among nNOS+ neurons; Cx43 hemichannel expression/activity in glia). Test whether transient prestress induces lasting increases in inhibitory tone and timing coherence that outlive the mechanical input. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4043341/?utm_source=openai))

Methods overview
- Devices: photopolymerized, elastomeric hydrogel rings with graded stiffness and microtextured mucosal interface; ex vivo tensile testing to calibrate prestress-strain curve. Biodegradable adhesive coatings calibrated for segment-specific residence times.
- Electrophysiology/imaging: in situ myenteric recordings; voltage-sensitive dye/two-photon calcium imaging to quantify phase-locking value, coherence spectra, and directionality (Granger/transfer entropy) within ENS microcircuits under prestress.
- Genetics/pharmacology: Piezo2fl/fl EC/EEC mice; Cx36−/− mice; 43Gap26 for Cx43 hemichannel inhibition; nitric oxide synthase inhibitors to dissect inhibitory pathway contributions.
- Systems readouts: dorsal horn and parabrachial recordings; hypothalamic photometry; automated feeding/metabolic cages; mixed-effects models on meal microstructure and weight regain.

Predicted outcomes and discriminators
- If prestress encodes a stable ENS timing state, we expect increased low-frequency inhibitory synchrony that is (i) reduced by Cx36 loss and (ii) attenuated when epithelial Piezo2 is absent. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6094143/?utm_source=openai))
- Meal termination will accelerate and weight regain will be blunted; effects will survive vagotomy but collapse with spinal afferent silencing, indicating a non-vagal route. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11583444/?utm_source=openai))
- Persistence after device removal with concomitant increases in Cx36 coupling and Cx43-mediated glial signaling would support a peripheral memory substrate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4043341/?utm_source=openai))
- Falsifiers: no change in ENS timing metrics under prestress; effects blocked by vagotomy but not by spinal silencing; or benefits vanish immediately on device removal without evidence of coupling/plasticity.

Risks and mitigations
- Risk: nociceptive activation of spinal pathways. Mitigation: operate below mechanonociceptive thresholds; real-time visceromotor monitoring; adaptive prestress control.
- Risk: motility disruption. Mitigation: segment targeting; titrated strain; off-cycle schedules; withdrawal criteria.
- Biological limit: excessive reliance on epithelial 5-HT could re-engage vagal circuits if applied proximally; regional restriction to distal colon/rectum avoids this.

Impact
A purely peripheral, non-hormonal, non-vagal gut intervention that writes a durable timing code into ENS networks addresses central desensitization by changing the format—not the amplitude—of the gut-to-brain message. If successful, this defines a new therapeutic axis for defending post-diet weight loss by exploiting prestress-mechanotransduction and intrinsic ENS electrical/glial coupling as a satiety memory substrate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6094143/?utm_source=openai))
