Title
Proximity-and-strain–enabled endogenous protease switching (PSEEPS) for irreversible, domain‑specific inactivation of rogue intracellular proteins

Central hypothesis-question
Can a single de novo intrabody that (i) binds an allosterically coupled surface on a pathological intracellular protein, (ii) mechanically exposes a latent, calpain‑susceptible loop, and (iii) conditionally docks endogenous calpain via non‑inhibitory calpastatin exosites, drive one‑cut, irreversible loss of function in living cells without globally elevating protease activity? The bet is that accessibility and nanoscale geometry—rather than protease abundance—are the bottlenecks for productive, limited proteolysis of many disease drivers. If true, “mechanics plus proximity” becomes a general intracellular safety‑switch modality orthogonal to degraders and receptor agonism/antagonism. Calpains are chosen because they perform physiological limited proteolysis and can inactivate signaling hubs when a correct site is presented; calpastatin’s modular exosites offer endogenous, tunable docking without overactivating the enzyme. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single causal lever: raise the effective rate of a specific endogenous, inactivating calpain cut at a cryptic site by simultaneously increasing (a) site accessibility via piconewton‑scale strain and (b) local calpain effective molarity and orientation via a short, non‑inhibitory calpastatin‑derived docking motif that is unveiled only upon target engagement. This mirrors natural force‑assisted proteolysis (e.g., ADAMTS13 on VWF) but is repurposed intracellularly for targeted inactivation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3179391/?utm_source=openai))

Aims and work plan

Aim 1. Identify inactivating, cryptic calpain sites on hard intracellular targets.
- Targets: β‑catenin (oncogenic Wnt effector) and YAP/TAZ (Hippo co‑activators) as exemplar undruggables where limited cleavage can rewire transcriptional programs. Prior work shows calpain can clip β‑catenin and modulate Yki/YAP ortholog stability; however, usable “off‑switch” bonds must be mapped precisely. Combine:
  - Sequence‑level prediction of calpain cuts (DeepCalpain/CalCleaveMKL/GPS‑CCD) to nominate P2/P1‑favored motifs within disordered loops that, if severed, disrupt TCF/TEAD binding or nuclear localization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))
  - Limited proteolysis‑mass spectrometry (LiP‑MS) with purified calpain on recombinant targets ± mild denaturants to reveal latent scissile bonds; validate in cell lysates with Ca2+‑titrated calpain. Use N‑terminomics to confirm single‑cut products and map neo‑N‑termini. Evidence that calpain can generate loss‑of‑function fragments for β‑catenin and cleave regulatory hubs motivates feasibility. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/64/20/7237/511898/Cleavage-of-Catenin-by-Calpain-in-Prostate-and?utm_source=openai))
  - Structural modeling (AlphaFold2/MD) to choose leverable epitopes whose mechanical perturbation would expose the nominated bond without global unfolding.
Go/no‑go: identification of at least one bond per target where a single in vitro calpain cut abrogates DNA‑binding or co‑activator function.

Aim 2. Build PSEEPS: a de novo intrabody that couples strain to conditional calpain recruitment.
- Construct: a rigid repeat‑protein or helical bundle “lever” bearing (i) a high‑affinity binder to a mechanically coupled epitope remote from the scissile loop; (ii) a short “tether arm” contacting a loop flanking the nominated bond to apply torsion/bending; and (iii) a calpastatin‑derived A/C exosite micropeptide (no B‑subdomain) as a low‑nM, non‑catalytic calpain docking tag. A de novo allosteric mask (LOCKR‑like) occludes the docking tag and only opens when the primary binder engages the target, implementing an AND gate for safety. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847431/?utm_source=openai))
- Rationale: calpastatin A/C bind calpain PEF domains away from the catalytic cleft (B mediates active‑site occlusion), enabling recruitment without inhibition; gating prevents off‑target docking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847431/?utm_source=openai))
- Optimization: vary lever length (2–6 nm), hinge stiffness, and docking‑tag affinity (μM→nM) to tune effective molarity/orientation. Readouts: (a) site‑specific cleavage by N‑term proteomics; (b) absence of bystander cleavage proteome‑wide; (c) loss of target function (TOPFlash for β‑catenin; 8xGTIIC for YAP/TAZ) with preserved cell viability at baseline Ca2+. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate intracellular, irreversible pathway rewiring with safety margins.
- Acute tests: transient expression in human cells; measure time‑resolved appearance of the exact neo‑N‑terminus, loss of target‑driven transcription, and lack of global calpain hyperactivation (spectrin breakdown product as sentinel). Compare to degrader controls to show distinct modality (single‑bond inactivation vs wholesale degradation). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6588652/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity: rescue with cleavage‑resistant target mutants (±single P1/P2 substitutions) and with PSEEPS lacking the docking tag or with docking tag locked; require geometric coincidence of lever and site.
- Safety: verify no activation of apoptotic caspases and no global proteostasis stress. Calpains are physiological limited proteases; recruitment without active‑site engagement and without Ca2+ elevation minimizes systemic risk. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Generalization and disease‑proximal models.
- Extend mapping to additional proteins where limited proteolysis is known to inactivate activity (e.g., EGFR kinase domain, MET juxtamembrane) to demonstrate portability across folds and compartments. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8055914/?utm_source=openai))
- In 3D tumor spheroids with constitutive Wnt/YAP signaling, quantify durable suppression after transient PSEEPS pulse; track clonal escape via sequencing of the targeted loop.

Key design controls and exclusion criteria
- Exclude targets where reported calpain cuts generate constitutively active fragments (e.g., PKC→PKM); pre‑filter with literature and in vitro mapping. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7607311/?utm_source=openai))
- Disallow constructs that increase global calpain activity or sequester calpain broadly; docking tag Kd and expression kept low; mask enforces binding‑dependent exposure.
- No recruitment of apoptotic caspases or lysosomal cathepsins.

Milestones
- M1 (Month 6): For at least one target, validated inactivating calpain bond and intrabody epitope pair; cleavage confirmed by LC‑MS neo‑N‑termini. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26796116/?utm_source=openai))
- M2 (Month 12): First‑gen PSEEPS drives >70% site‑specific clipping and >80% loss of reporter activity without spectrin breakdown at baseline. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))
- M3 (Month 18): Proteome‑wide off‑target cleavage <0.5% of quantified proteins (TAILS/ChaFRADIC); durable pathway rewiring in spheroids.

Why this fulfills the goal
- Defined intracellular consequence: single‑bond, irreversible switch‑off of a rogue function (e.g., TCF/TEAD co‑activation), distinct from receptor agonism/antagonism and from wholesale degradation.
- Solves an inadequacy of small molecules/antibodies: uses protein‑scale mechanics and geometry to expose and align a buried bond that occupancy inhibitors cannot access and antibodies cannot reach intracellularly.
- Feasibility and novelty: leverages native limited proteolysis and calpastatin exosites; to our knowledge, endogenously recruiting calpain via non‑inhibitory calpastatin fragments to inactivate unmodified intracellular proteins has not been demonstrated. Related induced‑proximity modalities focus on E3 ligases (PROTACs); our approach is protease‑centric and cleavage‑site specific. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsptsci.5c00730?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and decision points
- Success supports a new intracellular therapeutic class: “site‑specific protease switches.” Failure modes (no productive cut; activation fragments) trigger target re‑selection or switch to a different inactivating bond guided by N‑terminomics.

Selected references (supporting mechanistic premises)
- Calpains perform limited proteolysis that modulates signaling; predictors and assays exist. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanical force exposes cryptic scissile bonds in natural systems, motivating strain‑assisted accessibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3179391/?utm_source=openai))
- Calpastatin A/C exosites bind calpain PEF domains; B mediates inhibition—enabling non‑inhibitory recruitment designs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847431/?utm_source=openai))
- Calpain can inactivate key signaling proteins when the correct site is presented (e.g., β‑catenin; EGFR kinase domain). ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/64/20/7237/511898/Cleavage-of-Catenin-by-Calpain-in-Prostate-and?utm_source=openai))
- De novo allosteric masks (LOCKR) implement binding‑dependent motif unveiling for safety. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6733528/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverable
A minimal, genetically encodable protein “safety switch” that co‑opts endogenous proteolytic flux to permanently switch off disease‑causing intracellular proteins by one precise cut, with encoded geometric specificity and built‑in safety gating.

Title
A membrane-mechanics triage switch for organelle quality control: repurposing a HAMP transmembrane register to choose repair (p97/ESCRT) before clearance (LC3)

Rationale, question-as-hypothesis
Cells repair mildly damaged mitochondria and ER via local proteostasis and membrane repair (e.g., p97/VCP-driven extraction; ESCRT sealing; mitochondria-derived vesicles, MDVs). If stress persists or overwhelms capacity, selective autophagy removes organelle fragments or whole organelles via LC3-interacting receptors (LIR-containing mitophagy/ER‑phagy receptors). We ask whether a single de novo, organelle-embedded protein can sense membrane-state perturbations associated with damage, compute local repair capacity through occupancy, and then execute a binary choice: recruit repair machinery when salvageable; expose autophagy motifs when not. This aims to reduce unnecessary organelle loss while accelerating removal of irreparable segments. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4313695/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a bacterial HAMP-domain transmembrane register switch as an allosteric, reversible translator of bilayer physical state into alternative cytosolic interfaces. In the low‑damage state, the output surface presents short p97/ESCRT‑recruiting motifs; when local bilayer stress surpasses a threshold and/or repair capacity is saturated, the conformational register flips to expose tandem LIRs (± UBD) to commit that membrane patch to selective autophagy. HAMP domains natively convert small TM piston/rotation changes into large helical‑bundle reorientations; membrane lipid peroxidation and curvature/thickness changes provide the physical input. To our knowledge, HAMP has not been used in mammalian cells to control organelle‑autophagy decisions; current mammalian synthetic receptors rely on other architectures (synNotch, MESA, GEMS). ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev.micro.112408.134215?utm_source=openai))

Design overview (construct: TRIAGE-HAMP)
- Localization/topology: Single C‑terminal tail anchor targets the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) or ER; cytosolic N‑terminus carries the HAMP bundle followed by a short output coiled‑coil. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4313695/?utm_source=openai))
- Repair-first face (default): Surface displays one or more short p97-binding SLiMs (SHP box; VIM; VBM) and, for ER deployment, a minimal ALIX-binding LYPX(n)L to seed ESCRT when needed. These motifs enhance local extraction/sealing without global proteostasis activation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18208387/?utm_source=openai))
- Clearance face (switched): Surface exposes a tandem LC3/GABARAP‑binding LIR array (optionally a compact UBD such as UBAN/UBA) to nucleate selective autophagy microdomains only when revealed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7615515/?utm_source=openai))
- Steric exclusion gate: The repair-motif docking surface overlaps the autophagy‑motif surface so that bound repair factors physically occlude LIR/UBD exposure; only when local repair occupancy falls (capacity exceeded) does the autophagy face become available. This converts endogenous factor saturation into a decision point (no added signaling species).

Specific Aims

Aim 1. Calibrate a HAMP-based membrane-state sensor on the OMM/ER
Question/hypothesis: Does local bilayer perturbation characteristic of oxidative/morphological organelle damage drive a HAMP register change in situ?
- Engineering: Use Af1503/Tsr-derived HAMP with output coiled‑coil; create state‑locked mutants from literature models to define ONrepair and ONclearance references; fuse FRET reporters across the HAMP output to quantify state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2892831/?utm_source=openai))
- Perturbations: Induce graded lipid peroxidation (photosensitizers or iron-mediated Fenton chemistry), curvature/thickness shifts, and Δψm loss; measure sensor response independent of ubiquitin signaling. Use established biophysical links between peroxidation and altered packing/thickness/viscoelasticity as the physical basis. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42004-022-00809-x?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Monotonic FRET shift with peroxidation dose and curvature stress; no shift with unrelated cytosolic stresses; correct topology and membrane targeting.

Aim 2. Implement “repair-first, capacity-gated” output logic
Question/hypothesis: Can repair-factor occupancy enforce default repair and delay autophagy until capacity is exceeded?
- Design: Position SHP/VIM/VBM motifs to recruit endogenous p97 at the sensor site; for ER, include LYPX(n)L to access ALIX/ESCRT when needed. Place tandem LIRs on the alternative face; map steric overlap via structure-guided spacing and flexible linkers to ensure mutual occlusion. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18208387/?utm_source=openai))
- Assays: Live-cell recruitment (endogenous p97/ALIX/LC3 via knock‑in tags), proteomics of proximal interactors, and single-organelle readouts (mitoKeima or mito‑QC; ER‑phagy reporters). Titrate repair capacity by acute p97 inhibition or partial knockdown to reveal the autophagy face; quantify the switching boundary. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4313695/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Under mild stress, increased local p97/ESCRT without LC3 recruitment; as repair is titrated down or stress escalates, sharp transition to LC3 recruitment and autophagic capture at the same membrane patch.

Aim 3. Demonstrate functional triage: rescue when salvageable, removal when not
Question/hypothesis: Does TRIAGE‑HAMP reduce unnecessary mitophagy/ER‑phagy while accelerating removal of irreparable segments?
- Paradigms: Pulsed oxidative or proteotoxic insults that normally trigger MDVs/ERAD before organellophagy; and sustained insults that drive PINK1/Parkin mitophagy or ER‑phagy. Track MDV flux, OMMAD/ERAD throughput, and autophagic capture kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9189329/?utm_source=openai))
- Metrics: (i) Faster recovery of membrane potential/protein import after transient stress; (ii) increased MDV/ERAD throughput with reduced whole-organelle mitophagy/ER-phagy; (iii) under high damage, accelerated LC3 engagement and cargo delivery versus controls. Safety: no global proteostasis collapse (p97 activity assays; UPS markers), no chronic LC3 flux elevation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9189329/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and controls
- Minimal parts: All domains/motifs are short and genetically encodable; p97-binding SLiMs (SHP/VIM/VBM) are established; LIRs are modular and their spacing/adjacency tune LC3 vs GABARAP selectivity. Include state‑locked HAMP controls and motif‑dead mutants to isolate sensing vs effector functions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18208387/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinction from existing modalities: The switch acts at organelle membranes, reading bilayer mechanics unavailable to small molecules/antibodies, and computing capacity via occupancy—functions that demand protein‑scale interfaces and conformational switching. Reviews of mammalian synthetic receptors list no HAMP‑based, autophagy‑directing systems, supporting novelty. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-023-01680-5?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: HAMP is unresponsive in eukaryotic membranes. Mitigation: Use state‑locked variants to validate effector logic; screen alternative TMs with different hydrophobic lengths/tilt propensities to couple to HAMP rotation/piston; if needed, deploy on ER where curvature/thickness shifts are pronounced during stress and ESCRT repair is well documented. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9229795/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: p97 sequestration causes off‑target effects. Mitigation: Use low‑affinity SLiMs, decreased motif valency, and organelle‑restricted expression; verify no change in global UPS flux. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5559722/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Premature autophagy. Mitigation: Enforce steric occlusion geometry; tune LIR affinity and spacing; optionally incorporate a short multisite‑phospho IDR immediately downstream of HAMP as a temporal integrator to further delay LIR exposure under transient stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3001445/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Sensor calibration and topology validation; state‑locked references; peroxidation/curvature response curves established. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42004-022-00809-x?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Functional triage outputs demonstrated; occupancy‑dependent occlusion confirmed; quantitative switching boundary mapped versus repair capacity.
- Year 3: Efficacy and safety in disease-relevant cells (e.g., neurons or cardiomyocytes): improved recovery after transient stress; accelerated clearance under catastrophic stress; no global proteostasis or UPR activation.

Outcomes and significance
This work introduces a compact, programmable, membrane‑embedded protein that computes organelle health from bilayer mechanics and local capacity, executing repair-first triage before selective autophagy. It advances de novo intracellular therapeutic proteins beyond binding or receptor agonism by actively rewiring quality‑control pathways at their point of action. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev.micro.112408.134215?utm_source=openai))

Title: Valency-programmed condensate switches to triage intracellular damage: rescuing salvageable cells while clearing unsalvageable ones

Rationale (succinct prior art and gap)
- Protein triage in cells toggles between refolding/repair and degradation, with Hsp70–CHIP/HOP modules acting as key nodes; stress PTMs can bias the choice, but an engineered, context-aware switch that commits to repair first and degradation only upon persistent damage is missing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27863257/?utm_source=openai))
- Ubiquitin signaling and condensates are tightly coupled: polyubiquitin chain architecture controls phase behavior and client fate, yet natural UBQLN2/p62 hubs can either protect or clear substrates depending on valency and residence time—a controllable design lever. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
- Engineered ankyrin/DARPin scaffolds enable rigid, multispecific, geometry-controlled assemblies suitable for implementing multi-input logic and presenting mutually exclusive effector surfaces in cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5593856/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–goal–question
- Can a single, genetically encoded scaffold that senses local “damage valency” (exposed misfolded surfaces and accumulating K48/K63 polyubiquitin) undergo a reversible material-state transition that first enriches refolding/repair factors, but upon sustained high valency switches to recruit clearance machinery—thereby restoring function in salvageable cells while eliminating terminally damaged ones within the same tissue? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
- Encode a time-integrated threshold in a designer condensate: below a polyubiquitin/misfolding valency threshold, the scaffold forms dynamic, Hsp70/Hsp40-accessible microcondensates that accelerate client repair; above a sustained threshold, the same scaffold increases crosslinking and flips its client-interaction surface to reveal E3/adaptor docking sites, committing clients to proteasomal/autophagic clearance. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))

Design concept: ViDA (Valency-integrated Damage Assessor)
- Chassis: consensus ankyrin repeat scaffold (8–10 repeats) with two modular client-sensing rows:
  - Misfolding sensors: two repeats grafted with binders to generic exposed hydrophobic motifs (engineered to low µM affinity to avoid off-target binding when folded clients are scarce).
  - Ubiquitin valency sensors: a tandem array of engineered ubiquitin-binding modules with defined spacing/affinity tuned to preferentially bind ≥K48-Ub4 and/or K63-Ub3+ chains; spacing set to maximize cooperative partitioning as chain length and local density increase. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
- State control via sticker–spacer grammar:
  - Repair state (R): low-valency engagement yields small, dynamic droplets; ankyrin N-terminus presents Hsp70/Hsp40/HOP docking grooves; C-terminus masks E3/adaptor motifs.
  - Clearance state (C): sustained high valency (misfolds + polyUb) increases multivalent crosslinks, rotates terminal repeats to occlude chaperone grooves and expose E3/adaptor motifs (e.g., short VHL/SOCS-box or LC3-interacting regions for autophagy routing), biasing K48-ubiquitination or aggrephagy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
- Spatial variants: mitochondrial outer membrane-targeted ViDA (mito-ViDA) and cytosolic ViDA to evaluate organelle-specific salvage-versus-clearance without global proteostasis perturbation.

Specific aims
1) Build and calibrate ViDA’s two-state phase behavior and effector selectivity in living cells.
2) Demonstrate intracellular triage on mixed client populations: rescue refoldable clients while clearing irreparable ones in the same culture.
3) Test organelle-targeted ViDA for mitochondrial proteostasis: restore function where Δψm is recoverable and remove collapsed organelles via mitophagy.

Aim 1: Build and calibrate ViDA
- Constructs
  - ViDA-RC: full switchable scaffold.
  - R-locked and C-locked controls: terminal-repeat mutations that fix terminal geometry to permanently present chaperone grooves (R) or E3/adaptor motifs (C). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8229355/?utm_source=openai))
  - ΔUBD and Δmisfold modules to dissect inputs.
- Assays
  - Live-cell FRAP and partitioning: quantify droplet dynamics and client partition coefficients across graded proteotoxic stress; tune UBD spacing/affinity for desired threshold using Ub chain standards expressed in cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
  - Effector composition: proximity labeling mass spectrometry (TurboID fused to ViDA) to profile R vs C condensate proteomes; expectation: Hsp70/Hsp40/HOP enrich in R; E3s/proteasome (or LC3/SQSTM1) enrich in C. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
  - Switching hysteresis: stress-pulse protocols to confirm time-integration (residence time) and avoid oscillation.
- Success criteria
  - Bistable state occupancy with tunable threshold; mutually exclusive enrichment of repair vs clearance effectors.

Aim 2: Mixed-client triage in the same cell population
- System
  - Co-express two fluorescent clients: (i) repairable temperature-sensitive folding mutant (rescues at permissive chaperone levels), and (ii) irreparable truncation/misfold designed to accumulate K48-Ub chains.
- Readouts
  - Client fate mapping by single-cell imaging: track refolding kinetics and proteasomal degradation rates ± proteasome or autophagy inhibitors to validate pathway choice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
  - Function-first metrics: restoration of client enzymatic activity for the salvageable mutant vs elimination of irreparable client; cell viability and stress markers.
  - Comparative baselines: R-locked, C-locked, and Δmodules.
- Success criteria
  - Significant increase in functional rescue of repairable clients with no increase in their degradation; accelerated clearance of irreparable clients; net improvement in growth/viability under stress relative to controls.

Aim 3: Organelle-targeted triage (mito-ViDA)
- Design
  - Add outer-membrane targeting to ViDA; restrict to mitochondrial surface or intermembrane space as needed.
- Assays
  - Mixed-stress regime: transient Δψm drops (CCCP pulses) plus ROS bursts to generate salvageable vs terminally damaged mitochondria.
  - Outcomes: recovery of Δψm and respiratory capacity where salvageable; selective mitophagy (Parkin-independent) of collapsed mitochondria with C-state engagement; minimal impact on proteasome/autophagy flux outside mitochondria. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria
  - Improved mitochondrial network function and removal of collapsed fragments without global proteostasis disruption.

Key experimental choices and justifications
- Why condensate switching: Condensates are natural time-averaging integrators; chain-type/length-dependent Ub signaling alters valency, providing a physically grounded “timer” that distinguishes transient from persistent damage. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
- Why ankyrin repeats: repeat scaffolds allow rigid, multispecific geometry and mechanically coupled terminal reorientation with minimal parts, enabling mutual exclusivity between repair and clearance interfaces. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5593856/?utm_source=openai))
- Why not simply recruit E3s: in UBQLN2-like hubs, E3 recruitment can paradoxically protect from degradation; ViDA explicitly changes material state and interface geometry to permit proteasomal access or route to autophagy only after sustained high valency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980000/?utm_source=openai))

Bench plan and controls
- Tuning thresholds: vary UBD stoichiometry and spacing; use Ub-chain mimetics with defined linkages to program switching points; calibrate with cycloheximide-chase and proteostasis stressors.
- Orthogonality and safety: restrict expression with tissue-specific promoters; incorporate degron kill-switch on ViDA itself (small-molecule-controlled) to stop activity if off-target effects emerge; verify that global Hsp70 pools and proteasome capacity metrics are unchanged at baseline. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1873-3468.70371?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism falsification tests:
  - If R→C switching occurs without UBD occupancy, redesign misfold sensors to reduce avidity; if switching never occurs despite high K48-Ub, increase UBD affinity or add modest crosslinkers.
  - If E3 recruitment in R-state is detected, mutate masked motifs to confirm geometry-based occlusion.

Milestones
- M6: R/C-lock validation; FRAP-defined dynamics and effector proteomes distinct.
- M12: Mixed-client triage with functional rescue and clearance within one culture.
- M18: Mito-ViDA demonstrates selective mitophagy of terminal mitochondria with improved respiratory capacity.

Potential pitfalls and mitigations
- Over-sequestration of clients in R-state: engineer faster exchange by shortening stickers; reduce IDR content.
- Proteasome exclusion from C-state: bias C-state toward autophagy via LC3-interacting motifs; or lower crosslink density to admit proteasome. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target condensates: add localization domains (e.g., TOM/TIM tags) and reduce cytosolic LLPS propensity.

Validation of therapeutic relevance (cell and ex vivo)
- Neuronal or cardiomyocyte stress models with mixed salvageability; endpoints include contractility or synaptic activity recovery in salvageable fractions plus reduction of aggregate burden in terminal fractions. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1873-3468.70371?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and impact
- Converts polyubiquitin chain architecture and misfold density—ubiquitin’s native “grammar”—into a programmable, two-state, intracellular decision that preferentially repairs first, then clears only when damage persists. This differs from extracellular receptor agonism/antagonism and from single-function degraders by delivering pathway rewiring and condensate modulation with built-in safety thresholds. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility summary
- Grounded in: (i) established Hsp70–CHIP/HOP triage biology; (ii) well-documented coupling between ubiquitin chains and condensate valency; and (iii) clinically advanced, modular ankyrin/DARPin scaffolds for multispecific, geometry-controlled designs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27863257/?utm_source=openai))

Go/no-go criteria
- Proceed to animal models only if ViDA increases functional recovery of salvageable cells ≥30% and accelerates clearance of irreparable clients ≥2× without elevating global proteotoxic stress markers at baseline and without reducing viability of unstressed cells. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1873-3468.70371?utm_source=openai))

## Final Refined Idea: Cell‑Type‑Resolved, Raft‑Localized TRPV1/TLR4 Control of Diabetic DRG Excitability

### Core aim
Determine whether **diabetes‑induced lipid changes drive DRG hyperexcitability specifically by reconfiguring a raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4 module in nociceptors and SGCs**, and identify which compartment is the most effective, realistically targetable therapeutic lever.

We keep the two‑phase, decision‑gated design, but sharpen Phase 1 with one mechanistically specific perturbation and within‑cell analyses.

---

## Phase 1 – Existence and mechanistically specific causality

### Key questions
1. Do identified DRG nociceptors and SGCs in DPN show a robust, cell‑specific shift in membrane order?  
2. Is **raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4** required for diabetic hyperexcitability, beyond transcriptional/inflammatory regulation?  
3. Can local modulation of membrane order and TRPV1/TLR4 raft association normalize excitability in the *same cells* where order is measured?

### 1. Cell‑specific membrane order in nociceptors and SGCs

- Use diabetic and control mice with fluorescent reporters in **nociceptors (Nav1.8‑reporter)** and **SGCs (GLAST/GFAP‑reporter)**.  
- Prepare acute DRG slices or brief cultures preserving native architecture.  
- Apply Laurdan/Di‑4; perform two‑photon/confocal imaging.  
- **Segment analysis strictly to reporter‑positive plasma membranes** (nociceptor soma/initial neurites; SGC envelopes). Mitochondrial/ER regions are excluded by morphology and co‑stains.

Output: A cell‑type‑resolved GP distribution, giving a coarse but direct index of **plasma‑membrane order** in nociceptors and SGCs in DPN vs controls.

### 2. Raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4 module

Rather than inferring from bulk biochemistry, we focus on:

- **TRPV1/TLR4 abundance and responsiveness** in identified nociceptors/SGCs (immunostaining or tagged knock‑ins, plus calcium or current responses to capsaicin and TLR4 ligands).  
- **Mechanistically specific perturbation of raft association**:
  - Express in a subset of nociceptors/SGCs (via low‑titer AAV) **TRPV1 or TLR4 variants with impaired raft targeting**, e.g., palmitoylation‑deficient or cholesterol‑insensitive mutants, or peptides that selectively disrupt TLR4–TRPV1 proximity without ablating global expression.  
  - Neighboring cells in the same ganglion (no viral expression) serve as internal controls.

The logic: if diabetic hyperexcitability depends on **raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4**, then disrupting raft association should reduce excitability and inflammatory coupling **even if global transcriptional activation persists**.

### 3. Within‑cell/within‑ganglion perturbation–response

To move beyond group averages:

- In the same preparation, **record GP and excitability from the same cells** (e.g., GP imaging followed by patch‑clamp on identified cells) in diabetic vs control DRG.  
- Compare:
  - Cells with **intact** TRPV1/TLR4 versus those expressing **raft‑disrupted** variants within the same diabetic ganglion.  
  - Before/after **local DRG application** of AIBP/HDL mimetics or cyclodextrin (periganglionic/intraganglionic), tracking within‑cell changes in GP and excitability.

Readouts:
- GP change per cell → shift in membrane order.  
- TRPV1/TLR4 responsiveness and coupling (e.g., capsaicin‑evoked currents, TLR4‑evoked depolarization).  
- Firing properties (spontaneous activity, rheobase, firing frequency).

Decision gate:
- **Positive raft mechanism** if all three hold:
  1. DPN nociceptors/SGCs show a reproducible GP shift versus controls.  
  2. Cells with more ordered/disordered membranes exhibit systematically altered TRPV1/TLR4 responsiveness and hyperexcitability.  
  3. Disrupting TRPV1/TLR4 raft association or locally normalizing GP **reduces excitability in the same cells**, even when other injury pathways remain.
- If any of these fail—e.g., GP shifts without excitability change, or TRPV1/TLR4 raft‑disruption has no impact—the raft‑centric mechanism is not primary and the program stops.

Local behavioral measures (mechanical/thermal thresholds) are secondary confirmatory endpoints after electrophysiological causality is established.

---

## Phase 2 – Practical compartment hierarchy (only if Phase 1 is positive)

### Question
Given that raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4 in nociceptors/SGCs is mechanistically required, **which compartment is the most effective and practically targetable control point** for restoring normal membrane order and TRPV1/TLR4 raft state in DPN?

### Strategy
Use **compartment‑biased AAVs or nanoparticles** to deliver the *same kinds of raft‑modulating payloads* validated in Phase 1 (e.g., AIBP, raft‑disrupting peptides, TRPV1/TLR4 raft‑insensitive constructs):

1. **Nociceptor‑biased** (Nav1.8 promoter): normalize raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4 or membrane order in nociceptors.  
2. **SGC‑biased** (GLAST/GFAP promoters): reshape SGC membrane order and TRPV1/TLR4‑related signaling.  
3. **Endothelial/lipid milieu‑biased** (VE‑cadherin or lipid‑carrier–targeted): adjust local lipid supply/handling.

Use the same readouts as Phase 1 (cell‑specific GP, TRPV1/TLR4 function, excitability) to **quantitatively compare** how strongly each compartment‑biased intervention rescues nociceptor GP and hyperexcitability per degree of targeting.

The hierarchy outcome is thus practical and mechanistic: *which compartment, when modulated with realistic delivery tools, most effectively restores the raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4 state and normalizes diabetic nociceptor excitability?*

---

### Contribution
This final design:
- Provides the first **cell‑type‑resolved demonstration** (or refutation) of a diabetes‑induced, raft‑localized TRPV1/TLR4 mechanism in DRG nociceptors/SGCs.  
- Uses **within‑cell and within‑ganglion perturbation–response loops** and a **TRPV1/TLR4 raft‑specific perturbation** to avoid over‑attributing effects of broad cholesterol tools.  
- Yields a **practical, translational hierarchy** of where to intervene (neurons, SGCs, endothelium) to re‑establish healthy membrane order and TRPV1/TLR4 organization in painful DPN.

If Phase 1 fails, we efficiently rule out rafts as a primary driver. If it succeeds, we obtain a mechanistically tight and translationally actionable map of lipid‑driven nociceptor control in diabetes.

## Final Refined Idea: Stage‑Anchored Test of Neuron‑Only vs Dual Targeting at Defined DRG Leak States

### Core Translational Question

As DRG barrier leak progresses during diabetes, **at what stage(s)** is neuron‑intrinsic rescue (IGF‑1→AMPK→mitochondria support) **no longer sufficient** to normalize DRG neuron function, making **barrier repair mechanistically required**?

Instead of a single, idealized “DPN‑like leak,” the model uses a **small set of discrete, in vivo–anchored leak states** corresponding to meaningful disease milestones (e.g., pre‑symptomatic, early painful DPN, later conduction deficits).

---

### Mechanistic Axes (Constrained and Calibrated)

1. **Neuronal axis (intrinsic vulnerability)**
   - Diabetes reduces IGF‑1 signaling and AMPK activity in DRG neurons, impairing mitochondrial function (lower membrane potential, higher ROS, reduced ATP) and calcium handling.
   - These neurons become progressively less able to tolerate additional metabolic/inflammatory stress.

2. **Barrier axis (simplified DRG‑like leak states)**
   - In vivo, DRG/BNB permeability increases selectively to small solutes and certain tracers (e.g., [14C]mannitol) while macromolecular exclusion is relatively preserved, especially early, and changes are linked to claudin‑1/1‑like alterations.
   - We explicitly model a **simplified DRG‑like microvascular interface**, not full regional heterogeneity.
   - Barrier state is operationally defined as a **small set of tracer‑based leak phenotypes**, each anchored to in vivo data:
     - **State 0 (baseline)**: control small/large tracer permeability ratio (healthy DRG vessels).
     - **State 1 (early leak)**: modest increase in small‑molecule tracer flux, minimal change in large tracer—mapped to pre‑symptomatic or very early DPN.
     - **State 2 (established DPN‑like leak)**: larger increase in small‑molecule permeability with still‑preserved macromolecular exclusion—mapped to early painful DPN or onset of conduction slowing.
     - Optionally **State 3 (late, more severe leak)** if supported by in vivo tracer data.

Each state is defined by **paired (or triplet) permeability targets** to small and large tracers (and, if available, one intermediate tracer), derived from rodent DPN studies.

We do **not** claim to capture all cytokine, lipid, or albumin‑bound fluxes; these are acknowledged limitations. The barrier state is a minimal, calibrated phenotype, not the full chemical milieu.

---

### Experimental Architecture: Minimal but Stage‑Resolved

#### 1. Transwell DRG–Endothelium Co‑culture

- **Vascular side (top)**: DRG‑like microvascular endothelial cells + pericytes, grown to a monolayer with measurable TEER.
- **Neuronal side (bottom)**: DRG neurons plus satellite glia.
- Both compartments are kept under diabetic‑like glucose (static high or simple oscillatory), but glucose pattern is background context rather than a primary variable.

#### 2. Calibration to In Vivo Leak States

For each targeted state (0–2/3):

- Use controlled perturbations (e.g., mild junctional modulation, limited exposure to VEGF‑A or defined cytokine mixes, glycocalyx modulation) on the endothelial layer to achieve 
  - The desired **fold‑change in small‑molecule tracer permeability** and
  - The corresponding **minimal change in large tracer**, matching in vivo ratios as closely as feasible.
- Once a condition reproducibly produces a tracer profile within a predefined tolerance of an in vivo state, it is designated the **in vitro analogue** of that leak state.

Barrier measurements here are **instrumental**: they are used to establish and periodically verify that the system remains in the intended state.

---

### Intervention Logic: Necessity/Sufficiency Across Leak Stages

For each leak state, neuronal functional outcomes are the primary readouts.

#### Step 1: Neuron‑Only Rescue Across States

- Apply **neuron‑intrinsic rescue only** to the neuronal compartment:
  - e.g., IGF‑1 pathway agonist or AMPK/mitochondrial support compound, dosed and selected to minimize endothelial effects (verified in separate control wells without neurons).
- Maintain the pre‑established barrier state (no barrier‑directed repair in this phase).

**Primary neuronal readouts** (same across states):
- Mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS, and ATP proxy measures.
- Calcium handling and basic excitability/survival metrics.

**Barrier check (minimal)**:
- Periodic tracer assays to confirm that small/large tracer permeabilities remain in the calibrated window for that state.

**Question:** For each leak state (0, 1, 2, ±3), does neuron‑only rescue normalize neuronal function toward the non‑diabetic baseline?

- If neuron‑only rescue **fully normalizes** neuronal function at State 1 but fails at State 2, this suggests a **stage boundary** where barrier dysfunction becomes a mechanistic co‑determinant.

#### Step 2: Add Barrier Repair Only Where Needed

At leak states where neuron‑only rescue shows **incomplete** normalization:

- Introduce a **barrier‑directed intervention** on the vascular side (e.g., endothelial AMPK activator, tight‑junction/glycocalyx support), titrated with the aim to
  - Shift tracer permeabilities **back toward the healthier state** (e.g., from State 2 toward State 1 or 0), and
  - Avoid direct neuronal effects (confirmed in control).

Compare neuronal function across:
- Diabetic condition at leak State X, no rescue.
- Leak State X with neuron‑only rescue.
- Leak State X with neuron‑only rescue **plus** barrier repair (resulting in a lower effective leak state).

Crucially, the interpretation is **stage‑specific**:
- If neuronal function becomes normalizable **only** when barrier leak is also corrected (back toward State 0/1), this indicates that, beyond that stage, **dual‑compartment targeting is mechanistically required**.

---

### Optional Complement: Defined “Milieu” Without Endothelium

As a conceptual complement (not primary design):
- Prepare defined **milieu cocktails** mirroring measured concentrations of key soluble effectors (e.g., VEGF‑A, select cytokines, AGEs) in DRG interstitial fluid at the same in vivo disease stages corresponding to States 1–2.
- Expose DRG neurons directly to these cocktails (no endothelium) and repeat neuron‑only rescue tests.

This simpler system sacrifices structural realism but offers a **lower‑complexity check** on the intrinsic rescue capacity of neurons under stage‑matched molecular stress.

---

### Claim Scope and Limitations

- The endothelial layer is explicitly a **simplified DRG‑like barrier**; we make no claims about NRR vs FRR or perineurial specialization.
- Barrier states are defined by **tracer ratios plus minimal, specified modulators** (e.g., VEGF‑A presence/absence), not by exhaustive chemical characterization.
- Conclusions are restricted to: *At discrete, in vivo‑anchored leak states, in this simplified DRG interface, neuron‑intrinsic rescue is (or is not) sufficient to restore neuronal function.*

---

### Why This Design is Mechanistically and Translationally Useful

- **Mechanistic clarity**: By testing neuron‑only rescue across **stage‑defined leak states**, the study pinpoints where barrier pathology becomes a **necessary co‑target** for DRG neuron protection.
- **Efficiency**: The architecture stays minimal—transwell co‑culture, tracer calibration, targeted neuronal readouts—without organ‑on‑chip or global omics.
- **Translational leverage**:
  - If neuron‑intrinsic rescue suffices through State 2, this supports prioritizing neuron‑centric therapies (plus systemic metabolic control) even as leak emerges.
  - If full rescue requires barrier normalization at or before the transition to painful DPN/conduction slowing, this argues for **co‑targeted therapies** (neuronal support + barrier‑stabilizing agents) beginning at that clinical stage.

In sum, the final design is a stage‑resolved, calibrated test of **when** barrier repair becomes mechanistically indispensable, using the simplest system that still respects in vivo leak characteristics and keeps neuronal function as the deciding readout.

# Final Refined Idea: Minimal‑Genotype, 4‑HNE Dose–Response Test of ALDH2 Bottleneck vs Redundancy in DRG and Nerve Microvessels

## Core question

In early diabetic neuropathy, does **ALDH2 function set the effective 4‑HNE tolerance window** of DRG neurons and nerve microvessels—i.e., does changing ALDH2 shift how these cells respond to a given 4‑HNE load—*or* is its role largely buffered by other ALDH isoforms and scavengers?

The answer is expressed as how the **4‑HNE dose–response curves** for neuronal excitability and microvascular function move when ALDH2 is reduced vs intact, under early diabetic conditions.

---

## Meta‑strategy

1. Use a **minimal ALDH2 genetic series** on an early diabetic background:
   - WT ALDH2.
   - ALDH2 loss‑of‑function (e.g., ALDH2*2 knock‑in or a hypomorphic/conditional KO).

2. In these two genotypes:
   - **Map ALDH redundancy** in DRG and nerve microvessels (expression/activity of ALDH2 vs other ALDH isoforms and key scavenging systems).
   - Perform **controlled 4‑HNE challenges ex vivo** in DRG neurons and endoneurial microvessels to derive functional dose–response curves.

3. Ask whether **diabetes + ALDH2 status** re‑positions these dose–response relationships in ways that reveal ALDH2 as a bottleneck or as a buffered, interchangeable sink.

Systemic in vivo readouts (pain behaviors, basal perfusion) are retained but serve as context, not the primary bottleneck test.

---

## Step 1: Establish early diabetic context and ALDH landscape

In WT and ALDH2‑deficient mice:

- Induce **early diabetes** (e.g., STZ at a stage with clear pain hypersensitivity but minimal structural nerve loss).
- Confirm systemic **metabolic comparability** (glucose, lipids, general mitochondrial markers) so that downstream differences are not trivially due to gross metabolic divergence.

In DRG and endoneurial microvessels from these animals:

- Quantify **baseline 4‑HNE adducts and MG adducts**.
- Measure **expression and activity of ALDH isoforms** most relevant for lipid aldehydes (ALDH2, ALDH3A1, ALDH1A1, etc.), plus key non‑ALDH scavengers (aldo‑keto reductases, glutathione markers).

Interpretation:
- This mapping does *not* claim saturation from activity alone, but defines whether DRG/microvessels are ALDH2‑dominant or already heavily buffered by other isoforms.

---

## Step 2: 4‑HNE dose–response in DRG neurons

From diabetic WT and ALDH2‑deficient mice, prepare acutely dissociated DRG neurons or slices for patch‑clamp.

For each genotype:

- Apply **graded, controlled concentrations of 4‑HNE ex vivo** (short, defined exposures), with and without **Alda‑1** (as a functional ALDH2 enhancer in WT, inert in ALDH2‑deficient background).
- Measure a **small, biophysically specific panel** of 4‑HNE‑sensitive properties:
  - A defined shift in Nav channel inactivation or persistent current.
  - TRPA1 current potentiation or activation threshold changes.
  - Overall firing threshold/rheobase.

Key readout:
- Construct **4‑HNE concentration–effect curves** for these properties in WT vs ALDH2‑deficient neurons, with and without Alda‑1.

Bottleneck logic:
- If ALDH2 is a dominant 4‑HNE sink locally, then at a given exogenous 4‑HNE dose, **ALDH2‑deficient DRG neurons should show left‑shifted (more sensitive) curves**, and Alda‑1 should right‑shift the curves only in WT.
- If curves are similar between genotypes and minimally affected by Alda‑1, despite different ALDH2 status, and other ALDHs are abundant, this supports **redundant buffering** rather than ALDH2 bottleneck.

---

## Step 3: 4‑HNE dose–response in nerve microvessels

From the same animals, isolate endoneurial microvessel preparations enriched for endothelial cells and pericytes.

For WT and ALDH2‑deficient microvessels:

- Expose to **graded 4‑HNE concentrations** with/without Alda‑1 under controlled conditions.
- Measure **pericyte‑linked functional parameters**:
  - KATP‑dependent responses (e.g., changes in membrane potential or diameter with KATP modulators).
  - Ca2+ dynamics during constriction/relaxation.
  - Simple microvessel tone/diameter changes.

Again, build **4‑HNE concentration–effect curves** and compare between genotypes and ±Alda‑1.

Interpretation mirrors DRG:
- Strong genotype‑dependent shifts and Alda‑1 right‑shifts in WT indicate that **ALDH2 capacity shapes the functional tolerance to 4‑HNE** in microvessels.
- Flat or minimal differences, especially when other ALDH isoforms are robust, indicate that ALDH2 is not bottleneck at this compartment/timescale.

---

## Step 4: In vivo anchoring (optional but informative)

In the same animals, measure:

- **Pain behaviors** and simple nerve perfusion/oxygenation.
- Global oxidative stress markers vs 4‑HNE adducts in DRG/microvessels.

These data do not define the bottleneck alone but provide context: strong shifts in ex vivo 4‑HNE sensitivity curves with ALDH2 status that are mirrored by in vivo behavior/perfusion changes would strengthen translational relevance.

---

## Why this design is efficient and mechanistically sharp

- **Minimal genotypes, maximal interpretability.** Only two ALDH2 states (WT vs low) plus pharmacologic enhancement are used; this avoids a large cross of ALDH2 × glyoxalase/glutathione while still interrogating bottleneck behavior.
- **4‑HNE is the explicit axis.** We no longer normalize across different carbonyl species. Instead, we directly titrate 4‑HNE and see how ALDH2 status re‑positions the response curves.
- **Redundancy is measured, not ignored.** Parallel ALDH isoforms and scavengers in DRG/microvessels are quantified, so a weak ALDH2 phenotype can be interpreted as **redundant detox capacity**, not merely “no effect.”
- **Local vs systemic is disentangled by design.** The key tests occur in ex vivo DRG neurons and microvessels, under controlled 4‑HNE exposure, so systemic hemodynamics or CNS effects cannot explain the primary findings.
- **Success and null outcomes are both informative.**
  - If ALDH2 status strongly shifts 4‑HNE sensitivity curves and function, we have mechanistic evidence of a **true ALDH2 bottleneck** in DRG/microvessels.
  - If not, and redundancy is high, we can conclude that ALDH2 is **not a privileged 4‑HNE sink** at this stage, refining therapeutic priorities.

This final refinement preserves the core, reviewer‑endorsed framework but tightens it around a quantitative 4‑HNE dose–response paradigm and explicit ALDH redundancy mapping, yielding a decisive and interpretable test of ALDH2’s role in early diabetic neuropathy.

## Final Refined Idea: Macrophage-Anchored Test of Acidosis/GPR65 Dependence in Sciatic Nerve Neuropathy

### Core Question

In a diabetic or HFD neuropathy model where **sciatic nerve macrophages are already established as necessary for pain**, does **local acidosis and GPR65 signaling** at the nerve materially drive that macrophage-dependent pathology?

The project explicitly:
- Anchors all downstream interpretations to **macrophage dependence**, proven locally at the sciatic nerve.
- Treats **acidosis and GPR65** as *candidate modulators* of that macrophage-driven pathology, not as stand-alone explanations.

---

### Mechanistic Frame

Working hypothesis in the sciatic nerve:

1. Diabetic/HFD conditions induce **metabolic stress** in non-immune cells (axons, endothelial cells, possibly pericytes) via **PDK2/4 and related glycolytic pathways**, increasing local lactate and protons.
2. **Macrophages** accumulating at the sciatic nerve integrate this metabolic context; **local acidosis** is one input among others (ROS, AGEs, lipids).
3. Macrophage **acid-sensing machinery**, including **GPR65** where expressed, biases their cytokine/chemokine output, which in turn modulates **axonal excitability and pain behaviors**.

No assumption is made that the DRG LCN2–PDK2–lactate module directly copies into the sciatic nerve; rather, we test whether an analogous **metabolic–immune coupling via acidity** operates, conditional on macrophage involvement.

---

### Step 1 – Establish local macrophage dependence at the sciatic nerve

**Goal:** Confirm that pain behavior and nerve hyperexcitability in the chosen model depend on **sciatic macrophage-mediated inflammation**, providing a reference condition for all subsequent manipulations.

**Approach:**
- Use a **HFD or STZ model** with documented sciatic macrophage infiltration and mechanical hypersensitivity.
- Apply a **perineural macrophage-targeted intervention** at the sciatic nerve:
  - Either an established macrophage-depleting agent (e.g., Mac1–Saporin) or
  - A macrophage-focused **RAGE or LCN2/PDK2 pathway inhibitor** delivered perineurally.
- Readouts:
  - **Behavior:** mechanical/thermal sensitivity.
  - **Sciatic nerve hyperexcitability:** ex vivo nerve recordings.
  - **Macrophage metrics:** local macrophage density and cytokine profile (e.g., IL-1β, TNF) before and after intervention.

**Interpretation:** If local macrophage depletion or macrophage-pathway blockade **abolishes or markedly attenuates pain and hyperexcitability**, while sparing systemic glycemia, this establishes that **sciatic macrophages (or their RAGE/LCN2/PDK2-driven activation) are required** for the neuropathic phenotype in this model. Any later effect of pH or GPR65 modulation is interpreted against this established macrophage dependency.

---

### Step 2 – Confirm presence of metabolic stress and GPR65 in the sciatic niche

**Goal:** Ensure that mechanistic prerequisites for testing acidosis/GPR65 exist in vivo.

**Approach:**
- In sciatic nerves from neuropathic vs control mice, assess:
  - **Expression of PDK2/4 and LCN2** (and lactate transporters) in non-immune cells by immunostaining or targeted transcript analysis.
  - **Coarse pH evidence:** use pH-sensitive dyes or reporters in nerve slices to detect any shift toward extracellular acidification under neuropathic conditions.
  - **Gpr65 expression pattern:** via in situ hybridization or immunostaining to determine which sciatic cell types express GPR65 (macrophages vs T cells vs endothelial cells vs axons).

This step is intentionally coarse-grained: the goal is not to resolve microdomains, but to confirm that (a) **metabolic stress consistent with lactate production** is present, and (b) **GPR65 is expressed** in macrophages and/or other relevant cells near the site of pathology.

---

### Step 3 – Test whether local pH buffering alters macrophage-dependent pain and excitability

**Goal:** Ask whether **partial neutralization of local acidity** at the sciatic nerve modifies pain and hyperexcitability *in a setting where macrophage dependence is established*.

**Approach:**
- In neuropathic animals confirmed to be macrophage-dependent (Step 1), deliver a **moderate pH-buffering formulation perineurally** at the sciatic nerve (e.g., a biocompatible, mildly alkaline hydrogel or buffered solution) with:
  - Carefully titrated doses to avoid conduction block or ischemia.
  - Matching vehicle controls without buffering capacity.
- Readouts:
  - Behavioral thresholds (mechanical, thermal) over days.
  - Ex vivo sciatic nerve excitability.
  - **Macrophage state markers:** local cytokine profile and activation markers, to see whether buffering shifts macrophage output.

**Interpretation:**
- If **local buffering reduces pain and hyperexcitability**, and this effect is **lost or strongly diminished when macrophages are pre-depleted/inhibited** (Step 1), it indicates that acidosis principally acts by modulating **macrophage-driven pathology**.
- If buffering improves outcomes even when macrophages are suppressed, the effect likely stems from **direct actions on axons or Schwann cells**.
- If buffering has little impact, acidosis is unlikely to be a major driver relative to other metabolic signals, at least in this model.

This step ties acidosis dependence explicitly to macrophage presence/state rather than to the general microenvironment.

---

### Step 4 – Probe local GPR65 involvement as an acid-sensing axis (contingent)

**Goal:** Determine whether **GPR65 participates in acidosis-driven modulation** of macrophage-dependent neuropathic pain, contingent on tool availability.

**Approach (only if practicable tools exist):**
- Based on Step 2, if GPR65 is found in sciatic macrophages (and possibly other cells), perform **local GPR65 blockade** at the sciatic nerve:
  - Using a **perineural GPR65 antagonist**, if available, or
  - Local viral delivery (e.g., AAV) expressing a **GPR65 dominant-negative** or shRNA, with promoter choices biasing toward myeloid cells.
- Readouts mirror Step 3:
  - Behavior and nerve excitability.
  - Macrophage cytokine profile from sciatic tissue.
- Critical control: perform GPR65 modulation **with and without prior macrophage depletion/ blockade** (Step 1) to see whether any benefit of GPR65 blockade requires macrophages.

**Interpretation:**
- If GPR65 blockade **recapitulates the beneficial effect of pH buffering**, and that benefit is **absent when macrophages are suppressed**, the data support a model where acidosis acts largely through **macrophage GPR65 (and/or other macrophage proton sensors)**.
- If GPR65 expression or tools are limiting, or blockade yields no effect, the contribution of GPR65 is downgraded without undermining the broader inference about acidosis and macrophages.

GPR65 is thus positioned as a **testable, but not indispensable, mechanistic hypothesis** layered on top of the more fundamental macrophage–acidosis link.

---

### Why This Is Ready for Implementation

- **Scientific soundness:** The proposal no longer assumes DRG mechanisms in sciatic nerve; it uses them as conceptual guidance. It explicitly tests macrophage dependence first, then adds functional acidosis and GPR65 perturbations, all within a single, well-defined anatomical niche.

- **Problem–solution efficiency:** The work is centered on a small number of targeted experiments: local macrophage-dependency test, coarse metabolic/GPR65 mapping, and two local perturbations (pH buffering ± GPR65 blockade). There is no global omics, no whole-body depletion/rescue, and no multi-compartment comparisons.

- **Mechanistic attribution:** By repeating key interventions in the **presence and absence of local macrophages or macrophage signaling (via RAGE/LCN2/PDK2)**, any observed effect of pH or GPR65 is interpretable in macrophage-centric vs non-macrophage terms.

- **Feasibility:** Perineural delivery, transient macrophage depletion/ pathway blockade, and ex vivo nerve recordings are established techniques. pH buffering is technically demanding but manageable when modest in magnitude and short in duration; it is framed here as a mechanistic probe rather than a therapeutic end-point. GPR65 modulation is explicitly contingent on tool feasibility and does not compromise the core aims if not executed.

The refined project delivers a clear, macrophage-anchored test of whether **local acidosis—and, where possible, GPR65—meaningfully modulates sciatic nerve neuropathy**, within realistic experimental and temporal constraints.

## Final Refined Idea: Zonated Mapping of Diabetic DRG Permeability and Targeted Dampening of Caveolar Transcytosis

### Core goal

Rather than declaring a single “primary barrier logic,” the project aims to **define what kind of permeability is dominant where and when in diabetic DRG**, and to test **how much of that is therapeutically controllable via DRG‑endothelial caveolar transcytosis**.

Concretely:

1. Generate a **stage‑resolved, vascular‑segment‑resolved map** of permeability mode in diabetic DRG (small‑solute vs albumin‑class vs cellular ingress; arterial vs capillary vs venous segments).
2. Use **one high‑specificity manipulator of endothelial caveolar transcytosis in DRG** (Cav1 loss‑of‑function or equivalent) to test whether dampening this axis preferentially normalizes small‑molecule/albumin flux, leukocyte entry, and pain behaviors at defined stages.
3. Profile other candidate regulators (PI16, MLCK, VEGF‑A/GPR40, claudins) as **comparative modulators**, not as pre‑committed co‑levers.

### Mechanistic framing

Baseline DRG microvasculature is:
- **Transcytosis‑rich and heterogeneous**: caveolae and CD163+ perivascular macrophages are particularly abundant in specific segments.
- Embedded in a **neurovascular unit**: pericytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells co‑tune barrier function.

Diabetes overlays slow changes:
- **Basement membrane (BM) thickening**, altered pericyte/fibroblast coverage.
- **Endothelial metabolic rewiring** and oxidative stress.
- Documented **increases in Cav1 and pain behaviors**.

The project does **not** assume that enhanced transcytosis is the sole or earliest cause of leak. Instead, it asks:
- *What form of flux is dominant at each stage and in which vascular zones?*
- *If we selectively dampen caveolar transcytosis in DRG endothelium, what components of that flux remain controllable, and how does this relate to leukocyte ingress and pain?*

### Aim 1: Stage‑ and segment‑resolved mapping of diabetic DRG permeability

In a single diabetic model (STZ or db/db), at early, mid, and late stages, we:

1. **Apply size‑selective tracers**
   - Small solutes, intermediate dextrans, and albumin‑sized probes.
   - Quantify leakage not just at whole‑DRG level but along the **arteriovenous tree** using imaging that resolves arterial, capillary, and venous segments.

2. **Perform ultrastructural and structural analysis**
   - Electron microscopy in defined segments to quantify:
     - Caveolae/fenestrae density and vesicle profiles.
     - Junction morphology.
   - BM thickness, pericyte coverage, fibroblast proximity and morphology.

3. **Characterize leukocyte ingress and distribution**
   - Map which vascular segments are associated with immune cell adhesion and transmigration.

4. **Profile key molecular regulators (descriptive, not yet causal)**
   - Segment‑resolved expression/localization of Cav1, CD163+ macrophages.
   - PI16 in peri‑vascular fibroblast‑like cells, endothelial MLCK/MLC phosphorylation.
   - VEGF‑A, GPR40, claudin‑1, and other tight‑junction markers.

Outcome: a **topographical and temporal atlas** of how diabetic DRG flux shifts (e.g., from physiologic transcytosis in specific venous segments to broader capillary leak, or selective small‑solute leak without major macromolecular escape), and where leukocyte ingress occurs relative to these patterns.

### Aim 2: Test how much of this phenotype is controllable via DRG‑endothelial caveolar transcytosis

Using the same diabetic model, we introduce a **DRG‑endothelium‑biased Cav1 loss‑of‑function or equivalent tool** (e.g., endothelial Cav1 deletion under a promoter active in DRG microvessels). Specificity is maximized by:
- Restricting Cre drivers to microvascular endothelium (avoiding systemic macrovasculature where possible).
- Anatomically focusing analyses on DRG rather than whole nervous system.

At the same early/mid/late stages, we repeat the **exact readout set**:
- Zoned tracer leakage.
- Ultrastructure.
- Leukocyte behavior.
- Pain phenotypes.

Mechanistic questions:
1. **Flux mode control**: Does dampening caveolar transcytosis mainly reduce:
   - Small‑solute and albumin‑range flux in segments with high caveolae? or
   - Also broader macromolecular leak or leukocyte ingress?

2. **Stage‑dependent reversibility**: Is control strongest in early diabetes (before extensive BM thickening and capillary remodeling), with diminishing returns later, or is there still substantial therapeutic leverage even in a structurally remodeled DRG?

3. **Network adaptation**: How do segment‑resolved expression patterns of PI16, MLCK, VEGF, claudins, and pericyte/fibroblast markers change when transcytosis is dampened? Are there compensatory shifts suggesting alternative barrier control modes coming online?

Interpretation is explicitly framed in terms of **therapeutic leverage under chronic remodeling**, not pure historical causality.

### Role of other axes (PI16, MLCK, VEGF, claudins)

PI16, MLCK, VEGF‑A/GPR40, and claudin‑based sealing are:
- Quantified in Aim 1 and Aim 2 as **correlative modulators**: where and when they rise, and how they associate with specific flux modes and leukocyte behavior.
- Considered for **second‑pass perturbation** only if:
  - They show clear, stage‑specific engagement in diabetic DRG (not just sciatic nerve/perineurium), and
  - Residual leak or leukocyte ingress persists despite Cav1/endothelial transcytosis dampening, aligned with their expression patterns.

This avoids forcing PI16 or any single fibroblast module into the primary logic while still leaving room to identify and prioritize additional targets.

### Why this is efficient and implementable

- **Focused manipulation**: Only one high‑specificity manipulator (Cav1 loss‑of‑function in DRG endothelium) is built into the primary design, matching current tool specificity.
- **Zonated, stage‑resolved readouts**: Mapping along the arteriovenous axis and across disease stages ensures we do not over‑interpret whole‑DRG averages or equate all “more transcytosis” with pathology.
- **Clear separation of concepts**: The project distinguishes:
  - *Mechanistic flux mode* (what moves where and when), from
  - *Therapeutic leverage* (what can still be controlled by dampening transcytosis), acknowledging that chronic remodeling may lock in some aspects.
- **Expandable but not over‑committed**: Secondary axes are observed and only elevated if diabetic DRG data demand it, keeping the initial program tight and feasible while still allowing discovery of additional control points.

This yields a lab‑ready, mechanism‑centered program that can decisively answer: in diabetic DRG, what permeability modes dominate over time and vascular space, and to what extent can selectively reducing caveolar transcytosis in DRG endothelium normalize pathological flux, leukocyte ingress, and pain despite chronic structural remodeling.

## Final Refined Research Idea: DRG Vascular KATP as a Necessary Conduit for Systemic Vasoprotection in Diabetic Neuropathy

### Narrowed mechanistic claim

We now make a deliberately modest, testable claim:

> In diabetic neuropathy, **vascular KATP channels in DRG endothelial cells and pericytes are required for clinically relevant systemic vasodilation to translate improved systemic hemodynamics into better DRG capillary perfusion, oxygenation, and neuronal stability.**

This is a **necessary‑condition test**, not a claim that KATP is the only or absolutely dominant acute translator of local metabolic mismatch. Other pathways (NO, EDHF, prostanoids, angiotensin II/endothelin) clearly contribute. The question is whether, without DRG vascular KATP, systemic vasodilation still confers its usual benefit on DRG.

### Mechanistic framework

1. **Vascular KATP in DRG microvessels**  
   - Based on vascular and brain pericyte literature, we focus primarily on **Kir6.1/SUR2B‑containing KATP** as the canonical vascular form, while characterizing Kir6.2/SUR1 expression to confirm isoform predominance in DRG endothelium and pericytes.
   - These channels sense **intracellular ATP/ADP** and are modulated by **ROS/redox status**, providing a rapid link between local metabolic conditions and membrane potential in vascular cells.

2. **Role relative to other vasoregulators**  
   - Endothelial NO, EDHF, prostanoids, and altered angiotensin II/endothelin signaling strongly shape basal tone and long‑term vascular remodeling in vasa nervorum.
   - We hypothesize that vascular KATP contributes a specific *component* of control: enabling DRG microvessels to respond to changes in local energy balance—especially under diabetic stress—by adjusting capillary resistance and recruitment. It is not assumed to act alone, only that it is **necessary for systemic vasodilators to fully improve DRG perfusion**.

3. **Diabetes and KATP impairment**  
   - Diabetic glycoxidative stress, methylglyoxal, ROS, and miR‑9–mediated regulation reduce Kcnj8/Abcc9 expression and impair SUR2B/Kir6.1 function.
   - This likely blunts the capacity of DRG microvessels to use KATP to respond to metabolic cues, even when systemic perfusion pressure is pharmacologically improved.

### Experimental strategy (minimal, necessary‑condition test)

We work in a diabetic mouse model with three main conditions, using existing tools (vascular Cre lines with defined DRG expression patterns, AAVs, pimonidazole, focused laser Doppler/oxygen probes, and DRG electrophysiology).

1. **Baseline diabetic + no systemic vasodilation**  
   - Establish DRG microvascular lesion: hypoxia markers (pimonidazole), local perfusion/oxygen (high‑resolution, DRG‑focused measurements), and DRG neuronal excitability.

2. **Diabetic + systemic vasodilation with intact DRG vascular KATP**  
   - Administer a clinically relevant systemic vasodilator (e.g., ACE inhibitor or NO–cGMP enhancer) at a dose that modestly improves systemic hemodynamics and is known to benefit neuropathy in preclinical models.
   - Quantify how much DRG hypoxia is reduced and neuronal excitability is normalized relative to baseline. This defines the **reference benefit** of systemic vasoprotection when DRG KATP is intact.

3. **Diabetic + DRG vascular KATP loss‑of‑function (LOF) ± local rescue, under the same systemic vasodilation**  
   - Use endothelial/pericyte‑targeted Cre lines (acknowledging some spill‑over) to delete **Kcnj8/Abcc9** in DRG‑associated microvessels. We focus on the **Kir6.1/SUR2B isoform** as the primary vascular target, guided by expression profiling.
   - Induce diabetes and apply the same systemic vasodilator regimen as in condition 2.
   - Measure DRG hypoxia, local perfusion/oxygen, and neuronal excitability. Compare the **magnitude of benefit** from systemic vasodilation between KATP‑intact and DRG‑KATP‑LOF mice.
   - In a subset of LOF mice, perform **DRG‑localized wild‑type KATP rescue** via AAV engineered to express Kir6.1/SUR2B under an endothelial/pericyte‑biased promoter near DRG. Reassess the response to systemic vasodilation.

### Interpreting outcomes

- **Outcome A: KATP is a necessary conduit for systemic vasoprotection at DRG**  
  - With intact DRG KATP, systemic vasodilation substantially improves DRG hypoxia and neuronal excitability.
  - In DRG KATP‑LOF mice, the *same* systemic vasodilation produces little or no improvement at DRG, despite similar changes in blood pressure or overall flow.
  - Local WT KATP rescue in DRG microvessels restores much of the vasodilator’s benefit.
  - Interpretation: KATP is a **required component** for systemic vasodilators to impact DRG microcirculation; it has high control priority in this context, even if other pathways also contribute.

- **Outcome B: Systemic vasodilation works regardless of DRG KATP status**  
  - Systemic vasodilators improve DRG outcomes similarly in KATP‑intact and DRG KATP‑LOF mice.
  - Rescue confers little additional advantage.
  - Interpretation: NO/EDHF/prostanoid and structural mechanisms can compensate for KATP loss. DRG vascular KATP is not a bottleneck for translating systemic therapy into DRG benefit. Its control priority is low and should not be targeted as a privileged lever.

Either result is **informative**: a positive result elevates DRG vascular KATP as a key conduit through which systemic therapies protect nerves; a negative result rigorously downgrades its centrality, steering the field toward other regulators of diabetic neurovascular coupling.

### Scope and feasibility

- We explicitly **do not claim** to fully dissect acute burst‑level neurovascular coupling or to uniquely separate KATP from NO/EDHF in all timescales.
- We instead deliver a clean, lab‑implementable test of whether DRG vascular KATP is required for the protective effect of systemic vasodilation on DRG in diabetes, using:
  - Well‑characterized vascular KATP isoforms (primarily Kir6.1/SUR2B).
  - Realistic genetic tools for EC/pericyte‑biased manipulation.
  - Standard hypoxia, perfusion, and electrophysiological readouts.

This final refinement balances mechanistic ambition with feasibility and interpretability, providing a focused, falsifiable experiment on the **control hierarchy** of vascular regulators in diabetic neuropathy, without re‑introducing speculative constructs or excessive experimental surface area.
